# Introduction of Master Ramon Llull
## ¶ Here begins the introduction to the great general art of the most reverend and enlightened doctor, Master Ramon Llull, applicable to all sciences.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a heraldic shield with a cross motif, set within a frame of floral and foliate ornaments.</image-desc>
Since all science <note>original: "scientia"; in this context, it refers to organized knowledge or systematic study</note> is derived from universals—so that through universals we may know how to descend to particulars and provide an account of them—the following universals are set forth below. Through these, the intellect may be empowered to rise toward understanding in many different subjects. The principles of the general art are nine, and the rules are also nine, as appears in the following table.

---

| ¶ Transcendent Principles <note>The fundamental attributes of being that surpass any single category</note> | ¶ Instrumental Principles <note>The logical relations used to compare and analyze ideas</note> |
| :--- | :--- |
| **B** Goodness | Difference |
| **C** Greatness | Concordance |
| **D** Eternity <note>original: "Eternitas"; often used by Llull to denote duration or constancy</note> | Contrariety |
| **E** Power | Beginning |
| **F** Wisdom | Middle |
| **G** Will | End |
| **H** Virtue | Majority |
| **I** Truth | Equality |
| **K** Glory | Minority |

---

| ¶ Questions | ¶ Rules <note>These correspond to the questions and define the nature of the inquiry</note> |
| :--- | :--- |
| Whether? | Possibility |
| What? | Essence <note>original: "Quiditas"; the "what-ness" of a thing</note> |
| From what? | Materiality |
| Why? | Formality |
| How much? | Quantity |
| What kind? | Quality |
| When? | Temporality |
| Where? | Locality |
| How? | Modality and instrumentality |

---

| ¶ Subjects <note>The hierarchy of being, from God down to physical tools</note> | ¶ Virtues |
| :--- | :--- |
| **B** God | Justice |
| **C** Angel | Prudence |
| **D** Heaven | Fortitude |
| **E** Man | Temperance |
| **F** Imaginative faculty | Faith |
| **G** Sensitive faculty <note>The power of perception through the senses</note> | Hope |
| **H** Vegetative faculty <note>The power of growth and nutrition</note> | Charity |
| **I** Elementative faculty <note>The nature of the four physical elements</note> | Patience |
| **K** Instrumental faculty <note>The use of tools or external means</note> | Piety |

<margin>b</margin> ¶ **Goodness** is the being by reason of which a good thing does good: and thus to be is good, and not to be is evil.
<margin>c</margin> ¶ **Greatness** is the being by reason of which goodness or duration are the master of the encompassing extremity of being.
<margin>d</margin> ¶ **Eternity** or **Duration** is the being by reason of which goodness, greatness, etc., endure.
<margin>e</margin> ¶ **Power** is the being by reason of which goodness, greatness, etc., are able to exist and act.
<margin>f</margin> ¶ **Wisdom** is the being by reason of which a wise person understands.
<margin>g</margin> ¶ **Will** is the being by reason of which goodness, greatness, etc., are able to be willed.
<margin>h</margin> ¶ **Virtue** is the origin of the union of goodness and greatness into one great good, etc.
<margin>i</margin> ¶ **Truth** is that which is true concerning goodness, greatness, etc.
<margin>k</margin> ¶ **Glory** is the very delight in which goodness, greatness, etc., find their rest.

<meta>This page continues the introductory definitions of Ramon Llull’s "Art," a system of logic designed to find universal truths. The text transitions from defining the "Principles" (the fundamental qualities of being) to the "Species of Questions" (the logical framework for inquiry).</meta>

# Ramon Llull

<margin>Signature: a iii</margin>

¶ **Difference** is the property by reason of which goodness, power, etc., are distinct and unconfused concepts. <note>original: "rationes clare & inconfuse." Llull argues that while God's attributes are one, they must be logically distinct to be understood.</note>

¶ **Concordance** is that by reason of which goodness, will, etc., agree in one and in many.

¶ **Contrariety** is the mutual resistance of certain things because of diverse ends. <note>In Llull's system, this refers to moral or physical opposition, such as between virtue and vice.</note>

¶ **Principle** is that which relates to all things by reason of some property of priority.

¶ **Medium** <term>Middle/Mean: the bridge between a beginning and an end</term> is the subject itself through which the end flows into the principle, and the principle flows back to the end, sharing in the nature of both.

¶ **End** is that in which the principle finds rest.

¶ **Majority** is the image of the immensity of goodness and greatness.

¶ **Equality** is the subject itself in which the end of the concordance of goodness, power, etc., finds rest.

¶ **Minority** is being close to nothingness.

---

->**The Species of Questions**<-

<note>These questions correspond to the letters of Llull's "Great Art." They are the tools used to investigate any subject.</note>

**B: Whether?** <note>original: "Utrum"</note>
- Doubt.
- Affirmation.
- Negation.

**F: How much?** <note>original: "Quantum"</note>
- Continuous.
- Discrete.

**C: What?** <note>original: "Quid"</note>
- It is in itself.
- It has in itself.
- It is in another.
- It has in another.

**G: What kind?** <note>original: "Quale"</note>
- Properly.
- Appropriately.

**H: When?** <note>original: "Quando"</note>
- <note>These signify the letters E, D, and K in the Lullian combinatorial wheels.</note>

**D: From what?** <note>original: "De quo"</note>
- Primitively.
- Materially.
- Possessively.

**I: Where?** <note>original: "Ubi"</note>
- <note>These signify the letters E, D, and K.</note>

**E: Why?** <note>original: "Quare"</note>
- Formally.
- Finally. <note>Refers to the "Final Cause" or purpose of a thing.</note>

**K: In what manner?** <note>original: "Quomodo"</note>
1. It is a part.
2. A part is in a part.
3. Parts are in the whole and vice versa.
The whole transmits outside of itself its own likeness and that of its parts.

**And**
**With what?** <note>original: "Cum quo"</note>
1. It is a part.
2. A part is in a part.
3. Parts are in the whole and vice versa.
The whole transmits outside of itself its own likeness and that of its parts.

# Introduction to the Great General Art
## ¶ Types of Instantiating Principles

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Difference | | (The sensory and the sensible. |
| Concordance | Between | (The sensory and the intellectual. |
| Contrariety | | (The intellectual and the intellectual. |
| | | |
| | | (Causes. |
| Principle | | (Quantity. |
| | | (Time. |
| | | |
| | | (Of Junction. |
| Middle | | (Of Measurement. |
| | | (Of Extremes. |
| | | |
| | | (Of Perfection. |
| End | | (Of Termination. |
| | | (Of Privation. |
| | | |
| Majority | | (Substance and substance. |
| Equality | Between | (Substance and accident. |
| Minority | | (Accident and accident. |

¶ **Sensory** <note>original: "Sensuale"</note> refers to that being which perceives or can be perceived through the senses, namely by seeing or hearing; likewise, such as a stone, a tree, or any physical thing.

¶ **Intellectual** refers to that being which is spiritual by nature: such as God, an angel, the rational soul, etc.

¶ **Cause** is a principle through whose operation the "caused thing" follows, which is its effect.

¶ **Effect** is the name given to that caused thing which has been brought into being through the operation of a cause.

¶ **Efficient Cause** is that agent which effects or produces an effect: such as God who created the world, etc.

¶ **Material Cause** is that from which a thing is secondarily made: such as the body in a human, or iron in a knife.

¶ **Formal Cause** is that through which a thing principally exists and by which it is preserved in its being: such as the rational soul in a human, and the vegetative soul in a tree, etc. <note>In medieval philosophy, the "soul" was the "form" that gave life and structure to matter.</note>

¶ **Final Cause** is that for the sake of which a thing is principally made or effected: such as God, who is the final cause of every creature, or "to dwell in" being the final cause of a house, etc.

¶ **Substance** <term>Substance: that which exists independently</term> is that which exists by itself and in itself: such as God, an angel, a human, etc.

¶ **Accident** <term>Accident: a quality that must exist in something else</term> is that which does not exist by itself nor in itself: such as whiteness, health, virtue, vice, or knowledge. And there are nine types of accidents: namely of quantity, of quality, etc.

¶ **Quantity** is an accident through which beings are quantified, finite, and delimited, etc.

<summary>This page outlines the relational principles of the Great General Art, defining the four types of causes (efficient, material, formal, and final) and the distinction between substance and accident. It establishes the framework for understanding how physical and spiritual entities exist and interact.</summary>
<keywords>logic, scholasticism, four causes, substance and accident, sensory vs intellectual, metaphysics, Ramon Llull, Great Art</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical definitions of Ramon Llull, likely from his "Ars Brevis" or a similar introductory work on his "Art." The text transitions from defining the categories of accidents to the general subjects of his system, starting with God and Angels.</meta>

->By Ramon Llull<-

¶ **Quality** is an accident through which beings are "of a certain kind" or determined, such as the quality of grammar. <note>original: "qualitas grammatica"</note>

¶ **Relation** is that accident through which one being necessarily regards another: such as the relation of a teacher to a student, or a father to a son.

¶ **Action** is the operation of an agent upon a subject, as a lord over a vassal, or a hammer upon a nail.

¶ **Passion** <note>In this context, "passion" means being acted upon or receiving an action.</note> is the operation of the sufferer under the agent, as something being heated under the heater.

¶ **Habit** is an accident with which a subject is clothed, such as whiteness in a white thing, or knowledge in a knower.

¶ **Position** <note>original: "Situs"</note> is the proper and ordered placement of parts in a whole and vice versa, such as a roof on walls or a beam in a house.

¶ **Time** is an accident in which beings are named according to their beginning: such as the time of the world.

¶ **Place** is an accident through which beings are located and contained one within another, such as the place held by any bodily substance.

¶ **Medium of Joining** is that which joins diverse things into one, just as a nail joins two posts.

¶ **Medium of Measurement** is that through which equals or unequals are measured, as the other parts of a circle are measured by the center point of the circle, etc.

¶ **Medium of Extremities** is that which exists between extremes: such as a wall between the roof and the foundation.

¶ **End of Perfection** is said to be that in which a thing is perfected, or that for which a thing was ultimately made: just as God is the perfection of man, and man is the perfection of his own parts.

¶ **End of Termination** is called the limit of a thing: as the border of a kingdom is its limit.

¶ **End of Privation** is called the "non-being" into which a thing falls, or the non-being in which its existence ceases naturally, morally, or artificially: such as death, sin, destruction, etc.

### ¶ Concerning the nine general subjects.

The nine general subjects mentioned before must be treated with four conditions: namely, with **definition**, **difference**, **concordance**, and **majority**. With **definition**, so that every subject may have its own proper definition by which it is known and differs from any other. With **difference**, so that the difference between one subject and another is preserved. With **majority**, according to whether one subject is higher and nobler than another, higher and nobler principles and definitions, rules, and species should be attributed to it, following and preserving the definition and difference in concordance and majority, as was said before.

¶ In irrational, sensory beings, **instinct** is placed in the stead of wisdom; **appetite** in the stead of will; **delight** in the stead of glory; and **recollection** in the stead of memory.

<column-break/>

### ¶ Concerning the first subject, which is God.

**God** is that being in whom goodness, greatness, eternity, etc., which are His dignities <note>Llull uses "Dignities" to refer to the divine attributes like Power, Wisdom, and Will.</note>, are one and the same in number; and God is that being who has in Himself all fulfillment and needs nothing outside Himself. God is goodness, greatness, eternity, etc., His dignities being without contrariety, majority, or minority. <note>Meaning God's attributes never conflict and are all equally infinite.</note>

¶ A man can treat of God through the ten general questions by asking or investigating: **Whether** God is, **What** God is, **Of what** God is, etc., following the four conditions mentioned before, affirming in God every perfection and denying or removing every defect.

### ¶ Concerning the Angels.

An **Angel** is an intellectual substance created by God, nobler in nature and simplicity than any other creature. In an angel there is essential and natural goodness, greatness, duration, etc., except for "property" <note>Likely referring to the unique property of being uncreated, which belongs only to God.</note>. And it can be treated through the ten questions by asking **Whether** an angel is, **What** an angel is, etc., following the four conditions already stated.

<summary>This page defines the Aristotelian-Lullian categories of accidents (like Action, Time, and Place) and introduces the "General Subjects" of Llull's Art, specifically defining God and Angels.</summary>
<keywords>Ramon Llull, Scholasticism, accidents, definitions of God, angelology, logic, medieval philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page introduces the fundamental subjects of the "Great General Art" (Ars Magna), a philosophical system designed by Ramon Llull to categorize all knowledge. It follows the introductory definitions of the Art's principles.</meta>

# Introduction to the Great General Art

### ¶ Concerning the Heavens.
The Heaven is that body which possesses a greater extended magnitude than any other body.
¶ The Heaven possesses essential goodness, magnitude, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without any contrariety <note>original: "contrarietate"; meaning it is a perfect, harmonious substance without internal conflict</note>. And it can be examined through the ten questions by asking "Whether the heaven exists," etc., following the four conditions mentioned previously.

### ¶ Concerning Man.
Man is a sensory and intellectual substance, or he is a "man-making" animal, or one to whom "man-making" <note>original: "homificans"; a technical term in Lullian philosophy referring to the specific activity or essence that makes a human being human</note> properly belongs. Man possesses natural and essential goodness and magnitude, etc., in a twofold way: namely, sensory and intellectual. This is because he is composed of a rational soul and a body. The rational soul is the intellectual form that gives shape to the human body itself, giving it human being and preserving it within the human species. And it essentially possesses three powers: namely, memory, intellect, and will, with which it performs whatever it does. And the body of man is constituted of the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative powers, moved toward their operations through the aforementioned form <note>the rational soul</note>. And he can be examined through the ten questions by investigating concerning man through "Whether," "What," "Of what," etc., following the conditions already stated.

### ¶ Concerning the Imaginative Power.
The Imaginative is the power or part of the animal through which the animal itself imagines those things which were presented to it by the bodily senses. It possesses essential and natural goodness, magnitude, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without essential contrariety. And it has three powers co-essential to itself: namely, the instinctive, the appetitive, and the recollective. And it can be known by asking about it through "Whether," "What," "Of what," etc., following the four conditions mentioned above.

<column-break/>

### ¶ Concerning the Sensitive Power.
The Sensitive is the power with which an animal perceives sensible things, namely things visible, audible, etc. It possesses essential and natural goodness, magnitude, etc. It can be known by asking about it through "Whether," "What," "Of what," etc. And it has six particular senses: namely, sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell, and speech <note>original: "affatum"; Llull uniquely categorized the power of speech/expression as a sixth sense</note>, in which the power itself is diversified; and similarly, its essential principles and its particulars ought to be treated according to the four conditions.

### ¶ Concerning the Vegetative Power.
The Vegetative is the power through which a natural transformation occurs from one substance into another, such as from rain into a plant, and from food into flesh, etc. It possesses essential and natural goodness, magnitude, instinct, appetite, delight, etc., without essential contrariety. It also has four powers with which it operates naturally: namely, the appetitive, through which it seeks to draw [nutrients] to the subject; the retentive, through which it retains them; the digestive, through which it digests what is retained; and the expulsive, through which it expels that which does not suit the subject. And it can be treated with the ten questions, namely "Whether," "What," etc., following the four aforementioned conditions.

### ¶ Concerning the Elemental Power.
The Elemental <note>original: "elementatiua"</note> is a natural being or power within composite things, through which the elements enter into composition and exist so that they may act within those composite things which are formed from them. The elements are four: namely, fire, air, water, and earth. Fire is hot and dry...

<summary>This page defines the hierarchical levels of existence—from the celestial heavens and human beings down to the imaginative, sensory, vegetative, and elemental powers—using the systematic definitions of Ramon Llull's "General Art." It outlines the essential properties and internal powers of each level, such as the three powers of the human soul (memory, intellect, and will).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and systematic definitions of Ramon Llull, likely from his "Ars Brevis" or a related logical treatise. The text focuses on the categorization of reality and moral philosophy.</meta>

->Raymund Llull<-

light and bright. Air is moist, hot, light, and transparent. Water is heavy, cold, moist, and white. The **Elementative** <note>The power or category relating to the four physical elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth</note> possesses goodness, greatness, etc., along with contrariety by reason of the elements, which are distinct through their own appropriate qualities. It can be investigated through the ten general questions, namely: *Whether? What? From what?* and so on for any elementative thing, each of which has its own essential and natural goodness, greatness, etc. And it can be treated with the ten general questions by following the four aforementioned conditions.

### ¶ Concerning the Instrumentative.

**I**nstrumentative is the power or habit through which non-natural works are made, such as artificial things and the like. It contains three species: namely, moralities; the liberal arts and other sciences; and the mechanical arts. In the **Instrumentative** <note>The category of human skills, tools, and applied knowledge</note> there is goodness, greatness, etc., in its own general way; and each of its species has goodness, greatness, etc., differing from the others according as they are different among themselves. The general artist treats the instrumentative generally and specifically with the ten questions. This same method applies to the species, because they are contained in and under it; and also to anything contained under each, always regulating them by the four general conditions mentioned above, which are: definition, difference, concordance, and majority.

<column-break/>

### ¶ Concerning the Virtues.

**J**ustice is the virtue through which the just person renders to each what is his own: namely to God, to himself, and to his neighbor.
¶ **Prudence** is the virtue through which one acts prudently by choosing, avoiding, and foreseeing. Choosing, namely, the good and more quickly the greater good; and avoiding the evil and more quickly the greater evil; foreseeing, namely, regarding possibilities and impossibilities, the useful and the useless, etc.
¶ **Fortitude** is the virtue with which a brave man strengthens his soul against vices, so that he may be able to attain the virtues.
¶ **Temperance** is the virtue through which the temperate person moderates his soul and acts between two contrary extremes in quantity: namely, the greater, the equal, and the small.
¶ **Faith** is the virtue with which a man believes that to be true which he neither senses nor understands, and with which he can ascend to understanding beyond his natural powers in respect to the whole man.
¶ **Hope** is the virtue through which the one hoping expects help, forgiveness, and reward or glory from God.
¶ **Charity** is the virtue with which the will ascends to loving God and one's neighbor above one's natural power. Or thus: Charity is the virtue through which the charitable person loves God above all things, and himself and his neighbor equally in God and for the sake of God.
¶ **Patience** is the virtue with which a man suffers passion <note>In the sense of "suffering" or "enduring external action"</note> in peace and without anger of the heart.
¶ **Patience** is the habit with which the patient person conquers and is not conquered.
¶ **Piety** is the virtue with which the will moves itself to have sorrow for the weaknesses of one's neighbor.
¶ **Piety** is the habit with which one first grieves for the grief of his neighbor.

### ¶ Definitions of the Vices.

**A**varice is the vice diverting goods from the end <note>The "end" refers to the ultimate purpose or "telos" of a thing</note> for which they were created.
¶ **Avarice** is the vice with which goods are diverted from their end, which is to serve man justly, prudently, etc.
¶ **Gluttony** is the vice that more often deprives one of abstinence and temperance than any other vice; therefore it is the sin through which men die more than by any other sin.
¶ **Gluttony** is the vice through which the gluttonous person deprives himself of abstinence and temperance.

<margin>Definitions of the hundred forms.</margin>

<column-break/>

¶ **Entity** is that through which a being is a being, and it produces or acts as a being, just as goodness is that through which a good thing is good and performs good acts.
¶ **Essence** is that through which "to be" exists, just as through humanity one is a human, and through entity one is a being.
¶ **Unity** is the being through which one thing is one, and it acts or produces one.
¶ **Plurality** is an aggregation of things that are in some way diverse.
¶ **The Abstract** is the essence of things, such as the "whiteness" of a white object.
¶ **The Concrete** is the being in which the abstract—which is its essence—is sustained.
¶ **Nature** is the principle through which natural beings are produced naturally. Nature is twofold: namely, **Nurturing Nature** <note>original: "natura naturans," referring to God as the creative source</note> and **Nurtured Nature** <note>original: "natura naturata," referring to the created world</note>. Therefore, nature must be treated differently according to how it is diversified through different subjects.
¶ **Genus** is a being that is predicated of many things differing in species, such as "stone," which is predicated of marble, ruby, and sapphire; or "animal," of man, ox, lion, etc.
¶ **Species** is that which is predicated of many things differing in number <note>i.e., individuals</note>, such as "man" of Peter, etc.
¶ **Disposition** is the privation of some thing, by reason of which the thing itself is disposed toward some end; such as disposing natural or artificial matter toward a form.
¶ **Proportion** is the ordering of degrees toward one thing, such as the elements.
¶ **Intention** is the act through which beings apply themselves to work by reason of some natural, artificial, or rational end. It is twofold: namely, primary and secondary. The primary regards the end.
¶ **The Instant** is the beginning and the end of time.
¶ **Intensity** is that which is closer to the simple than the composite, like simple fire.
¶ **Extensity** is the opposite, like fire entering the elements.

# Introduction to the Great General Art
<note>original: "Introductoriū magne artis generalis". This refers to the system of Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher who sought to create a universal system of logic.</note>

**Contiguity** is the act of joining things at their extremities: such as bones and flesh in the body.

**Continuity** is the mixing of parts where some are within others, such as the elements within a compound body. <note>original: "elementato" - a physical thing made of the four elements.</note>

**Chaos** or **Matter** <note>original: "yle" from the Greek hyle</note> is the first existing body, the principle of all things that can be generated or corrupted. It is a body constituted from universal form and primary matter.

**The Individual** is a being that is predicated of only one thing, such as Peter is of himself, and it is further removed from the "genus" than the "species" is.

**Simplicity** is the being through which beings are simple, because they are not composed of multiple essences: like God, who is a simple being and supreme in simplicity. This is because He is one single essence which is His very goodness, greatness, etc. Regarding **Pure Simplicity** in creatures, something is called simple in which there is one by its own number or in respect to another, such as an angel, the soul, or fire.

**Composition** is the gathering of several essences into some proposed being: from many things, such as a human who is composed of body and rational soul, or like a compound body made of the four elements, and a created substance made of matter and form.

**Form** is the essential principle through which action chiefly exists.

**Matter** is the essential principle to which "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" means the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> properly belongs: by reason of matter, a composite substance is passive.

**Body** is a substance having length, breadth, and depth: such as a stone, a tree, etc.

There are six **rectitudes** <note>directions or orientations</note> of bodies, namely: upwards, downwards, forwards, backwards, to the right, and to the left.

**The Point** is the smallest part of a body.

**The Line** is a certain extended length composed of continuous points, the extremities of which are two points.

**The Sphere** is the proper place which every element seeks—

<column-break/>

—as fire seeks the upward and earth the downward. The **Celestial Sphere** is called the circle in which the signs <note>of the Zodiac</note> and planets are situated.

**Reason** is the light of the intellect for knowing the realities of things.

**The Vacuum** is that object in which no entity is considered. **The Full** is the opposite.

**The Universal** is that being which contains many particulars within itself. **The Particular** is the opposite.

**Property** is the being with which an agent acts specifically: such as an animal or a plant.

**Transmutation** <note>original: "Trāslatio"</note> is the act of a thing naturally transformed, having stripped off its old form and put on a new form.

**Alteration** is a change from one quality into another while the substance remains the same: such as wine into vinegar, health into sickness, or virtue into vice.

**Generation** is a natural operation through which that which exists in potentiality naturally exists in actuality by causing a new form.

**The Angle** is a part of a figure in which the ends of lines meet sharply or squarely.

**Figure** is an "accident" <note>a non-essential quality</note> constituted from the position of lines and the condition of the surface or colors.

There are three **General Figures**, namely: the triangular, the quadrangular, and the circular.

**The Triangular** is a figure that has three acute angles contained by three lines.

**The Quadrangular** is a figure having four angles, whether right or oblique, contained by four lines.

**The Circle** is a figure contained by a single circular line.

**The Surface** is the upper extremity of a body in which its color appears.

**Instinct** is the principle by which natural beings are regulated toward their natural operations according to their species and nature: such as fire or an animal. It is a likeness of the intellect.

# Of Ramon Llull

**Appetite** <note>original: "Appetitus"; in Llull’s philosophy, this refers to a natural inclination or "desire" inherent in all things to fulfill their purpose.</note> is the principle through which natural beings desire that which is suitable to them according to their nature: as fire desires to ascend, or a man to drink and eat; and it is the likeness of the will.

**Motion** is the principle through which moving beings move movable things toward some end. And it is twofold, namely natural and artificial (or violent) motion. Natural motions are six: namely generation, corruption, increase, decrease, alteration, and change of place.

**Corruption** is a natural work through which that which is in act passes into privation by corrupting the old form—namely that form through which it existed in its actual being before it was corrupted.

**Privation** is the medium between generation and corruption, through which being passes into non-being. These three general principles exist in the three things by which the course of nature is sustained in general and corruptible things: namely in the elements, vegetables, and animals.

**Infinity** is being without limit and measure. And it is threefold: namely in magnitude, duration, and number. Infinity of magnitude is immensity. Infinity of duration is eternity. Infinity of number is from the perspective of the one counting, who does not reach the end of the number, even though the thing numbered itself may have a finite number.

**Comprehension** is the likeness of finitude and apprehension, just as the sense of taste, when it tastes, apprehends the salt sea.

**Capacity** is the form through which a capable thing can comprehend and reach the beings that are comprehensible by it.

**Existence** is the essence of a being that exists. **Agency** <note>original: "Agentia"</note> is the being of acting; but to act is the act of the existing thing: just as heating is the act of the hot, or doing good is the act of the good.

**Power** <note>original: "Potentia"</note> is that which, together with its act, relates to an object: such as sight with seeing, or hearing with hearing. And there are ten natural powers in man: namely hearing, sight, taste, touch, smell, speech <note>original: "affatus"</note>, imagination, memory, intellect, and will, to which ten modes of objects subsequently correspond. In another way, power is taken for a being that is not yet, but can be: such as knowledge in the intellect, or fruit in the tree.

<column-break/>

**Object** is that being which is apprehended through a power, such as flavor through taste.

**Act** is the work of a power by which an object is taken up by the power, as seeing is the act of sight; similarly, act is twofold: first, when a being is in its state of existence; second, for its very operation.

**Immobility** is the property of an immobile being which has no appetite to move itself, such as God, who is an immobile being since He is an eternal and infinite being, having His perfection in Himself eternally and infinitely.

**Succession** is the change from one thing into another through motion.

**Attraction** is the act of a power which desires to attract something according to its nature and the property of the attractor and the attracted: as the magnet attracts iron, or treacle <note>original: "tiriaca"; a traditional medicinal compound used as an antidote.</note> attracts poison.

**Reception** follows attraction relatively.

**Signification** is the revelation of secrets, demonstrated with a sign.

**Novelty** is the being through which a subject is habituated with new habits or a new quantity.

**Monstrosity** is the deviation of the motion of nature from the beginning to the end through excess or great deficiency: such as a sixth finger, or having only four; and from this, it is called a monster.

**Color** is a quality <note>original: "habitus"</note> contained by a figure, and there are four general colors: namely the two of light <note>original: "lucis duo"</note>, transparency, whiteness, and blackness.

**Shadow** is a quality of the privation of light or brightness; and it is the quality of the air blackened by the opposition of the earth.

**Necessity** is that being which cannot be otherwise. The **Necessary** is that which can in no way be avoided.

**Contingent** is that which happens without necessity; and it is twofold: namely simple and...

# Introduction to the Great General Art

necessary. Simple contingency is that which is in no way a necessity: such as being a blacksmith. Necessary contingency is the future necessity of one of two contradictories: such as Peter being saved or damned.

¶ **Fortune** is an accidental finding without the intention of the one favored by fortune.

¶ **Opportunity** is a being that has an intention toward those things which can happen: as a man putting wood into the fire so that it may burn is the opportunity for the burning; or a doctor for health.

¶ **Definition** is a certain and express manifestation of a thing and its properties.

¶ **Question** is a petition for the unknown through which the powers of the soul are stretched out so that they may rest in their own acts; it is made in ten ways in the art of questioning: namely through *whether*, *what*, *of what*, *why*, *how much*, *what kind*, *when*, *where*, *how*, and *with what*. <note>These are the ten Lullian questions used to investigate any subject.</note>

¶ **Obstinacy** is an excessive action of the memory and the will regarding an object, through which the intellect stands fixed by a false affirmation against a true negation, as occurs with vice and [obsessive] love.

¶ **Opinion** is a supposition or belief in something accompanied by doubt.

¶ **Supposition** is a certain established blending of the possibility of an affirmation and its contrary negation, so that truth may be found by investigating.

¶ **Demonstration** is the manifestation of the unknown through the known, or the less known through the more known. It occurs in three ways: namely through the *what* (or through the cause); through the *because* (or through the effect); and through equivalence. First, as in "the sun is, therefore it is day." Second, "it is day, therefore the sun is." Third, as in "the divine goodness is infinite and eternal, therefore the divine power is [infinite and eternal]": because the goodness and power of God are equal. Or, demonstration is the necessary or consequent apprehension of some particular position or privation proceeding from a necessary or fitting position, or from an impossible privation of definitions and proper-

<column-break/>

ties of universal principles, and of the distinctions and rules of the General Art.

¶ **Preaching** is the art with which a preacher informs the people to hold good morals and avoid evil ones.

¶ **The Transcending Point** <term>Punctus transcendens: a Lullian term for the limit where human reason reaches toward divine truths it cannot fully grasp</term> is an instrument of the human intellect with which it reaches its object according to the natures of the lower powers, and reaches a celestial object above its own nature.

¶ Or, the **Transcending Point** is the height or difficulty of the reality of an object, implying a potential contradiction because the power, by its own nature, cannot fully reach it.

¶ **Idea** in God is a being or object eternally [held] through divine wisdom concerning things to be produced in time: and this idea in God is God himself. An idea in time is a likeness of the eternal idea, and such an idea or likeness in a creature is a created thing.

¶ **Predestination** in divine wisdom is the act which understands men as eternally chosen with justice for salvation: and this predestination in God is an idea which is God. [Reprobation] is the act of divine wisdom which understands those to be rejected with justice for damnation; it is in God an idea of God.

¶ **Liberty** is an intellectual property given to the rational creature so that it may freely love the good and avoid the evil. **Free Will** is that in the rational soul through which it freely moves itself toward good or evil by loving or hating, accepting or leaving. And it is twofold: namely, *speculative*, when it considers whether it will act or not; and *practical*, when the choice has been made.

¶ **Creation** in eternity is an idea: and because it is eternally known through divine wisdom and loved through divine will, this creation in eternity is an idea which is God. Creation in time is the production of a being from nothing: and this is the creature.

¶ **Mercy** is sparing with compassion for sins: and mercy in eternity is an idea which is God: but in the one predestined or shown mercy, it is a created thing.

# Of Ramon Llull.

Grace is the choosing of a person beyond their merits, giving good things to those who have not earned them.
Science <note>original: "Scientia"; here meaning systematic knowledge or a branch of learning</note> is a necessary habit of knowledge concerning things, held through true understanding.
General Science is a certain universal habit that stands applicable to reason, by which all knowable things of the other sciences are within the power of the human intellect to know. It is imagined that the intellect creates science in three ways in this world: first, through the nature of the senses and imagination; second, through its own nature above its imagination;
Third, above its own nature in the nature and perfection of the Supreme <note>referring to God</note>, and thus the reason of the human intellect is threefold according to the three modes of understanding mentioned above.
Art is the ordering and rule of knowing the end <note>purpose or goal</note> of that which one wishes to have knowledge; and it has two species, namely the mechanical art and the liberal art.
Mechanical Art is a lucrative manual method for sustaining the subject of physical life.
Liberal Art is a certain method of knowing through which the intellect reaches toward expressing the quantities of things, and they are seven: namely grammar, logic, rhetoric, music, geometry, arithmetic, and astrology <note>original: "astrologia"; in this period, astrology and astronomy were often treated as a single discipline</note>.
Moral Art is a method of ordering the powers of apprehension through the multitude of their actions and notifications.
General Art is a universal standing for all sciences through its primitive and general principles, in which the unities of those sciences shine forth. Likewise, the General Art is a certain gift of God, so that it may be a general instrument for the human intellect, necessary for knowing the truths of beings in which it may rest, so that through true understanding it may be removed from opinions and errors.
Theology is the science preparing the human intellect and will to know and love our Lord God.
Philosophy is the science through which the intellect is illuminated to know the First Cause, through whose effect we know the secret natural or moral works of the wise.

<column-break/>

Astrology is the science for knowing the virtues and motions which the heavens have in the lower elemental bodies according to the nature of the superior bodies, namely the signs and the planets.
Geometry is the art through which instruction is had for measuring lines, angles, and figures, and the lengths, breadths, and depths of physical things.
Arithmetic is the art invented for counting many units.
Music is the art for ordering many voices according to harmony in one song.
Rhetoric is the art of ordering words beautifully and ornately.
Logic is the art teaching how to discern truth from falsehood.
Grammar is the art teaching how to speak, pronounce, and write congruously and correctly.
Medicine is the science teaching how to preserve health or restore it when lost, according to the possibility of nature in a sentient body.
Morality is a habit outside of nature through which one is disposed to doing good or evil through virtues or vices.
Law <note>original: "Ius"</note> is to attribute to each person that which is their own.
Soldiery <note>original: "Militia"</note> is a habit with which a soldier assists his prince so that he may uphold justice.
Politics is the art with which citizens ensure the public liberty of the city.
Preaching is the art with which a preacher informs the people to have good morals and avoid evil ones.

### And first concerning theology.
God is the subject in theology: and He is called the subject because all things treated in theology itself are directed toward giving knowledge of God. The end of theology is to know, love, honor, praise, and serve God, and with theology itself and the virtues, to pursue the vices for the attainment of perpetual blessedness.

<meta>This page serves as an introductory classification of the sciences, likely following the Lullian tradition (Ars Generalis). It establishes the definitions, subjects, and goals of Theology, Philosophy, Law, Medicine, and Geometry.</meta>

# Introduction to the Great General Art
<note>original: "Introductoriū magne artis generalis". This likely refers to the system of Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher who sought to create a universal system of knowledge.</note>

The principles of theology are the divine essence: life, dignities <note>The "Dignities" are the divine attributes such as Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity</note>, acts, form, relation or ordering, and action; the articles, precepts, exposition, the primary intention, and the secondary intention.

### ¶ Concerning Philosophy.

**D**elight in knowing is the subject in philosophy; the goal is to know the first cause and secrets. The effects of the principles are the first cause, motion, the intelligence of the sphere, universal form, primary matter, nature, simple elements, appetite, potential, habit, act, mixing, digestion, composition, and alteration.

### ¶ Concerning the Division of Philosophy.

**P**hilosophy is divided into three parts, of which one is natural, another moral, and another discourse-based <note>original: "sermocinalis", referring to the language arts</note>. Natural philosophy is the science held concerning natural things, of which there are three parts: namely metaphysics, physics, and mathematics.
¶ Metaphysics is the science of spiritual and transcendent things, which has three considerations: namely the divine, the angelic, and the rational soul.
¶ Physics is the science of lower natural things in the elements and those things composed of elements.
¶ Mathematics is the science of natural things considered in quantity, of which there are four parts: namely geometry, astrology, music, and arithmetic. Geometry considers immobile quantity in a body; astrology considers the quantity of moving things in a celestial body.
¶ Arithmetic concerns number in the absolute. Music concerns number in relation to sound.
¶ Moral philosophy is the science of moral things, of which there are three parts: monastic, economic, and political.
¶ Monastic <note>In this context, "monastic" refers to the ethics of the individual or "self-rule"</note> is the science of the governance of one person over themselves. Economic is the governance of one over many <note>referring to the management of a household</note>. Political is the governance of many over many.

<column-break/>

¶ Discourse-based philosophy is the science considering speech, of which there are three parts: namely grammar, logic, and rhetoric. Grammar concerns congruent speech; logic concerns true speech; rhetoric concerns ornate speech.

### ¶ Concerning Law.

**J**ustice is the subject in law; the goal is that there may be peace and concord among peoples, and that God may be served with judgment and honesty. The principles are to love God, to live honestly, and to render to each what is their own. To love God is the principle for using the virtues and escaping vices. To render to each what is their own is the principle for satisfying God Himself regarding oneself, oneself regarding oneself, and one's neighbor regarding oneself.
¶ Alternatively, the principles of law are these: form, matter, general law, common law, special law, natural law, positive law, canon law, civil law, customary law, theoretical, practical, military, comparative, ancient, and new.

### ¶ Concerning Medicine.

**H**ealth is the subject in medicine; the goal is that the sentient body may be able to have its operations which are suitable to it. There are three principles: namely things natural, things non-natural, and things against nature. Natural things are seven: namely elements, complexions <note>the balance of humors</note>, humors, members, virtue, operations, and species; and four things are annexed to the aforesaid: age, color, figure, and the distance between male and female. Non-natural things are ten: namely food, air, drink, sound, waking, exercise, action, fullness, emptiness, and the accidents of the soul. Things against nature are three: namely disease, cause, and accident.

### ¶ Concerning Geometry.

**I**mmobile continuous quantity is the subject in geometry. The goal is to know lengths and widths...

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the encyclopedic overview of the sciences according to the system of Ramon Llull, likely following a section on geometry or physics given the opening reference to "depths of corporal things."</meta>

# Of Raymond Llull

...and the depths of corporal <note>physical or material</note> things. The principles are ten, namely: point, line, angle, figure, quantity, center, capacity, length, breadth, and depth.

### ¶ On Astronomy

**C**ontinuous mobile quantity, or celestial influence, is the subject in astronomy. The goal is to know the powers and movements which the heavens possess effectively over lower things <note>referring to the influence of stars on Earthly affairs</note>. The principles are the signs and the planets. There are twelve signs: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. There are seven planets, namely: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.

### ¶ On Arithmetic

**N**umber in its absolute sense is the subject in arithmetic. The goal is to sum many units by counting and to retain them more easily by number. The principles are parity <note>evenness</note> and imparity <note>oddness</note>. There are three types of numbers: the "article" <note>multiples of ten</note>, the "digit" <note>1 through 9</note>, and the "composite" <note>combinations like 12 or 25</note>. There are ten species of number: numeration, addition, subtraction, mediation <note>halving</note>, duplication, multiplication, division, progression, the extraction of square roots, and the abstraction of cubic roots.

### ¶ On Music

**T**he harmony of voices or melody is the subject in music. The goal is to produce delight in song by harmonizing diverse voices. The principles are ten, namely: height, depth <note>original: "infinitas," likely referring to the low bass range</note>, the middle range, length, shortness, thickness, thinness, subtlety, proportion, and the accent of vowels and consonants.

### ¶ On Grammar

**C**ongruity and correctness of speaking is the subject in grammar. The goal is to speak, pronounce, and write congruously and correctly. The principles are the letter, the syllable, the phrase, the word—or the eight parts of speech—and the agreement of substantive and adjective, of subject <note>original: "suppositi"</note> and predicate <note>original: "appositi"</note>, of relative and antecedent, and the modes of signifying.

<column-break/>

### ¶ On Logic

**A**rguments or the significance of reasoned argumentation is the subject in logic. Indeed, the goal is that through arguing, the true and the false may be found and the one discerned from the other. The principles are the term and the proposition.

### ¶ On Rhetoric

**T**he order and beauty of words is the subject in rhetoric. The goal is to move the will of the listener toward some desired end through ordered and beautiful words. The principles are form, matter, and end. There are five parts, namely: invention, disposition, style <note>original: "loquutio"</note>, memory, and pronunciation.

¶ Since General Science <note>Llull's "Ars Generalis"</note> possesses principles, questions, and general rules for all arts and sciences and for every particular thing contained within them, the unity of an art or science is revealed in the General Art by following its own process—just as a particular is found within its universal—by inquiring into its goodness, greatness, etc., and by inquiring about it through the questions "Whether?", "What?", "Of what?", etc. Therefore, the General Art itself is a mirror for the human intellect in which the truths of all knowable things shine back and appear. The goal of speculative science is truth; of practical science, however, it is work.

¶ Here ends the introduction to the Great General Art of the most reverend Illuminated Doctor, Master Raymond Llull, most useful for all sciences, which has very recently been brought to light. In the year of our Lord 1515, on the 28th day of the month of April.

# The Great and Ultimate General Art of the most distinguished Master **Ramon Llull**, professor of the illuminated sacred pages:

The pursuer and key-bearer of all the arts and sciences of **Llull** himself, providing an easier entry to them. Never before has it been *more elegantly commended to the printing press*, and polished by Master **Bernard de Lavinheta**, *a most faithful interpreter of that art*. Together with **figures** properly **inserted** in their places, which clarify the entire work. Furthermore, **parts, chapters, rubrics, titles**, and annotations have been included, with an added alphabetical index or directory containing **select sentences**, referring back to the page numbers.

# Epigram by Laurentius Theobaldus Cenomanus <note>Laurentius Theobaldus of Le Mans</note> to the reader, concerning the doctrines of this art devised by Ramon Lull, a man divinely skilled in every language and every art.

What a harvest this small, refined book holds for you, reader:
Though it be slender, the honor of a rare agate is within.
It explains here what the choir of doctors—
(That very model of Pallas Athena)—did not reveal in bright Athens.
What neither our age nor antiquity knew better:
Lullius gave by a heavenly, ethereal art.
Whatever Aristotle, whatever famous Greece
Considered; whatever King Croesus <note>Symbol of immense wealth</note> or the Sorbonne <note>The famous theological faculty in Paris</note> possesses.
With easy genius, he penetrated to the celestial axes:
And by pure virtue, he completed a grand work.
If rash Icarus had skimmed the low seas
With his wings, he would then have fallen into icy waters.
And because he desired to see the starry seats,
He was cast down when the sun’s help was withdrawn.
Lullius twisted his flight from the depths to the heights
And the heavens: yet the sea does not hold the man.
Among the heaps of books, refined reader (for he holds
The trophies), choose this work and be wise.

### A Concatenated Poem <term>Concatenated Poem: A verse form where the end of one line or phrase is repeated at the start of the next, like links in a chain</term> concerning the work.

The work touches on mystical things / but the work which touches on mystical things
Lays up a grand burden / but the burden which it lays up as grand:
Seeks wide baths: or the work which touches on mystical things.

->The Author to Choerilus<-
<note>original Greek: αυτ. προς Χαιριλ.</note>

You strike ten thousand muses with many-folded forms:
Choerilus does not easily sow a double-wisdom.
<note>original Greek: μυριαδα τας τυπεις αυθις πολυειλια μουσας: ουκ ευσπειρει απλους Χαιριλος αμφισοφον. This likely refers to Choerilus of Samos, an epic poet often contrasted with more refined styles.</note>

This great art, both general and final, was begun by the Blessed Ramon <note>original: "Raymundo"; referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic</note> at Lyon upon the Rhône in the month of November, in the year of our Lord 1305. It was finished by him in the city of Pisa, in the monastery of Saint Dominic, to the praise and honor of God, in the month of March in the year of our Lord 1308 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. May it be commended to Him and to the Blessed Virgin Mary, His mother. AMEN.

### A SHORT PRAYER TO THE BLESSED RAMON LLULL.

To you, Ramon, who bears the palm of martyrdom,
I flee for refuge; break the dog-like teeth <note>A metaphor for harsh critics or detractors</note> set against you.
May your science, now revealed to every mortal,
Flow forth as a truly clear fountain of doctrine
Into the whole world; let it be open, for it has lain hidden from the world too long.

### The title of the Great Art published by the Blessed Ramon Llull.

**O God, with Your highest perfection, the final general art begins.**

<meta>This is the opening page (folio 1) of the "Ars Magna" (Great Art) by Ramon Llull. It establishes the foundational principles and the symbolic alphabet used throughout the system.</meta>

# The Great and Ultimate General Art of the Enlightened Doctor and Master Ramon Llull.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral motifs and a central circular design.</image-desc>

Since we have created many general arts, we have proposed to explain them more clearly in this one, which we call the "ultimate," because we do not intend to create another hereafter; indeed, we compile it from the others and explicitly add some new things.

<margin>The human intellect consists more in opinion than in science <note>original: "scientia" - here meaning certain, demonstrated knowledge</note>.</margin>
¶ Since the human intellect is established far more in opinion than in certain knowledge—because every science has its own principles that are distinct from the principles of other sciences—the intellect therefore requires and desires a single general science for all sciences, containing its own general principles in which the principles of other particular sciences are implied and contained, just as the particular is contained in the universal. The reason for this is so that other subordinate principles may be ordered and regulated by these primary principles, so that the intellect may rest in those sciences through true understanding and be removed and distanced from erroneous opinions.

<margin>This science is a shortcut to others.</margin>
¶ Through this science, indeed, other sciences can be acquired very easily. For the particular principles shine forth and appear in the general principles of this art, provided that the particular principles are applied to the principles of this art, just as a part is applied to its whole.

<margin>The general principles of this art.</margin>
¶ The principles of this art are these: Goodness. Greatness. Eternity or duration. Power. Wisdom. Will. Virtue. Truth. Glory. Difference. Concordance. Contrariety. Beginning. Middle. End. Majority. Equality and minority. ¶ And they are called "general" because all the "goodnesses" of other sciences are applicable to one general Goodness. And I say the same of all "greatnesses" in relation to one general Greatness. And so it is to be said of other similar things in their own way.

<column-break/>

<margin>Why it is called a general science.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, this science can be called general because it has general questions applicable to all other questions, whatever they may be. For all are implied in these. And they are these, namely: Whether it is. What it is. From what it is. Why it is. How much it is. Of what kind it is. When it is. Where it is. How it is. And with what it is. And there are ten, as they appear numbered.

¶ Likewise, this art is general by reason of the mixture of principles and rules which it possesses, as will appear below. For just as a proposition taken in common is general to all propositions, so in their own way these composite principles, taken in common, are general to all particular composite principles.

<margin>Note well.</margin>
¶ But so that doubt may be removed, I say that all other principles are particular in respect to these principles of this art. Just as "great goodness," which is composite, is common to the goodness of Peter and William, and of a horse, and so on for others.

### On the division of this art.

<margin>Division of this art</margin>
¶ This art is divided into thirteen parts: namely, the Alphabet. The Figures. The Definitions. The Rules. The Table. The Evacuation of the Third Figure. The Multiplication of the Fourth Figure. The Mixture. The Nine Subjects. The Application. The Questions. Habituation. And the Method of Teaching.

# The first principal part: On the Alphabet.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' with geometric and floral patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>The first principal part of this work.</margin>
The Alphabet of this art is this:

<margin>Explanation of the alphabet</margin>
¶ **B**: signifies Goodness. Difference. Whether. God. Justice. And Avarice.
¶ **C**: signifies Greatness. Concordance. What. Angel. Prudence. And Gluttony.
¶ **D**: signifies Eternity or duration. Contrariety. From what. Heaven. Fortitude. And Lust.
¶ **E**: signifies Power. Beginning. Why. Man. Temperance. And Pride.
¶ **F**: signifies Wisdom. Middle. How much. Imagination. Faith. And Sloth.
¶ **G**: signifies Will. End. Of what kind. The Sensitive <note>The power of sensing/feeling</note>. Hope. And Envy.
¶ **H**: signifies Virtue. Majority. When. The Vegetative <note>The power of growth/life</note>. Charity. And Wrath.
¶ **I**: signifies Truth. Equality. Where. The Elementative <note>The physical/elemental realm</note>. Patience. And Falsehood.

<insert>
Through this science others are very easily acquired.
This science is general, having general questions for all other questions.
Likewise general by reason of the mixture of principles and rules.
</insert>

**A** signifies glory <note>original: "gloriā"</note>, minority, the manner and the "with what," the instrumental, piety, and inconstancy. ¶ A practitioner must know this alphabet by heart; for if they do not, the artist will be least able to use this art or put it into practice. ¶ This alphabet is established in this art so that the principles and questions of this art—and those things contained within them—may be signified through it, and so that the subject of inquiry may be brought to a conclusion, ensuring the understanding is true and certain, and not doubtful.

# On the Figures.
<margin>Four figures.</margin>
There are four figures: as is evident on the present page. <margin>On the first figure / which is circular.</margin> The first figure is designated by the letter **A**: and it is circular / divided into nine chambers. In the first chamber: stands **B**: in the second indeed **C**: and so on for the others. And it is called circular: because the subject is changed into the predicate and vice versa: as when it is said: great goodness / good greatness. eternal greatness: great eternity. God is good: good is God. and so on for the others: in their own way. <margin>What the circulation of the first figure is useful for.</margin> Through such circulation indeed the artist <note>The "artist" refers to a practitioner of Llull's Art, a system of logic.</note> will be able to recognize those things which are convertible / and those which are not convertible: such as "God is good" / and things of this sort: which can be converted. However, "God" and "angel" are not convertible: nor "goodness" and "angel": nor "his goodness" and "greatness": and so on for other terms.

<column-break/>

In this figure: all things are implied / such as when it is said: God is good / great / eternal / and so on for the rest. An angel is good / great / durable: and the rest. Greed is not good / but evil: and so on for others in their own way. In this figure: the proper and appropriated <term>passions</term> <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the attributes or properties belonging to a subject.</note> existing between the subject and predicate are recognized. <margin>Proper passions.</margin> Proper / such as "God is good / great" / and things of this sort. And the angel who has innate goodness / greatness and similar things. <margin>Appropriated passions.</margin> Appropriated / such as the evil angel who has appropriated malice: and this is meant morally. And so it is with fire: which has a good and great dryness through the earth. And man morally: good and great prudence / justice / and so on for the rest. <margin>A notable point for the artists of this art.</margin> Indeed, the artist of this art ought to familiarize and imagine this figure: and apply it to the purpose / according to those things we have said about it. So that the intellect through it may be able to reach truths: and this truly and in reality.
->The explanation of the first figure ends.<-

---

# On the Figures.

<margin>
The second triangular figure.
</margin>

**S**<insert><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' at the beginning of the text, featuring foliate patterns.</image-desc></insert>econd figure: this consists of three triangles: namely, of **difference**, **concordance**, and **contrariety**, as appears in the figure itself. ¶ Above the angle of **difference** are written: *sensual and sensual*; *sensual and intellectual*; *intellectual and intellectual*. And likewise for the angles of **concordance** and **contrariety**: to signify the difference that exists between the sensual and the sensual, such as between one body and another; and between the sensual and the intellectual, such as between the body and the soul; and between the intellectual and the intellectual, such as between God and an angel. And the same applies to concordance and contrariety. ¶ Above the angle of the **beginning** <note>Latin: *principium*</note> are written: *cause*, *quantity*, and *time*. By *cause*, the substantial principles are signified, which are the efficient, formal, material, and final principles. By *quantity* and *time*, the accidental principles are signified, such as the nine categories <note>The Aristotelian categories of accidents, excluding substance.</note>. ¶ Above the **middle** angle are written: *conjunction*, *measurement*, and *extremity*, to signify the three species of the middle: namely, the middle of conjunction, of measurement, and of the extremities. The middle of conjunction is like a nail that joins two posts. The middle of measurement is like a center point which exists equally in the middle of a circle. The middle of the extremities is like a line in the middle of two points. ¶ Above the angle of the **end** are written: *termination*, *privation*, and *final cause*, to denote that there are three species of end. For there is an end of termination, such as the boundary of a kingdom or a field. Likewise, there is an end of privation, such as death which ends life. And there is a causal end, such as God, who is the end and cause of all things. ¶ Above the angle of **majority**—and likewise for the angles of **equality** and **minority**—are written: *between substance and substance*, to signify that one substance is greater than another, such as the substance of a man which is greater in goodness or virtue than the substance of a stone. ¶ Likewise, *between substance and accident*, to signify that substance is greater than accident, just as the substance of a man is greater than his quantity and the like. ¶ And *between accident and accident*, to denote that one accident is greater than another, such as understanding being greater than sensing. And it can be spoken of in the same way regarding minority, since they relate to each other relatively. And between substance and substance there is equality, such as a man and a stone which are equal in the genus of substance. And between accident and accident there is equality, such as understanding and loving, which are equal in the genus of accident. And between substance and accident there is equality, such as quantity and its subject, which

<column-break/>

are equal through extension and surface. ¶ The **green triangle**, which consists of difference, concordance, and contrariety, is general to all things. For whatever exists is either in difference, concordance, or contrariety. Moreover, in this triangle, whatever exists is implied. However, difference is more general than concordance and contrariety. For more things can be different than can be concordant or contrary. Just as Peter and Martin differ, and they agree in species <note>i.e., they are both human</note>, but in their characters they are contrary: for one is just, the other indeed is unjust; and so of others in their own way. ¶ Difference indeed is the cause of plurality, but concordance is the cause of unity. Since just as difference distinguishes between one and another, so concordance composes many things into one. Contrariety, however, corrupts and dissolves. And therefore, just as the green triangle exists in a subject naturally, so the intellect is discursively active in a moral sense: by distinguishing, concordancing, descending, and ascending through the three species of difference, concordance, and contrariety mentioned above. And therefore the intellect with difference is simply general to the object. And likewise for concordance and contrariety. But when it is contracted through the scale constituted in the three species, it is not entirely general, nor entirely specific. As when it is said: "difference exists between the sensual and the sensual," and the rest; but when it descends to individuals, it is entirely particular in a moral sense. ¶ The **red triangle**, which consists of beginning, middle, and end, is general to all things: because it contains all things in itself; since whatever exists is either in the beginning, the middle, or the end. And outside these three terms, no being can exist. The **beginning** indeed is a being to which all other beings are subordinate. Yet a universal beginning cannot exist without nature or morality, having in itself the *beginner*, the *begun*, and the *beginning* <note>Lull's characteristic "triadic" logic where every principle has an active, passive, and verbal form.</note>. For just as the nature of heat cannot exist without that which heats, that which is heated, and the act of heating. So the nature of the beginning can by no means exist without the nature of the three aforesaid. And thus the artist <note>The practitioner of Lull's Art.</note> ought to know these three in the universal beginning, because they are of its essence causally and through the proper passions of the subject. But not occasionally; for they are acquired morally. Causal principles indeed imply necessity; occasional ones, however, imply contingency and "for the sake of well-being." ¶ And thus the artist ought to ascend and descend from the universal to the particular and vice versa. ¶ The **middle** moreover is as universal as the beginning. For just as the agent with the beginning

# Second Part

As the beginning acts as a principle, so also the middle acts as a mediator. And indeed, through the middle: it joins distinct beings into one composite or mixture. But through the middle of measurement: it measures acts—just as the intellect measures its own act of understanding existing in the middle between the one who understands and that which is understood; and sight measures its own seeing; the generator its generating; and the judge his judging; and so it is with other similar things.

<margin>He measures</margin>
<margin>his own understanding: The Act. <note>The following abbreviations are obscure, likely referring to grammatical or logical relations: "beg. r. ob- utij genis. r. a- genit."</note></margin>
<margin>Extremity.</margin>

¶ Through the middle of the extremities: there are essences and continuations—just as goodness, which is a simple essence existing as a middle between greatness and duration, having within itself the act of "bonifying" <note>term: bonificare (to make good). In Lullian philosophy, this describes the active function of the attribute of Goodness.</note>, existing in the middle of the "bonifier" and the "bonifiable," which join together in the act of bonifying: and all three are one undivided goodness; though morally, this is by no means the case. Indeed, these three species of the middle are the ladder through which the intellect descends and ascends while investigating the middles of beings. And in a similar way, it follows concerning the end, with which the efficient cause brings beings to rest in the ultimate term. But in a privative term <note>A term defined by the absence of something.</note> it does so least of all, because it is privative; and in a terminative term, one being is indeed separated from another, and one rest from another. Such an investigation is very useful and clear to the intellect for reaching the essences of things.

<margin>the end</margin>
<margin>The yellow triangle.</margin>

¶ By the yellow triangle is understood one universal majority <note>term: maioritas (greatness/superiority). One of the "Relations" in Llull's system.</note> to which all other majorities are subordinate. For with that majority, the agent "majorifies" <note>acts to make greater</note> just as it "principates" with the beginning. And this same thing is true of equality and also minority in its own way. ¶ Just as goodnesses and other substantial things are placed in majority, so goodnesses and other accidental things are reduced to the genus of minority. And in innate substantial goodness, the bonifier, the bonified, and the act of bonifying are equal by essence. And the same can be said of the intellect and the will, "fire-ness" <note>term: igneitas. The essential quality of fire.</note> and similar things in their own way. And so it is regarding the equality of causal and moral accidents. Indeed, through these three aforementioned species, the intellect shall ascend and descend so that it can reach the truths of things, both as to the genus of majority, equality, and minority, and also as to the substantial and accidental genus. ¶ And this ascent and descent is highly systematic for acquiring the sciences.

<column-break/>

<margin>Epilogue</margin>

¶ We have spoken of the second figure, which is the instrument of the intellect with which it acts upon the first figure; since through "difference" it distinguishes between goodness and greatness and the like; and with "concordance" it accords them. And so with others in their own way. Likewise, it distinguishes with difference within the essence of goodness: through the bonifier, the bonified, and the act of bonifying. And with concordance, it indeed accords that they are the same by essence naturally; but morally not so: because the difference is not innate but acquired, in that they are principles by occasion.

# On the Figures.

<margin>
Explanation of the third figure, divided into thirty-six chambers. <note>original: "Expositio tertie figure perviginti sex cameras divise." Note: The text says 26 in the margin but 36 in the body; 36 is the correct mathematical number for this table.</note>
</margin>

The third figure is composed of the first and second figures; it contains within itself thirty-six chambers <term>chambers: the cells or compartments in the table where two principles meet</term> as appears in the figure itself. In each chamber there are two letters: in the first, **b.c.**; in the second, **b.d.**; and so on for the others. And it is said to be composed of two figures because its **b** is equivalent to the **b** in the first figure and the **b** in the second. And likewise for **c**, which is equivalent to the **c** in the first and the **c** in the second, and so on for the others.

<margin>
The purpose of the figure.
</margin>

¶ The purpose for which this figure is placed in this Art is for signifying how, with one principle, a person may apply or associate another principle. Just as one applies **c, d,** and so on up to **k** to the letter **b**, so that with **c** and **d** one may have knowledge of **b**, according to whatever knowledge one seeks concerning **b**. And just as we speak of **b**, so it is to be understood of **c**: such as looking at **c** with **b**, and afterwards with **d**, and so on until the chamber of **c. k.** And so on for the other chambers in order until the chamber of **i. k.** This is done at will, according to how much a person wishes to multiply the arguments toward the same conclusion, and by observing this, applying the meaning of the chambers to the proposition at hand.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Application of the figure.
</margin>

¶ This figure teaches how to descend from the universal to the particular, step by step in four ways. First: by speaking through the chamber of **b. c.**, thus: "Goodness has great Difference and Concordance." <note>In Llull's system, B=Goodness, C=Greatness, and the second figure provides the relations of Difference and Concordance.</note> Second: when the intellect considers the "angles" of Difference, it descends from the universal to the particular by understanding that Difference and Concordance exist between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, as was said in the second figure. Third: it descends further when it considers that Difference and Concordance are good in fire and air through their Concordance in heat. Fourth: it descends by understanding that good Difference and Concordance exist between the "bonified" <note>original: "bonificatum." A Lullian term for the object or result of the action of Goodness.</note> etc., which are of the essence of Goodness. And just as we have spoken of **b. c.**, so it can be said of the other chambers of this figure.

It demonstrates how to move from abstract universal truths to specific, particular examples using these combinations.</summary>

Definition occurs in many ways, but is reduced to two, and each has four species <note>original: "species," here meaning types or categories.</note>

* **Power**: This is the Being <term>Being: Latin *Ens*, referring to anything that exists</term> through which matter has its own properties. <note>original: "passiones." In scholastic philosophy, these are the attributes or "passions" that a substance undergoes or possesses.</note>

# On Definitions.

<margin>On the fourth figure having three circles.</margin>
The fourth figure: has three circles as appears in it/ and it encompasses the first figure: the second and the third: and in it are gathered those principles from which the table is composed. Since the chamber of b.c.d. makes a column in the table composed of b.c.d. And the chamber of b.c.e. makes a column composed of b.c.e. <note>Llull uses letters to represent divine attributes or principles; these "chambers" are combinations used for logical deduction.</note>

<margin>Why the 4th figure is placed in this art.</margin>
¶ The intention why this figure is placed in this art: is so that from it the table may be made in order/ and so that a person may know how to find many reasons and many conclusions/ with the aforesaid reasons applied to one conclusion/ by looking at the meanings of the letters/ and applying them to the proposition/ in such a way/ that neither an inconsistency nor an impossibility follows through the aforesaid meanings.

<margin>What the middle circle is useful for.</margin>
¶ The middle circle: teaches how to find the middle <term>medium: the middle term in a logical syllogism</term> of a conclusion just as .c. and so of the others which is the middle through which .b. and .d. participate in greatness. And so .d. being between .b. and .e. which does not permit participating in goodness and power through its property: therefore the middle of concordant or conjunctive things causes an affirmative conclusion: and of contrary or disjunctive things, a negative one.
¶ End of the second principal part of this work.

### On definitions: and it is the third principal part.

<margin>The third principal part of this work: which is about definitions.</margin>

This third part: is about the definitions of the principles: such as the definition of goodness/ which is this. Goodness: is that being by reason of which the good acts good. And greatness: is that being by reason of which goodness/ duration and the rest/ are great. And this word "and the rest": signifies the other principles/ yet not simply/ just as saying/ in God there is goodness/ greatness etc. it is not understood/ that therefore there are majority/ minority/ or property. <note>Llull distinguishes between the absolute principles like Goodness and the relative principles like Majority.</note>
¶ Duration: is that by reason of which goodness/ greatness etc. endure.
¶ Power: is that by reason of which goodness/ greatness and such: are able to exist and act.
¶ Wisdom: is the property by reason of which the wise one understands.
¶ Will: is that through which goodness/ greatness and similar things/ are desirable/ and through which a good/ great etc. subject/ is willing.
¶ Virtue: is the origin of the union/ of goodness/ greatness/ and such things which are similar.
¶ Truth: is that which is true concerning goodness/ greatness and similar things.
¶ Glory: is the very delight in which goodness/ greatness and others rest.

<margin>Concordance</margin>
¶ Concordance: is that by reason of which goodness and greatness and the rest agree in one and in many.

<margin>Contrariety</margin>
¶ Contrariety: is the mutual resistance of certain things because of diverse ends.

<margin>Principle</margin>
¶ Principle: is that which relates to all things by reason of some priority.

<margin>Middle</margin>
