<margin>End</margin>
¶ End: is that in which the principle rests.

<margin>Majority</margin>
¶ Majority: is the image of immensity/ greatness/ eternity and the rest.

<margin>Equality</margin>

<margin>Minority</margin>
¶ Minority: is a being close to nothingness.

And those which are accidental/ accidental ones: just as for goodness which is substantial/ "to bonify" is appropriate. And for accidental goodness an accidental definition is also appropriate with which the agent bonifies the "bonifiable" things accidentally.

# Fourth part.

<margin>Definitions at will and through terms</margin> Just as we have spoken concerning goodness, so it can be said of the other principles. Through the two aforementioned modes, the practitioner can indeed define all things. ¶ There is, however, a third mode which is confused or manifold; namely, when definitions are made at will or by contingency, without considering the proper and appropriated definitions existing between the subject and the predicate. This occurs, for example, when it is said: "God is an infinite and eternal being," and "Man is a rational animal." And again: "He is an animal to whom alone it belongs to ride, to write," and so on in his own way. ¶ Furthermore, definitions are made by composition, namely when one principle is defined with another: <margin>Definitions by Composition</margin> as when it is said "Great Goodness is a being by reason of which a great good [agent] acts upon a great good [object]." And if "Eternity" is added, this means that Great Goodness is eternal. Indeed, Great Goodness itself is defined thus: "Great and Eternal Goodness is a being by reason of which a great and eternal good [agent] acts upon a great and eternal good [object]." By such a method, the practitioner can make demonstrations through presumptive and true principles, and even necessary ones, which cannot be held in any other way. ¶ Further, just as it is said "Goodness is a being by reason of which a good [agent] acts upon a good [object]," so it can be said of Magnitude. "Magnitude is a being by reason of which a great [agent] acts <margin>Rules and questions are one and are like the word in the 'bonificative' etc. <note>Lullian technical terms for the active, passive, and verbal functions of a principle.</note></margin> upon a great [object]," and "Eternity produces an eternal [object]." And so with the others. ¶ Furthermore, to explain the definitions of the principles, the practitioner can explain and declare them along with their nature; for goodness would not have a nature without the innate *bonificative* <note>the active power of goodness</note>, *bonificable* <note>the capacity to receive goodness</note>, and *bonifying* <note>the act of being good</note>. Neither would Magnitude exist without the *magnificative*, *magnificable*, and *magnifying*; nor Eternity without the *eternizing*, *eternizable*, and *eternizing*. And so with the others. And if the principles did not have a nature, goodness would not be a being by reason of which a good [agent] acts good naturally. Nor would Duration be a being by reason of which goodness, magnitude, and the rest endure. And therefore, if the definitions were destroyed, the principles would be nothing; nor would the whole universe exist, which is false, because we have experience of the universe, that it exists. <margin>Wisdom and Intellection</margin> Likewise, through this principle "Wisdom," it is to be understood that it is understood by the intellect; and in every other being besides rational substance, "instinct" is understood through wisdom, and "appetite" is understood through will. ¶ Furthermore, someone perhaps having a canine tooth and a serpentine tongue <note>A metaphor for a sharp-tongued or malicious critic.</note> will scorn and slander our principles and their definitions. <margin>Substance and the sensible. Against the emulators of this art.</margin> But the Art requires that one principle help another, as if it were said: granted that Magnitude is a being by reason of which Goodness is great, and that all goodnesses are equally great; this must be denied through the principles of Majority, Minority, and Contrariety, which do not permit <margin>Prudence</margin> all goodnesses to be equally great.

->¶ The end of the third principal part of this work.<-

<column-break/>

### The fourth principal part, which is about the rules.

<margin>Rubric of the fourth part of this work, which is about the rules.</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative initial 'R' containing a figure of a scholar or saint holding a book and a staff, set against a background with a landscape and a building.</image-desc> The rules are ten: namely, *Whether*, *What*, and the rest, as is already marked in the alphabet. These rules are ten general questions through which every inquiry must be made; and how that which is sought is placed within them is illuminated, colored, and even signified to the intellect according to the essence and nature of the rule, just as is evident in grammar. For just as all declinable noun-words are included in the five declensions and can be declined through them, so in their own way all other questions besides these of this Art (which can be made) are included in these ten, and are indeed reduced to them, and are also regulated by them by reason of the generality they possess. And just as these questions are general, so are their species. For just as Goodness is entirely general with its generalities—the *bonificative*, *bonificable*, and *bonifying*—without which it cannot be entirely general, so it is with the ten questions of this Art, which are general along with their species.

### Concerning Rule B.

<margin>Question 1. Concerning Rule B.</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative initial 'R' containing a figure of a man in a robe, possibly a scholar, pointing towards text.</image-desc> The rule of B is *Whether* [Latin: *utrum*], and it concerns possibility: whether this thing which is asked about exists or does not exist. Such possibility causes faith, or belief, or supposition, because it supposes that both parts are possible, namely the affirmative and the negative. This rule of B has three species: which are Doubt, Affirmation, and Negation. <margin>This rule has three species.</margin> Through the first species, one must suppose that it is or is not, so that the intellect is not obstinate or bound, but investigative, so that it can pass through to reaching the affirmative or negative as true. And this with such a condition: that it always concedes that which is more "recollectible" <note>worthy of being remembered</note>, intelligible, and lovable to be true in the conclusion, aiding itself with the principles and their definitions, and with the other rules. For example, if it is asked *whether* the intellect exists: it is seen that it does, because it is more recollectible, intelligible, and lovable for it to be than not to be. And this is according to the aforementioned investigation of the principles. When it is said that that which is more recollectible and lovable is to be chosen, it must be understood that it is chosen with greater intelligibility and not with less. For when the affirmative or negative is chosen with less...

# On the Rules.

<note>The text begins by discussing the choice of a subject based on its ability to be remembered and loved.</note> ...the ability to be remembered and the lovability of the subject: such that the choice is not of the genus of philosophy or science, but rather of the genus of faith and belief. Since, however, a choice with a greater degree of intelligible equivalence generates a greater ability to be remembered and loved, it follows that true science is necessary, in which the intellect truly rests because it truly attains the object. And in this step consists the entire power of this rule.

### .C. On Rule C.

<margin>Question 2 regarding Rule C, which has four species.</margin>
<margin>First species.</margin>
The Rule of C concerns "quiddity" <note>The "what-ness" or essence of a thing</note>: because it is the subject and source of the definitions of beings, just as B is figured in the definitions of principles. This rule also has four species. The **first species** concerns the definition and the thing defined, which are interchangeable with the definition itself; as when it is said: the intellect is an essence to which "to understand" belongs, and so on for others in their own way.

<margin>Second species.</margin>
The **second species** is when it is asked what a thing has in itself essentially and naturally, without which the thing itself cannot exist. For example, when it is asked what the intellect has in itself essentially and naturally, without which it cannot exist: the answer is that it has an innate *intellective* [power], an *intelligible* [object], and the act of *understanding*. And this "intellect through the intellect" is the agent and the understander; and with its own innate *intelligible*, it is the "possible intellect" in which it understands "foreign" intelligibles <note>External data or concepts not innate to the soul</note> which are not of its essence; and its *understanding* is an innate and intrinsic act. And all three are one intellect and one indivisible essence. Indeed, in that intrinsic understanding of the intellect itself, "foreign" understanding is characterized, just as a "foreign" intelligible is characterized in the intrinsic intelligible. And this is indeed necessary: so that passion corresponds with passion, and act with act, and they relate to each other appropriately. I say this, however, when the intellect is "practical"; but when it is "theoretical," not at all. Rather, the intellect itself is that which it is simply, like a whole which exists through its parts which are co-essential to it. ¶ Through what has been said about the intellect, one understands how the intellect is both universal and particular: it is universal as an instrument by which it can understand this or that. And so it is with the intelligible act, which is universal for receiving this or that intelligible successively. And so with the intrinsic act: namely, understanding with foreign acts successively. That what has been said of the intellect is true is probable enough through the definitions of the principles and the Rule of B. For if it were not true, the intellect would not have imaginative goodness, nor duration, etc., nor would it have a nature by which it is universal and particular; nor would the Rule of B be entirely true, which is impossible.

<margin>Third species.</margin>
The **third species** is when it is asked: What is a thing in another? And the answer is that it is according to the genus of quality: just as the intellect is active through its intellective power when it attains an object, and is passive when it receives species <note>Mental images or forms</note>. And it is "great" when it has a great and difficult object; and it is "true" when it understands truly; and "false" when falsely. And it is bound and necessitated by memory when it believes; but it is in liberty and in God <note>original: "dete" likely for "deo"</note> when it understands truthfully.

<margin>Fourth species.</margin>
The **fourth species** is when it is asked what a thing has in another; such as what the intellect has in an object. And the answer is that it has action and passion as signified in the third species: and it has action in grammar, logic, and geometry; and passion in the positive sciences; and it has goodness through moral virtues, and fault through sin; and so with other qualities. ¶ We have spoken of Rule C and its species. And just as we have exemplified it through the intellect, so in its own way it can be exemplified in corporeal subjects: as in fire, to which it properly belongs to "ignite" substantially and to "heat" accidentally; fire having the *ignifier*, the *ignitable*, and the *igniting*. And in a lamp and in a wick there is fire, having its action in the elements. And just as the vegetative [power] is in a vegetated body, and the sensitive in a sensed body, and the imaginative in an imagined body; in the celestial [body], however, it is not so. For a star does not produce another star, nor an angel another angel: because they lack substantial generation, since they are incorruptible and indivisible substances. Concerning God, it is understood in another way according to the definition and nature of divine goodness and essence.

<column-break/>

### .D. On Rule D.

<margin>Question 3 regarding Rule D: which has three species.</margin>
<margin>First species.</margin>
The third question concerns "materiality" <note>The "from what" of a thing</note> and has three species. The **first** is "of what a thing is" [made]: as when it is asked what the intellect is of, absolutely. And the answer is that the intellect is of itself: that is, it was not made from anything but was created in its totality where it previously was not.

<margin>Second species.</margin>
The **second species** is when it is asked of what something is made or constituted: such as asking of what the intellect is [composed]. And the answer is that it is of its co-essential principles: namely, of its *intellective*, *intelligible*, and *understanding*. And so of man, who is constituted of his body and his soul. And a nail which is of iron, and so with similar things.

<margin>Third species.</margin>
The **third species** is when it is asked "whose" something is: such as asking whose is the intellect and whose is the kingdom. And the answer is that the intellect is man's, and the kingdom is the king's. Through this rule, it is asked what a thing is. ¶ We have spoken of Rule D and applied it to the intellect, and thus it can be applied to other subjects in its own way: as is evident regarding the whole universe, that it is of itself according to the first species, and not from any other pre-existing principle. And through the second species, it is granted that it is [composed] of form and substantial matter and as a constituted whole. From...

# Fourth Part

->**Man is, so to speak, a source**<- <margin>Man as a source of something</margin>
from which particular forms descend. And from which matter, particular matters descend. The universe itself belongs to God, because it is His creature. And this can also be understood regarding universal and substantial goodness, magnitude, etc., which are primitive <note>original: "primitiva"; meaning primary or foundational</note> in respect to their genus. Through the second species of this rule: goodness indeed consists of the "bonifying" <note>the active power to make good</note>, the "bonifiable" <note>the capacity to be made good</note>, and the act of "bonifying"; and magnitude consists of the "magnifying," the "magnifiable," and the act of "magnifying"—all in a universal sense. And so it is with the others in their own way, because these are its parts. The same can be said of all particular goodnesses, magnitudes, and so forth. These goodnesses descend from the aforementioned goodness, and magnitudes from the aforementioned magnitude, and so on for the others; similarly regarding the elements and things composed of elements in their own way. However, it is not the same for man according to the second species; for he is a composite of soul and body, which differ in genus and nature, just as corporeal and incorporeal substance differ. And so it is with substance and accident: just as quantity is not of the essence of a substance, but is its "habit" <note>a condition or state</note> by reason of which it is "how much" <note>quantitative</note>. And so with quality, by reason of which it is "of what kind." And so with other accidents. Nevertheless, substance and accident are composed in the body, without which composition a body cannot exist.

<margin>3. As the Soul is</margin>
Through the third species of this rule: accidents belong to substance, for they do not exist through themselves but through substance. The reason for this is: because the same accident is not made of "this and that" <note>i.e., it lacks internal essential parts</note>. Substance, however, is so: since it is constituted of this matter and that form, by reason of which it is self-existing. And an accident is its likeness, its figure, and its instrument.

<margin>Accident / Quantity</margin>
Furthermore, an accident such as quantity is of itself according to the first species, in which it is primitive (insofar as it is general); all other quantities are from it and descend from it. It is indeed undivided insofar as it is primitive, but it is divided into many particular qualities <note>The text likely means "quantities" here, following the logic of the paragraph</note>, just as general quality is divided into many particular qualities. This division is "by accident," namely through substantial division, which divides through the breaking and generation of species, differences, and number.

<margin>Accidents from which sciences are known</margin>
Furthermore, there are other accidents from which the sciences are formed, as appears in Logic, which concerns "second intentions" <note>logical concepts about concepts</note> joined to "first intentions" <note>concepts of real objects</note>. And so it is with mechanical accidents, such as the shape of a chest which is the shape of the wood. And the shape of a tower, from the shapes of the stones. And so with others in their own way.

<margin>
1. Species
2. Composite
3. Rule by possession
</margin>
Through this rule, the artist <note>the practitioner of this "Art" or system of logic</note> inquires into primitivity and simplicity through the first species. Through the second, composition. Through the third, dominion and possession. This rule is general to all things. We have spoken of Rule D, and that which is true is evident through itself, and through all the definitions of the principles and through Rules B and C. It is indeed quite probable: for if substantial goodness (and likewise for intellect and such things) were not according to the second species of this rule, it would lack its own species, and thus would have nothing from which it was made; whence it would follow that it would not be self-existing, but would be like an accident which lacks the second species of D. Nor would goodness itself be a reason substantially, nor would the "good" produce "good" substantially from the essence of goodness; and thus some goodness would not be a substance but an accident. And thus the definition of magnitude, duration, and the rest would be destroyed. Furthermore, all things would then be accidents, which is impossible and against Rules B and C. And in this passage, the doctrine is given by which the artist of this Art may prove one truth with another, by applying the definitions of the principles and Rules B and C, which has been said here regarding D.

<column-break/>

### The fourth question, which is about "Why"

<margin>Question 4, which is about "Why," contains two species.</margin>
<note>Decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a human face in profile.</note>
The fourth question is about "Why," which has two species: one is through **existence**, the other is through **agency**. For example, to ask through existence *why* the intellect is: the answer must be according to the existence of the intellect, which is because of this: that it is made of its own "intellective," "intelligible," and "to understand" <note>the act of understanding</note>; just as everything that exists is what it is through its co-essential parts of which it is made. And the intellect acts through agency so that it may understand and move itself toward its end, which end is that it may understand God and the truths of other beings. And so that man may have the habit of knowledge through this rule, he asks: *why are things?* That the intellect exists through a "formal why" as said above seems to be true through the definition of goodness, magnitude, and the rest, and through Rule B and the second species of Rule C, without which the intellect would have neither the nature of existing nor of acting. Furthermore, as has been said of the intellect, so it can be said of substance, which exists through its causes and its occasions. Through its causes, such as through form, matter, efficient, and final cause. Through occasion, such as through definition, habituation, and contingency. And so with other accidents. Through "Why" itself, there are indeed genera, species, individuals, the liberal arts, trades, virtues, and vices.

# On the Rules.

<margin>
Question 5. regarding F.
</margin>

The fifth question asks about **quantity**, which has two species: namely, simple and composite. For example, it asks: how great is the intellect? And one must respond according to the simplicity of its essence: that the intellect is as great as the being of its essence. However, regarding its composition, one must respond: that it is as great as it is through its existence and agency, or through its own <term>intellective</term><note>the power of understanding</note>, <term>intelligible</term><note>the object being understood</note>, and <term>understanding</term><note>the act of understanding</note> of which it consists. Through this rule, the measurements of beings and their number are sought. How what has been said about the intellect is true seems probable enough through the definition of **goodness**, **greatness**, and the rest, according to the second species of the rule (C. D.). Since goodness, insofar as it is a simple essence and form, has a continuous quantity distinct from other essences by reason of its genus and nature; but insofar as it is the reason for producing good, it has a discrete nature through the <term>bonificative</term><note>the power to make good</note>, the <term>bonificable</term><note>that which can be made good</note>, and the <term>bonifying</term><note>the act of making good</note>. And from this indeed flow foreign and discrete quantities through the composition it has in an individuated subject, in which goodness has both continuous and discrete quantity. And just as was said of goodness, so it can be said of other superior forms which cause inferior continuous and discrete quantities. Just as in a stone, which is <term>habituated</term><note>clothed or characterized</note> by one continuous quantity while having discrete quantities by reason of the essences of the elements from which it is composed. And so it is for a plant through the elemental and vegetative powers; and for a man through the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and reasoning powers from which he is composed. And so for a tower or a ship constructed by art. Yet not as continuously as a natural subject, but more discretely than a natural subject, by reason of its integral parts.

### On the sixth rule. G.

<margin>
Question 6. regarding G.
</margin>

The sixth question asks about **quality**, which has two species: namely, *proper* and *appropriated*. Thus it asks by the first species: What kind is the intellect? And it must be answered: that the intellect is such as its own proper intellectivity, its intelligibility, and its own proper understanding. And if it is asked by the second species: It must be answered that the intellect is such as its <term>habit</term><note>a stable disposition or learned quality</note>, or such as its appropriated intelligibility through the action placed in its own proper intellectivity, through which it reaches other

<margin>
moral forms seen in themselves

intelligible beings. And this is the same if it is asked: What kind is fire by its own proper quality, which is its heat? And it must be answered that it is hot, heating; and through its dryness, which is a quality appropriated to it through the earth, it is "dryable." But in the air, it is "drying" through dryness. And so for others; through this rule, one inquires about proper and appropriated quality. Proper qualities are superior causes, and appropriated ones are inferior; just as the heat of fire is a superior quality, and its dryness is inferior. And so of natural goodness, which is superior, while moral goodness is inferior. Through this rule, the artist inquires into those things which are superior and inferior between the subject and the predicate. I say that proper qualities are proper <term>passions</term><note>attributes or properties arising from an essence</note>, and appropriated qualities are likewise appropriated passions.

# Part Four.

<margin>
The Modal Rule.
</margin>
By the first species of rule **d**, we say that **time** is subject to the agent in the thing to be done through the act of doing: because substance clothes itself in time either naturally or morally. ¶ By the **modal rule**, it is to be understood that time consists in the mover, the moving, and the mobile (or the motion); and this is held habitually, just as a part exists substantially within a part. And the likeness of time consists of its form—past, present, and future—just as in the habit of heat there is a form, a heater, a thing to be heated, and the act of heating. And in motion: moving, the mover, and the mobile (or the motion).

<margin>
The second instrumental species.
</margin>
¶ By the second instrumental species of rule **R**: **Time** is the instrument of substance along with motion, so that substance can act; in the subject, however, there is the "ability to be acted upon," and its "actability" is a form shaped through time and motion. And in this step, it appears in what manner the intellect truly and really reaches the essence of time. And that this is true is provable indeed through the definitions of the principles and rules **b. c. d. e. f. g.** Nevertheless, it is necessary that the intellect be exceedingly high and clear, and also removed from confusion and doubt, by reason of the preparation of the material both subjectively and objectively.

Just as one is habituated in a habit: namely, the good in goodness, the white in whiteness, the great in greatness, and such. And the form of this instrument appears through sense and imagination in the mixing of flour in water, and water in flour, and such things. ¶ We have spoken of place through the discourse we made about it by means of rules **c. d. R.**; we have notice and knowledge of it, and to this the definitions of the principles and rules **b. c. d. e. f. g. h.** bear witness.

And *concordance* accords many things in one composite; and likewise it is modal by joining. And thus follows the mode by which a part is in a part and the whole in its parts. Just as in a coin in which gold is in silver and silver in gold, each remaining in its own essence and its own being. Such modality is a general being under which all particular modalities fall, and its subject is "likeness." Just as figure is the likeness of substance, and color is the likeness of the colored thing, and such like. And moral modality is the likeness of natural modality. ¶ And that what has been said about modality is true, seems probable by reason of the definitions of the principles. ### On Rule K: which is about Instrumentality.

<margin>Tenth question: on instrumentality.</margin>
<margin>First species.</margin>
The tenth rule is about instrumentality: this is to ask *with what* things are, or *with what* they act. And it has four species similar to those which are of the rule of modality. ¶ The first species is, such as asking with what the understanding is a part of the soul. And it must be answered that the understanding is a part of the soul with *difference*, *concordance*, and *power*; and so with the other principles, except for *contrariety*. ¶ The second <margin>Second species.</margin>

<column-break/>

species is: with what does the understanding understand things other than itself? And it must be answered that the one who understands does so by acquiring and joining one species <note>a mental image or concept</note> with another, and placing them in its own intelligible: just like an eye which reaches its own likeness in a mirror. ¶ <margin>Third species.</margin> The third species is: when it is asked with what the understanding is universal and particular. And it must be answered that it is universal insofar as it has one active, intellective, formal power with which it reaches many things in one universal intelligible—which is of the essence of the understanding itself—with which and in which (namely, the universal intelligible) many species are intelligible, just as in one mirror many images are visible. And it is particular when it descends by practicing, namely by understanding some specific species which it has acquired and preserved in the memory. ¶ <margin>Fourth species.</margin> The fourth species is: when it is asked with what the understanding transmits its likeness outside of itself. And it must be answered: with its own *intellective*, *intelligible*, and *to understand*, with which it makes species to be understood, and through memory to be recallable, and through the will to be eligible for loving or hating. ¶ <margin>Division of instruments.</margin> Through this rule, inquiry is made into the instruments of things, whether spiritual or corporeal. ¶ Furthermore, of instruments, one kind is **substantial**: <margin><insert>Substantial</insert></margin> such as the male and female who have a substantial instrument with which they generate the offspring. Another is **accidental**: <margin><insert>Accidental</insert></margin> such as fire which with its heat warms the thing capable of being warmed. And just as a man who with justice makes himself just. <margin><insert>Universal</insert></margin> Another is **universal**: such as the understanding which with its intelligible makes this or that foreign thing intelligible. And just as the male who with one and the same rod generates many sons; and fire with its heat warms many things; and just as the blacksmith who with one and the same hammer makes many nails. Truly, **particular** instruments are this and that and the rest, with which <margin><insert>Particular</insert></margin> a builder constructs a house. And just as two propositions with which a conclusion is made. And so of others in their own way. <margin><insert>Intrinsic</insert></margin> Another is an **intrinsic** instrument: such as the intelligible which is of the essence of the understanding. <margin><insert>Extrinsic</insert></margin> Another is **extrinsic**, which is the "stranger" <note>external information</note> with which a teacher generates knowledge. And just as the hammer with which the blacksmith forges a nail. That what we have said about instrumentality is true, all the definitions of the principles of this Art and all the rules attest and prove. And similarly what has been said of the ten rules: which rules are vessels for all things that can be understood and are proportionate to the human understanding.

->**The end of the fourth part.**<-

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the rule of Modality and introduces the rule of Instrumentality, explaining how the mind uses internal and external "tools" to process knowledge and perform actions. It categorizes instruments into substantial, accidental, universal, particular, intrinsic, and extrinsic types.</summary>
<keywords>instrumentality, modality, intellect, memory, will, universal vs particular, scholastic logic, Ramon Llull, cognitive theory</keywords>

### ¶ Rubric concerning the Table.

<margin>
.T.
</margin>

<margin>
.b c r b.
</margin>

This Table is composed of 84 columns, as has been stated. It is the subject or instrument in which the solutions to questions are investigated, by taking up the matter at hand through affirming or denying, harmonizing the principles through the rules, and avoiding their contradiction. Furthermore, the letter **t.** in the table signifies that the letters appearing before it are principles from the First Figure <note>The First Figure represents the nine attributes of God: Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory.</note>, and the letters appearing after it are from the Second Figure <note>The Second Figure represents relational concepts like Difference, Concordance, and Contradiction.</note>. For example, in the chamber **b.c.t.b.**, the **b.** preceding the **t.** signifies Goodness, and the **c.** signifies Greatness. The **b.** after the **t.** signifies Difference; and so it goes for the others. Moreover, the investigation performed in the Table is at a higher level of signifying truths than that which is performed in the Figures. ¶ Indeed, the Table of the Fourth Figure is derived by rotating the second and third circles, as appears in the Table itself, up to 84 columns. In this revolution consists the binding of the columns: **b.c.d.** <note>Goodness, Greatness, Eternity</note> which converts itself with column **b.c.f.** <note>Goodness, Greatness, Power</note>. And so it proceeds successively from column to column until the final one, which is **h.i.k.** <note>Truth, Glory, Justice</note>, as appears in the Table. Thus, in any given column, all columns are implied; by reason of this implication, every column is helpful to every other. ¶ For any solution to a single question, all the meanings of all the questions—both abstract and those guided toward that specific question—can be applied. In this step, the great universality of this Table of this Art becomes apparent. ¶ Furthermore, in every column there are twenty questions arranged on the surface. We shall give an example of this in the first column, which is **b.c.d.**, by predicating first of Goodness, then of Greatness, and afterwards of Eternity, as follows: ¶ The first is: Whether goodness is so great that it is eternal? ¶ Second: Whether there is any goodness so great that it contains within itself things that are different yet co-essential to it? ¶ Third: Whether goodness is so great that it contains within itself things that are concordant yet co-essential to it? ¶ Fourth: Whether goodness containing within itself contrary things is great? ¶ Fifth: Whether eternal goodness is different? ¶ Sixth: Whether eternal goodness is con-

The first chamber is **b.c.d.**, the second is **b.c.t.b.**, and so on until the twentieth, which is **t.b.c.d.** From each chamber we have extracted one question, as shown above. And just as we made 20 questions in the first column, so another 20 can be made in the second, and another 20 in the third, and so on in order until the final column, which is **h.i.k.** ¶ Through these questions and solutions, the intellect itself raises the mind to a high level of universality, so that it is rendered immeasurable and inestimable. This is by reason of the generality of the predicate and the subject. In this step, it is clear in what way this Art is highly general and useful. ¶ To provide the doctrine and method for solving questions, we wish to solve the aforementioned questions by applying the meanings of the letters to the proposition in such a way that the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules are not destroyed. ¶ And first: to the first question, one must respond with **b.** <note>Rule B: "Whether?"</note>: Whether goodness is so great that it is eternal? I say that it is. And this is indeed manifest through the definitions of Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity. For if Goodness is the being by reason of which a good [agent] does good, and Greatness magnifies Goodness and Eternity, and the definition of Eternity makes Goodness and Greatness endure, it is necessary that the act of Goodness be infinite and eternal, and consequently the essence of Goodness. Thus it is concluded that Goodness is great and eternal. For without Greatness and Eternity, it could not have an infinite and eternal act—namely, "to bonify" <note>original: "bonificare" - a Lullian term for the active expression of goodness</note>—and this is affirmable through Rule B and through the second species...

# On the Table
## Folio 15

Furthermore, through the first type of Rule D <note>The "Rules" and "Dignities" refer to the combinatorial logic system of Ramon Llull’s "Ars Magna."</note>, the affirmation must be held: because eternity is the primary essence beyond which there is no other preceding it, and its primary nature is good and great; and thus it follows by necessity that there is some goodness that is great and eternal. ¶ Furthermore, through the third type of Rule D, it is signified that there is no other contrariety that has dominion in eternity, but rather the opposite: for contrariety would have dominion if eternity did not have primary and great goodness; therefore, goodness is so great that it is eternal.

<margin>b c b To the second question.</margin>
¶ To the second question, when it is asked whether there is any goodness so great that it is differentiated? **Solution.** I say that it is so. And this is indeed manifest through their definitions. For if goodness is the being by reason of which a good thing acts for the good; and greatness is the being by reason of which goodness and difference are great; it is indeed necessary that in goodness there are differing things coessential <note>Sharing the same underlying substance or essence.</note> to itself: namely, the **bonifying** <note>The active principle: that which makes good.</note>, the **bonified** <note>The passive principle: that which is made good.</note>, and the **act of bonifying**. For this belongs to the nature of goodness, greatness, and difference: that in the essence of goodness there are things distinct really and simply. And that this goodness is essentially undivided, great, and without confusion. ¶ Likewise, the question must be held as affirmative through Rule B, as is evident through itself, and also through Rule C. For through the first type, goodness itself is defined with its concrete forms and is converted essentially and concretely. And through the second type, difference is placed with greatness: that goodness has in itself the bonifying, the act of bonifying, and the bonified; which indeed it would not have by nature without distinction; nor could goodness be the reason for a good thing to produce good from itself. And thus goodness itself would be empty of the nature of greatness if difference were lacking. ¶ Moreover, regarding the same, greatness and difference are in goodness naturally, as is clear through the third type of Rule C. And also goodness is in them naturally. And through the fourth type, greatness and difference have their acts in goodness,

<margin>b c c To the third question.</margin>

And in this passage appears the height of the intellect which truly and actually has reached this: to which height it could not ascend except with God helping.

It must be answered that it is not: because it lacks concordance, which is indeed more absolute than contrariety. The reason for this is that concordance with goodness posits being by generating. And contrariety with malice posits the privation of goodness by corrupting: and this is what the definitions of goodness, greatness, and contrariety intend: that what we have said is true. Rule B indeed requires this, and also the first type of Rule C. Since if great goodness contained in itself contrary things, it would indeed be a great evil to it; and greatness and smallness would be converted into that goodness: which is impossible. And also through the second type of Rule C, which posits in goodness the bonifying, the bonified, and the act of bonifying with greatness: therefore, the negative must be held regarding this question. Likewise, the third type says that contrariety could not be in a good subject with greatness. And the same judgment applies to the fourth type, which says that contrariety could not have its act in great goodness.

-># Part Five.<-

The eternity of the world <note>The author is arguing against the Aristotelian idea that the universe has no beginning</note> posits an eternal evil that is never at rest; whereas the eternity of God posits an eternal good that is at rest. The eternity of God allows for eternal evil to be durable <note>i.e., lasting in punishment</note>, and the eternity of the world posits that good is durable according to the definition of eternity. The second species of Rule D posits that eternal good and eternal evil are joined in a composite. The definition of magnitude posits a great conjunction, and the third species of Rule D posits subjection on both sides. The second species of Rule E posits a contrary and a preserved contrary. Indeed, eternity deviates in the eternity of God and in the eternity of the world, having dominion in both, by producing an eternal, unquieted contrary—which is impossible. By reason of this impossibility, the world cannot be eternal.

### To the 13th question.
<margin>c t b c</margin>
<margin>To the 13th question.</margin>
When it is asked: what is great difference and concordance? It must be said that in the essence of magnitude there is a "magnifier," a "distinguisher," and a "concordant" <note>The author uses active Latin participles to describe the internal mechanics of the Trinity</note> which are one person in number; that the "magnified," "differentiated," and "concorded" is another person; and the "to magnify," "to differentiate," and "to concord" is yet another person. All these three persons are the same through essence, nature, magnitude, difference, and concordance. This is to be seen through their definitions, and through the first and second species of Rules C and D, and through the third species of C, so that magnitude, difference, and concordance are acting and concording in reality, separate from emptiness and idleness. Through the fourth species of C, one has an act in the other, without which acts their definitions would not be true—which is impossible, as Rule B testifies.

### To the 15th question.
<margin>c t b d</margin>
<margin>To the 15th question.</margin>
It is asked: what is great difference and contrariety? It must be answered that it is that cause causing one contrary in another, as in an element in which fire and water are mixed; similarly air and earth; and between innate natural good and moral evil—namely, sin and the like. This is evident through the definitions of magnitude, difference, and contrariety. Difference declares and distinguishes the contraries themselves. Contrariety in a subject deprives it of concordance and generates contrary appetites and ends. This is signified through Rule B, and through the first and second species of Rules C and D, and through the third species of Rule C. Similarly, it is quite clear that one contrary is the agent and the patient <note>The "agent" performs the action; the "patient" receives it</note> in the other. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one has action in the other; through the third species of Rule D, it has subjection. In this passage, the great pains of Hell are prefigured. Through the fourth species of C, one has an act in the other, without which acts their definitions would not be true—which is impossible, as Rule B testifies.

### To the 16th question.
<margin>c t c d</margin>
<margin>To the 16th question.</margin>
When it is asked: what is great concordance and contrariety? It must be said that it is that being which places concording and contrariety-forming things in the same subject, generating and corrupting within the element. For example, fire and earth have concordance through generation with air, as air is hot and dry, receiving dryness from the earth and giving heat to the air. Through the third species of Rule D, it is dominant over dryness and moisture, in which it places great contrariety by corrupting. Just as we have spoken of fire, so it can be said of the other elements according to their qualities. Thus it is to be seen through the first and second species of Rules C and D, and through the definitions of magnitude, concordance, and contrariety, and by what mode the elements enter a mixture and compose a "thing made of elements" <term>elementatum: a physical body composed of the four elements</term>. Through the third species of Rule C and D, one element is the agent and patient in another. Through the fourth species of Rule C, one element has action and passion in another, and also motion, by generating and corrupting.

<column-break/>

### To the 17th question.
<margin>d t b c</margin>
<margin>To the 17th question.</margin>
When it is asked: from what does the difference of the concordance of eternity arise? It must be answered that it is from nature and relation. For difference posits things that are distinct and naturally related through a "distinguisher," a "distinguished," and "to distinguish" in eternal concordance. According to its definition, this concordance posits a "concordant," a "concorded," and "to concord," and one essence and nature. In this, eternity posits an "eternizer," an "eternized," and "to eternize" by reason of its definition. This is manifest through Rule B and through the first and second species of Rules C and D. The third species of Rule C posits action and passion without matter. The fourth species of the same rule posits eternal natural acts. To this, the third species of Rule D cannot contradict, because it is separate from the primary acts of differing and concording.

On the doctrine of this art.

¶ The doctrine of this art is that the explicit terms which are in the question should be taken: as when it is said "whether the world be eternal." In that question is "eternity," which is an explicit term since it is in the first figure. And through eternity, D is required <note>In the Great Art, 'D' often represents Eternity or Duration.</note>, and through D the terms signified by D itself are acquired. And the scale which is in the angle of D, namely contrariety, which is between the sensual and the sensual: and between the sensual and the intellectual: and between the intellectual and the intellectual. ¶ Likewise, through "whether" <note>original: "utrum"</note>, B is acquired, and through B those things which exist under it are acquired: as is clear in the Alphabet. And since we wish to apply C in the question, it being implied in the question, whatever C contains is acquired. ¶ And thus the doctrine is given for applying the first column: for solving the aforesaid question, for finding the explicit and implied terms, applying them to the proposition: namely to the solution of the question in such a way that the definitions of the principles and the rules remain unharmed: helping oneself with the species of other rules: to give the doctrine of how a man can help himself with others. ->Fifth Part.<-

<margin>Question 1 regarding chamber B.C.D.</margin>
When it is asked whether the world is eternal: we say through B.C.D. that it is not. For if it were eternal, its <term>reason</term><note>Latin: ratio; here meaning the underlying principle or logic of its existence</note> would be from eternity producing an eternal good: and <term>greatness</term><note>Latin: magnitudo; one of the divine dignities in this system</note> would magnify that good reason from eternity and in eternity, as is evident through its definition: and eternity would cause that production to endure from eternity and in eternity. And thus no evil would be in the world, because good and evil are contraries: but evil is in the world, as is evident through experience. It is concluded, therefore, that the world is not eternal. ¶ Furthermore, rule B. posits that the negative side of the question must be held according to the definitions mentioned above, and according to what we propose to say through rule C.D. by saying thus: if the world is eternal, its eternity causes as much duration of malice as duration of good. This is evident through the first species of rule C. and through the first species of rule D.: evil would be as <term>primordial</term><note>Latin: primitiuum; meaning original or first-principle</note> as good. For no day would be primordial nor last. And through the second species of rule C. and D., the world would indeed be composed of good and evil from eternity and in eternity. And through the third species of rule C., the world is infinite in eternity, and finite in goodness and malice. And through the fourth species of rule C., it has rest in things that can be generated and corrupted: in generable things by reason of good, and in corruptible things by reason of evil. And through the second species of rule D., divine eternity and its goodness would necessitate evil and rest by causing the eternity of the world. And since all these things are impossible, it is clear that the negative side of the question must be held.

### Regarding chamber B.C.T.B.

<margin>Question 2 regarding chamber B.C.T.B.</margin>
If the world is eternal, there are two different eternities: namely, the eternity of God and the eternity of the world. And thus the <term>difference</term><note>Latin: differentia; another of the author's fundamental principles</note> which exists between the sensual and the sensual, between the sensual and the intellectual, and between the intellectual and the intellectual, would posit three different general eternities. And goodness would posit them as good, and greatness as great: but this is false and impossible: because difference posits them as evil in a certain respect, and thus the greatness of goodness fails. And consequently, the goodness of greatness posits confusion: which is impos-
<column-break/>
sible. It is concluded, therefore, that the negative side of the question must be held.

### Regarding chamber B.C.T.C.

<margin>Question 3 regarding chamber B.C.T.C.</margin>
If the world is eternal, the innate <term>concordance</term><note>Latin: concordantia; the principle of harmony or agreement</note> which is of the essence of the world between the sensual and the sensual, etc., is eternal: and thus there are three subordinate general concordances and three eternities with greatness of goodness and eternity: and with the eternal duration of greatness and goodness: which is false and impossible, because there are three subordinate <term>contrarieties</term><note>Latin: contrarietas; the principle of opposition</note> opposite to them with greatness of malice and eternity. ¶ Furthermore, through rule B. and through what we said of the definitions, the negation must be held: and this same thing is evident through the first species of rule C. and D. since the most general concordance, through its scale, posits that the eternity of God and the eternity of the world concord in one good with greatness, which is false: because great and eternal contrariety prevents this. ¶ Likewise, regarding the same, the second species of rule C. and D. posits that if the world is eternal, then a good, great, and eternal concordance encompasses the entire essence of the world, separated from all contrariety, which is false. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species of rule C., assuming the world were eternal, the essence of the world would be eternal with the greatness of eternity, which is false: since in the world there is corruption and guilt, which are the effects of greatness and contrariety and malice. ¶ To the same point, through the fourth species of rule C., concordance has great goodness and eternity in the subject in which it exists, which is false: since the subject is habituated with great malice and eternity through contrariety. ¶ To the same point, through the third species of rule D., it is signified that the world is eternal: and it is as much subject to malice as to goodness: which is not to be said: as is manifest through divine eternity, which is the first cause with great concordance of goodness, duration of reason, etc.

### On Chamber B.D.T.B.

<margin>Question 5: On chamber B.D.T.B.</margin>
Supposing that the world were eternal, the difference <note>original: "differentia"</note> which exists between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, etc., posits that there are three eternal things, good and eternal, in which goodness is the reason producing an unconfused and eternal good, which is false and unthinkable. If it is posited that the world is not eternal, the difference that existed between the sensible and the intellectual—and likewise for other deceased men—can indeed be led back into eternity through the resurrection with a good and eternal habit given by God through merit. ¶ Likewise, Rule B affirms this same thing, as does the first species of Rule C, for God is a being rewarding into eternity. Furthermore, the first species of Rule D says that the eternity of God is simply primary through an eternity differing from all time. ### Concerning Chamber B.T.B.C.

<margin>Question 8: concerning chamber B.T.B.C.</margin>
If the world is not eternal, the goodness and the difference existing between the sensual and the intellectual <note>Refers to the physical senses versus the human intellect</note> etc., can have a concordance in eternal time <note>original: "euo eterno"</note>. But if it is from eternity, by no means: since there would never have been a first man, nor will there be a last. And thus the world is a confused subject in which moral goodness would not have concordance from eternity; nor would concordance within it have its own definition: which is evident through the everlasting corruption, privation, and guilt, which is against the first rule. And through the first type of Rule C, the world is a subject in which goodness has neither concordance nor rest. And through the first type of Rule D, goodness, difference, and concordance are primitive forms and innate, yet separated from perfection; and the world is confused through the second type of Rule D. And through the second type of Rule C, it has innate: the *confusing*, the *confusable*, and the *act of confusing*. By the third type of Rule D, however, there is some dominating being that renders the world confused. Furthermore, through the third type of Rule C, the first cause of the world is evil, having dominion within the world itself. And this is by reason of the fourth type of Rule C, which is impossible: therefore it is concluded that the world is not eternal.

### Concerning Chamber B.T.B.D.

To the same point, the first type of Rule C posits that if the world is eternal, then contrariety is an impediment to every good divided through the sensual and the sensual, etc. And eternal goodness is indeed a being perfecting the scale existing between the sensual and the sensual, etc. And the difference existing between the sensual and the sensual is a being distinguishing between good and evil. And again, through the second type of Rule D: the world is composed of primitive contrarieties that are both good and different. Which is indeed false and manifest through the first type of Rule D. Through the second type of Rule C, and the third type of the same rule, and the third type of Rule D, it is clear that the world is subject to its innate parts. Furthermore, through the third type of Rule C, it exists in its innate corruptible parts, while having an eternal habit <note>A "habit" or "habitus" in medieval logic refers to a stable quality or state of being</note> by reason of the fourth type of rule. And since all these things are impossible: therefore, etc.

### Concerning Chamber B.T.C.D.

### On Chamber C. D. T. B.

<margin>Question 11. Regarding chamber C. D. T. B.</margin>
Assuming that the world is eternal, it is asked: what is the great difference of its eternity through the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc.? <note>The "scale of the sensual" refers to the ladder of being or the relationship between physical objects perceived by the senses.</note> And it must be answered that it is that essence which places a distinct eternity between one sensual thing and another through the "eternizer," the "eternized," and the act of "eternizing" <note>original: "eternantē/ eternatum ꝛ eternare." This is Lullian terminology where a principle is divided into its active, passive, and verbal components to show its internal function.</note>: which is impossible. For those things capable of being generated would then be incorruptible, which is contrary to their own definitions. Rule B regarding the aforesaid also bears witness in the negative. Furthermore, the first species of Rule C posits and agrees that the aforementioned definition is false and impossible. ¶ Moreover, the first species of Rule D affirms that the primary things are corruptions and incorruptions: great through "Greatness," eternal through "Eternity," and different or clear through "Difference." ¶ Likewise, the second species of C and D posit that the world is composed of these very things. ¶ Furthermore, the third species of Rule C says that the world is incorruptible in the heavens and corruptible in elemental things, with the world having an incorruptible nature by reason of the fourth species of Rule C; and it is eternally incorruptible with a great difference, which is a contradiction, and also against the third species of Rule D; therefore, etc.

### On Chamber C. D. T. C.

<margin>Question 12. Regarding chamber C. D. T. C.</margin>
If the world is eternal: it is asked, what is the great concordance of its eternity? And it must be answered through the definitions of Greatness, Concordance, and Eternity, and through the second species of Rule C: that it is a being having within itself the innate "eternizer," "eternized," and "eternizing." ¶ Furthermore, through the second species of Rule C and the first and second species of Rule D: that it consists of these things with all contrariety removed; and that it has through Greatness such extensiveness just as it has through Eternity an infinite duration according to the fourth species of Rule C; and through the third species, that it exists in infinite greatness just as in eternity, separated from the third species of Rule D: which is false, as is evident through the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc.

### On Chamber C. D. T. D.

<margin>Question 13. Regarding chamber C. D. T. D.</margin>
Granted that the world is eternal: it is asked, what is the great contrariety of Greatness and Eternity? And it must be answered through the first species of Rule C: that it is an infinite resistance between divine Greatness and Eternity. And to this the first species of Rule D bears witness, for divine Eternity causes an infinite duration similar to itself, but Greatness causes the finite greatness of the heaven, dissimilar to itself. And through the third species of Rule D, the Greatness of God is hindered in its effect of acting, but Eternity is not at all. Whence it follows by accident that there is a great and eternal contrariety between divine Eternity and Greatness through the second species of Rule C and D. Whence it follows that the Greatness of God is contrary in His Eternity and vice versa. And it also appears that divine Eternity has a higher power and vigor than His Greatness: which is false and impossible; and this is proved through Rule B and the definitions of Greatness, Goodness, and Eternity. Therefore, etc.

Therefore, etc.

### Concerning Chamber C. T. C. D.

<margin>Question 16. Concerning chamber C. T. C. D.</margin>
**P**ositing that the world is eternal, it is asked: what is the great distance existing between its great concordance and contrariety? <note>Concordance and contrariety are two of Lull's "General Principles"; the former represents harmony/agreement and the latter represents opposition.</note> It must be answered through the first species of rule C and D that it is that form which causes contradiction: which appears through the eternal scale existing between the sensual and the sensual, etc., because it joins itself in eternity, which is a simple principle in which things are composed through the second species of rule C and D. And one principle is indeed subject to another through the third species of rule D. And the second and third species of rule C posit a great and eternal distance: since concordance and contrariety are opposites in a subject, one having in the other a contrary nature through the fourth species of rule C. And because the eternity of the world posits for itself a coessential contradiction—which contradiction can by no means exist—it is therefore concluded that the world is not eternal.

### Concerning Chamber D. T. B. C.

<margin>Question 17. Concerning chamber D. T. B. C.</margin>
**P**ositing that the world is eternal: it is asked, from what is its eternity derived? It must be answered through the first species of C and D that it is from the primitive infinite and finite differences and concordances sustained in the scale of the sensual and the sensual, etc. Eternity, indeed, as to its genus, is the infinite duration of difference and concordance which are in the scale according to their genus: and they are finite in extension, quantity, as well as habit and position: and in eternity they are eternal. Whence it follows through the second species of rule C and D that the world is composed of infinite and finite parts, with eternity having dominion through the fourth species of rule C and through all other innate parts which are finite. Furthermore, it has subjugation through the third species of rule D, which is false and impossible; and it is also proven through the rules of B and through the definitions of the aforementioned principles. Therefore, etc.

### Concerning Chamber D. T. B. D.

<margin>Question 18. Concerning chamber D. T. B. D.</margin>

And it is also manifest through rule B and through the definitions of the principles. Therefore, etc.

And it must be answered through the first species of rule D that they are from themselves: and through the first species of rule C, eternity is a being composed of contraries: which is evident through the second species of rule C and D, it having in itself the concorder, the contrarier, and the eternizer; and the concorded, the contraried, and the eternized; and the acts of concording, contrariating, and eternizing: <note>Lull often uses these active/passive/verbal triads (e.g., "eternizer, eternized, eternizing") to describe the internal mechanics of a principle.</note> which is indeed to posit an opposite in the object. It is concluded, therefore, quite clearly, that the world is not eternal.

# Sixth principal part: On the evacuation of the third figure.

<column-break/>

<margin>Heading of the sixth part. 79</margin>
**T**he third figure is divided into thirty-six chambers <note>original: "cameras," referring to the cells in a combinatorial grid</note> as is evident in the figure itself: and in each chamber are implied twelve propositions and twenty-four questions and 
<margin>What it means to "evacuate."</margin>
their solutions. ¶ And we use the term "to evacuate" when we extract the propositions, questions, and their solutions: and we lead the doctrine from implication to explication, providing the artifice and practice of this art. For just as we solve questions here with the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules, so can the practitioner of this art solve "foreign" questions <note>questions from outside this specific system</note> with them, provided however that the practitioner knows the meaning of the names.

### Concerning chamber B. C. 102

<margin>The first chamber is B. C.</margin>
**I**n this chamber, we will first make propositions by changing the subject into the predicate: then we will make questions. And just as we shall exemplify with the twelve propositions of chamber B. C., so it can be exemplified with the other chambers contained in this third figure. And afterward, we will provide solutions by proving through three propositions in each chamber. And just as we give an example of those, so it can be given for other propositions contained in the same chambers. ¶ Regarding the first, it must be said thus: It should be known that in the third figure, the intellect "evacuates" the chambers because it abstracts from them as much as it can, receiving from each chamber those things which the letters signify, and applies those significations to the purpose at hand. And thus the intellect makes itself applicative, investigative, and inventive. And of this we shall give an example from one chamber containing the twelve aforementioned propositions. And as it follows for that one, so it will follow for the others. And it is thus: From 
<margin>Twelve propositions of the 3rd figure.</margin>

Magnitude is good; magnitude is different; magnitude is accordant. Difference is good; difference is great; difference is accordant. ### Concerning the chamber B. D.

<margin>Second chamber B. D.</margin> Goodness is enduring. Is goodness enduring? # On the evacuation of the third figure.

The destruction of the whole follows from the destruction of the parts. And this is signified through rule B, and also through rule G. <note>In Lullian logic, the "rules" refer to specific questions: B is "Whether?", G is "How?" or "By what?".</note>

And it must be answered that it is: for goodness is more good through substance than through accident <note>term: accident <gloss>a non-essential quality, like color or shape, as opposed to the core essence or substance</gloss></note>; and through substantial relations rather than minor and accidental ones. And goodness is greater in one subject than in another, just as in the scale of the sensual and the sensual, and in the scale of majority existing between substance and substance, etc. ¶ How is goodness virtuous? And it must be answered that it is virtuous then when it is its own being; but morally it is virtuous then when it is habituated by the habit of justice and prudence, etc. And this is demonstrated through the definitions of goodness, virtue, majority, and difference: and through rule B. ¶ When is goodness differentiable? It must be answered: then when it is its own being. And this is through the difference which posits real relations without which it cannot have its nature. And also it is differentiable then when it is moral. For one habit is through justice; another truly through prudence, etc. And it is proved through the definitions of the aforementioned principles. ¶ When is goodness greater? And it must be answered that it is then when it is substantially and not [merely] morally. Furthermore, it is greater then when it is habituated by moral virtue existing in practice, than when it is not in practice. Further, it is greater when it acts with charity than when with justice. And thus that same judgment applies to substantial acting and accidental acting. And this is indeed provable through rule B.

# Part Six

<margin>How</margin>
It must be understood that just as it is evident in the scale of the senses <note>original: "scala sensuali"</note> and the scale of substances, and so forth. Goodness is indeed lesser in a stone than in a plant; and in a plant it is lesser than in a brute animal; and in a color it is lesser than in the act of seeing; and in seeing it is lesser than in understanding, and so with others. And this is affirmable through the rule of B. K. <note>Llull uses letters to represent specific principles and logical rules in his system.</note> ¶ In what way is glorious Goodness? It must be answered that glorious Goodness has its mode through "Difference," which posits that it is a single substantial essence distinct from all others: and that it has different substantial things which are of its own genus and nature, with which it has an intrinsic nature placed in rest. And this is indeed glorious to it, while it exists in glory, and glory exists in Goodness itself. It also has a moral mode in causing distinct, good, and glorious moral habits. And to this, the rules of B. K. bear witness. ¶ With what is Goodness <margin>With what</margin> different? It must be answered that it is different through itself, and with the "Difference" which posits that the essence itself is distinct from all other essences that are not of its species and nature. And there is another mode with which Goodness is different: namely, with its relatives which are co-essential and substantial to it, with which it causes accidental goodnesses. And this is signified in the scale of the senses and the scale of substances, and so forth.

### Concerning Chamber C. D.

<margin>What is eternal Greatness?</margin>
<margin>The ninth chamber, which is C. D.</margin>
Greatness is eternal. What is eternal Greatness? It must be answered through the definitions of Greatness, Eternity, Concordance, and Contrariety, by saying this: Eternal Magnification is a being having in itself—through the first and second species of rule C. D.—concrete things that are great, infinite, eternal, and primitive. And through the third species of rule C. D., the said concrete things exist with an infinite greatness of Concordance and also Contrariety, and are separated from all subjection, with each concrete thing existing in another concrete thing. ¶ Indeed, the whole essence of Eternity exists in each of the aforesaid concrete things; and similarly the whole being of Concordance; and each has its own distinct number from the other in the other, the three concrete things existing as one essence and not as many. ¶ What is <margin>What is it?</margin> Great Concordance? Great Concordance is that essence which stands through the second species of rule C. D., and through the third species of rule C. is in another as the whole essence of Concordance, and every concrete part of Concordance is the whole essence of Concordance. And it is also the mistress of all other accidental or foreign concordances. ¶ What is Great Contrariety? It must be answered that it is that form which causes corruptions in elevated things, and causes habits of privation: namely, injustice, lust, etc. ¶ It is asked: eternal Greatness, concordant Greatness, and contrary Greatness—from what do they come? <margin>di. g. o.</margin> And it must be answered through what was said above, as is clear to one who looks closely. ¶ And we do it in this way for the sake of brevity, and so that boredom is not generated in the intellect of the learner because of repetition.

<margin>Great Power</margin>

What is Great Power? It must be answered that it is a being in which Greatness and Power are convertible <note>In Llull's logic, "convertible" means the terms are interchangeable in their scope and essence.</note>. And this is signified through the first species of rule C. And through the second species of rule C. E., it is Great Power because it has formal and co-essential concrete things: namely, the Magnifier, <margin> -ing, -ed, -to </margin> the Magnified, the Power-maker, the Power-made, and the acts of Magnifying and Power-making <note>original: "magnificantem, magnificatum, possificatum, magnificare, possificare." Through the third species of rule C, it is in other essences so that through it they are able to exist and act. Through the fourth, however, it has actions and passions of acting and being acted upon in an appropriate subject. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species of rule E, Great Power exists so that all things other than itself are magnificently possible; and this is proved through the definition of Greatness and Power. ¶ Greatness is concordant. What <margin>What is Great Concordance?</margin> is Great Concordance? It must be answered through what was said in chamber C. D. Greatness is a Great Principle. What is a Great Principle? To which it must be said that it is a being in which Greatness and Principle are convertible without any matter or accident. And this is signified through the second species of rule C and the first of E. But the Magnifying <margin> -ing, -ed, -to </margin> Principle exists so that there may be a Magnified Principled-thing, and that from both may proceed the act of Magnifying and the act of Principiation, with the definitions of Greatness, Power, Concordance, and Principle. ¶ Great Power, Great...

Concordance and the Great Principle: why do they exist? It must be answered that they exist through that which is signified by the types of Rule C <note>Rule C refers to the third rule of Lull's Art, often dealing with "Why?" or "How?"</note> and through the definitions of the aforementioned principles.

### 11 On the chamber C. F.

<margin>Great intellect</margin>
<margin>The eleventh chamber, which is concerning C. F.</margin>
Great intellect exists. What is great intellect? It must be answered that it is a being in which Greatness and Intellect meet. And this is signified by the first type of Rule C. Furthermore, the greatness of the intellect is that it possesses concrete things co-essential and relative to itself: namely, the **one who understands**, the **thing understood**, and the **act of understanding** <note>original: "intelligentem/intelligibile/& intelligere"</note>; with these it possesses a discerning nature, and its essence is continuous and indivisible. And this is signified by the second type of Rule C. Moreover, the greatness of the intellect is such that all things capable of being understood are within its essence; and this is signified by the third type of Rule C, so that the intellect itself may be magnificently practical. Furthermore, through the fourth type, the intellect is such that it has a general relation to all things, like an intellect that understands "this" and "that"; and that it has an "understandable" in which it understands this and that; and with these it is practical, particular, and successive, both through the defensive and sensual scale, etc., and through the scale of the medium of conjunction, etc. What is Great Concordance? It must be answered by that which was said in chamber C. D. Greatness is a mediating force. What is a Great Medium? To which it must be answered through the scale of the medium and the scale of concordance, and through the first and second types of Rule C. F. For without these, a great medium could not exist at all; and also without such a medium, greatness would be empty and idle; and similarly, without such greatness, the medium could not be great. And that what has been said is true is proven indeed by the definitions of the principles and the types of rules, and also by the successive scales of ascending and descending, by which sciences are acquired and made into habits. It is asked: How great is the greatness of the intellect, and how great is its concordance, and likewise for its medium? And it must be said that it is as great as it has been signified. However, regarding what has been said of its greatness, concordance, and medium in the paragraphs placed in chamber C. F., we leave this to the man who well contemplates the aforementioned things and who knows this Art. And we do this for the sake of brevity.

<column-break/>

### 12 On the chamber C. G.

<margin>What is Great Will</margin>
<margin>The twelfth chamber, which is concerning C. G.</margin>
What is Great Will? Through the first type of Rule C, it must be answered: that it is a being in which all great things are lovable; and through the second type of Rule C and the first type of G, it possesses a great **lover**, a **beloved**, and the **act of loving** <note>original: "amantem/amatū & amare"</note> formally; in which beloved, it is formally active with the act of loving. And through the fourth type, it has all lovable things within itself. And through the second type of G, it causes appropriate lovable habits of the genus of Quality. And it is probable enough through the definition of Greatness, Will, Concordance, and also the End; and through the scales of C. G. placed in the second figure. What is Great Concordance? It must be answered by that which was said above concerning it. What is a Great End? It must be answered through the first type of Rule C that a Great End is that being which, in the essence of greatness, has its own proper relations: namely, the **one resting**, the **thing rested in**, and the **act of resting** <note>original: "qētātem/quietatum & quietare"</note>; in which, from its own intrinsic rest, all things capable of rest—whether foreign or appropriate—are set at rest. And this is signified through the first and second types of Rule C, and also through the definitions of the principles of chamber C. G. What kind of will is great, and what kind of concordance, and what kind of end? To this question, it must be answered by what was said above. For the solutions are implied in what was said above, and they can be skillfully explained for the purpose at hand.

Furthermore, through the second type: Great Virtue is that which has within itself virtuous relations—the **one magnifying**, the **thing magnified**, and the **act of magnifying** <note>original: "magnificantem/magnificatū & magnificare"</note>—naturally and substantially related outside itself and existing within itself. ### 14 Concerning Chamber C. I.

Greatness is true. What is true greatness? It must be answered that it is that substance which is most distant from falsehood and from accident; it possesses, through the second species of Rule C, true things / the magnified / the magnifiable / the act of magnifying / existing outside of place and in place infinitely, without contradiction. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species, it is the cause causing true greatnesses existing in place and not false ones, both substantial and accidental. ¶ Moreover, through the fourth species, it has great and true actions in every new subject. And this is proven through the definitions of the principles of Chamber C. I., as through the rules. ¶ What is great concordance? It must be answered as before: but if it is asked what is "greater concordance"? It must be answered that it is a greater substance having in itself substantial and greater relations, removed from all accidents. ¶ There is great equality. What is great equality? It must be answered that it is an instance <note>original: "iustantia," likely a scribal error for "substantia" (substance) or "instantia" (presence)</note> having within itself its relatives, segregated from all majority and minority. Furthermore, through the second species, it is the cause of all related majorities and minorities, existing itself in a place without being confined, and infinite outside of place. Furthermore, through the fourth species, it has in place whatever it wills. And this is probable through the rule and through the definitions of the principles of Chamber C. I. ¶ Where are great virtue, great concordance, and great equality? It must be answered that they are in themselves through the second species of Rule C.
