Great glory: it is asked, what is it? It must be answered that it is that substance which is most distant from depravity and punishment; and it is a being having within itself, through the second species of Rule C, the glorious / the magnifying / the magnified / and the act of magnifying. Through the third species, it is the cause in all foreign substances and accidents. And through the fourth species, it has great glory in the great glorified one, and vice versa. And likewise for magnifying and glorifying. And this is affirmable through the rules of C. K. and the definitions of the principles of Chamber C. K. ¶ What is great concordance? It must be answered as before. But if it is asked: what is the great concordance of glory? It must be answered through all four species of Rule C that it is that which is signified through them. And to this, the definitions of the greatness of concordance and of glory bear witness. ¶ What is great minority? And it must be answered that it is an accident closer to non-being than to substance. Likewise, it is a being not having relatives co-essential to itself through the second species of Rule C. But through accident, there are nevertheless some substantial greatnesses, as is evident in the <term>sensual scale</term> <note>The "scala sensualis" refers to the ladder of being perceptible to the senses (animals, plants, etc.)</note> etc., joined to the scale of substance and substance, etc. And this is proven through the rules of C. K. and through the definition of minority. ¶ How is great glory? And likewise for great concordance? It must be answered through the third species of Rule C, with the relations themselves existing one in another by magnifying, glorifying, and concording, segregated from all minority. ¶ With what is great glory? And likewise for great concordance? It must be answered that it is with the magnifying / glorifying / and concording; the magnified / glorified / and concorded; the act of magnifying / glorifying / and concording; and also with the <unclear>turning</unclear> of identity of essence, substance, and nature, with these three relatives through the second species of Rule C, and each one distinct from the other by its own number. ¶ Furthermore, there is great glory, and likewise great concordance, with the sensual scale, etc., and similarly with the substantial scale, etc. But this is not as great as the first, because the first is the cause, while the other is the second <note>i.e., the secondary effect</note>.

The text uses a combinatorial method where letters (D, F, G, H, I) represent fundamental principles like Duration, Power, Wisdom, and Will. The "evacuation" of the chambers refers to the process of exhausting all logical questions (What? Of what? Why? How much?) for each combination.</meta>

# On the evacuation of the third figure.

Of what?
The seventeenth chamber, which is D. F.
</margin>

Powerful duration, according to the first species of rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "What is it?" or "Of what is it?" in Llull's system</note>, of what is it? It must be answered: that it is of itself, since it is primitive in regard to its own essence and power, which gives it the ability to exist and act. And through the second species of rule D, it is asked: of what things is powerful duration composed? It must be answered: it is of its own relatives <note>term: relatives (relativa). In Lullian logic, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, e.g., the endurer, the endurable, and the act of enduring.</note> and of the relatives of power. And through the third species of the same rule, it is asked: to whom does powerful duration belong? It must be said that it is substantial to duration and power, since it is the habit <note>term: habit (habitus). A stable disposition or quality.</note> by which substantial duration and power are able to endure. ¶ Of what is the duration of contrariety? It must be answered that it is of the primitive qualities, truths, and vices which endure because they are able to endure. ¶ Of what is the duration of principles? It must be said: it is of the primitive durations and primitive principles, with duration communicating its essence to the principle, and the principle communicating its essence to duration. ¶ Why does power endure? It must be answered: it endures because it is of the powerful, the enduring, the durable, and the possibility of enduring, and of the power within the composite subject in which they exist. ¶ Why does the contrariety of power endure? It must be said: because it is of the habitualized contrary relatives, and of the duration and power in the composite subject in which they exist. ¶ Why do the principles of power endure? It must be said: they endure by reason of the habitualized substantial relatives of the genus of duration and power.

It must be answered: it is as great as its essence is, and as its concrete parts are. ¶ How great is the duration of contrariety? It must be answered: it is as great as the contrarieties or moralities are in the subject in which they exist. ¶ How great is the duration of the mean <note>term: mean (medium). The middle point or mediating force between extremes.</note>? re. <note>Syllable carried over from the previous page.</note> ¶ Where is the duration of truth? It must be answered that it is in all species <note>original: "speciebus"</note> of the first type. ¶ Where is the duration of contrariety? It must be said that it is in the subject in which there are contrary qualities having contrary acts. And it is in a disputation in which there are debaters. ¶ Where is the duration of equality? It must be answered that it is in correlatives signified by the second species of the letter "C" and "D". And it is in modality and instrumentality.

### 21 Concerning the chamber of D. K.

<margin>The twenty-first chamber concerning D. K.</margin>
<margin>The duration of glory, about which it is argued: whether, in what way</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
Duration is capable of glory. ¶ Concerning what is the duration of glory? It must be answered that it concerns the enduring/durable and the act of enduring; and the glorifying/glorifiable and the act of glorifying. ¶ Concerning what is the duration of contrariety? It must be said just as was stated before. ¶ Concerning what is the duration of minority? It must be answered that it concerns the enduring/minorifying/durable/minorifiable and the acts of enduring and minorifying. ¶ In what way is the duration of glory? It must be said that it is by the mode through which duration and glory act upon the durable and the glorifiable, with these active principles entering into them; and the durable and the glorifiable have a passive mode under duration and glory. Enduring and glorifying have a neutral mode proceeding from the active and passive. ¶ In what way is the duration of contrariety? It must be answered that it is by the mode which qualities have when one exists in another. ¶ In what way is the duration of minority? It must be answered that it is by the mode of duration, division, and corruption. ¶ With what is the duration of glory? It must be said that it is with the relatives of duration and glory. ¶ With what is the duration of contrariety? It must be said that it is with the contrary parts influencing their own likenesses. ¶ With what is the duration of minority? It must be answered that it is with the relatives of division in a subject habituated toward corruption.

### 22 Concerning the chamber of E. F.

<margin>Power</margin>
<margin>The twenty-second chamber concerning E. F.</margin>
<margin>Why</margin>
Power is knowable. Why is power knowable? It must be answered that it is because the intellect has its own correlatives, and power likewise; and thus, with one principle communicating its essence and nature to the other, it follows that power is knowable. ¶ It is asked: why is power a principle? It must be said that it is for this purpose: so that other principles may be able to exist and act. ¶ It is asked: why is it <term>mediable|the quality of being or having a middle</term>? It must be answered: so that its "being able" <note>original: "posse"</note> may be in the middle of the one who is powerful and that which is placed, with which "being able" they are joined. ¶ Wisdom is powerful: how much is it powerful? To which it must be said that it is as powerful as the power communicates and diffuses itself within it. ¶ How much is the principle? It must be answered that it is as much as the "middle" enters into it. ¶ It is asked: how much is the middle? It must be said that it is as much as its species are in the subject in which they exist.

<margin>How much</margin>

### 23 Concerning the chamber of E. G.

<margin>The twenty-third chamber concerning E. G.</margin>
<margin>Of what kind</margin>
Power is lovable. Why is it lovable? It must be said that it is because it causes the will to be powerful in existing and acting. ¶ Why is power a principle? It must be answered as before. ¶ Why does power rest? It must be answered that it is because, according to its genus, it can exist and act. ¶ Of what kind is power? It must be said that one kind is proper, such as its possibility; the other is appropriated, such as its lovability. ¶ Of what kind is a principle? It must be answered that one kind of principle is substantial, while the other is accidental; and the substantial is habituated by the accidental. ¶ Of what kind is the end? It must be answered that one end is perfective, another is terminative, and another is privative, as is evident in the "ladder" of the second figure. <note>Refers to Llull's mnemonic diagrams.</note>

### 24 Concerning the chamber of E. H.

<margin>The twenty-fourth chamber concerning E. H.</margin>
<margin>When</margin>
Power is virtuous. Why is it virtuous? It must be said that it is because it is situated in virtue and habituated by virtue. ¶ Power is greater. Why is it greater? It must be said that it is because it has greater relations and rests in a greater faith. ¶ Why is power in time? It must be said because it was created in time and with time, and its act is in time. ¶ When is power? It must be said that it is then, when it is the cause so that other principles can exist and act. ¶ When is the principle? It must be said that it is then, when its "primitivity" <note>The state of being first.</note> is present, and when it has its correlatives, etc. ¶ When is majority? It must be said that it is then, when powers have greater acts or effects.

<margin>The twenty-fifth chamber is E.I.</margin>
### 25 On chamber E.I. <note>E represents Power; I represents Truth.</note>

Power is true. Why is it true? It must be said because it is habituated <note>In scholastic philosophy, "habituated" refers to a stable quality or disposition of being.</note> by Truth and its species. ¶ When and why is Power a principle? It must be said as before. ¶ Why does Power have equality? It must be answered that it has equality since it is situated within its correlatives <note>Correlatives: the internal structural components of a principle, typically the active agent, the passive recipient, and the act of the principle itself (e.g., the Powerer, the Powerable, and Powering).</note>. ¶ Where is Power? It must be said that it is in its correlatives and in the Truth by which it is habituated. ¶ Where is the Principle? It must be answered that it is in its correlatives; and it is in Power, since through Power it is able to exist and act. And it is in Truth, because it is habituated in Truth. And it is in Equality, since its correlatives are equal. ¶ Where is Equality? It must be said that it is in the intrinsic correlatives of Power, Principle, and Truth.

<margin>The twenty-sixth chamber, which is E.K.</margin>
<margin>why</margin>
<margin>how</margin>
### 26 On chamber E.K. <note>E represents Power; K represents Glory or Minoritas (Smallness/Lesser), depending on the specific Lullian alphabet used here.</note>

Power is glorious. It asks why it is glorious: It must be answered, because it has its substantial correlatives in which glory is impressed and habituated. ¶ Why is Power a principle? It must be answered as before. ¶ Why is Power "lesser" <term>minoritas: the principle of Smallness or being lesser</term>? It must be said because its correlatives are situated in "lesser-ness," and are habituated by it, by reason of which it causes divisions and the "less" which belongs to the genus of minority, just as the "greater" belongs to the genus of majority. ¶ How is Power? It must be answered that it is by way of modality, when it is habituated by modality. ¶ How is the Principle? It must be answered that it is by the mode which it has in its correlatives from which it exists, having that mode since it is habituated by the Power with which it can act as a principle. And likewise concerning Glory, with which it has a mode of glorying, when in its intrinsic "principle-able" <note>The passive aspect of a principle</note> it originates foreign beings that are not of its own genus. ¶ How is Minority? It must be answered that its mode is to participate in division, emptying, corruption, and nullification. ¶ With what is Power glorious? It must be said that it is glorious with Glory, just as Glory is powerful with Power. ¶ With what is the Principle? It must be said that it is with its correlatives and with Power, without which it cannot be. ¶ With what is Minority? It must be said that it is with division, corruption, and emptying.

<column-break/>

<margin>The twenty-seventh chamber, which is F.G.</margin>
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
<margin>how much</margin>
<margin>of what kind</margin>
### 27 On chamber F.G. <note>F represents Wisdom/Intellect; G represents Will/Virtue.</note>

Wisdom is lovable. It asks how much it is lovable: It must be answered that it is as purely lovable as the Will is "knowable," because it has equal correlatives. ¶ The Medium <note>The "Middle" or "Mean" between extremes.</note> is lovable. It asks how much it is lovable: It must be said that it is as much lovable as there is loving in the Will through joining and measuring. ¶ The End <note>The "Final" or "Purpose."</note> is knowable: It must be answered that it is as much knowable as Knowledge is able to rest in the End. ¶ It is asked what kind of "knowability" is the proper passion <note>A "passion" in this sense is a characteristic property or attribute.</note> of the Intellect: It must be said that it is that through which the Intellect has an intrinsic passion in which are born "intelligibilities" or foreign species, these being placed in the genus of intelligibility through the second species of G. ¶ What kind is the proper Medium? It must be answered that it is the "mediatable" in which there are foreign or appropriated "mediatabilities." ¶ It is asked what is the proper End of the Intellect: It must be said that it is the thing understood, quieted in its own intelligibility.

<margin>The twenty-eighth chamber, which is F.H.</margin>
<margin>when</margin>
### 28 On chamber F.H. <note>F represents Intellect; H represents Virtue/Greatness.</note>

The Intellect is virtuous. It asks how much it is virtuous: It must be said that it is as much as it is habituated by virtue. ¶ The Medium is virtuous: It must be said that it is as much as its scale <note>original: "scala"</note> is habituated by the medium. ¶ How great is the Greatness of the Intellect? It must be answered that it is as great as the Intellect surpasses in reaching objects with a greater understanding. ¶ When is the Intellect virtuous? It must be answered that it is then when it is habituated by natural and moral virtue. ¶ When is Virtue mediated? It must be answered that it is then when Virtue enters the medium, by reason of which entry Virtue consists in the middle. ¶ When is Greatness understood? It must be said that it is then when the Intellect reaches the essence and the act of virtue.

### On the Discovery of Middle Terms

<margin>
b c d
On the discovery of middle terms.
</margin>
In chamber b.c.d. (and so with the others in their own way), "c" stands in the middle circle because it exists between "b" and "d." And because "c" is joined with "b" and with "d" through certain positions—namely, the habituations and situations existing between the subject and the predicate. When the artist <note>artist: a practitioner of Llull's "Great Art" (Ars Magna)</note> wants a middle term, he should always investigate in the middle of the circle. For just as "animal" is suited to stand as a measure and a link between "substance" and "man" when it is concluded that "man is a substance," so the letter in the middle circle must stand between the letter in the upper circle and the letter in the lower circle. For example, when one argues thus: Every c is b, and every d is c, therefore every d is b. ¶ And just as it is necessary through certain conjectures and properties that an animal be a substance and a man be an animal, so the artist of this Art must conjecture through those things which b and c signify—namely, their subordinate principles. For instance, b sounds or signifies Goodness, Difference, and "Whether." And c signifies Greatness, Concordance, and "What." And d signifies Duration, Contrariety, and "Of what." And in this sounding or signifying consist the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules with which the artist must conjecture the middle term

with the upper letter and the lower letter in its own way. ¶ And in this step, the intellect creates knowledge concerning the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative; and concerning instances, demonstration, and guidance; and also concerning the possible and the impossible. ¶ The intellect habituates itself to these five modes in this way: when it is said, "every c is d and every b is c," let it be granted by making a distinction. Such as Greatness which is good through Goodness, and Goodness which is great through Greatness. And Goodness which has "great" correlatives <note>correlatives: Llull's theory that every principle has an active, passive, and verbal form (e.g., Greatening, Greatened, and to Greaten)</note> through the second species of c signified, and Greatness which has "good" correlatives through Goodness through the second species of c signified; and so with Greatness and Duration in their own way. ¶ Furthermore, when it is said "every c is b and every d is c," there arise the universal affirmative and the universal negative; and this is by reason of the Difference subordinate in b. And in d, Contrariety is subordinate; just as when it is said: "no stone is an animal, every man is an animal, therefore no man is a stone." For the reason for this is that a stone has no sense, etc. ¶ "Every animal is a substance, some man is an animal, therefore some man is a substance." And thus: "every c is b, some d is c, therefore some d is b." The reason for this is that the Contrariety which is subordinate in d cannot be the Concordance which is subordinate in c, nor can great malice be great goodness. For if it were so, one would be placing opposites in the same object, which is impossible and against the correlatives of the second species of rule c. And when it is said "no animal is a stone, some man is an animal, therefore some man is not a stone." Just as when it is said: "no c is b, some d is c, therefore some d is not b." And it also recognizes possibilities and impossibilities. # On the multiplication of the fourth figure.

<margin>
The contraction of the first most general and particular principles.
</margin>
is g. ¶ Furthermore, the artist finds the middle term by contracting—namely, when a principle that is entirely general is drawn toward a principle that is neither entirely general nor entirely special. For example, "Difference," which is a most general principle <note>original: "generalissimum"</note>, is drawn toward the differences that exist between one sensual thing and another sensual thing, which are neither most general nor most specific. And when they are contracted to the most specific things <note>the "specialissima"</note>, such as to *this* animal or *this* plant or *this* stone—an individual being constituted from these differences substantially and also accidentally through its own quantity, quality, etc., with the individual itself placed in its own species—then those differences are the "middle" between the most general and the most specific principle. And what has been said of Difference can also be said of Goodness, etc. For Goodness is an entirely general principle. When it is contracted to Greatness, etc., then it is neither a most general nor a most specific principle. But when "Great Goodness" is contracted to *this* concrete thing constituted of that Great Goodness as to its form and matter, and also its quantity and quality, etc., so that it is placed in its own species and individuated under it: then Great Goodness (which is neither most general nor most specific) is the middle existing between the abstract and the concrete, tasting of the nature of the extremes. By this nature, the artist can find the middle term existing naturally between the major and minor proposition: and through such a middle, demonstrations are made from first, true, and necessary principles against which no objection <note>original: "instantia"</note> is found. ¶ Furthermore, he finds the middle through its own letter and its own circle: namely through **f.**, which signifies the middle, and through the middle circle, such as placing **f.** under **b.** and above **c.** which is below; considering that through **b.** one has Goodness and Difference, and through **c.** Greatness and Concordance. And thus they stand between **b.** and **c.**, by reason of which **c.** passes to **b.** through the middle; as when it is said: "Every **f.** is **b.**, and every **c.** is **f.**, therefore every **c.** is **b.**" But this pertains only to the middle genus. And as we have said in the chamber **b.f.c.**, so it can be said in the chamber **c.f.d.** and in the chamber **d.f.e.** etc. ¶ By what has been said concerning the middle, the artist can have very general material for finding many middle terms. And this is clear with the definitions of the principles and with the species of the rules.

Proof is general, and its species are: through demonstration of "the reason why" <note>original: "propter quid"</note>; through demonstration of equivalence; and through "that it is" <note>original: "quia"</note> separately. We propose to give an example through this syllogism: ¶ *Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance.* And first we will prove the major premise, then the minor. ¶ And first, through the demonstration of "the reason why" <note>propter quid</note>: an animal is constituted of the sensual and the sensual, because it is composed of elements, vegetated, sensing, and imagining. ¶ And thus it follows that it is a substance, because it is composed of substantial parts. And because "substance" is the higher term and "animal" the lower, the animal indeed has higher causes—namely, the form and matter from which it is constituted—and its parts are lower, because they are caused by the form and matter which are general principles. ¶ And thus it is truly concluded "the reason why" an animal is a substance. ¶ Through the demonstration of equivalence <note>equiparantie</note> it is proved thus: General form and general matter are equally primitive causes. And this is evident through the first species of Rule D. And because an animal is caused from its own proper form and matter, running through the elemental, vegetative, etc., these are equal principles of the animal itself; by reason of which it follows that an animal is a substance constituted of its own proper form and matter, which descend equally from equal most general principles—namely, from the first form and the first matter. This is evident through the second species of Rule D, the first of E, and through Rule B. ¶ Through the demonstration of "that it is" <note>quia</note> it is proved thus: an animal is, because it is; or rather, the causes are present—namely, the form and matter from which it exists, and without which it cannot be. And because form and matter constitute a substance, it truly follows that an animal is a substance. ¶ Now we intend to prove the minor premise through the same three species. And first, "the reason why" <note>propter quid</note>: when the embryo is constituted in the womb from the elemental, vegetative, etc., and is itself delineated and formed with human members; and when the rational soul, which is a substance, is introduced into that embryo. Then, from itself and its lower parts, it constitutes a man; and thus the animal which is an embryo is transmuted into a man through the human species in which it is placed with all its coessential parts. ¶ And thus it follows that the soul is the cause why man is a substance; and this is clear through the first species of Rule C. ¶ Through equivalence I prove it thus: The rational soul has...

# Seventh Part.

The co-essential parts are equal—namely, intellect, will, and memory—and consequently the embryo is equally constituted from the elemental, the vegetative, and so on. Because its principles are substantial, it is equally a whole man through its substantial principles joined to the rational soul with the human body. And this is clear through the rules of **b. c. d. e.** <note>These letters refer to the symbolic alphabet used in Ramon Lull's "Ars Magna" to represent specific principles or categories.</note> that man is an animal. ¶ Through <margin>through "because"</margin> demonstration, which is proven thus: Socrates is that which an animal is, without which Socrates cannot exist. The minor premise is proven through the three aforementioned species, through two of which—namely, "on account of what" <note>original: "propter quid"</note> and through "equivalence"—the most powerful conclusions are made. However, this is not done through "because" <note>original: "per quia"</note>, since the cause contains more within itself than the effect. ¶ Furthermore, just as we gave the example of man being a substance through "animal," so it can be said of a brute beast, a plant, and a stone. And thus the intellect creates knowledge by proving the major and minor premises through this Art, with which the intellect is disposed toward all conclusions, as is evident through the things already said.

### On the Knowledge of Fallacies.

<margin>How fallacies are known.</margin> The falsity of the "middle" <note>The "middle term" in a syllogism, which connects the two premises.</note> is the genus of fallacies, and the letter **f.** signifies this middle. The **f.** which is in the middle circle is the instrument for finding and knowing fallacies, by placing and turning it under the letters in the upper circle and over the letters in the lower circle, thus composing "chambers" <note>A "chamber" (camera) in Lullian logic is a specific combination of letters on the rotating wheels of the Art.</note>. For example, placing **f.** under **b.** and over **c.**, and observing how **b.** and **c.** relate to **f.** in fallacies, and vice versa. Afterward, by multiplying the revolutions, the variation of the middle in which the error lies will appear. We shall give an example of this in the fallacies.

### On the Fallacy of Equivocation.

<margin>What the fallacy of equivocation is.</margin> Equivocation is the different signification of one and the same name, which arises because one name signifies several different things. A paralogism <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> is formed thus: *Every dog is capable of barking; a celestial constellation is a dog; therefore, a celestial constellation is capable of barking.* <note>The Latin "canis" means both a literal dog and the constellation Canis Major.</note> We assign this to the chamber **b. f. c.** Through **b.**, we understand the difference between an animate body and an inanimate body. Through **f.**, we understand that an animate and inanimate body are not joined by reason of the same species. Through **c.**, we understand that an animate body has sensible correlatives, while an inanimate one does not. And thus the artist <note>The practitioner of the Lullian Art.</note> recognizes the manner in which the reasoning fails by reducing

<margin>Equivocation: one name signifying different things.</margin>

<column-break/>

it to the impossible. By reason of this knowledge, the intellect recognizes that a logician cannot stand against nature, especially by using this Art to reduce the argument to the impossible—such as a star, which is a being in which it is impossible to possess the nature of "bark-ability." ¶ Furthermore, through the chamber **d. f. e.** and others, one recognizes where the paralogism fails. For this dog, which is composed of the elemental, vegetative, and sensitive, can bark according to the second species of rule **d.**; but a star, if it does not have such correlative principles, cannot bark because it is not constituted of those principles. This is evident through the second species of rule **d.**, the first of **c.**, and also through the scale of the middle.

### On Amphibology.

<margin>What amphibology is.</margin> Amphibology <note>A fallacy resulting from ambiguous grammatical structure rather than a single word.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that a single sentence signifies several things. A paralogism is formed thus: *Whatever belongs to Aristotle is possessed by Aristotle; but this book belongs to Aristotle; therefore, it is possessed by Aristotle.* ¶ To this fallacy we assign <margin>d. f. h.</margin> the chamber **d. f. h.** Through **d.**, we know that its third species signifies that this book is not possessed by Aristotle, since it is not possessed except by a man joined with the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational powers, as is clear through the second species of rule **d.** But **f.** signifies the middle of measurement, conjunction, and continuation in the subject in which it exists. **h.**, however, signifies that the book which exists in this "now" is not possessed by Aristotle, because he is dead. And this <margin>b f g</margin> same thing can be known through the chamber **b. f. g.**, etc. For **b.** places a difference between a dead man and a living one. And **f.** places a conjunction between the sensual and the intellectual in a dead man. Not **g.**, which signifies "appropriation"—namely, that Aristotle made such a book as this, but it is not properly possessed by Aristotle because he is dead.

### On the Fallacy of Composition.

<margin>What the fallacy of composition is.</margin> The fallacy of composition is a deception arising from the potential multiplicity of a sentence whose words can be combined with one another in different ways. A paralogism is formed thus: *Whatever is possible to be white, it is possible that it is white; but it is possible for a black thing to be white; therefore, it is possible that a black thing is white.* And assign...

By **f.** we understand that white and black do not exist joined together by a medium between the extremes in color. By **e.** we understand that this is possible according to the principles from which it originates, as is clear through the first species of rule **e.** It is concluded, therefore, that it is impossible for white to be black. Through chamber **g.f.h.** etc., the deception <note>the logical error</note> is recognized. By **g.** it is signified that one accustomed to whiteness cannot, because of that habit, be accustomed to blackness. By **f.** it is known that whiteness and blackness do not join together, nor do they measure one another, nor do they even constitute a continuous medium between extremes; for if they did, one would have to grant an object in opposition. By **h.** we know that one accustomed to whiteness in this "now" <note>the present moment</note>—such as this white cloth—it is possible that he may be accustomed to blackness in another future "now."

### On the fallacy of division.

<margin>What the fallacy of division is:</margin> The fallacy of division is a deception arising from the potential multiplicity of a statement whose parts can be divided from one another. It forms a <term>paralogism</term> <note>a piece of illogical reasoning</note> thus: Every animal is either rational or irrational; but not every animal is rational; therefore every animal is irrational. To this deception, we apply chamber **c.f.g.** By **c.** we know that when one word is in one subject, with the agreement of the subject's correlative, a single meaning follows through the second and third species of rule **c.** But when it is placed in the contrary without the relatives of the subject, it varies the meaning by dividing it, as is clear by the scale **b.c.** in the second figure. By **f.** we know that the beings "rational" and "irrational" are not joined, nor do they measure themselves in the same species through a continuous medium. By **g.** we know that the property of a rational being is the ability to laugh, but not so for an irrational one. Through chamber **e.f.i.** etc., the deception is known. By **c.** and **f.** as was said above. By **i.** we know that truth does not posit in what is true that diverse things are the same; nor does equality posit that they are equal in species, nor in the same place relative to each other.

### On the fallacy of accent.

<margin>What the fallacy of accent is:</margin> The fallacy of accent is a deception arising from the fact that a word pronounced in different ways signifies different things. It forms a paralogism thus: What *populus* <note>original: "populus" with a long 'o' means poplar tree</note> is a tree? But a certain nation is a *populus* <note>original: "populus" with a short 'o' means people/nation</note>; therefore a certain nation is a tree. To this deception we apply chamber **b.f.c.** By **b.** we understand the difference between one accent and another accent; by **f.** the conjunction and measurement; and by **c.** they agree to one meaning according to the voice. *Populus* with the first syllable long signifies a tree, and with a short one, a people. Through chamber **b.f.k.** etc., the deception is recognized. For there is a contrariety between a long and short syllable. By **f.** it is understood that they are not joined nor measured in the voice when it is understood as a tree as it is when understood as a people. By **k.** the modes of accenting are understood; they do not produce a similar meaning when the syllables are mixed.

### On the fallacy of the figure of speech.

<margin>What the fallacy of the figure of speech is:</margin> The fallacy of the figure of speech is a deception arising from the fact that one word is similar to another word. It forms a paralogism thus: Whatever you saw yesterday, you see today; but yesterday you saw a white thing; therefore today you see a white thing <note>This is a classic sophism: you see the *object* today, but not necessarily its *color* if it was painted overnight</note>. To this paralogism we apply chamber **b.f.g.** By **b.** we understand the difference between "what" <note>substance</note> and "of what kind" <note>quality/accident</note>. By **f.** that they do not join themselves, nor do they measure themselves to the same object as one, since they are diverse. By **g.** we understand that "what" requires its own meaning, and "of what kind" similarly; but the deception consists in the appropriation in which the principle does not rest. Through chamber **d.f.h.** the deception is recognized. By **d.** the contrary ends are known, because whatever is changed is changed into a quality. And by **f.** the privation of continuity between the past "now" and the present "now" is known. By **h.** it is known—and through the fourth species of rule **e.** and the first of **d.**—that it has one meaning through "what" and another through "of what kind": because "what" speaks of <term>substance</term> <note>the essential nature of a thing</note>, while "of what kind" speaks of <term>accident</term> <note>a non-essential quality, like color</note>.

### On fallacies outside of language.

<margin>On the fallacy outside of language.</margin> Fallacies outside of language differ from fallacies in language in this: the first motive [in language] is without an apparent cause on the part of the voice. In fallacies outside of language, however, it is on the part of the thing itself.

# Part Seven: What a Refutation Is

<margin>On the fallacy of the accident.</margin>
The **fallacy of the accident** <note>Latin: *fallacia accidentis*; a logical error where a general rule is applied to an exceptional case, or where a property of an accident is attributed to the subject itself.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that something is said to belong simply to two things which are, in some way, only united by accident. A false argument <term>paralogism<note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note></term> is formed thus: *I know Coriscus; but Coriscus is the one coming toward us; therefore, I know the one coming toward us.* <note>A classic Aristotelian example: you might know the person, but not recognize them as they approach.</note> ¶ For this deception, we assign the chamber **b.f.c.** Through **b**, we understand the difference between what is perceived by the senses and what is perceived by the mind; for Coriscus is one thing, and "the one coming" is another. Through **f**, it is known that "the one coming" and "Coriscus" are not in a continuous middle ground between the extremes. Through **c**, we understand that Coriscus can be sitting in the street while another man is the one coming. ¶ Furthermore, the deception is recognized through chamber **g.f.h.** Through **g**, we understand that Coriscus has his own proper number and the other man coming has another; similarly, that a name is specifically assigned to him despite the deception. Through **f**, it is known that Coriscus is not joined with any man coming in one and the same measure. Through **h**, it is known that Coriscus "the sitter" is not the same at the time when he is "the comer."

<margin>b f c.</margin>
<margin>g f h</margin>

### On the fallacy of "in a certain respect" and "absolutely."

<margin>On the fallacy of *secundum quid* and *simpliciter*.</margin>
The **fallacy of "in a certain respect" and "absolutely"** <note>Latin: *secundum quid et simpliciter*; the error of arguing from a qualified statement to an unqualified one.</note> is a deception arising from taking a statement made in a certain respect as if it were spoken absolutely. A false argument is formed thus: *Every man who has whiteness in him is white; Socrates is white as to his teeth; therefore, Socrates is white.* ¶ To this deception, we apply the chamber **c.f.i.** Through the fourth type of rule **c**, we understand that an Ethiopian <note>Latin: *ethyops*; a standard medieval logical example for a person with dark skin.</note> has whiteness in his teeth, eyes, and nails, but blackness in his body. Through **f**, we understand that this whiteness is not continuous throughout the whole body. Through **i**, we understand that he is white in one place and black in another. ¶ Furthermore, through chamber **g.f.k.** Through **g**, we understand that he is properly white in his teeth, and "appropriately" white only when one falsely concludes he is white overall. Through **f**, it is known that the Ethiopian is a subject in which there are several distinct quantities. Just as there is the quantity of a tooth and the quantity of a foot—the tooth being characterized by whiteness and the foot by blackness. Through **k**, we understand that the Ethiopian is colored only with whiteness in the tooth and blackness in the body.

### On the fallacy of the ignorance of the refutation.

<column-break/>

<margin>On the fallacy of *ignorantia elenchi*.</margin>
The **fallacy of the ignorance of the refutation** <note>Latin: *ignorantia elenchi*; missing the point or failing to address the actual argument of the opponent.</note> is a deception arising from not observing those things necessary for the definition of a refutation, especially regarding the nature of contradiction. ¶ Now, a **refutation** <term>elenchus<note>A logical refutation, specifically one that proves the contradictory of the opponent's conclusion.</note></term> is a syllogism of contradiction, which is sometimes one syllogism and sometimes two. It is one when the syllogism concludes the contradiction of some previously given proposition; for example, if it is granted that "some animal is incorruptible," one proceeds thus: *Everything composed of contraries is corruptible; every animal is such a thing; therefore, every animal is corruptible.* This is the contradictory conclusion of the first given proposition, by which the syllogism constitutes a refutation. It is two when a contradiction is concluded from two syllogisms; as in the aforementioned syllogism, a second syllogism is placed against it: *Nothing blessed is corruptible; some animal is blessed; therefore, some animal is not corruptible.* ¶ Therefore, the essence of a refutation consists of a syllogism and a contradiction. Whatever, then, is against the definition of a syllogism and a contradiction is also against the definition of a refutation. A false argument is formed thus: *Two is the double of one; two is not the double of three; therefore, two is double and not double.* ¶ This is not valid because the omission of the phrase "in the same respect" means there is no true contradiction; and this was declared through the second type of rule **c**. ¶ To this deception, we apply **b.f.c.** Through **b**, we understand that two differs from one and vice versa. Through **f**, we understand that two is more than one in discrete quantity. Through **c**, we understand that two agrees in being an even number, and three agrees in being an odd number. ¶ Furthermore, through chamber **d.f.e.** Through **d**, we understand that an even number, namely two, is composed of two units according to the second type of rule **d**. One is the principle of number according to the first type of rule **d**. Through **f**, we know that two and one are not measured equally in number according to the first type of rule **e**, because two is a double and one is not a double.

### On the fallacy of the consequent.

<margin>On the fallacy of the consequent.</margin>
The fallacy of the consequent <note>original: "fallacia consequentis"; a formal error where one assumes that because the "then" part is true, the "if" part must also be true.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that the consequent is thought to be entirely the same as the antecedent. A paralogism <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> is formed thus: If a donkey is an animal, and an animal exists, therefore you are a donkey. This is not valid. ¶ For the consequence first placed is not converted. ¶ To this deception we apply the chamber **b. f. d.** By **b.** we understand the donkey and the rational animal differing in species, because the difference which is between the sensual and the sensual is not that which is between the sensual and the intellectual. By **f.** we understand that the sensual and the intellectual are joined in man, not in the donkey. By **d.** we understand that in man the sensual and the intellectual are joined in the constituting of man himself; but in the donkey, they are not. Through the chamber **d. f. e.**, by **d.** we understand that the subject which is of the sensual and the sensual is not converted with the subject of the sensual and the intellectual. By **f.** we understand that man and donkey do not enter under one continuous medium of extremities. By **e.** we understand that man exists so that he may understand; but the donkey does not.

### On the fallacy of non-cause as cause.

<margin>On the fallacy of non-cause as cause.</margin>
The fallacy of non-cause as cause <note>original: "non causam vt causa"; treating something as a cause that is not actually the cause of an effect.</note> is when among the premises from which a conclusion follows, some proposition is placed which does nothing toward the conclusion, and thus is not the cause. However, "cause" is said here to be that which is a cause in inferring, according to which premises are said to be the causes of the conclusion. And a paralogism is formed thus: as soul and life are the same. And death and life are contraries. Generation and corruption are contraries; but death is corruption; therefore life is generation, and to live is to be generated—which is impossible. ¶ To this deception

we apply **b. f. c.** By **b.** we understand the difference between a soul and life, since life is higher, as is evident in brutes through the vegetative and sensitive soul being continued; and by the reasoning soul continued from the sensual and the intellectual, we understand the difference. By **f.** we understand the life of the rational soul not continued to the life of a brute. By **c.** we understand that in the rational soul, life is a continuous magnitude of intellect, will, and memory. In brutes and in plants, this is by no means the case. ¶ Furthermore, we recognize the deception through the chamber **d. f. e.** By **d.** we know that life in plants and in brutes is of corruptible correlates; in the rational soul, however, not at all, since it is not made of contraries. By **f.** we know that the cause and the non-cause are not joined in the subject. By **e.** we know that the soul lives by resting in its end, namely in God; but death does not.

### On the fallacy of multiple questions.

<margin>On the fallacy of multiple questions.</margin>
The fallacy of multiple questions <note>original: "plures interrogationes"; the error of demanding a single answer to a question that actually contains multiple hidden questions.</note> is a deception arising from the fact that to a question which is multiple, one response is given, because it is proposed as a single way of questioning. A paralogism is formed thus: Do you think that man and donkey are a rational animal? And if it is said "yes," one proceeds thus: man and donkey are not a rational animal; therefore man is not a rational animal. ¶ To this deception we will apply this chamber **b. f. c.** By **b.** we understand that the difference existing between the sensual and the sensual differs from the difference existing between the sensual and the intellectual; by reason of which man and donkey cannot be the same. By **f.** we understand that man and donkey are not under one continuous medium of extremities. By **c.** we understand that man and donkey do not agree in the same species nor in the same number. ¶ Likewise, through the chamber **d. f. g.** the deception is recognized. By **d.** we understand that man is constituted of three souls: namely, of the vegetative, sensitive, and reasoning soul. The donkey, however, is not; but of the vegetative and sensitive only. By **f.** we understand that man can have knowledge as a habit; the donkey, however, cannot. By **g.** we understand that "risibility" <note>The capacity to laugh; a classic logical example of a property unique to humans.</note> is a proper passion of man, and also "intelligibility" is substantial to him; but these do not apply to the donkey.

# Eighth Part

<margin>
On the fallacy of contradiction.
</margin>

The fallacy of contradiction is a deception: and it depends on the eight aforementioned propositions which evidently conclude a contradiction, which we have composed in the *New Logic* <note>original: "logica noua"; likely referring to Lull’s own logical system</note> discovered by way of a general art. And a <term>paralogism</term> <note>a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</note> is formed thus: No stone is visible; a certain stone is visible; therefore, a certain stone is visible and not visible. ¶ To this paralogism we apply this chamber **b.f.c.** Through **b.** we understand that there is a difference between a visible and invisible stone, because an invisible stone is not visible in itself, as it is not endowed with a sensitive <term>habit</term> <note>a disposition or quality</note>. However, a stone becomes visible by accident, because sight adapts itself to its color and position. Through **f.** we understand that when a stone is invisible, it is not joined with the species of visibility; but when it is visible, it is so joined. Through **c.** we understand that sight is not acting upon the invisible stone through the fourth species of the same rule; nor does it have a <term>passion</term> <note>the state of being acted upon</note> under the visual power. But regarding the visible stone, the total contrary can be said. ¶ Furthermore, through chamber **g.f.h.** the deception is recognized. Through **g.** we know that visibility is not a proper quality of man; but by accident, sight appropriates visibility to him, because color, figure, and position are its objects. Through **f.** we understand that the stone is not with the sensitive [faculty]. Through **h.** we understand that a stone is sometimes visible and sometimes not visible. ¶ We have spoken of fallacies applied to the rules so that the intellect may recognize the deceptions of fallacies. And through what we have said, the intellect recognizes that the logician with his fallacies does not dare to stand before the natural philosopher; granted that it be as you, the logician, say, this indeed would be impossible and that and other things would follow in the nature of things, as is evident in the nature of definitions, principles, and rules. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that in a dispute one logician does not rest at the end with another logician, because they do not descend to the truth of the thing; but they only stand upon the name and the likenesses of things through the definition of contrariety. But if a logician disputes with a natural philosopher, the truth of the thing is quickly sought and they quickly rest at the end. Because the logician can by no means deny the experiences which they reach with the sensitive, imaginative, and reasoning [faculties], as was said above.

### On the Method of Teaching.

<column-break/>

<margin>
On the method of teaching.
</margin>

Through the fourth figure more truly, and through the others, a method is given by which other sciences can be easily and briefly acquired, such as theology, philosophy, etc. And this is by finding a "middle" <note>a middle term in a syllogism</note> that is neither most general nor most specific. The reason for this is: because this science has the most general principles and also the most general rules. Other sciences, however, have subordinate principles, and thus their "middle" is imperfect without this science. And so men learn with difficulty over a long time. And when they doubt, they do not have the most general principles to which they may recur artificially, as the artist of this art does. ¶ Furthermore, other sciences will be taught through this part by placing a chamber in which **f.** stands for the middle in the authorities of other sciences, explaining the authorities in the chamber according to that mode by which **f.** could enter those authorities, explaining and reducing them to a syllogism according to that doctrine which has already been stated above. And of this we shall give an example. Thus it is read in theology that **God is pure act.** This authority is provable through these two chambers: namely **b.f.c.** and through chamber **d.f.e.** And this in this manner: through **b.** we shall have goodness and difference. Through **c.** that goodness is a great reason having in itself great and good and distinct correlatives. Through **d.** eternal and primitive. Through **e.** they are quieted by reason of the end; and through the second species of rule **d.** and through the first of **e.** they are necessary. And through **f.** they are joined and measured well, infinitely, eternally, separated from every accident. ¶ And thus, this explanation having been made, it is seen and clear that God is pure act in existing and acting. ¶ Furthermore, it is read in philosophy that **from nothing, nothing comes.** <note>original: "de nihilo nihil fit"</note> To explain and clarify this authority, we assign chamber **d.f.e.** Through **d.** we explain that "nothing" is not a principle; because if it were so, "nothing" would already be "something." Likewise through **d.** that "nothing" is not the matter for anything. For if something could be made from it, it would already be something. The same is understood concerning the third species of **d.** For if "nothing" were subject to anything, it would indeed be something. **f.** also sounds or signifies that from nothing, nothing is made. Nor can "nothing" have a middle; because if it had a middle, it would already be something. Through **e.** it is understood that "nothing" cannot be a material, formal, efficient, or final cause; and it can be endowed with no power; because if it were in the opposite, it would already follow that it was something. And thus the aforesaid authority is clarified and explained through the aforementioned chamber. I do not, however, say that the mode is eternal;

But that authority which says that the world was created out of nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note> can be explained through the aforementioned chamber D. Indeed, it posits that God is primary through eternity, power, and intellectuality. And through the third species of D <note>referring to the specific logical rules of the author's system</note>, His power is not subject to anything; thus He can understand and produce the world, which was not in act nor in potentiality, out of nothing. It follows, therefore, that the world exists in act through creation, with God measuring His infinite power, intellectuality, primitivity, etc. ¶ Furthermore, one reads that Being and One are interchangeable <note>A central tenet of Scholastic metaphysics: whatever exists is, by virtue of existing, a single thing</note>, as are Truth and One, and Good and True. These authorities can be explained through chamber B.F.C., and likewise for other chambers such as B.F.G. For in B we have differences, such as between the sensual and the sensual. For in a stone, "one" is one kind of being; in a plant, it is another kind of being; and in a sentient creature, another, etc. And so it is with One and True, and Good and True. ¶ These goodnesses, unities, and truths are not interchangeable <note>in a literal, identical sense</note>; for if they were, difference would be destroyed, and consequently the medium <note>the middle term or connecting link</note>. And likewise for concordance, which is impossible. For there is one measurement in a stone, and one continuous medium, and one quantity in a stone, another in a plant, etc. And thus, regarding the literal sense, the authorities cannot stand [as identical], because the chamber cannot enter the authorities according to the literal exposition, but enters with the allegorical sense, and this with rule G. ¶ Since correlatives <note>terms that exist only in relation to each other</note> regarding unity are not the same as they are regarding entity, goodness, and truth; but they are "appropriated" thus because every principle communicates itself to another. And so there remain principles that are differentiable, concordable, and capable of being mediated, as well as qualitative reasons; and every principle has its own proper rest through its own proper essence and act, and no inconsistency follows. And to this, rule B consents with all other rules. ¶ Just as we gave an example concerning theology and philosophy, explaining and declaring them with the chambers, so it can be done for other sciences: namely medicine, law, and morals, etc. ¶ For if an authority contains within itself the truth of a chamber of the fourth figure, they can enter that authority with its definitions and species, affirming or denying. And thus it is not impossible for the authority to be true. ¶ For no authority constituted from first, true, and necessary principles contradicts reason. And this rule is infallible and necessary.

<margin>
General rule.
</margin>
->¶ End of the seventh principal part.<-

<column-break/>

## Eighth principal part: On the mixture of principles and rules.

<margin>
79. 102
Rubric of the eighth part.
Mixtion of principles.
On the principles and rules.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a floral or foliate design within a square frame.</image-desc>
This part is divided into two parts: namely, the mixture of principles where one is deduced with another. ¶ The second part is about principles deduced through the rules. ¶ In this part, instruction is given on how one principle may be known through other principles by deducing it through those very principles and through all species of rules. Therefore, when there is doubt concerning any principle, let one recur to this part. There, one will indeed be able to find the truth about it with the aforesaid principles and the species of rules: for example, if it is asked whether any goodness is a substantial being <note>term: "substantial being" (ens substantiale) refers to something that exists in itself rather than as a quality of something else</note>. ¶ Again, whether any moral goodness is a habit and a real being. And then, at that time, let one recur to the chapter on goodness deduced through other principles and through the rules; and let that be held which seems most rational through rule B, with other rules and the definitions of the principles mixed in. ¶ This mixture is the center and subject of this art. ¶ Nevertheless, in the third figure, a mixture of the rules of the principles was made. But in this part, we shall declare in order, with one principle deduced through all principles and through all rules by deduction and union, so that the intellect may be discursive <note>moving logically from one point to another</note> singularly through every principle. ¶ And first, we shall speak of the first part.

<margin>
The center and subject of this art.
</margin>

### On goodness deduced through the principles.

<margin>
On goodness deduced through the principles.
Greatness.
Duration.
Power.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'B' with foliate patterns.</image-desc>
Goodness is, in itself, the reason for a good thing to act or produce good; and because it is great through magnitude <note>term: "magnitude" (magnitudo) in this context refers to the "greatness" or scale of a principle's influence</note>, it is a doubled reason for a good thing to produce a great good. ¶ Goodness through duration is durable; and thus it is the reason for a good thing to produce a durable good. And because it is great through magnitude—as has been said—it is a tripled reason: so that the good may act as a good that is great and durable. ¶ Goodness through power <note>term: "power" (potestas) refers to the capacity or potential to act</note> can exist and act; and thus goodness—through that which it has of itself, and through that which it has from power, and through that which it has from magnitude, and through that which it has from duration—is a quadrupled reason for a good thing to produce and act as something good, great, durable, and powerful; and so with the other principles with which they can be manifoldly mixed, holding to the manner we have given.

# Part Eight.

<margin>Exclusion from goods</margin>
However, we exclude contrariety and minority <note>original: "minoritatem"; referring to the state of being lesser or smaller</note> with which Goodness cannot have a multitude. And because we avoid prolixity, we do not wish to provide examples of how it might be fivefold or sixfold, etc.; but we will exemplify and show how it is that all principles are combined. ¶ Goodness through **Wisdom** is knowable. And thus there is a reason for a "good" in a scientific way <note>meaning "pertaining to knowledge" or "scientifically"</note> that it should act as a known or scientific good. ¶ Goodness through **Will** is lovable; therefore there is a reason for a "good" through love that it should act as a lovable or beloved good. ¶ Through **Virtue**, goodness is virtuous. And thus there is a reason for a virtuous "good" that it should act as a virtuous good. ¶ Goodness through **Truth** is true. And thus, rightly and truly, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a true good. ¶ Goodness through **Glory** is glorious: and thus there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a glorious good. ¶ Goodness through **Difference** is clear and not confused. And thus, rightly, distinctly, and clearly, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a good clearly distinct from itself. ¶ Goodness through **Concordance** is accordable; and thus, rightly and concordantly, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a concordant, accorded good. ¶ Goodness is against **Malice**, which is its contrary. And thus concordance is against contrariety, because they are opposites. And thus goodness, rightly and concordantly, is against malice and contrariety. ¶ Goodness through **Principle** has the nature of a principle. And thus there is a reason for a "good," rightly and principally, that it should produce a principled good <note>original: "bonum principiatum"; a good that originates from a principle</note>. ¶ Goodness has the nature of a **Middle** through the middle. And thus, rightly and mediately, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a good with a middle. ¶ Goodness through the **End** has the nature of an end. And thus, rightly and finally or perfectly, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a perfect and quieted good. ¶ Goodness through **Majority** has the nature of majority; and thus, rightly and "majorifically" <note>a Lullian neologism meaning "in a magnifying or increasing manner"</note>, there is a reason for a "good" that it should act as a magnified good. ¶ Goodness through **Equality** is of the nature of equality. And therefore, rightly and equally, there is a reason for a "good" that it should produce a good made equal from several things. ¶ Goodness which is **Minority** has the nature of minority through minority. And therefore there is a reason, rightly and "minorifically," for a lesser good that it should act as a diminished good; and this is said respectively or comparatively. ¶ This has been said concerning Goodness as it is deduced linearly through all the principles. And because we have spoken of it generally, the artist <note>the practitioner of Llull's Art</note> can find many things at will in the line of Goodness.

**Magnitude** is good through **Goodness**, and goodness is great through magnitude. And thus from these follows the concrete thing, which is a "great good." ¶ Magnitude is lasting through **Duration**, and duration is great through magnitude: and from these follows the concrete "great and lasting" thing. ¶ Magnitude through **Power** can exist and act, and power through magnitude is great. And thus magnitude with power is the reason why there is a great concrete thing having great power of existing and acting. ¶ Magnitude is knowable through **Wisdom**, and wisdom through magnitude is great: and these two cause a "great and scientific" concrete thing having great knowledge. ¶ Magnitude is lovable through **Will**, and will is great through magnitude: and thus they cause a great "beloved" concrete thing, in which they have their sustenance. ¶ Magnitude through **Virtue** is virtuous, and virtue through magnitude is great: and from these is caused a "great and virtuous" concrete thing, in which they have their sustenance: and the concrete thing itself is the "being," and they themselves are the "essences." And in this step it appears how several essences compose one "being" with themselves. ¶ Magnitude through **Truth** is true, and truth through magnitude is great: and from them follows a "great true" concrete thing, in which they have their sustenance. ¶ Magnitude through **Glory** is glorious, and through magnitude glory is great. And from them follows the subject, in which they have magnificence and delight. ¶ Magnitude through **Difference** is distinct, by reason of which distinction in the essence of magnitude there are distinguished: the *magnifying*, the *magnifiable*, and the *magnifying act* <note>Llull's triad of agent, patient, and action</note>. And difference is great through magnitude, and therefore in the same subject they participate through magnifying and distinguishing. ¶ Magnitude through **Concordance** is accorded, and concordance is magnified through magnitude: and therefore in the same subject they participate through magnifying and according. ¶ Magnitude is contrariable through **Contrariety**, insofar as it is through transmutation; but naturally it is not against itself. And contrariety through magnitude is great: just as fire and water, which through magnitude have great contrariety by heating and cooling. ¶ Magnitude through the nature of **Principle** has in itself principles co-essential to itself: namely, the magnifying, the magnifiable, and the magnifying act. And the principle through magnitude is magnified, having, namely, a naturally great originating nature.

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

<margin>Greatness</margin> Greatness <note>original: "Magnitudo"</note> has the capacity to be a principle and to act as a principle. ¶ Greatness, by means of the Medium, possesses the logic of mediation; and the Medium, by means of Greatness, possesses the logic of magnifying—provided, however, that they exist within the same subject. ¶ Greatness is the cause why the End is great; and the End is the cause why Greatness is at rest; and this occurs within the same subject. ¶ Greatness is greater by means of Majority; and Majority is great by means of Greatness. This is necessary so that within a subject, each may have its own action: namely, Greatness to magnify, and Majority to make greater. ¶ Greatness, by the logic of Equality, contains things within itself co-equally: namely, the magnifier, the magnifiable, and the act of magnifying <note>These are the "active," "passive," and "verbal" components of a principle in Lullian philosophy</note> are co-equal parts of Greatness. And Equality, by reason of Greatness, contains within itself great things co-essential to it: namely, the great, the equalizer, the equalizable, and the act of equalizing. ¶ Greatness, in regard to the "Greater," is distinct from Minority; for Greatness could not be what it is if joined with it. The reason for this is that Smallness and Minority are interchangeable: namely, in regard to the subject in which they exist; just as sin is "nothing," so it is with an accident that cannot exist by itself.

### On Duration derived through the principles.

<margin>On Duration derived through the principles.</margin> Duration is good through Goodness, and Goodness lasts through Duration. Therefore, Duration directly causes duration, while Goodness does so indirectly—that is, by happenstance. The reason is that it belongs to a good thing to perform a lasting good. ¶ Duration is the cause why Greatness lasts, and it is great through Greatness; therefore, in the subject in which they exist, they participate through "lasting" and "magnifying," assuming there is no preexisting obstacle to hinder their actions. ¶ Duration is the cause why Power lasts, and Power is the cause why Duration can exist and act; thus, in the subject in which they exist, they participate through "lasting" and "being able." ¶ Wisdom lasts by the logic of Duration, and Duration is knowable through Wisdom; thus, in the subject in which they exist, they participate through "lasting" and "knowing." ¶ Duration is lovable through the Will, and the Will is durable through Duration; therefore, in the subject in which they exist, they agree through "lasting" and "loving." ¶ Duration is virtuous through Virtue, and Virtue is durable through Duration; therefore, in the subject in which they exist, Duration is distant from vice through Virtue, and Virtue is distant from privation through

Duration. ¶ It is in the nature of Duration to last. It is in the nature of Truth to verify; and Truth lasts through Duration, and Duration is true through Truth. ¶ Glory lasts by the logic of Duration, and Duration is glorious by the logic of Glory; therefore, Duration is distant from punishment through Glory, and Glory is distant from privation through Duration. ¶ Duration is clear and unconfused through Difference, and Difference lasts through Duration; thus Duration, through Difference, possesses the "laster," the "lastable," and the "lasting" in a differing and distinct way. And Difference, through Duration, possesses the "laster," the "lastable," and the "lasting" permanently and enduringly. ¶ By the logic of Concordance, Duration contains within itself concordant things; and by the logic of Duration, Concordance contains within itself lasting and permanent things. ¶ Duration contradicts its contrary and they destroy each other as much as possible; and Contrariety destroys Duration as much as it can. The reason for this is that Contrariety agrees with "non-being," while Duration speaks of "being." ¶ Duration, through the Principle, possesses the logic of a principle; for all things that last, last under the logic of Duration. And so the Principle lasts by the logic of Duration. ¶ Duration, by reason of the Medium, possesses a middle—namely, the act of "lasting" existing in the middle between the "laster" and the "lastable." And the Medium, by reason of Duration, lasts in the subject in which it exists. ¶ Duration, by reason of the End, is perfect and at rest; and the End lasts by the logic of Duration in the subject in which it exists. ¶ Duration, by reason of Majority, is "made greater" in some subject; and Majority, by the logic of Duration, is sustained enduringly in the subject. ¶ Duration, by reason of Equality, possesses the logic of co-equalizing; for it has between the "laster," the "lastable," and the "lasting" things co-essential to itself. And Equality, by reason of Duration, lasts in the subject in which it exists. ¶ Duration, in the subject in which it exists by reason of Minority, is close to nothing; and Minority, by reason of Duration, lasts and has value in relation to being.

### On Power derived through the principles.

<margin>On Power derived through the principles.</margin> Power is good through Goodness. And Goodness, through Power, is able to exist and act. Therefore, they mutually move the subject in which they exist—according to the nature they possess—to act and exist well and powerfully with them. ¶ Power is great through Greatness, and Greatness is able to exist and act according to Power. Therefore, in the subject in which they exist, what one lacks, the other supplies according to its own logic. Power is lasting through **duration**. And duration can exist and act through power: and if duration is eternity, existing and acting are necessary, because in eternity there is no novelty <note>i.e., no change or new beginning</note>. ¶ Power is knowable through **wisdom**. And wisdom can exist and act through power: and if they are interchangeable <note>original: "convertuntur"; a logical term meaning they are co-extensive or identical in essence</note>, existing, understanding, and acting are of necessity because they cannot be otherwise. But this is understood of God alone. ¶ Power is lovable through **will**, and will can exist and act through power: and if they are interchangeable, the subject in which they exist can of necessity exist, act, and love. ¶ Power is virtuous through **virtue**: and virtue can exist and act through power: and thus the subject in which they are can powerfully and virtuously exist by existing and acting. ¶ Power is true through **truth**: and truth can exist and act through power. And if in the subject in which they are they are not interchangeable: the lack of interchangeability implies that the subject in which they are can be false and idle. ¶ Power is delightful through **glory**: and similarly glory can exist and act through power. And if in the subject in which they are they are interchangeable: power is necessarily distant from pain, because it is distant from impotence. ¶ Power is an unconfused and clear reason through **difference**: and difference can exist and act through power. And if in the subject in which they are they are interchangeable: it follows of necessity that the subject is actually in a state of "being able" and in distinguishing well from itself. ¶ Power is accordable through **concordance**: and concordance can exist and act through power. And if they are not interchangeable, the lack of interchangeability implies it is impossible for "being able" and "concordance" to be in the subject. ¶ Power cannot be against itself through **contrariety**: nor can contrariety be powerless through power. And because they are not interchangeable, the lack of interchangeability implies that some power is separate from contrariety. ¶ Power has the nature of beginning through **principle**: and principle has the nature of "possifying" <note>making possible</note> through power: and if they are interchangeable, "being able" and "beginning" are separate from contingency and novelty. ¶ Power has the nature of mediating through the **middle**: and through this nature, "being able" exists in the middle of the "power-er" and the "powered." And the middle can exist and act through power: and therefore the middle posits influences from the end, and refluxes from the principle, and to know their nature. ¶ Power is able to rest through the **end**: and the end can exist and act through power. And difference is intelligible through **wisdom**: because in the differentiating end <note>original: "fine differentiativo"</note>, the thing to be differentiated, and the act of differentiating, it would not otherwise be understood. ¶ **Wisdom**, through **concordance**, contains within itself concordant things: namely, the intellective power, the object of the intellect, and the act of understanding; these agree in the essence that is formed from them. And they agree in existing as a plurality, because one is not the other. And the principle, through wisdom, is an object of the intellect. And if they are interchangeable in the subject in which they exist, they exist by necessity and cannot be otherwise. ¶ Understanding, through the nature of the **middle**, consists in the middle ground between the one who understands and the thing understood. And the middle is intelligible through wisdom. **Wisdom**, through the **end**, is capable of rest; and the end, through wisdom, is knowable. And in a subject where they are not interchangeable, there can be understanding without rest, and rest without understanding. ¶ **Wisdom**, by reason of **majority**, can receive within itself a greater understanding; but because it is not interchangeable with majority, it cannot increase infinitely, but only finitely, beyond which limit it cannot extend itself. ¶ **Wisdom**, by reason of **equality**, has within itself equal essential reasons: namely, the innate, the intellective, the intelligible, and the act of understanding; and equality is intelligible through wisdom; this intelligibility is drawn out through the equalizer, the equalized, and the act of equaling, objectively. ¶ **Wisdom**, or the intellect, is not interchangeable with **minority**; for if it were, it would always have a lesser understanding, and it would be more fitting for it to be ignorant than to understand, which is impossible.
