### On the Will as derived through the principles.

<margin>On the Will derived through the principles.</margin>
<margin>Greatness</margin>
<margin>Duration</margin>
The **Will**, through **goodness**, is good. And goodness, through the will, is lovable; and if they were interchangeable, the subject in which they existed would always be acting well and loving, and could not be otherwise. ¶ The **Will**, through **greatness**, is great; and greatness, through the will, is lovable; and therefore the lovability of the will is great, and the lovability of greatness is also great. And if they were interchangeable, there would be a "loving-ness" and a "lovability" in the infinite, consisting of the magnifier, the magnified, and the acts of magnifying and loving. ¶ The **Will**, through **duration**, is durable. And duration, through the will, is lovable; and if duration (which is eternity) and the will were interchangeable, then by necessity the act of eternalizing and the act of loving would exist from eternity and into eternity. ¶ The **Will**, through **power**, is able to exist and to act. And power, through the will, is lovable. And in a subject where they are not interchangeable, the will can be powerless and power can be unloved. ¶ The **Will**, through **wisdom**, is knowable; and wisdom, through the will, is lovable. And if this exists alongside greatness and eternity, it follows that understanding and loving exist by necessity. ¶ The **Will**, through **virtue**, is virtuous; and virtue, through the will, is lovable; but if they are not interchangeable, virtue can be hateful and the will can be vicious. ¶ The **Will**, through **truth**, is true. But where will and truth are not interchangeable, truth can be hateful and the will can be false. ¶ The **Will**, through **glory**, is delightful; and thus glory, through the will, is lovable; and thus the will, through glory, is distant from pain; and glory, through the will, is distant from hatred. ¶ The **Will**, through **difference**, contains within itself the distinction between the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving; and these are clear within it and not confused. And difference, through the will, is lovable. ¶ The **Will**, through **concordance**, has within itself concordant things: namely, the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving; and concordance, through the will, is lovable. And because it is lovable along with goodness, greatness, duration, power, etc., there are within it the lovable things: the concorder, the concordable, and the act of concording. ¶ The **Will**, with **contrariety**, hates vice and sin; and if the will and contrariety were interchangeable, the will could never love the virtues through concordance. ¶ The **Will**, through the **principle**, is the principle of loving. The reason for this is: because all lovable things are lovable by reason of the will. It follows that the principle, in regard to the reason of the will, is lovable. And in this step it appears how one being causes something from itself so that it may receive some utility from it. ¶ The **Will**, by reason of the **middle**, has within itself a middle: namely, the act of loving; and the middle, by reason of the will, is lovable. ¶ The **Will**, by reason of the **end**, is perfectly at rest when it sees that it has within itself a rest that is good, great, lasting, and capable of loving, without which the end cannot be sufficient for itself. ¶ The **Will**, with **majority**, is in a greater act of loving; so that it may have a greater act, majority is lovable. ¶ The **Will**, in regard to the reason of **equality**, has a nature of equaling through the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving. And equality, through the will, is lovable.

->Part Eight.<-

<margin>Minority</margin>
The will, when associated with minority <note>original: "minoritate"; refers to the state of being lesser or decreasing in the author's logical system</note>, is focused on nothingness, and with nothingness it exists outside in emptiness or idleness. If the will and minority were interchangeable, non-existence would be more desirable than existence, which is impossible.

### Concerning Virtue as derived through the Principles.

<margin>Concerning Virtue as derived through the Principles.</margin>
Virtue is good through goodness, and goodness is virtuous through virtue. Thus, virtue, by means of goodness, is the reason for a good person to act well, and by its own nature, it ensures that the act itself is virtuous. <margin>Greatness</margin> ¶ Virtue is great through greatness, and greatness is virtuous through virtue. This would not be the case if it did not possess a "virtuifier," a "virtuifiable," and the "act of virtuifying" <note>The author uses these technical terms—virtuificans, virtuificabile, virtuificare—to describe the internal mechanics of a quality: the part that acts, the part acted upon, and the action itself</note>, which are of its essence and identical with it. <margin>Duration</margin> ¶ Virtue lasts through duration; and if it is numerically one with duration, then the virtuifier, the virtuifiable, and the act of virtuifying always endure in their essence. <margin>Power</margin> ¶ Virtue is powerful through power, and thus it has power against vice and sin. But it has no power when a person does not wish to act with power; the reason for this is that such a person is vicious and idle. <margin>Wisdom</margin> ¶ Virtue is knowable through wisdom, and wisdom possesses virtuous knowing through virtue—provided, however, that the act of the will passes through, which creates the lover. ¶ And in this step, it appears how one virtue assists another. <margin>Will</margin> ¶ Virtue is lovable through the will, and the will is virtuous through virtue; thus they agree through the acts of loving and virtuifying. <margin>Truth</margin> ¶ Virtue is true through truth, and truth is virtuous through virtue. If they were identical in the subject in which they exist, there would never be falsehood or sin in that subject. <margin>Glory</margin> ¶ Virtue is delightful through glory <note>In this context, "glory" often refers to the highest joy or the radiance of perfection</note>, and that delight is virtuous through virtue. ¶ And in this step, it appears how the virtuous person, in taking delight, seeks glory. <margin>Difference</margin> ¶ Virtue is clear and not confused through difference, because difference establishes a distinction between the virtuifier, the virtuifiable, and the act of virtuifying, even though they are identical in essence. Thus, it establishes that difference possesses the power to do this. <margin>Concordance</margin> ¶ Virtue, through concordance, contains within itself concordant essential things from which one essence is made. Virtue establishes that concordance is virtuous for this purpose. <margin>Contrariety</margin> ¶ Virtue is set against its contrary, namely vice and sin; it stands against them with goodness, greatness,

<column-break/>

and so on. ¶ Contrariety is against virtue through the deprivation of its habit <note>A "habit" in medieval philosophy is a stable disposition or quality of the soul</note> and through the deprivation of the habits of will, greatness, and so forth.
<margin>The First</margin>
Virtue is primary through priority, because whatever is primary is primary through priority, and whatever is virtuous is virtuous through virtue. Therefore, the principle is virtuous through virtue. <margin>The Middle</margin> ¶ Virtue is capable of mediation through the middle, and the middle is virtuous through virtue. <margin>The End</margin> ¶ Virtue is perfected and at rest through the end. Thus, the just tend toward rest along with virtue. <margin>Majority</margin> ¶ Virtue possesses a greater nature through majority, and majority possesses a virtuous essence through virtue. <margin>Equality</margin> ¶ Virtue, through equality, possesses a nature that balances justice with providence, and so on. The same applies to understanding and loving, which are sometimes equally virtuous. <margin>Minority</margin> ¶ Virtue is sometimes lesser by reason of minority, just as it is sometimes greater. Thus, when it is lesser, it accords with non-existence, just as when it is greater, it accords with existence.

### Concerning Truth as derived through the Principles.

<margin>Concerning Truth as derived through the Principles.</margin>
Truth is good through goodness, and goodness is true through truth. If they are interchangeable, the "good" and the "true" are always the same. But when they are not interchangeable in some subject, someone may desire to have a "good" in a false way—neither truly nor virtuously. In this step, it appears that in man, goodness and truth are not always interchangeable. <margin>Greatness</margin> ¶ Truth is great through greatness; it would not be great unless it essentially contained a "verifier," a "verifiable," and the "act of verifying" within itself. <margin>Duration</margin> ¶ Truth endures through duration, because the verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying endure within it. Similarly, in moral action, the internal corresponds with the external, just as in the senses the radical moisture corresponds with the nutritional. <margin>Power</margin> ¶ Truth is powerful through power; and if it is identical with power, no falsehood can prevail against it. <margin>Wisdom</margin> ¶ Truth is knowable through wisdom. Wisdom desires truth so that it may relate truly to that which is known. <margin>Will</margin> ¶ Truth is lovable through the will, so that the will may truly possess its beloved. <margin>Virtue</margin> ¶ Truth is virtuous through virtue, and virtue is true through truth; therefore, they participate through the act of verifying against falsifying and sinning. <margin>Glory</margin> ¶ Truth is delightful through glory, and glory is true through truth.

It emphasizes that these qualities are composed of internal active and passive elements that ensure their consistency and power over vice and falsehood.</summary>

And thus the just truly and gloriously tend toward eternal glory. ¶ **Truth through difference** is clear and separated from confusion. And difference establishes that in truth there is one who is the verifier, another who is the verified, and another which is the act of verifying <note>original: "verificans/verificatus/et verificare." This tripartite structure—the doer, the object, and the action—is central to Lullian logic</note>; and truth establishes this within that which is true. ¶ **Truth through concordance** has within itself co-essential things that agree, namely: the verifying, the verifiable, and the act of verifying: which agree in essence; and they agree that they are many; and truth establishes that concordance truly possesses what it has. ¶ **Truth is against falsehood**: and it stands against it with its verifying, its verifiable, and its act of verifying. And this is because they are not interchangeable. ¶ **Truth by reason of equality** has within itself equally the verifier, the verifiable, and the act of verifying; and equality through truth truly possesses that which it has. ¶ **One truth is smaller** than another: and that which is smaller participates with non-being: because it has less of being / and truth establishes this in the true: and minority also establishes this in its own kind.

And thus, by reason of the goodness which it has, it is the reason for the good, that it may act for the good and through itself: and that this acting may be glorious. ¶ **Glory through greatness** is great: and greatness is not without its own glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorifying: and if its greatness is infinite in its glorifying, it is infinitely so. ¶ **Glory through duration** lasts: and if it is eternity, its lasting is through "eternizing" <note>original: "eternare," the active state of being eternal</note> in which there can be no innovation. ¶ **Glory through power** is powerful in acting and existing: and if it is the same as power, it is impossible for it to be in defect or idleness. ¶ **Glory through wisdom** is knowable: and wisdom through glory is delightful. And therefore the glorifier without the glorified and the act of glorifying cannot be at rest. ¶ **The greater the glory**, the more it is in delight: and the greater the majority, the more it is the image of delight. ¶ **Glory without equality** essential to itself cannot be at rest through itself, because it would fail in having equally the glorifier, the glorifiable, and the act of glorifying. ¶ **Glory with minority** is near to pain and non-being: therefore with majority it stands apart from pain and non-being.

# Eighth Part

The two [Difference and Magnitude] share a path that is inseparable from their essence. And thus, the difference is so great that it contains within itself a diversity; indeed, magnitude is distinct through differentiation because it places it in its own number or genus: and within it, it places a distinction between the *magnifier*, the *magnifiable*, and the *act of magnifying* <note>original: "magnificattuū / magnificabile et magnificare"</note>, which belong to the essence and nature of magnitude.
¶ Difference lasts through duration, and duration, through difference, possesses within itself distinct things that belong to its essence: namely, the *enduring*, the *endurable*, and the *act of enduring*. And difference lasts through duration: the distinction which is converted with eternity lasts from eternity to eternity, distinguishing between the *eternizer*, the *eternizable*, and the *act of eternizing*; and this is signified through the most blessed Trinity.

<margin>Corollary: It lasts</margin>
¶ Difference is an innate power in an absolute sense: and it is powerful through power, because it causes within power a distinction between the *powerful*, the *powered*, and the *act of being able*. And power is capable of this along with difference.

<margin>Corollary: Power</margin>
¶ Difference is knowable through wisdom. And wisdom, through the nature of difference, can understand the distinction between the *intellectual*, the *intelligible*, and the *act of understanding*—so that they may be intelligible things; for without difference, they could not be objects of thought or be understood.

<margin>Wisdom. Corollary: Will</margin>
¶ Difference is desirable through the will: so that the will can have within itself the nature of loving, and so that a clear rational structure may exist between the *lover*, the *lovable*, and the *act of loving*; without which distinction, the rational structure would be confused and powerless to love.

<margin>Truth, Virtue</margin>
¶ Difference is virtuous through truth: and virtue, through difference, has within itself distinct things in which it has its agency and existence; and virtue, through difference, is set apart from vice. Indeed, without it, all things would be numerically the same.

<margin>Corollary: Glory</margin>
¶ Difference is true through truth; and truth, through difference, establishes true things, just as it is true that there is a distinction between the *verifier*, the *verifiable*, and the *act of verifying*; and between the *knower*, the *knowable*, and the *act of knowing*.

<margin>Concordance, Corollary</margin>
¶ Difference is delightful through glory: and glory, through difference, can possess delight through the *glorifier*, the *glorifiable*, and the *act of glorifying*; which could not exist in glory without distinction.
¶ Difference, through concordance, possesses within itself concordant things which it receives into itself by distinguishing between the *concordant*, the *concordable*, and the *act of concording*. And difference does this with its own *differentiator*, *differentiable*, and *act of differentiating*; and together, difference and concordance in the subject in which they exist establish that subject as one in common, which possesses within itself many concordant and differing things, from which it is constituted—just as one substance, one man, etc.

<column-break/>

<margin>Against</margin>
¶ Difference and innate contrariety differ. And this is because sometimes difference agrees with innate concordance by distinguishing, concording, and generating. And sometimes difference acts with contrariety against concordance by distinguishing, opposing, and concording; and this is so that the corruption of one may be the generation of another, and vice versa. And this happens in a similar way in moral matters, as we shall indicate.

<margin>Principle, Corollary</margin>
¶ Difference, through the principle, possesses the rational quality of priority, so that it may be a general principle for all differences: and this with its own proper *differentiator*, *differentiable*, and *act of differentiating*; without which it could not exist in that height, nor have the rational quality of a principle.

<margin>Medium</margin>
¶ Difference, through the medium, possesses the nature of a middle; and it has within itself a middle, namely the *differing* <note>original: "differre"</note>, by which it distinguishes one thing from another; and this "differing" exists between the differentiator and the differentiable.

<margin>End, Greater</margin>
¶ Difference, through the end, is in a state of rest: and its rest is to distinguish between one thing and another so that it may have subjects in which to exist and may possess agency.
¶ Difference, by reason of majority <term>maioritas: the quality of being greater or superior</term>, is greater in one subject than in another. For it is greater in substantial essences than in accidental ones. Hence, difference has a greater action in distinguishing substantial goodness from accidental magnitude, and it has a greater action in distinguishing within the same essence the many things constituting that essence than in distinguishing one essence from another essence: as was signified in the intellect, in which the *intellectual*, the *intelligible*, and the *act of understanding* differ through difference; these are innate and equal parts of the intellect. Nevertheless, between one essence and another, it applies itself more extensively.

<margin>Corollary: Equality</margin>
¶ Difference, through equality, possesses within itself equal things: just as equality, through difference, possesses within itself distinct things. And therefore, in the subject in which they exist, they communicate with each other through *differing* and *equalizing*.

<margin>Minority</margin>
¶ Difference is lesser through minority, just as it is greater through majority: and because minority is a small subject or a small "something," difference cannot enter it with its full magnitude; nor can it differ much through it: and according to how much the "small" enters, it distinguishes smallly.

# On the mixing of principles and rules.
## folio 34.
### ff ij

<margin>Derivation of Concordance through the principles.</margin>
Concordance <note>Latin: *Concordantia*; the principle of harmony or agreement</note> is good through Goodness: and Goodness is concordant through Concordance: and thus, in the subject in which they exist, they participate by making good and by making concordant. ¶ Concordance through Greatness is great: and it would not be great if it lacked the "concordant-maker," the "concordable-object," and the "act of concording" <note>Llull uses these three-part active/passive/verbal terms to describe the internal mechanics of every essence</note>: which belong to its very essence. Indeed, Contrariety would be greater if it could impede this; however, Concordance is greater than Contrariety, because it prevents it from being a substantial principle, as has been proven in the *Great Art*. ¶ Concordance is durable through Duration, while the concordant-maker, the concordable-object, and the act of concording—from which it is made—endure within it. ¶ Concordance through Power is able to exist and to act; and Power through Concordance possesses concordant things: and therefore, in as much as Concordance and Power join together in the subject in which they exist, they distance themselves by that much from Contrariety. ¶ Concordance is knowable through Wisdom or Intellect: and when the intellect makes it an object by understanding its essence, and its essential concordant-maker, concordable-object, and act of concording, it perceives and attains it more than by making it an object through essence alone; and Concordance communicates itself more to the intellect by concording. ¶ Concordance through Will is lovable: because Concordance places its own act within the Will, so that the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving may meet in identity of essence. ¶ Concordance accords virtue with virtue in the subject in which they exist: and it does this in its own essence and in the essence of the virtue, for it could not do this outside of them, because its act would have no subject in which it could be sustained. ¶ Concordance through Truth is true: and Truth through Concordance is made concordant: and therefore, in the subject in which they exist through the acts of concording and verifying, they stand apart from Contrariety and Falsehood. ¶ Concordance through Glory is delightful: and Glory through Concordance is made concordable: and therefore one reason hungers for the other. ¶ Concordance cannot exist without Difference: but Difference can exist without it, insofar as it coincides with Contrariety. And in this step it appears that Difference is a more general principle than Concordance. ¶ Concordance and Contrariety are opposites: because what Concordance builds, Contrariety destroys, and vice versa: but Concordance is a higher principle than Contrariety, because it aligns with Being by concording, while Contrariety aligns with Non-being by contradicting. ¶ Concordance, by the nature of a Principle, is general to all concordable things: because a Principle requires that Concordance have one active principle, another passive, and another neutral: with which it contains within itself all lower concordances held beneath it. ¶ Concordance through the Middle is inflowing and outflowing: through the concordant-maker, the concordable-object, and vice versa: and the act of concording is the middle between them. ¶ Concordance rests through the act of concording, the concordant-maker, and the concordable-object: outside of which it could not rest, nor could the End be a state of rest without Concordance. ¶ Concordance is sometimes greater, sometimes lesser. The reason for this is: because in one subject greater things accord than in another, just as in a human more than in a rose, and in a rose more than in a stone. ¶ Concordance coincides with Equality, so that it may have within itself equally the concordant-maker, the concordable-object, and the act of concording, which are co-essential to it; without these, Equality could not be the subject in which the end of Concordance could find rest. ¶ Some Concordance is lesser than another: and it is lesser because it cannot enter into Greatness and Majority with Minority. And therefore, Concordance with Minority is concerned with nothing: that is, with Contrariety, which is its opposite.

Contrariety is sometimes good through Goodness, and sometimes evil through Malice. # Part Eight.

and another is innate and moral, such as through heat and cold. Moral: just as it is possible to sin, yet contrariety in the act of sinning does not in itself have the power of opposing <note>i.e., it is not a force of nature</note>, but is a habit acquired by a person, with which that person sins. ¶ Contrariety is knowable by reason of objective wisdom: not that contrariety causes one to know, rather it is against knowing through ignorance. ¶ Contrariety is in one way desirable, and in another way not desirable: such as the contrariety of the elements <note>the balance of fire, air, water, and earth</note>, and the contrariety through which virtue stands against vice. Undesirable contrariety: such as the contrariety through which death is against life, and vice against virtue. ¶ The contrariety between vice and virtue places and communicates itself so that a person may be against vice through it, or, if the person wills, may be against virtue through vice: not that the contrariety itself forces the person to act upon it, because the person has free will to act with it, for good or for evil. ¶ Some contrariety is true, others false. True, such as justice against injustice. False, such as an injury which is truly a habit against the habit of justice. ¶ Some contrariety is through pleasure, others through sorrow. Through pleasure: such as a person who, in committing a vice, rejoices over virtue <note>perhaps meaning the subversion of it</note>. Through sorrow: such as one who has grief for things committed. ¶ Contrariety has three different modes as was said in its own chapter in the first part of the first distinction. ¶ Contrariety whose mode is against concordance, and vice versa: as appears in the chapter on concordance and in the chapter on contrariety in the first part of the first distinction. ¶ Contrariety by reason of its origin is naturally innate: as all natural contrarieties contain within themselves; however, moral contrariety is a habit acquired by a person, as was said above. ¶ Contrariety is a middle point, and this in two ways: namely naturally and morally. Naturally, such as heating which contradicts cooling, and vice versa. Morally, such as acting well: this is because one person who acts well and another who acts poorly are in a certain way opposed through contrariety. ¶ Contrariety is never in itself at rest: because if it were, its rest would be perfect, and thus contrariety with perfection would agree with non-being; and being with non-being, which is impossible. ¶ Of contrarieties, one is greater, another lesser. Greater, such as vice against virtue. Lesser, such as heating against cooling. ¶ Contrariety in one way agrees with equality, in another way not: as is evident in the four elements. Absolutely it does not agree with equality: as in virtue and sin, which have no agreement. ¶ Contrariety always agrees with minority <note>the state of being "lesser"</note> by reason of its kind. The reason for this is: because it inclines being toward non-being. ¶ And therefore, he who pricks more, pricks through it, is more pricked, and placed in danger and tribulation, and distanced from patience. And from such contrariety, may Almighty God wish to deliver us.

### On the Principle deduced through the principles.

The Principle <note>original: *Principium*, meaning the beginning or source of all things</note> is good through goodness, and goodness through the reason of the principle acquires the name of "principle." Since whatever is capable of being made good as a "bonifier" exists through the reason of goodness. And therefore, to begin <term>principiare|the act of a Principle exercising its function</term> what is good, is good. And goodness is the reason and principle for a good thing to do good. And if a good man does not do good: he does evil, because it is against his own reason, and against the reason of the good principle. ¶ The Principle is great through greatness. Since whatever is capable of being begun or has been begun is under the reason of the principle. And because so many and such great things are capable of being begun and have been begun: therefore the principle is great. However, it is not great if it does not begin something great, since it is able to begin something great. # On the mixing of principles and rules.

<column-break/>

A **beginning** <note>original: "principium"; in Llull's system, this refers to the source or origin of an action or being</note> is a principal virtue: and if in the subject in which they exist, the acts of "beginning" and "giving virtue" are hindered, then the beginning and the virtue are not the same. ¶ A beginning is true through **truth**: and if it is identical with truth, and eternity is identical with truth, it is necessary that in that very beginning there exist the acts of beginning, verifying, and eternizing. ¶ Through **glory**, a beginning is glorious and delightful: and if it were interchangeable with glory, then to be glorious and to act as a beginning are necessarily interchangeable. ¶ A beginning is clear and unconfused through **difference**: and if the beginning is the **intellect**, then "beginning" and "understanding" are interchangeable: and difference establishes that one is the "understander" and the other the "understood"; one the "beginner" and the other the "begun." Otherwise, beginning and intellect could not be distinguished from confusion.

<margin>Difference</margin>
¶ A beginning, through **concordance**, has a nature of according, which it could not have without concordance: and the "beginning-maker," the "able-to-be-begun," and the "act of beginning" would be of the essence of the beginning. ¶ **Contrariety** is against a beginning when it hinders its act, namely "beginning": but in a subject in which the beginning is identical with **power**, contrariety cannot hinder the beginning from being begun. Since it has nothing with which it might have power, which is of the genus of power. ¶ A beginning goes toward the **end** through the **middle**, without which middle it could not go to the end: and when the middle is hindered, the power of the beginning and the end fails: and the appetite suffers, and sadness and labor follow: but when **goodness**, **greatness**, and **duration** supervene, power is multiplied and the hindrance is destroyed. ¶ A beginning rests through the end, and it could not rest through the end without the act of beginning: but when the "beginner" believes it finds rest in the "begun" (which is of its essence) through the act of beginning (which is an accident), it cannot: and in this step it appears that God alone is the beginning and the rest.

# On the mixing of principles and rules.

<margin>Greatness</margin>
The product itself is placed within the substantial species of goodness and majority. ¶ Majority is great, and some magnitude is greater; from which it follows that it is a substance: for if it were not greater, a substance could not be "more great" through an accident <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself, while an "accident" is a quality (like color or size) that only exists in a substance.</note>.
<margin>Duration</margin>
¶ Majority lasts through duration, and duration is greater through substance: for if not, an accident would endure by itself and not through a substance; and a greater thing could be greater through minority rather than majority, which is impossible.
<margin>Power</margin>
¶ Majority is able to exist and act through power, and power can be greater through majority; from which it follows that majority and power can be substantial parts in the subject in which they exist.
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
¶ Majority is knowable through wisdom, and thus it is a substantial object. If majority were not knowable through itself but only through an accident, it would be impossible. Majority is lovable through the will, so that the will, through majority, can have a greater object.
<margin>Will</margin>
<margin>Virtue</margin>
¶ Majority is the image of the immensity of virtue; from which it follows that some majority is a subject <note>i.e., a fundamental reality</note>: for if not, it could not be the image of the immensity of virtue, because an accident could not suffice for this, since an accident implies minority, and substance implies majority.
<margin>Truth</margin>
¶ Majority is true through truth, and truth is greater through truth; from which it follows that some truth is substantial: because if not, it could not be greater than an accident, nor could majority be true through substantial truth.
<margin>Glory</margin>
¶ Majority is delightful through glory, and glory has greater delight through majority; therefore, it is necessary to grant some substantial majority, so that there may be greater glory through substance than through accident.
<margin>Difference</margin>
¶ Majority is unconfused through difference, which distinguishes between substantial and accidental majority; without this distinction, majority would be confused.
<margin>Concordance</margin>
¶ Without concordance, majority could not be the image of immensity, virtue, magnitude, etc. This concordance posits that some majority exists as a subject in its being and acting.
<margin>Contrariety</margin>
¶ Majority overcomes a lesser contrariety with a greater concordance; however, majority with a greater contrariety could not overcome a greater concordance. The reason for this is that majority belongs to its own genus. ¶ And in this passage, it appears in what manner sinners sin who bear guilt, because virtues are positively greater and vices are privatively smaller <note>The author argues that good has a "substantial" reality (majority), while evil is a "privation" or lack of that reality (minority).</note>.
<margin>Principle</margin>
¶ Majority is a principle by reason of being a principle; and a principle, through majority, has the character of a substance. If it did not, it could not be "greater" to the point that a principle is so great it can be no more; it must have in itself coessential parts from which it is made. For if it could be greater potentially and not actually, then a greater majority could exist in potentiality than in act, which is impossible.

<column-break/>

¶ Majority without a medium coessential to itself—namely, "to majorize" <note>original: "maiorificare" - a technical term meaning the act of making or being greater</note>—could not exist in its own genus; nor could the medium be a substantial being without majority.
<margin>Middle</margin>
¶ Majority causes greater rest; from which it follows that some end is substantial by reason of absolute majority: since God is not made in respect to minority, but in respect to the being of majority. The reason for this is so that God may be separated from pride, envy, and the like.
<margin>End</margin>
¶ Majority without equality could not be the image of immensity, goodness, magnitude, and so forth, because it would have nothing with which it relates; therefore, it has things equal and coessential to itself: namely, the "majorizer," the "majorizable," and the act of "majorizing."
<margin>Equality</margin>
¶ Majority and minority are opposed in the subject in which they exist respectively, just as substance and accident are; however, not naturally, because substance and accident agree in constituting one term, such as a body. Therefore, majority by itself agrees with "being," and minority with "non-being." Nevertheless, some majority agrees with non-being, because it causes sin or corruption.

### On Equality deduced through the Principles.

<margin>On Equality deduced through the Principles.</margin>
Good equality is the reason for a good thing to act equally for the good. And this definition is the fountain from which natural and moral justice arises.
<margin>Great</margin>
¶ Equality is great through magnitude; and magnitude, by reason of equality, has things equal and coessential to itself within it. Indeed, equality could not be great through magnitude without a "co-equating" nature through the "co-equater," the "co-equatable," and the act of "co-equating," which are coessential and natural to it.
<margin>Duration</margin>
¶ Equality lasts through duration, because that which endures suffices for that which is co-equative, for it makes the co-equatable and the act of co-equating endure. And if equality and eternity were the same in lower things as they are in the Eternal, then "co-equating" and "eternalizing" would endure in them from eternity without the corruption of one and the generation of another; which is impossible <note>The author distinguishes between the perfect equality of God and the changing equality found in the physical world.</note>.

# Part Eight

->**Equality**<-

<margin>Power</margin>
Equality is capable through power, and power through equality possesses within itself things coequal and coessential to it. Thus, in the subject in which they exist, they cause "co-equaling" and "being able." If these were the same in lower beings <note>i.e., in the physical world as opposed to the divine</note>, they would necessarily cause co-equaling and being able to such an extent that they would eliminate all inequalities from the world; everything would be equal and equally powerful, which is impossible. In this step, it appears how one impossibility leads to another.

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
Equality is knowable through wisdom; and because wisdom is great through greatness, and equality is likewise, it follows by necessity that equality exists in act through coessential, coequal, and coequatable things, and the act of co-equaling. If equality is the same as the intellect, it follows that in it there is always co-equaling and understanding.

<margin>Will</margin>
Equality is lovable through the will; the reason for this is so that the will can possess these things through the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving. Because will and equality are great through greatness, powerful through power, and resting through the end <note>the final purpose</note>, they exist in act by necessity.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
Equality is virtuous through virtue; and virtue through equality possesses within itself equal things. Therefore, in this step, it appears that the virtues are coequatable, and that co-equating is virtuous.

<margin>Truth</margin>
Equality is true through truth; because it could not receive the habit of truth without its own nature, it must imprint its habit and nature upon truth, so that truth, by reason of equality, possesses within itself coequal and coessential things.

<margin>Glory</margin>
Equality is delightful through glory, and glory is coequatable through equality. Therefore, in glory, the one glorifying delights in co-equaling to himself the glorified and the glorifiable.

<margin>Difference</margin>
Equality, through difference, is a clear, demonstrative, and unconfused reason. The reason for this is that difference establishes that one is the "co-equaler," another the "coequatable," and another the "co-equaling" <note>the act itself</note>. But if difference were removed from equality, equality would be emptied of clarity and would be overshadowed and filled with darkness.

<margin>Concordance</margin>
Equality, through concordance, possesses concordant things; and concordance, through equality, possesses co-equaling things. If they are interchangeable, they are always permanent through co-equaling and concording.

<margin>Contrariety</margin>
Contrariety and equality cannot act as principles together. Equality and contrariety are not friends, because equality and concordance are friends; in this step, it appears that justice arises from equality and concordance, while injury <note>injustice</note> arises from contrariety and inequality.

<margin>Principle</margin>
Equality is a principle by the nature of a principle; and a principle, by reason of

<column-break/>

equality, possesses within itself things equal and coessential to it. If they are interchangeable, they are always permanent through "principling" <note>acting as a source</note> and co-equaling.

<margin>Medium</margin>
Equality, through the medium <note>the middle point or bridge</note>, has a mediating nature, and the medium, through equality, has a co-equating nature; thus they agree with each other through co-equaling and mediating.

<margin>End</margin>
Equality is the subject in which the end of concordance rests; and in that rest itself is "majority" <note>greatness</note>, so that rest is not without the majority of equality, being utterly distinct from "minority," which is not of the nature of rest.

<margin>Majority</margin>
Equality is greater through majority; and equality, as to its essence and nature, requires things equal and coessential to itself so that it is in every way distinct from minority, its enemy. In this step, it appears how majority outside the soul is a real, natural thing.

<margin>Minority</margin>
Equality and minority are enemies. The reason for this is that where there is equality, there cannot be minority; for if there were, it would destroy equality. Nevertheless, insofar as some equality is less than another along with minority, it has some agreement through which it coincides with non-being.

### Concerning Minority deduced through the Principles.

<margin>Concerning Minority deduced through the Principles.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' with floral/foliage patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc> Minority, through goodness, is not concerned with nothingness, because goodness is always concerned with something; but goodness, through minority, is concerned with nothingness. Therefore, when a good person does not attain the good, he is idle; from goodness, goodness is minor and concerned with nothingness, but this happens by accident.

<margin>Greatness</margin>
Minority is not of the nature of greatness in respect to majority, which is its contrary; yet it is "great" insofar as it is a substance, and it is the substantiating factor of substantial beings, which differ specifically through majority and minority.

<margin>Duration</margin>
Minority lasts through duration in its own kind, which would be impossible if it were of eternity, for eternity is not of the nature of minority. In this step, it appears that the world is not eternal. For if it were, it would be of the nature of eternity; that eternity would be "minor" compared to the eternity of God, just as the goodness of the world is minor compared to the goodness of God.

<margin>Power</margin>
Minority, through power, can be what it is, but not beyond what it is. And so it is regarding its agency.

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
Minority, by reason of wisdom, is knowable; and wisdom, by reason of minority, is minor—I say minor when it is in potential...

# Folio 37.
## On the mixing of principles and rules.

->**[Left Column]**<-

<margin>Will</margin>
Minority <note>Latin: *Minoritas*; refers to the state of being lesser in quantity, quality, or power</note> is not something that acts or remains idle by itself, because being in potentiality and idleness are consistent with a "lesser" state. Truly, actual deeds and active agents are consistent with a "greater" state <note>Latin: *Maioritas*</note>.
<margin>Whether</margin>
¶ Minority through the **will** is lovable, not in the sense that the will directs minority toward itself, but that it loves minority in some object so that it may love majority. For example, in water, the will loves the heat which causes a "lesser" state in the water <note>i.e., reducing its coldness</note>, so that a person may be warmed and bathed by that water.
<margin>Virtue</margin>
¶ Minority through **virtue** <note>or power/potency</note> is virtuous, because virtue restores what the subject of minority possesses through a small quantity; just as a mustard seed has great power through its sharp taste and multiplies into many seeds.
<margin>Truth</margin>
¶ Minority through **truth** is true. The reason for this is that truth truly posits that it is concerned with "non-being," and minority, by diminishing, posits that one truth is lesser than another.
<margin>Glory</margin>
¶ **Glory** through minority is lesser; thus glory through minority is not rest. Rather, glory, by reason of its abundance, would multiply its delight in the subject in which there is minority, unless minority hindered this—and it does hinder it, because it cannot contain great delight within itself.
<margin>Difference</margin>
¶ Minority through **difference** is a clear <note>unconfused</note> reason; but according to its kind, its charity is small.
<margin>Concordance</margin>
¶ Minority participates with **concordance**, as it is constituted from several concordant things. But that concordance is small, because it cannot enter minority with greatness.
<margin>Contrariety</margin>
¶ Minority with **contrariety** is against majority; and minority with contrariety is against minority. In this step, it appears how easily minority can be overcome.
<margin>Principle</margin>
¶ Minority through a **principle** belongs to the nature of a principle; thus it is a principle under which all agents are lesser and of small value.
<margin>Medium</margin>
¶ Minority through the **middle** <note>or medium</note> is capable of being mediated: namely, it is the middle point between equality and majority, through which things tend toward the "non-being" in which they are not, until they pass through minority itself and receive their own nature, and come to nothing.
<margin>End</margin>
¶ Minority, as far as it concerns itself, is less at rest. The reason for this is that it is concerned with non-being; but **majority** knows this, because it is concerned with being, and it makes minority its handmaid.
<margin>Minority</margin>
¶ Minority and majority cannot be the same thing, because majority speaks of "being" and minority of "non-being"; yet they agree well toward one end, like a mistress and a handmaid.
<margin>Equality</margin>
¶ Minority and **equality** cannot be the same in species. The reason for this is that minority stands between equality and non-being, while equality stands between majority and minority.

<column-break/>

### The second part of the eighth principal part, in which the principles are deduced through the rules.

<margin>Second part of the eighth part. The discourse is conducted via commentary on the figures.</margin>
**L**though the principles have been discussed in the third figure through the "chambers" <note>the compartments of the logical machine</note>, here the discourse will be continuous through the **rules**, so that the intellect may have knowledge of everything through the rules in a straight line.

<margin>These principles are general.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, in this part, we intend to prove that every principle is general, so that it may be known that this **General Art** <note>The *Ars Generalis* of Ramon Llull</note> is proven to be general through the aforementioned principles; and likewise for this reason: so that those wishing to "bite" <note>criticize or attack</note> this Art cannot resist the aforementioned principles.

<margin>Against the rivals of this Art.</margin>

These ladders are indeed general and good through Goodness; which Goodness they could not have if General Goodness were lacking.
<margin>Whether Goodness...</margin>

# On the mixture of principles and rules.

fo. xxxviij.

[Greatness] <note>The text refers to the principle of "Magnitude" or "Greatness" from Lull's Art.</note> causes to magnify, or that with which it causes a great magnifying. And this is seen through rule B. <note>Rule B typically asks "Whether?" or "What?"</note>
<margin>in itself</margin> ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does Greatness have in itself? And the answer is that in corporal things it has a signifier, a magnified thing, and a magnifying act, and essentials with which it causes substantial extensions in a subject, from which quantities are caused, with which it measures itself and other principles in the corporal subject in which it exists. But in a spiritual Greatness, it causes great acts: namely, great understanding, remembering, and loving, practiced by spiritual greatness, while that greatness exists in the spiritual principle. And this is the same for spiritual "bonifying" <note>The act of making good</note>, enduring, judging, etc., as is proved by rule B.
<margin>in another</margin> ¶ Further, through the third species: what is Greatness in another? And it must be said that it is a form forming a great formed thing and a great materialized thing: as was signified through the first species of D.
<margin>in another</margin> ¶ Furthermore, through the fourth species it is asked: what does Greatness have in another? The answer is that it has a great action and passion <note>In the philosophical sense of "undergoing" or "receiving" an action</note> in the great subject in which it exists, with which it is natural. And this was signified through the first rule of D.
<margin>D: of what, from what, etc.</margin> ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: of what is Greatness? The answer is that it is of itself, so that it may be primary in the act of magnifying: for if it did not magnify, it would not have that of which it was; nor consequently would there be a magnified thing, which is impossible: this, however, is evident through rule B.
<margin>from what</margin> ¶ Through the second species it is asked: from what is Greatness? And the answer is that it is from its natural correlatives <note>The internal components of a principle: the active, the passive, and the act itself</note> signified in the second species of C.
<margin>whose it is</margin> ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: whose is it? And the answer is that it belongs to the subject in which it exists: because the subject acts with it in itself naturally or morally. And this was signified through rule B.
<margin>E: why it is</margin> ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why is Greatness? And the answer is through the second species of rule C, because it is from a magnifier, a magnifiable thing, and a magnifying; by reason of which Greatness has the nature of existing as that which it is.
<margin>for what reason</margin> ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is Greatness? And the answer is: so that other principles may be great through it. And this is signified in the figure through all the other chambers in which C <note>C represents Greatness in Lull's symbolic alphabet</note> is present.
<margin>F: how much</margin> ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: how great is Greatness? And the answer is that it is as great as its essence is continuous in the subject, designated by the scale of the third figure through B-C and C-D up to the chamber C-K.
¶ Through the second species it is asked: how great is Greatness? And the answer is that it is as great as it can receive from its correlatives signified through the second species of C. And likewise concerning the habits of greatness flowed from it, sustained, situated, and numbered in the first and second figure.

<column-break/>

¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked: of what sort is Greatness? And the answer is that it is such as it is through the first species of rule C and the first and second of D, E, and F. And rule B testifies to this.
<margin>G: of what sort (Proper/Appropriated)</margin>
¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: of what sort is Greatness? And the answer is: such as are its habits, diffused and discoursed in the third figure through the scale B-C and C-D up to C-K.
<margin>H: when</margin>
¶ Through the first species of H, it is asked: when is Greatness? And the answer is that it is then when its subject is, in which it is sustained and joined. And it is provable through the scale of the third figure constituted by B-C and C-D up to C-K: in which scale all fifteen species of rule H are implicated, since greatness in motion consists in time, and time in it: but to explain this would be very long; rather, it belongs to the artist who knows this art.
<margin>I: where</margin>
¶ Through all species of rule I, it is asked: where is Greatness? And the answer is that it is with all species of I in the chambers designated in the third figure. And through the art, it is applicable to the purpose of a person looking upon and knowing this art.
<margin>K: in what way / with what</margin>
¶ It is asked through the species of the first rule K: in what way is Greatness? And the answer is that it is through that mode which it has in rules C, D, E, F, G, H, and I, as signified in the scale of the third figure.
¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked through all species: with what is it? And the answer is that it is with its correlatives signified in the second species of C. And it is with the first and second species of rules D, E, F, G, H, and I, and with the first modal, without which it cannot be that which it is.
¶ Furthermore, it is with other principles, without which it could not be that which it is; nor would it have the nature which it has in itself and in others. And that which has been said is known through itself and is also confirmed through B.
¶ We have spoken of Greatness discoursed through the rules, by reason of which it has been shown in what way the human intellect has a very general subject for attaining many and great operations caused and deduced by Greatness into the subject in which they are. And therefore, since it is so, what wonder is it if through this general art the human intellect is very general for causing great and many sciences, easily discovered.

### On power deduced through the rules.

<margin>Whether power is deduced through the rules.</margin>
It is asked whether there is any infinite power? And it must be answered that there is. And this is attested through the chapter on eternity. For if there were no infinite power, then eternity, which is infinite, would have nothing with which it could be infinite; and this is proven through rule B. Likewise, through the third species of rule D: for unless there were infinite power, it would follow that a finite power could prevent it from being. Whence it would follow that power would be a privative habit <note>A "privative habit" is a state defined by the absence of a quality, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note> subjected to a finite and positive habit, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked through the first species of rule C: what is infinite power? And it must be answered that it is a being to whom "to be able infinitely" properly belongs. And this was seen through the first species of rule D. And also rule B bears witness to this. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does infinite power have in itself? And it must be said that it has natural and essential relations with which it can well be that which it is. And this is demonstrable through rule B and through the second and third rules of D. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is power in another? And it must be said that it is a being causing actions and passions in a subject, by reason of which the subject can have actions and passions: and this is affirmable through rule B. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does power have in another? And it must be said that it has actions just as a cause has in an effect, and it has passions in the subject in which it is, the power itself being clothed <note>original: "habituata"</note> with goodness and magnitude, etc. And this was seen through rule B. ¶ Through the first species of rule D it is asked: from what is power? It must be said that it is from itself, because it is a general principle. And this is provable through rule B. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: from what is power? It must be said that it is from the *power-er*, the *power-able*, and the *act of powering*. <note>original: "possificante, possificabili & possificare." These are Lullian neologisms describing the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle.</note> And this is provable through the second species of C. ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: whose is the power? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is: which indeed acts upon the patient <note>The "patient" is the entity receiving the action.</note> with its power. And this is evident in itself. ¶ Through the first species of rule E it is asked: why is there power? It must be said that it is because it is from the *power-er*, the *power-able*, and the *act of powering*: but accidentally it is a habit in the subject in which it is: just as whiteness exists because its subject is white. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species it is asked: why is there power? It must be said so that other principles may have existence and agency through it. ¶ Through the first species of rule F it is asked: how great is the power? It must be said that it is as great as can enter its own nature: and this is manifest through the second species of C: so that from them there is one continuous existence. And to this, rule B and the first and second species of rule D bear witness. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: how great is the power? It must be said that it is as great as its discrete correlates seen through the second species of rule C, and through the first of G, and through rule B. ¶ Through the first species of rule G it is asked: what kind of power is it? It must be said that it is such as is the proper passion <note>In logic, a "proper passion" is a characteristic uniquely and necessarily following from a thing's essence.</note> of the subject: such as the infinity and eternity of God, without which God could not be that which He is. ¶ Likewise, through the second species it is asked: what kind of power is it? It must be said that it is such as is the habit in the subject, like goodness or magnitude, which can be what they are through power; and a judge can be [a judge] through power. And this is manifest through rule B. ¶ It is asked through all species of rule H: when is power? And it must be said through the first species of the rule that it is then when its definition is. And through the second of the same, it is then when it has correlates coessential to itself. ¶ Further, through the third, it is then when it is a habit in a subject. ¶ Furthermore, through the fourth of the same, it is then when it has actions and passions in a subject. ¶ And through the first species of rule D, it is then when time can exist through power and through motion, and motion in time. ¶ Further, through the second of D, it is then when it is from its correlates. ¶ Furthermore, through the third of D, it is then when it is the instrument of the subject in which it is. ¶ And through the first species of the modal rule, it is then when it has its mode through itself. In medieval philosophy, this refers to a stable disposition or "habit" of the soul, like a skill or a moral character trait.</note> in time and in motion. For difference abstracts the habit from all other habits, and property establishes that it is the specific habit of the intellect: so that through the second species of rule C, any relative term may be habituated in another, and all its relative terms may be mutually habituated in one habit; and this is clear through rule B and through all species of rule K. ¶ Through all species of rule K, it is asked: **With what is wisdom?** It must be said that it is with its correlative foundations, so that they themselves may be habituated. And it is with the act of goodness, because it is good. And it is with the act of truth, because it is true. And it is with the act of power, for it is possible. And it is with the act of will, since it is desirable. And it is with the act of virtue, for it is virtuous. And it is with the act of glory, for it is indeed delightful.

### On the Will, deduced through the rules.

<margin>whether</margin>
<margin>On the Will, deduced through the rules.</margin>
<margin>what</margin>
<margin>in itself</margin>
<margin>in itself</margin>
It is asked: **Whether the will is immortal?** And the answer is yes, as to its essence: because it is not composed of contrary relatives, as is clear through the second species of rules C, D, and E. Nevertheless, it is mortal when it is habituated by sin, because it deviates from the second species of E; and to this, rule B bears witness. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: **What is the will?** And the answer is that it is a being to which "willing" and "not-willing" <note>original: "velle et nolle"</note> belong, so that through the second species of rule E, it might be at rest. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **What does the will have naturally in itself?** And the answer is that it has the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving <note>The "Lullian Trinity" of the will: amantem, amatum, amare</note> constituted from its own relation; and this substantially, with which it habituates itself with a good habit or a bad one, and with a great or a small one; and this morally. And this is proven by rule B.

¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: **Why is there a will?** And the answer is: because it is constituted from its natural correlatives. Morally, however, it exists because in the subject in which it is, it is clothed in its habit, just as a cloaked man is clothed in his cloak. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **Why is there a will?** The answer is so that beings may be lovable or loved: for without the will, they could not be objects in relation to the category of the will. And thus "rest" would be emptied of goodness and greatness, which is impossible; and this is clear through rule B.
¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: **How great is the will?** And the answer is that it is as great as its essence, differing from all others. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **How great is it?** And the answer is that it is as great as it is from its essential relatives from which it is designated through the second species of rules C, D, and E. And this is proven by rule B. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked: **What kind is the will properly?** And the answer is that it is a proper substantial passion in the subject in which it is: just as a man cannot exist without his will. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **What kind is it by appropriation?** And the answer is that it is good through a good habit, or evil through an evil habit, with which the will clothes itself to will well or poorly. And this is clear through rule B.

# Part Eight

<margin>
L: Where
c, d, k
</margin>
Where is the will? It must be answered that it exists both subjectively and objectively when it is led through all the species of c, d, and k <note>In Lullian logic, these letters refer to specific principles: c (Greatness), d (Duration), and k (Difference)</note>. In this matter, it is not necessary to explain further: for it is clear enough to an intellect that observes well and is practiced in this Art. And this has been proven through the rule of b, e, f, and g. ¶ Through all the species of rule i <note>Rule I usually concerns "When"</note>, it is asked: where is the will? And it must be answered through all the species of that same rule that it is in the subject in which it exists subjectively and objectively. And this is clear enough to one who looks closely at rules e, f, g, and h.

<margin>
R: In what manner
</margin>
¶ Through all the species of the rule of modality <note>Rule R: "How?"</note>, it is asked: in what manner does the will exist subjectively and objectively? And it must be answered that it exists through that mode by which it was discussed through all the other rules and their species, as was clearly seen. To recount this, however, would be very tedious; therefore, we leave it to the practitioner of this Art.

<margin>
K: With what
</margin>
¶ Through all the species of instrumentality <note>Rule K: "With what?"</note>, it is asked: with what does the will exist? We leave this answer to the reader of this Art, who can find the answer in the chapter on Wisdom in the final paragraph. ¶ But here it is asked: with what does the will "objectify" its object? <note>The term "obiectat" refers to the act of the will turning something into an object of desire or thought.</note> It must be answered: with its freedom, which is indeed an innate habit <term>habit: a stable disposition or quality of the soul</term> within it. Furthermore, it objectifies with its relatives <note>Lullian "relatives" are the internal components of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving</note>: because the "willer," joined with the sensitive and imaginative faculties, extracts and brings forth foreign species from things perceived by the senses and the imagination. It imprints these upon its own pleasure; once imprinted, things "willable" are generated and arise through desire, and things "hatable" through anger. This occurs in the intrinsic act of willing, from which arises a foreign "willing" or "nilling" <note>nolle: the act of "not-willing" or rejection</note> by accident. And in this step, it appears that "nilling" is not of the essence of the will, because it is caused by irascibility <note>anger or the "irascible" faculty</note>. This irascibility is the opposite of "willability." In this step, the understanding is very profound.

### Concerning Truth deduced through the rules.

<margin>and truth deduced through rule B</margin>
<margin>what</margin>
<margin>if it [converts] with itself</margin>
<margin>according to itself</margin>
It is asked: whether created truth converts with its own truth? It must be answered that it does not: because if so, it would be too similar to the truth of God: which indeed converts with its own unity. And further, it would convert with goodness, greatness, duration, etc., by reason of which it would extend itself outside of time and place, which is impossible. And this is evident through rule B. ¶ Through the first species of rule C <note>the rule of Greatness</note> it is asked: **what** is truth? And it must be answered that it is an incorruptible being. For if it were corruptible, a contradiction would be implied: namely, that it would be and would not be: which contradiction is impossible. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does truth

<column-break/>

have in itself essentially and naturally? And it must be answered that it has its correlatives without which it cannot be: in which and with which all things are verifiable: and outside its essence no being can be true: as was seen through the first species of D. ¶ Further, <margin>in another</margin> through the third species it is asked: what does truth have in another? And it must be answered that it has the "habit" <note>a stable quality or disposition</note> with which it verifies the subject in which it is. ¶ Through <margin>D: of what? Primary</margin> the first species of rule D it is asked: **of what** is truth? And it must be answered that it is of itself: so that falsehood, which is its contrary, may not be lying before it: and so that it might be able to rest in its own essence: and this was seen through the second species of rule C. ¶ Through the second species <margin>Material</margin> it is asked: **of what things** is it? And it must be said that it is of its correlatives: otherwise it would not be the foundation of its habit with which it passes over to verifying other principles. ¶ Through the <margin>Possessive</margin> third species it is asked: truth being a habit, **whose** is it? And it must be answered that it is of its substantial foundation in which it is sustained: and this is evident through rule B. ¶ Through <margin>E: why? Existing, Acting</margin> the first species of rule E it is asked: **why** is truth? To which it must be answered: because it is from its substantial correlatives. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **why** is truth? And it must be answered: so that other principles may be verifiable through truth itself. ¶ Through <margin>F: how much? Co-measuring</margin> the first species of rule f it is asked: **how great** is truth? And it must be answered that it is as great as the other principles verified through truth itself. ¶ Through the <margin>Distinguishing</margin> second species it is asked: **how great** is truth? To which it must be answered that it is so great as it is habituated by its own proper habit with which <margin>G: of what kind? Proper, Appropriated</margin> it causes foreign acts. ### On Difference deduced through the rules.

<margin>whether</margin>
<margin>On Difference deduced through the rules.</margin>

**W**hether Difference is a general and real principle? And we say that it is: as is evident through Rule B: for if not, the world would not naturally consist of its parts, which are naturally primitive through Difference, and concordant through Concordance, and contrariating through primitive Contrariety. These could not exist without primitive Difference, without which the world would be emptied of primitive concordances and contrarieties: and also in the second species of Rule E, and natural appetite and rest: and all things would indeed want to be numerically the same, and thus the world would not be what it is. It is concluded, therefore, that the affirmative of the question is to be held. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C <margin>what it is formally</margin> it is asked: what is Difference? It must be answered that it is the cause of many beings through its act, namely, *to differ*. And this is proven through Rule B and through the "ladder of difference" placed in the Second Figure, or in the Third from chamber B. C. all the way to chamber B. K., in which Difference is discoursed <margin>what it is substantially</margin> and diffused by causing many things. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does it have in itself naturally and essentially? And it must be answered that it has

<column-break/>

its correlatives: namely, the *differing*, the *differentiated*, and the *act of differing*, without which it cannot exist; with which it contains in itself all its species differing among themselves. ¶ Further, through the third species it is asked: what does Difference have in another? <margin>it is in another</margin> And it must be said that it is a being having in its essential "differentiable" foreign differences with which it causes plurality habited by that very Difference. ¶ Further, through <margin>it has in another</margin> the fourth species it is asked: what does Difference have in another? And it must be said that it has plurality thus habited by itself, just as coals are habited by heat; and this is shown through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of D <margin>From what, where, Primitive</margin> it is asked: from what is primitive Difference? And it must be answered that it is from itself: for if not, all things would desire to be one and the same in number, which is impossible. For I do not desire to be you, <margin>Materially</margin> nor a stone etc., nor vice versa. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species it is asked: of what things is Difference? And it must be answered that it is of the *differing*, the *differentiable*, and the *act of differing*: which are indeed co-substantial to it, with which it makes all things differ with its own habit, which without it would not be existing through themselves: nor would they have a foundation: nor could substance and accident differ. ¶ Through the third <margin>Of what</margin> species it is asked: whose is Difference? And we say that Difference existing is the habit of substantial difference: and all things are provable through Rule B. ¶ Through the <margin>Wherefore, Formal existence</margin> first species of Rule E it is asked: why is Difference formally? And it must be answered: because it is from its co-essential relatives. ¶ Further, through the second <margin>They act finally</margin> species it is asked: why is Difference finally <note>original: "finaliter" (referring to the 'final cause' or purpose)</note>? And it must be answered: so that there may be many things which cannot exist without it. And if the world were deprived of the aforesaid Difference, it would indeed be emptied and annihilated: because it would not be, nor would it have an end. ¶ Through the first species of F it is asked: <margin>How much, Continuous</margin> how great is Difference? And it must be said that there are two most general differences: one of which is substantial, causing substantial differences that differ substantially, because Difference diffuses itself in them by reason of mixture. ¶ There is also another habitual difference with which substantial Difference makes principles differ from one another. <margin>Discrete</margin> ¶ Further, through the second species: how great is Difference? To which it must be said that it is as great as quantity extends itself in its correlatives: for just as Difference habits quantity by containing it in its genus, so quantity measures Difference by containing it in its genus. And this can be seen through Rule B.

¶ Through the rule of Modality <note>Rule K</note>, it is asked: in what manner is difference? And it must be answered: that it is through that manner which it has in its correlatives <note>term: correlatives (original: "correlativa") — Llull's theory that every principle has an active, passive, and verbal form (e.g., Differing, Differed, and to Differ)</note>, and also through that manner which it has in clothing other principles with itself. For just as a man has a manner of writing by moving his hand, and with his hand moving the letters, and with the pen moving the ink, and with the motion of the ink moving and shaping the letters; so difference has its manner by way of differentiating one thing from another substantially. And this is demonstrable through all species of the rules.

<margin>

</margin>
¶ Through the rule of Instrumentality <note>Rule L</note>, it is asked: difference is with what? And it must be answered: that it is with its relatives, with its habit <note>term: habit (original: "habitus") — a state of being or "clothing" of a substance</note> with which it clothes other principles by diversifying them; and also with goodness, greatness, etc., and with motion, quantity, quality, etc. Without these principles, difference cannot exist, and with difference itself, the principles are what they are; for if difference were taken away, the principles would certainly not be what they are.

### Concerning Concordance deduced through the rules.

¶ Through rule B <note>Rule B refers to "Possibility" or "Whether a thing exists"</note>, it is asked: whether **concordance** is substantial? For if concordance were not substantial without substances, the whole essence of form and the whole essence of matter would not be concordant to constitute a third substantial thing. And thus that third substantial thing would be an emptying of the whole mixture and composition, which is impossible. It is concluded, therefore, that concordance is a substantial part in the subject in which it exists; and this is evident through rule B.

Just as a crystal placed upon a green subject receives a green color from it, and upon a red one, a red color: so concordance placed in Goodness receives one mode, and in Magnitude another mode, etc. Similarly, this can be said of the species of the rules; and this is plain in itself. ¶ Through the rule of Instrumentality, it is asked: with what is concordance? # Eighth Part

<margin>G: What kind of Property</margin>
"Being ignited" and "to ignite" belong to the habituated state itself: and this is to be seen through Rule B <note>Rule B usually refers to the question "Whether it is?"</note>. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: what kind of contrariety is it? And it must be answered that it is the **proper passion** <note>A "passion" in this context is a property or attribute that follows from the essence of a thing</note> of the subject: just as the contrariety of the world is innate. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what kind of contrariety is it appropriately? It must be said that it is an **appropriated passion** in the subject in which it exists: just as a sinner who habituates himself to sin against virtue: and likewise deafness, sadness, and the like. And this is made manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through all species of Rule H, it is asked: when is there contrariety? It must be said that it exists then when the subject is habituated by it. Furthermore, it is then when its subject is practical modally and instrumentally. And this is seen through itself. ¶ Through all species of Rule I, it is asked: where is contrariety? And it must be said that it is in the species where it has its action, such as in an elemental body during generation and corruption. And it is between "willing" and "not-willing," and it is between good and evil, and it is in all privative habits. And this is evident through itself. ¶ Through the Modal Rule <note>Rule J</note>, it is asked: how is there contrariety? And it must be answered that contrariety has a mode by imposing one contrary upon another, so that it expels **concordance** from the subject in which it is; and it has a privative mode by depriving and "con-flicting" with "con-cording," and it has a mode of hindering the end. And it has a mode of multiplying by persevering, and the like. And this is provable through itself. ¶ Through the Rule of Mentality <note>Rule K</note>, it is asked: with what is there contrariety? And it must be said that it is with mixed contrarieties in the subject in which they are, and it is with privative habits. For just as concordance is a matter of "being" with its substantial correlatives, so contrariety is a cause of "not-being" with its accidental correlatives: and just as concordance with generation produces "being," so contrariety with the deviation of the end causes "not-being" and the like.
