### Concerning the Principle, deduced through the rules.

<margin>B: Whether. Deduction of the principle through the rules.</margin>
<margin>C: What it is in itself / What it has in itself</margin>
Through Rule B, the question arises: whether it is a substantial principle? And it must be answered that it is. Because if not, substance would not belong to the genus of "principle," but would be a primitive accident; and thus substance would not be existing through itself, but through an accident: which is against the species of Rule D and E, and Rule B. Therefore, etc. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: what is a principle? And it must be said that it is a being outside of which no being can begin <note>original: "principiare"</note>. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does it have essentially in itself? And it must be answered that it has its substantial correlatives, in which all foreign principles are "principled" <note>derived from the principle</note>. ¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: what is it in another? It must be answered that the principle which is the **agent** is in the "principled" as the actor, and the "principled" is in the "principant" as the **patient** <note>the receiver of action</note>, and both are joined in the act of "principating." And the principle which is a **habit** is in the substantial principle habituated by it, and in the "principled" there is motion. ¶ Likewise, through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? It must be answered that the principle existing formally has action in matter, and matter has passion from it, and from the agent it has mobility, and in the end, rest; and this is manifest through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: from what is the principle? And it must be said that it is from itself, so that it can be primitive, otherwise it would not be a general principle. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what things is it? And it must be said that it is from the efficient form, matter, and end. An accidental principle, however, is from similarity substantially, and they together compose a corporal principle through quantity (how much) and through quality (what kind) and the like. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species, it is asked: whose is it? It must be answered that the principle existing as a habit belongs to the principle existing substantially: just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man. And all these are necessary, as is to be seen through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: why is there a principle? And it must be said in two ways. In the first way: it is because it is constituted of the "principant," the "principled," and the "principating." In the second way: it is an accidental principle because the substantial principle is habituated by it. And in this step, the intellect creates science, and also recognizes the demonstrations of "why" <note>propter quid</note> and "that" <note>quia</note> from which they arise. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: why is it so finally <note>regarding its purpose</note>? And it must be said: so that other principles may be subordinated under it, which is the most general. And this is plain of itself. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: how great is the principle? And it must be answered that it is as great as its essence is: as is manifest through the middle of the extremities. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: how much is it? And it must be answered that it is as great as its correlatives are, through the difference of dominion and through the concordance of the concording. And they are the same by essence. And this is proven through Rule B. And of this we have experience in man, in whom the elemental is one principle, the vegetative another, the sensitive another, the imaginative another, and the reasoning another. And all five under the number five are one man. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: what kind of principle is it? And it must be said that the **proper principle** is the most general one which we investigate; the **appropriated** is a foreign principle, acquired and subordinated: as signified by the second species of Rule G—

# On the mixing of principles and rules.
## fo. xliiii.
<margin>Rule H: When?</margin>
Through all species of Rule H, it is asked: **When is the beginning?** And it must be answered that it was then when its <term>correlatives</term><note>In Lullian logic, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving.</note> existed, with which it is most general; and it was then when the subordinate principles existed, such as Being, Quality, etc., which are the <term>Categories</term><note>The Aristotelian Predicaments.</note>; and it is also then when there is a "course" under which there are the mover, the movable, and the acts of moving; and these are passing from one "now" into another successively through one place, and from one "now" into another "now" through another place, generating motion with a turned course; and this is plain through all species of Rule H. ¶ Through all species of Rule I, it is asked: **Where is the beginning?** And it must be answered that it is in its correlatives because it exists within them; and it is in all subordinate principles, just as a cause is in its effect; and it is in motion, because it is habituated by it; and it is in position, because it is situated within it; and this is both modally and instrumentally; and this is provable through Rule B. ¶ Through the Rule of Modality, it is asked: **How is the beginning?** And it must be answered that it is a causal beginning by way of the correlatives from which it is made; and it is a habitual beginning by the way which a causal beginning has in habituating other foreign principles with its own habit, so that they may be principles, by multiplying its own likenesses within them; and this is seen through itself. ¶ Through all species of the Rule of Instrumentality, it is asked: **With what is the beginning?** And it must be answered that it is with its correlatives from which it is made, and it is with its own nature without which it cannot exist; and the principles which are general are with the most general substantial principle in which they are situated; and this is manifest through the second species of Rule C.

### On the Middle deduced through the rules.

<margin>
Whether
</margin>

<margin>
On the Middle deduced through the rules.
</margin>

**Whether** in the substance of the world it is possible to grant one most general **Middle**? And it must be answered that yes, otherwise there would be no subordinate "middles," and thus the world would be emptied of the middle that is <term>continuative</term>, <term>mensurative</term><note>measuring</note>, and <term>conjunctive</term>; nor would Concordance have any being; nor would the Beginning have a subject through which it might pass to the End in which it might rest; and thus there would be no motion; and many other inconveniences would follow, which is impossible, as is evident through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: **What is the Middle?** And it must be said that it is the subject in which the Beginning and the End meet one another and join themselves together, so that the Beginning may rest in the End; and the most general Middle is the cause of all bodily middles.

<column-break/>

<margin>
What it has in itself
</margin>
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **What does the Middle have in itself essentially?** And it must be said that it has its correlatives, namely: to join, and to apply and continue extremity with extremity, as is signified in Angle F in the second figure. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **What is the Middle in another?** And it must be answered that it is the junction in form and matter, as "to ignite" in fire; and it is "to heat" in heat; and "to vegetate" in a plant; and "to sense" in a sense; and "to imagine" in the imaginative faculty; and "to reason" in the reasoning faculty; and "to move" in motion; and "to generate" in generation, and such like. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **What does it have in another?** And it must be answered that it has the "habit" from which it is habituated, and with which it causes secondary acts which are not of its own kind; and all these things are manifest through Rule C. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: **Of what is the Middle constituted?** And it must be answered that it is of itself, so that it may be a general principle by itself. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **From what things is it?** And it must be answered that it is from the essence of form and matter in which it exists; and it is from motion and such like. ¶ Furthermore, through the third species, it is asked: **Whose is the Middle?** And it must be answered that it belongs to the whole subject in which it is; and this is evident by itself and is proved through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: **To what is the Middle formally related?** That it is constituted of its correlatives, as is manifest through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **Why is there a Middle finally <note>i.e., regarding its final cause or purpose</note>?** And it is said that it is so that subjects may be full and continuous, and so that the Categories may have secondary acts, just as substance "sustentates" <note>supports</note>, and quantity "measures"; and thus the agent acts, and the mover moves; and so of the rest in their own way, just as lines "linearize" etc., without which acts the powers could not be at rest; and this is clear both by itself and through Rule B. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: **How great is the Middle?** And it must be said that it is as great as the "continuative" is in the subject in which it is: such as "joining" in a conjunction; and "generating" in a generation; and "running" in a course; and "composing" in a composition; in the third way, such as a human being, who is a third "middle" constituted of soul and body; and such like. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **How much is the Middle?** And it must be answered that it is as much as the part of the whole Middle is: such as in an elemented body, "to ignite," "to aerify," "to liquefy," and "to earthify," from which there is one common elementary thing; and so of others in their own way. And this is clear. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: **Of what quality is the Middle?** It must be answered that it is of such a quality as is the proper <term>passion</term><note>A characteristic property or attribute.</note> of the subject in which it is: such as "to ignite" in fire, and "to run" in a course, and such like.

### Concerning the End deduced through the rules.

<margin>
6 Whether
Concerning the End deduced through the rules.

It is asked through rule B: whether there is an **ultimate end**? And it must be answered that yes: otherwise the middle would be determined by the part of the beginning, and not by the part of the end. And thus there would be motion and process from the rear part unto infinity, and the beginning would never reach the end and rest: which is impossible, and against the first species of rule D and the second of E.

¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is the end? And it must be answered that it is the principle outside of which there is no rest. ¶ Further, through the second species it is asked: what does it have essentially in itself? And it must be answered that it has its correlatives: namely, the "quieter" <note>the thing that brings rest</note>, the "quieted" <note>the thing put to rest</note>, and the act of "quieting," in which all other principles rest. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is it in another? And it must be answered that it is good in goodness, great in magnitude, differing in difference from all other principles; and in concordance, it is concording with all other principles, except for contrariety. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be answered that it has in goodness the habit of the good, and also the situatedness of other principles; and in difference it has an act differing from all acts of other principles: and this is self-evident through rule B.

# On the mixture of principles and rules.

<note>original: "De mixtione principiorum et regularum." This section explains how the abstract principles of Llull's system are defined by asking specific logical questions.</note>

it must be answered that it is such as it can be through its appropriate passion <note>In medieval logic, a "passion" is a property or attribute arising from a thing's nature.</note>; just as the will is such as is appropriate through hatefulness, and the intellect through ignorance; and similarly, power is sometimes through impossibility, since impossibility does not depart from the nature of power itself; and so concerning others in their own way. And just as deafness is to a man, or justice, or injury, and such things. And this is manifest through Rule B <note>Rule B usually asks "Whether?" or "What?" regarding the essence of a thing.</note>. ¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H asks "When?" (When is it?).</note>, it is asked: when is the End? And it must be answered that it is then when it is in all the species of its rules in which it can by no means exist without time; just as time itself cannot exist without the End itself. And this Rule B signifies to an intellect that understands well. ¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I asks "Where?" (Where is it?).</note>, it is asked: where is the End? And it must be answered that it is in all species as if in its primitivity and its correlatives <note>Correlatives are the active, passive, and verbal forms of a principle, e.g., the Lover, the Beloved, and Loving.</note>; and it is a perverse habit in privation and in injury; and a right habit in the limit and justice: and this is clear to one investigating subtly. ¶ Through all species of modality <note>Rule K, asking "How?"</note>, it is asked: how is the End? And it must be answered that it is by way of difference, which posits that its correlatives are different from all other principles and their relatives. And it is by way of concord, which accords the End with all other principles, except however for contrariety. Again, it is by way of the middle, because it mediates the End itself through all other principles; and it is by way of appetite, which desires to rest in the End itself; and so of the rest in their own way. ¶ Through all species of instrumentality <note>Rule L, asking "With what?"</note>, it is asked: with what is the End? And it must be answered that it is with its correlatives, and with all species of its rules without which it cannot be; and it is good with goodness; just as a hooded man <note>original: "cappatus"</note> is good with a good hood. And with appetite it is desirable, and such things.

# Eighth Part.

<margin>
K: In what way
</margin>
It is asked: where is **greatness**? And it must be said that it is in a greater subject, habit, place, and the like; and this is clear through all the species of rule I <note>Rule I usually refers to "Where" (Ubi) in this system</note>. ¶ Through the rule of modality, it is asked: in what way is greatness? And it must be responded that it is by way of the difference that causes its correlatives to be greater by differing. ¶ Likewise, it is by way of the concordance that causes them to be greater by according. And it is by way of rule G <note>Rule G refers to "Quality"</note> by reason of greater appropriations and the like; nevertheless, these greatnesses exist under a "greatness" which is the genus to those aforementioned greatnesses; just as particular whitenesses are under a universal whiteness, and this is evident in itself. ¶ Through all species of instrumentality, it is asked: with what is greatness? And it must be said that it is with its correlatives and with its greater habit, with which the subalternate greatnesses are habited; or rather the greater acts in which their likenesses shine forth.

### On equality deduced through the rules.

<margin>
B: Whether
On equality deduced through the rules.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a floral or foliate motif within a square frame.</image-desc>
It is asked: whether there is any **equality** that is a most general principle? And it must be responded that it is just as is evident through the subalternate and individuated equalities of plants, which are the same in species; and similarly it is manifest in fruits which are equally individuated; and this has been seen through rule B <note>Rule B refers to "Whether" (Utrum)</note>. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is equality? And it must be said that it is a being to which "to co-equalize" properly belongs. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: what does it have in itself essentially? And it must be responded: its innate <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Lullian philosophy, these are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle</note> from which it is constituted: namely, from the *co-equalizer*, the *co-equalizable*, and the *co-equalizing*. ¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: what is it in another? And it must be said that it is active and passive; because it is equally constituted from form and matter. ¶ Likewise, through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be said that it has its habits with which individuals are equally habited; just as in an orchard the apples are equally of the same species; and so it is concerning elemental, sensible, imaginable, rational, and mechanical things, and the liberal arts; and also concerning moral things. ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: of what is equality? And it must be responded that it is of itself; otherwise, subalternate equalities would not have a genus without which they cannot exist. ¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: of what things is equality? And it must be said that it is of its essential correlatives

<column-break/>

without which it can least be that which it is; and if they were lacking, foreign equalities would fail. ¶ Further, through the third species, it is asked: when is equality? And it must be said that the equality of acts is the equality of powers; just as the equality of understanding, remembering, and willing is of the equality of the intellect, memory, and will; and so it is of sensible things, and this is evident in itself. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why is there equality? And it must be responded that it is because it is from its equal, substantial, true, and necessary relatives with which there is a "demonstration of the cause" <note>original: "demonstratio propter quid"</note>; and also a demonstration by equivalence. ¶ Again, through the second species, it is asked: why is there equality? And it must be responded that it is in the soul: so that God may be equally understood, remembered, and loved by it; and in sensible things it is so that objects may be equally sensible and the like. ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: how great is equality? And it must be said that continuous equality is as great as that which is sustained in its subjects. ¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: how much is it? And it must be responded: as much as is in its correlatives and in an unequal foreign number; and this is clear in itself. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked: what kind of equality is it properly? And it must be said that it is such as can be through the proper <term>passion</term> <note>A "passion" here refers to a logical property or attribute of a subject</note> of the subject in which it is. Just as the equality of substance, form, and matter. And just as there are innate equalities of sensual beings, etc. ¶ Likewise, through the second species, it is asked: what kind is it appropriately? And it must be said that it is such as can be through the appropriated passions of foreign subjects in which it is: such as two logicians in logic, and two judges in justice, and two hooded men in hoods; and the like. ¶ Through all species of rule H, it is asked: when is equality? And it must be responded that it is then when it truly is in the species of H, as in its concretes, etc.; just as in a race which equally consists between the runner and the "runnable" <note>the path or distance to be run</note>; and the present time between the past and the future; and so of others in their own way. ¶ Through all species of rule I, it is asked: where is equality? And it must be responded that it is in itself: because it is in its correlatives; and in the subject in which it is equally deduced through action and passion; and it is in goodness, greatness, etc., in which it is equally present, so that the principles may be equal. And it is in difference so that its correlatives may be equally differing; and it is in concordance so that its correlatives similarly may be equally according; and it is in modality so that it may be modally; and it is in instrumentality so that it may be instrumentally; and the whole...

<meta>This page continues the systematic application of the "Art" (Lullian logic), moving from the principle of Equality to the principle of Minority. It follows the established pattern of questioning each principle through the "Rules" (Questions) labeled B through K.</meta>

<margin>Rule B</margin>
This is made manifest through Rule B <note>Rule B usually refers to the question "Whether it is?"</note>. ¶ Through the Rule of Modality <note>Rule K, "How?"</note>, it is asked: **How is equality?** And we say that it exists through the mode it has in its correlatives <note>Lullian "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, e.g., the equalizer, the equalized, and the act of equaling</note>; and it exists through the mode of justice, weight, measure, and proportion in the subject in which it resides; and this occurs both naturally and artificially. This is sufficiently clear in itself.
<margin>With what?</margin>
¶ Through all the species of the Instrumental Rule <note>Rule K, "With what?"</note>, it is asked: **With what is equality?** It must be answered that it is with its correlatives: and with the Difference by which the agent distinguishes; and it is with the Concordance with which the agent equally accords; and with the proper Property with which it causes its own specific habits: as is evident in elemental and vegetative things, etc. This is signifiable through Rule B.

### On Minority deduced through the Rules.

<margin>Whether</margin>
<margin>On Minority deduced through the Rules.</margin>
It is asked: **Whether minority is one way as a substance and another way as an accident?** And it must be answered that it is so: because if it were not, the substantial relation existing between majority and minority would be destroyed, and all principles would be equal; furthermore, the royal relation of majority and minority would not exist between substance and accident, which is impossible. Rule B proves this.
<margin>What is it?</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C: "What?"</note>, it is asked: **What is minority?** And let us say that it is a being to which it properly belongs to "minorate" <note>To make smaller or diminish</note> and to distance itself from majority.
<margin>In itself</margin>
¶ And through the second species, it is asked: **What does it have in itself?** It must be said that it has its innate correlatives, in which and with which all other principles are capable of being minored, by dividing and annihilating the subject in which it exists.
<margin>In another</margin>
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **What is it in another?** It must be said that it is a consummating being, such that it can exist near to nothingness.
<margin>In another (possessions)</margin>
¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **What does it have in another?** It must be answered that it has a lesser essence, a lesser being, and a lesser nature, quantity, quality, etc. This is clear in itself.
<margin>From what?</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D: "From what?"</note>, it is asked: **From what is minority?** It must be answered that it is from itself, so that it may be a general principle without which subordinate minorities could not exist within the genus of minority.
<margin>First</margin>
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **From what is substantial minority?** It must be said that it is from its correlatives, without which it could have no nature or existence. Accidental minority, however, is from itself insofar as it is a "habit" <note>A quality or disposition</note> with which substantial minorities are habited; and the minorities of powers are of their own kind.
<margin>Matter / Possible</margin>
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **Whose is minority?** It must be said that it belongs to the agent, insofar as the agent causes minorities from it and with it. All these things are evident in themselves and also through the rules of B.

<column-break/>

<margin>E: How much / Why</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E: "Why?"</note>, it is asked: **Why is there minority?** It must be said that it is because of the correlatives by reason of which it is a principle regarding its own genus.
<margin>It acts</margin>
¶ Further, through the second species, it is asked: **Why is it?** It must be said: so that there may be lesser beings in their own genus, without which there could be no motion, division, generation, corruption, or privation <note>The loss or absence of a quality</note>. This is quite graspable in itself.
<margin>F: How much (quantity)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule F <note>Rule F: "How much?"</note>, it is asked: **How great is minority?** It must be answered that it is as great as that which is outside the genus of majority and equality.
<margin>Distinction</margin>
¶ Furthermore, through the second species, it is asked: **How great is minority?** It must be said that it is as great as its correlatives, its subordinate minorities, and the individuals that belong to its genus.
<margin>G: What kind (Quality)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule G <note>Rule G: "What kind?"</note>, it is asked: **What kind of thing is minority?** It must be answered that it is such as can exist through the proper "passion" <note>A property or attribute acted upon</note> of the subject in which it resides: just as one substance is smaller than another through its own proper passion, without which it cannot be.
<margin>Appropriated</margin>
¶ Likewise, through the second species, it is asked: **What kind is it?** It must be said that it is such as the lesser predicament <note>Category</note> appropriated to it, such as a lesser quantity, quality, etc.
<margin>H: When</margin>
¶ Through all species of Rule H <note>Rule H: "When?"</note>, it is asked: **When is minority?** It must be answered that it is then when it is actually sustained through all species of Rule H which are of its genus; and it is also then when it is in practice through the act of "minorating," and all this is plain to one who looks closely.
<margin>I: Where</margin>
¶ Through all species of Rule I <note>Rule I: "Where?"</note>, it is asked: **Where is minority?** It must be said that it is in itself, since it is in its correlatives with which it exists; and it is in a composite subject of lesser substance and accident: just as a cloaked man is in a smaller cloak; and water is in a lesser heat; and a horse is in a lesser gallop, and such things; and a man in a lesser mode; and a craftsman in a lesser craft.
<margin>K: From what / How</margin>
¶ Through the Rule of Modality <note>Rule K: "How?"</note>, it is asked: **How is minority?** It must be said that it is through the mode it has in its correlatives, so that it is lesser in being and acting than some other principle; just as a man in moral matters who has a mode of existing in lesser virtue, doing a small amount of good; and a horse in running sometimes has a small run. This is clear in itself.
<margin>K: With what</margin>
¶ Through the Rule of Instrumentality, it is asked: **Minority [with what?]**

# Part Nine.

And it must be answered that it is with all others that are of its own kind, existing together in the subject in which it is, along with lesser essences and with lesser acts of powers: namely, with a lesser running, heating, and the like. ¶ We have spoken of the principles deduced through the rules: and from what has been said of them, a doctrine is given with which a person can deduce other implicit and foreign principles. And through such a method and doctrine, the intellect is made very general for finding many means to investigate true conclusions.

## The ninth principal part: Concerning the nine subjects named above in the alphabet.

<margin>Through the nine subjects, everything that exists is implied.</margin>
<margin>The ninth principal part concerning the nine subjects named above in the alphabet.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a floral or foliate pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>
Since in the nine subjects everything that exists is implied, and outside of them there is nothing, we therefore wish to place them in this Art. Thus, with them, the Art may be general, because they are general to all things. Therefore, by running through the aforementioned subjects by means of the principles and rules of this Art, we will be able to have knowledge of these subjects. And if any doubt arises concerning any subject, let it be applied to its own subject, as we will exemplify below, according to what is indicated in the treatise on application. ¶ And first, we shall speak of the first subject, which is God, signified by the letter **b**.

### Concerning the first subject, which is God.

<margin>God</margin>
<margin>Concerning the first subject, which is God.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a figure or stylized floral elements within a square frame.</image-desc>
This subject is divided into two principal parts. ¶ The first part concerns the discourse of God through the principles. ¶ The second part concerns the discourse of God through the rules. ¶ Now, the first of these parts is divided into five parts. ¶ The first part is about the investigation of the divine <term>dignities</term> <note>original: "dignitatum"; these are the divine attributes or perfections such as Goodness and Greatness</note> or reasons. ¶ The second part is about their intrinsic, co-substantial acts. ¶ The third is about the infinity of the dignities. ¶ Fourth is about the infinity of their acts. ¶ Fifth is about the discourse of God through the principles. Furthermore, the second part is divided into ten rules, as appears in them; and first, we must look at the first part.

<column-break/>

### Concerning the investigation of the divine dignities.

<margin>Concerning the investigation of the divine dignities</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a stylized figure or floral motif.</image-desc>
First, I suppose that God exists, which we proved in the second principal part of the aforementioned division. ¶ God exists: and His being is good; but His being could not be good without goodness, just as a colored thing cannot be colored without color. Therefore, His goodness exists, since His being is good; and this is by necessity. ¶ God exists: and His being is great. For if it were not great, it would no longer be worthy of being God; whence it follows that divine greatness is a real being. ¶ God exists: and His being is eternal; for if it were at any time begun, it would no longer be worthy of being God. There is, therefore, eternity, without which an eternal being cannot exist. ¶ God exists: and since He is, He is able to be; therefore, there is power <note>original: "potestas"</note> without which God cannot exist. ¶ God exists: and He Himself knows Himself. Otherwise, His being would not be worthy of being God. There is, therefore, divine wisdom, without which God could not know Himself. ¶ God exists: and He loves Himself; for otherwise He would not be worthy of being God. ¶ There is, therefore, divine love, without which God could not love Himself. ¶ God exists: and His being is virtuous; otherwise God would be vicious, and thus would not be worthy to be God. ¶ There is, therefore, divine virtue, without which God cannot be virtuous. ¶ God exists: and His being is true; if not, it would be false, and consequently He would not be worthy to be God. ¶ There is, therefore, divine truth, without which God could not be true. ¶ God exists: and His being is glorious; if not, it would no longer be worthy of being God. There is, therefore, divine glory, without which God cannot be glorious. ¶ We have proved that the divine dignities exist in reality, without which God could not exist; therefore they are numerable, each existing in its own proper number. The reason for this is: for unless each existed in its own proper number, God would not exist. And so, for God to exist, it is necessary that there be in Him several reasons or real dignities. Nevertheless, as to essence, they do not differ. For all are one and the same divine essence; or one is another essentially. For otherwise goodness would be great by accident, and vice versa. And the same can be said of the others. ¶ And in this step, the human intellect recognizes that God, insofar as He considers the unity of His essence, does not consider several reasons; but insofar as He considers that He cannot exist without several reasons, He numbers them in reality. Just as a person who, insofar as he does not consider being one, does not consider many things; but insofar as he considers that he cannot exist without many parts, he understands and knows that there are many things in himself. ¶ We have searched into the divine dignities, and we have found them to be co-essential to God.

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the nature of God's attributes, specifically addressing the necessity of internal divine actions to avoid the logical fallacy of an "idle" or "empty" deity. It maintains the scholastic tone of the previous folios.</meta>

# On the nine subjects. Against the Saracens <note>original: "Sarracenos" — a medieval term for Muslims. The author is engaging in a common scholastic debate regarding the nature of God's unity versus His attributes.</note>

->folio 47<-

...and substantial from eternity and in eternity. Indeed, the reason why they exist is within themselves and not outside of them. For otherwise, they would exist by accident <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like the color of a shirt, whereas "substance" is the essential nature of a thing.</note>, and likewise God would be accidental, which is impossible. ¶ And this is against certain Saracens who believe they have a high and subtle knowledge of God, who say that God is one and has no dignities <term>dignities: the divine attributes or perfections, such as Goodness, Greatness, and Eternity</term> in regard to Himself, but possesses them only so that He may act with them upon creatures: namely, that He is good so that He may perform good acts for the creature, and He is great so that He may create a great creature, and He is eternal so that the creature may be durable, etc. ¶ From this it is clearly evident that in their words or sayings they imply a contradiction; for if it were as they say, since God is infinite in His reasons, He would surely create infinite and eternal creatures—which He does not do, nor do they themselves say He does. For they say the world is new <note>meaning "created in time" rather than eternal</note> and quantified or limited. ¶ Furthermore, they imply a contradiction by saying God is the First Cause; for He would not be the First Cause if His reasons existed for the sake of the world, and thus God would exist with His dignities so that the world might exist, which is a very absurd thing to say.

### On the intrinsic acts of the divine reasons.

<margin>On the intrinsic acts of the divine reasons.</margin>
It is said that power is in vain if it is not brought into action. ¶ Furthermore, it is said that power is known through acts, and acts are known through their objects; and thus it is signified that the divine dignities have acts without which the dignities of God would be in vain in infinity and eternity, and God would not know His own dignities, nor would He make Himself an object of His own thought. From this it would follow that God is not God through His dignities, which is false, as was proven above. ¶ Further, if divine Goodness did not have an act—and likewise for the others—it would then have no nature, and would be idle and empty, and would not relate to any end, which is impossible and against rule 'e' and also against the second species of rule 'c' <note>These refer to specific logical rules in the author's philosophical system, likely the "Ars Magna" of Ramon Llull.</note>. Therefore, etc. The divine dignities thus have intrinsic, coessential, and natural acts. ¶ Further, if the dignities did not have coessential acts, each would indeed be a privative habit <note>A "privative habit" is the absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness is the absence of sight.</note>. For just as blindness is a privative habit because it does not have the act of seeing, so divine Goodness would be a privative habit if it did not have an intrinsic act coessential to itself, namely, "bonifying" <note>original: "bonificare" — the active exercise of being good</note>; and similarly Greatness without "magnifying," and Eternity without "eternizing," and Power without 

<column-break/>

being able, Wisdom without knowing, Will without willing, and Virtue without "virtuifying," and Truth without "verifying," and Glory without "glorifying"; and God would not be worthy to be God with habits that are privative and coessential to Him, which is impossible. ¶ Therefore, the divine dignities have intrinsic acts that are coessential and real. ¶ Furthermore, it is known: every perfect goodness has an act; and so it can be said of divine Greatness and Eternity, etc. Therefore, etc. ¶ Further, no goodness is perfect without an act; and so it can be said of divine Greatness and Eternity. Therefore, etc. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, by affirming and denying, that the divine dignities have intrinsic and coessential acts.

<margin>No dignity is perfect without an act.</margin>

### On the infinity of the divine reasons.

<margin>On the infinity of the divine reasons.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a figure, possibly a scholar or saint, in profile.</image-desc> Divine Goodness is the reason for a good thing to produce good, and it has already been proven that it has an act, namely "bonifying." And therefore, if Greatness is the being by reason of which Goodness is great, then Goodness is the reason for a good thing to produce a great good. And since Eternity is the reason through which Goodness and Greatness endure, Goodness is therefore the reason for producing a great and eternal good. But Goodness could not be such a reason unless it were itself infinite and immense; therefore, Goodness is necessarily infinite. ¶ Divine Greatness exists, as has been proven, and it likewise has an act, namely "magnifying"; and since Eternity is the being by reason of which Greatness endures, and Power is that by reason of which Greatness can exist and act. ¶ There is therefore an infinite and immense subject through which "magnifying" can spread itself from eternity and in eternity; and such a subject we call infinite Greatness. ¶ Eternity is a measure existing all at once and together, having nothing on the side before nor on the side after; and its subject is eternal from eternity; and thus Eternity is an infinite reason; and this is indeed good and great, and through Power it is able to be. ¶ Eternity exists, as has been proven, and it has an act, namely "eternizing"; and because Eternity can exist and act infinitely, it follows of necessity that Power is infinite, without which Power, Eternity could not have an act nor an infinite essence. ¶ The Wisdom of God, or the Intellect, exists, as has already been proven above; and Eternity is that by reason of which it endures, and through Power it can exist and act; and Greatness...

<summary>This page argues that God's attributes (Goodness, Greatness, etc.) must have internal, eternal actions—such as "bonifying" or "magnifying"—to be perfect and distinct from the created world. It refutes the idea that God's attributes only exist to interact with creation, asserting instead their infinite and coessential nature within the divine essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the systematic proof of the infinite nature of the Divine attributes (Dignities), moving from the attributes themselves to the infinity of their internal actions. The author employs a scholastic method of "reductio ad absurdum" to show that if God's attributes were finite, it would result in logical contradictions.</meta>

# Part Nine.

<margin>will</margin>
The will is that through which He can diffuse Himself immensely: and through goodness, it is infinite. The intellect is good, and through the will, it is lovable; for this reason, the infinity of the intellect is necessitated, as it cannot be otherwise. ¶ The Divine will exists, as does its act, as has already been proven above. If the will itself is infinite in eternity and from eternity, it is indeed infinitely intelligible. But if it were finite, it would be understood as such, and would not be infinitely intelligible; consequently, the Divine intellect would not be lovable nor loved from eternity and into eternity. Thus, the definitions of goodness, greatness, etc., would fail, which is impossible. ¶ It is therefore proven that the Divine will is infinite.

<margin>virtue</margin>
¶ The Divine virtue <note>original: "virtus"; in this context, it refers to moral excellence as well as "power" or "potency"</note> exists, and its acts exist, as proven above. Now, if it is infinite, all is well; but if not, it would be defective through some vice or flaw preventing it from being infinite. Consequently, all other reasons that would allow it to be finite—even while they themselves remain infinite—would fail. Because that which is finite cannot extend or diffuse itself as far as the infinite, it clearly appears that the other Dignities would be partly flawed and partly not, which is quite impossible. ¶ Therefore, Divine virtue is infinite.

<margin>truth</margin>
¶ Divine truth exists, and its acts exist, as proven above. Since truth is goodness, greatness, etc., these are reasons that are infinite in reality. It is therefore necessary that truth be infinite; otherwise, the infinity of the aforementioned reasons would not be true, as truth would have nothing to correspond with.

<margin>glory</margin>
¶ Divine glory exists, and its acts exist, as proven above. But the essence of glory itself is either infinite, or finite, or partly finite and partly infinite. If it is absolutely infinite, all is well, because no inconsistency follows regarding itself or the other Dignities. But if it were partly finite and partly infinite, a most great inconsistency would follow. For all the other Dignities would not have an infinite subject of glory and rest; thus, the finiteness of glory would be a "privative habit" <note>a philosophical term for the absence of a quality that should be present</note> through which the other Dignities would suffer pain, which is quite impossible. ¶ It follows necessarily, therefore, that Divine glory is infinite.

### On the infinity of the acts of the Divine reasons.

<margin>goodness</margin>
<margin>On the infinity of the acts of the reasons.</margin>
Divine goodness is the reason for the good to produce good. And because greatness is the reason why goodness is great, it is also eternal through eternity; through power, it can exist and act; through the intellect, it is understood; through the will, it is loved; through virtue, it is virtuous; through truth, it is true; and through glory, it is glorious. ¶ It follows therefore of necessity that the act of goodness—namely, *to bonify* <note>original: "bonificare"; the active process of making or doing good</note>—is infinite in relation to the infinity of goodness, and also in relation to the infinity of all other Dignities or reasons.

<column-break/>

<margin>Greatness</margin>
¶ The greatness of God is infinite, and possesses this act, as proven above. Therefore its act—namely, *to magnify*—is either infinite or finite. If infinite, all is well; but if not, it is like a tree in which the "elemental" nature <note>the basic physical matter</note> is more extended than the "vegetative" nature <note>the life-force that causes growth</note>, because at the extremities of a tree there are sometimes dry branches in which the vegetative power is absent, but the elemental remains. Thus, a finite act would correspond to infinite greatness, rather than an infinite one; this would be evil against good, and small against great. Consequently, *to magnify* and *to eternize* could not be converted <note>interchanged logically</note>, and all other acts of the Divine reasons would fail the act of greatness, and the act of greatness would fail them, by reason of which they would be small. ¶ It would not follow that the infinity of the essence should fail in the finiteness of its act, distancing itself from an infinite act; this is against its nature. It would rest more in a small act than a great one, which is dissonant to reason and against the infinity of *bonifying* which we proved above. ¶ He concludes, therefore, that the Divine *magnifying* is infinite.

<margin>Eternity</margin>
¶ *To eternize* exists, as proven above, as do infinity and eternity. The act of eternity—namely, *to eternize*—is either infinite or finite. If it is infinite, all is well, for no inconsistency follows. But if it is finite, a great inconsistency follows: because *to eternize* would be limited by time, and consequently eternity would be the subject of time from eternity and in eternity, which is quite impossible and against the infinity of the Divine Dignities already proven above. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that *to eternize* is an infinite act.

<margin>Power</margin>
¶ *To possify* <note>original: "possificare"; the act of making something possible or exercising power</note> is the act of power, as proven above. But *to possify* is either an infinite act or a finite one. If it is infinite, all is well; for just as a finite *possifying* suits a finite power, so—and much better—does an infinite *possifying* suit the infinite power proven above. If only a "created" *possifying* belonged to infinite power, then the power would degenerate from its nature regarding God and the creature. ¶ Furthermore, *to bonify*, *to magnify*, and *to eternize* could not be infinite acts, because no one gives what they do not have. From this a contradiction follows, because *to bonify*, *to magnify*, and *to eternize*, which are infinite acts as proven, could not be infinite; and because...

<summary>This page argues that God's attributes—Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory—must be infinite, otherwise they would contradict His perfect nature. It further establishes that the active expressions of these attributes (such as "bonifying" or "magnifying") must also be infinite to match the essence of the attributes themselves.</summary>

<meta>Catchword: God; ink bleed-through from verso; Gothic typeface (Textura)</meta>

...a contradiction cannot stand. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that the divine "power-to-be" <note>original: "possificare," a technical term for the active power of being</note> is infinite. ¶ Divine understanding is either finite or infinite: if infinite, that is well; if indeed it is finite, a great inconvenience follows: namely, that the essence of the intellect, insofar as it is infinite, would not be understood. Thus, in part, it would be a subject of ignorance, which is a privative habit <note>A "privative habit" refers to the absence of a quality that ought to be present</note> through which the infinity of the aforementioned reasons is unknown—which is evil against good, small against great. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that divine understanding is an [infinite] act. <note>The Latin text says "finitus," but the logical conclusion of the argument requires "infinitus." This is likely a period printer's error.</note> ¶ Divine loving or willing is either infinite or finite: if infinite, that is well. But if it is finite, then the infinity of the divine reasons and their acts would not be infinitely lovable nor loved. And thus the infinity of the intellect and its act would not be infinitely lovable. And the same can be said of the infinity of goodness, etc.: which is impossible. ¶ It is concluded, therefore, that divine loving is infinite. ¶ The act of divine virtue <note>term: "virtus" (virtue/power) refers here to God's inherent strength or capacity</note> is either infinite or finite in the essence and number of virtue. If infinite, that is well; if however it is finite, it follows that there is infinity in the essence and number of the other dignities—because they are virtuously infinite—and not in its own number: which is quite impossible. ¶ The act of divine truth is either infinite or finite. If infinite, that is well. If however it is finite, it follows that there is infinity in the essence and number of the other dignities—because they are truthfully infinite—and not in its own number: which is impossible. ¶ The act of divine glory is either finite or infinite in essence and number. If it is infinite, that is well. If it is finite, it follows that there is infinity in the essence of the other dignities—because they are truthfully infinite—and not in its own number: which is quite absurd and impossible. For no act is greater in another than in itself.

### On God deduced through principles.

<margin>On God deduced through principles.</margin>
In this chapter, we shall discourse upon God through principles in two ways. ¶ The first will be intrinsic: and regarding His own nature. ¶ The second truly will be extrinsic and voluntary: regarding Himself toward His creatures. And in every chapter we shall discourse through these two modes: and so by that means (God nevertheless helping), the human intellect will be able to have knowledge of the essence of God, and of His intrinsic operation, and also of the manner He holds toward creatures: and this is as follows.

<column-break/>

### On God deduced through goodness.

<margin>On God deduced through goodness.</margin>
God is good: and He is His very own goodness. Whence it follows that His goodness is the reason for Him why He should produce a necessary good. <note>In Llullian philosophy, God's internal activity (the Trinity) is seen as a "necessary" production of His nature.</note> The reason for this is: because goodness and God are interchangeable in the unity of nature. This is evident through the definition of goodness, just as in a plant in which the vegetative power is the reason why it produces a necessary vegetative [product]—the plant nevertheless having its conditions for vegetating. Just as God has His own [conditions] for producing an intrinsic "bonified" <note>term: "bonificatum" (the bonified), the result of the act of making good</note>; therefore God produces an intrinsic bonified: and this with His infinite "bonifying" <note>term: "bonificare" (to bonify), the active verb of goodness</note> through all His infinite goodness. ¶ While God knows Himself as good in producing the bonified, He considers that it is indeed good to produce a created good, so that His intrinsic bonifying may be understood, loved, remembered, and praised through it; and so that God may "bonify" those powers when He is well-objectified by them. And for this reason, He created the power of intellect, will, and memory in the angel and in the rational soul. And consequently, all His conditions pertaining to them, so that they can perfectly enjoy God and acquire good merit. And in this step, the human intellect recognizes the first intention which God had for creating good creatures.

<margin>Extrinsic Mode</margin>

### Discourse on God through greatness.

<margin>Discourse on God through greatness.</margin>
<margin>Intrinsic Mode</margin>
God is great: and He is His own infinite greatness with which He has an infinite "magnifying" <note>term: "magnificare," the active exercise of greatness</note> without which He could not have infinite greatness, nor even His infinite act. And because greatness is that by reason of which goodness and eternity are great, therefore these dignities with their acts concur to produce an infinite "magnified" <note>term: "magnificatum," the result of greatness</note>, and likewise a bonified, eternized, etc.; and further so that each dignity may have its infinite act in the infinite magnified. ¶ While God knows Himself thus great and also infinite, in existing and in acting: and consequently He knows Himself well-conditioned and disposed to produce a great creature: and this to such an extent that He would produce an infinite creature if the creature were capable of receiving infinite greatness; just like a fire which, if it had an abundance of wood, would magnify and multiply its flame up to the sphere of the moon: and so God...

# Ninth Part

He created a great created thing: such as the heavens, the angel, and the rational soul; and similarly other creatures that are endowed with greatness. ¶ And in this step, the human intellect recognizes one great created being that is greater than all other creatures, which I do not dare to announce or demonstrate. ### Concerning God as deduced through Eternity.

<margin>Intrinsic mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God as deduced through eternity</margin>
God is eternal, and He is His own eternity. And thus God necessitates Himself to produce an "eternized" being <note>original: "eternatum" — a technical Lullian term for the internal object of a divine attribute's action</note> without which eternity would not be infinite, nor would it have an infinite act. And to this end, all the Dignities <note>The "Dignities" are the primary attributes of God in Lullian philosophy, such as Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, etc.</note> concur with their own acts, so that the "eternized" being may be infinitely "bonified" <note>made good</note>, magnified, etc. And so that these Dignities with their acts may be in act within the infinite eternal. ¶ And at this sublime production, the human intellect marvels greatly.

<margin>Extrinsic mode</margin>
¶ And while God thus considers Himself by eternizing and understanding Himself as disposed and ordered toward producing the world from eternity and in eternity—with respect to Himself—yet He cannot create the world from eternity by reason of the world's own defect regarding its beginning. For it is finite, like the heavens, which are not from eternity, just as they are not infinite or immense. For its body is endowed with quantity, surface, figure, and motion; nevertheless, it can exist in eternal time <note>original: "euo eterno" — likely referring to 'aevum', the duration of angels</note> so that angel and man may know, love, recollect, and praise the supreme divine production.

### Concerning God as deduced through Power.

<margin>Intrinsic mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God as deduced through power.</margin>
God is powerful, and He is His very own power. And thus God is necessitated to produce an infinite "possificated" being <note>original: "possificatum" — that which is made possible or the object of Power's act</note> so that His power may be infinite and have an infinite act. And because through infinite power the divine Goodness, Greatness, etc., can exist and act infinitely, therefore all the other Dignities with their acts concur infinitely to produce the "possificated" being, so that it may be "bonified," magnified, etc. ¶ And while God thus recognizes Himself as powerful in existing and acting, He recognizes

<column-break/>

Himself as disposed and ordered toward producing a created power that is neither infinite nor eternal. For God knows Himself intrinsically with absolute and ordered power, but extrinsically with ordered power only; this is because God does not produce creatures out of His own nature, but produces them effectively <note>as an external effect</note>. Just as a real man who paints a man on a wall: the painting is not of his own nature. ¶ And thus the human intellect knows with what intention God created the created powers: namely, so that creatures might be able to understand, love, recollect, and praise God with them. And thus the human intellect knows that the infinite and intrinsic "possificated" being is the cause of all finite and extrinsic "possificable" things.

### Concerning God as deduced through Wisdom.

<margin>Concerning God as deduced through wisdom</margin>
<margin>Intrinsic mode</margin>
God is wise, or Intellect; and He is wisdom itself. And wisdom itself is that by reason of which the Wise One understands Himself to be necessitated to produce an "understood" being <note>original: "intellectum" — here used as the internal object of the act of understanding</note> in the infinity of wisdom itself, with an infinite "understanding" through the whole infinite essence of the Intellect itself. Just as fire, which with its natural appetite, necessitates itself to produce an "ignited" thing or to "ignite" through its own essence. And therefore all other reasons concur to produce the infinite "understood" being, so that in that production every Dignity may have an infinite act, and this naturally. ¶ While God thus knows Himself, He knows that it is worthy and just that there be a created intellect that honorably recognizes the supreme infinite Intellect. And thus He created the intellect of angels and of men. ¶ But the human intellect marvels, after it has been created to understand the supreme Intellect, as to what is the cause why it is ignorant of that same created intellect; but afterwards it recognizes that sin is the cause, which indeed deviates evil angels and sinful men from the end for which they exist.

### On God deduced through Virtue.

<margin>On God deduced through Virtue.</margin>
<margin>Internal mode</margin>
God is virtuous: and he is his own virtue, and his acts are co-essential and natural to him. And therefore, just as he loves himself as being necessitated to produce an infinite beloved: so he loves and knows himself as being necessitated to know and produce an infinite virtuous object: and to this all the dignities concur with their acts: so that through infinite virtue they may be virtuous and infinite: and they cannot behave otherwise. God, thus loving and knowing himself intrinsically, inclines himself and passes over to loving and knowing that he is ordained and disposed to create natural virtues: such as are the figures and signs of infinite and eternal virtue, etc., with which created virtues the infinite and eternal virtue may be known, loved, remembered, and praised.

<margin>External mode</margin>
¶ Furthermore, he passes over to creating moral virtues, of which we shall speak below in the ninth subject, because they are the way to paradise; and so that God might reward men with them from his virtuous glory. And while the intellect considers this, it marvels why men in this life are not more morally virtuous than vicious, since their virtues have their origin from the supreme virtue, but vices do not. But then it recognizes that this is because men have free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity to choose between different courses of action</term> to do good or evil. But they incline themselves more toward the sensitive power <note>The physical senses and desires</note> and love it more than the reasoning power. ¶ Furthermore, the divine intellect asks why he permits this to happen, since he himself is virtuous and not vicious, and is spiritual and not sensual.

<column-break/>

Then the intellect recognizes that the reason for this is so that the justice of God may have a subject in which it can act. Nevertheless, it should be known that free will relates to two different parts: namely, to the good created part with which it does good, and to the evil uncreated part with which it acts wickedly and sins. This is the "uncreated part" on the side of the uncreated "nothingness" by accident. For man, insofar as he is drawn out of nothing, has an inclination toward nothingness, which is contrary to Being. Whence it is manifested that free will partly agrees with Being, and partly with non-being (or nothingness, which is the same thing), and this equally.

<margin>If man sins to his damnation, why did God create him?</margin>
¶ But still the intellect asks: since God knows that man will sin, why did he create him? And it recognizes this for this reason: because he created a good free will for him, with which he can remove himself from sin and hate it if he wishes. If, however, he had not created man, he would do injury to his own justice, because he would not have a subject in which he could act.

Thus God, loving and knowing himself as necessitated to produce an infinite truth: thence loves and knows that it is indeed true to create created natural truth, and also moral truth: so that through them the infinite verified object may be understood, loved, remembered, and also praised.

# On the nine subjects.
<note>The "Nine Subjects" refer to the fundamental categories of being in Ramon Llull's philosophical system: God, Angel, Heaven, Man, Imaginative, Sensitive, Vegetative, Elementative, and Instrumentative.</note>

...for there are many reasons: the bonifying <note>original: "bonificativus" - the active power of doing good</note>, the magnifying, the eternifying, etc. There is another number: to bonify, to magnify, to eternify, etc. There is another number: the bonified, the magnified, etc. And all these three are relatives referring to one absolute being, namely, God. ¶ While God considers himself in this way by reason of the definition of concordance, he creates one world by reason of his unity; and he creates many diverse things by reason of his plurality: namely, many signified things, as is evident in the scale of concordance <note>A "scale" or "ladder" refers to the hierarchical levels of being in Lullian logic</note> from which one world is constituted. ### Concerning God deduced through contrariety.

<margin>Internal mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God deduced through contrariety.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a face in profile.</image-desc> God is contrasting, but he is not contrariety; he is indeed appropriate. For he effectively gives penitence to the sinner; nevertheless, he causes contrarieties, as is shown in the scale of contrariety. ¶ God indeed is not contrariety. For concordance itself is infinite, having an infinite and eternal act. But at this step the intellect doubts: since God is infinite concordance, why then does he permit contrariety to exist? And to this it is answered that a property exists between God and man the sinner, so that the justice of God can extract its act in the sinner; for just as a mirror is disposed to receive all figures impressed upon it, so God is disposed to the tormenting of sinners. ¶ Furthermore, unless God created natural contrarieties in the world, the world would not be such as it is. ¶ Still, the intellect doubts here: since in the divine will there is an infinite "willing," why then does God have a "nilling" <note>original: "nolle" - the act of willing against something</note>? And so that it may understand this, it helps itself with the example given above. For just as a mirror receives the likeness of whiteness and blackness, so God loves the virtuous man by willing, but hates sinners by nilling.

### Concerning God deduced through principle.

<margin>Internal mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God deduced through principle.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a face in profile.</image-desc> God is the beginning-maker <note>original: "principians"</note>, and he is also his own principle; just as in his goodness in which God is the beginning-maker of the begun <note>original: "principiatum"</note>, namely, the bonified. And he is the beginning-maker not having anything pleasing to himself <note>outside of his own nature</note>; just as in his coessential "to bonify," which is not in the nature of his goodness as the beginning-maker, but is only begun from the beginning-maker and the begun; just as "to love" is begun from the lover and the beloved. ¶ While God considers that he is such a perfect principle, he passes to creating the world from nothing in such a way that one individual generates another individual, just as one man another man and one plant another plant similar to itself. And this is with substantial and natural beginning-making. ¶ Furthermore, he creates another principle: such as the one who understands, who causes the intellect objectively. And the one understanding and the intellect cause the act of understanding accidentally, so that the intellect can acquire knowledge; and thus it can be said of the will, that it may be clothed with the habit of love.

<margin>Internal mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God through the middle discourse.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a face in profile.</image-desc> In God there is a middle, just as in his goodness there is "to bonify," and in his greatness "to magnify," etc. And he himself is his own middle because he is infinite, with which God measures himself insofar as he is infinite through his intrinsic acting just as through his existing; in which "to mediate," the mediating and the mediated join themselves so that they are one continuous and absolute middle. ¶ While God thus knows himself to be the middle, he then passes to the causes created by him, as is evident in the definition of the middle, and also in the scale of the middle placed in the second figure: such as "to act," which is the middle existing between the agent and the actable; and such as "to love" between the lover and the lovable or the beloved.

<margin>External mode</margin>
<image-desc>A triangle diagram with the letter 'E' at the top apex, 'F' at the bottom left, and 'G' at the bottom right. A horizontal line connects F and G, and a vertical line drops from E to the center of that line.</image-desc>

### Concerning God through the discourse of the end.

<margin>Internal mode</margin>
<margin>Concerning God through the end discourse.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a face in profile.</image-desc> God is his own end, and he is not a privative end <note>an end that is merely a stopping point or absence</note>, but in that end there are many terms; just as in his goodness in which the bonifying is one term, the bonified another term, and to bonify another term: and all these three rest in one goodness. ¶ While God thus knows himself, by reason of the end he passes to creating many ends in the world, such as the habit of goodness which is one end morally, from which the bonifier habits himself by producing the bonified which is another end. And thus concerning "to bonify" in its own way. And all these three terms rest in that goodness which is their end; but when a man passes to sin, the habit of goodness and its terms are deprived. And consequently, man deviates from his end, by reason of which he tends toward eternal labor.

<summary>This page explores how God's internal attributes—specifically contrariety, principle, middle, and end—serve as the archetypes for the physical and moral structure of the created world. It explains that while God is a perfect unity, his internal "relatives" (the actor, the action, and the object) allow for the creation of a diverse yet harmonious universe.</summary>

# Part Nine

### On God through the discourse of Majority.

<margin>Intrinsic mode</margin>
<margin>On God through the discourse of Majority.</margin>
God is greater than the world and also greater than everything contained within it; for His reasons <note>The "reasons" or "dignities" are God's attributes like Goodness and Greatness</note> are infinite and possess infinite acts. And for this reason, just as He is greater than the world with His goodness and greatness, so He exists before the world with His majority <note>term: majority (Latin: *maioritas*). In this system, it refers to the state of being greater or superior in essence and scale.</note>. Furthermore, just as God with His substance is greater than the world with its majority, so indeed God with His eternity is greater than the world, while the world exists with its novelty <note>term: novelty (Latin: *novitas*). This refers to the world having a beginning in time, as opposed to God's eternity.</note>. Likewise, just as divine substance is greater than an accident <note>term: accident. A philosophical term for a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size.</note>, so divine substance exists before the accidents of the world. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that it is impossible for the world to have existed from eternity.

<margin>Extrinsic mode</margin>
While God thus recognizes His own majority, He proceeds to create majorities with which He may be known and loved—His own majority which is signified on the scale of the Second Figure.

### On God through the discourse of Equality.

<margin>Intrinsic Mode</margin>
<margin>On God through the discourse of Equality.</margin>
In God there is equality, as appears in His co-essential goodness, etc. For since the "Bonifier" <note>original: *bonificans*. A term used to describe the active principle of Goodness within God.</note> has two actions substantially: because he "bonifies," there is the "Bonified" and the "Bonifying" <note>The author is describing the internal relations of the Trinity using grammatical analogies: the Actor, the Object, and the Act itself.</note>. The Bonified indeed receives one passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon.</note> from the Bonifier, and has one action: because it "bonifies" the act of bonifying; which "bonifying" indeed has the two aforementioned passions. And since divine goodness is infinite and has an infinite act, as has already been proven above, therefore that divine equality is infinite, separated from every accident. For in an infinite subject, no accident can exist.

<margin>Refers to the Second Tree of the Art</margin>
<margin>Extrinsic mode</margin>
God, thus considering His infinite equality, proceeds to create finite substantial equality and also accidental equality. He creates substantial equality so that through likeness, infinite equality may be known. Likewise, He creates accidental equality so that through unlikeness, infinite equality may be known; for one opposite is known through the other.

### On God deduced through Minority.

<column-break/>

<margin>Intrinsic mode</margin>
In God there is no minority <note>term: minority (Latin: *minoritas*). The state of being lesser or inferior.</note>, because God Himself is infinite majority and eternal. Otherwise, one opposite would be the other opposite, which is impossible. And for this reason, it is fitting for God to "majorize" <note>To make greater or act through greatness.</note>, but not to "minorize." But because the world cannot exist at all without minorities, God disposed Himself to create minority in the world, so that through finite minorities, His infinite majority might be known. For one opposite is better known through the other; whence the intellect knows that God is greater absolutely, by reason of eternity, while the world is lesser, by reason of minority or novelty.

<margin>On God through the discourse of Minority.</margin>
<margin>Extrinsic mode</margin>
God, thus knowing Himself disposed to create majority rather than minority, therefore creates minorities for the sake of majorities—just as the body of a man exists for the sake of the rational soul. And all corporeal things exist for the body of man, and leaves and flowers for the fruit; and so it is with other secondary intentions in relation to primary intentions. We have investigated God through the aforementioned explained principles so that we might have knowledge of Him; and just as we gave an example through the aforementioned explained principles, so it can be given through the implied principles, by following the method we have held.

### On God deduced through Rule B.

<margin>Whether</margin>
<margin>On God through the discourse of Rule B.</margin>
The question is asked: *Whether God exists?* To prove that God exists, we wish to follow the method of the Art: namely, to mix the principles with the rules to investigate and prove that God exists, making Eternity the subject, applying it to other principles, and first through Goodness.

<margin>Goodness</margin>
Eternity exists. For if it did not, the world would have indeed originated itself. And thus it would have existed before it existed, which is impossible; for no being can originate itself. Therefore, eternity exists through its concrete form, namely an "Eternal Being" <note>original: *ens eternum*. The author argues that an abstract quality like eternity must exist in a concrete subject.</note>; for no essence can exist without its concrete form, and vice versa. This infinite duration exists, and its infinite goodness exists. Whence it follows that goodness is the reason for the Eternal One to act well eternally. That being is infinitely good, for whom goodness is the reason to act well infinitely and eternally; and such a being we call God. Therefore, it is clear through the aforementioned that God exists; and the human intellect, following the method of the General Art, cannot deny this.

<margin>Greatness</margin>
Eternity exists, as has already been proven above; and it is great through greatness in so...
