### Eternity is:
<margin>Power</margin>
(as was proved above) and since it is, its power is infinite, without which it could not be infinite; indeed, this power is the reason for eternity so that it can exist and act infinitely: and such a subject of the aforementioned eternity we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Appetite <note>original: "ap." likely referring to Appetitus or the desire for the good</note></margin>
and its being is infinite and intelligible; from which it follows that some eternal being is living or possessing life, without which it could not be an eternal intelligible being: and such an infinite and eternal being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Will</margin>
and it is infinite duration; it is indeed lovable: from which it follows that the eternal being has life, without which it cannot be loved from eternity and in eternity; and such a loved and eternal being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Virtue</margin>
infinite, and thus it is virtuous; for without infinite virtue it could by no means be virtuous. From which it follows that its virtue is infinite, so that vice is not present in it; from which it follows that its eternity has an act, namely *eternizing* <note>The act of making or being eternal</note>, in which act all the principles of the first figure <note>The primary divine attributes in Lullian logic: Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Power, Wisdom, Will, Virtue, Truth, and Glory</note> have eternal acts: just as goodness has *bonifying*, eternity has *eternizing*, and power has *powering* <note>original: "possificare"</note>, etc. Otherwise, the virtue itself would be vicious and injurious, which is impossible; and such an eternal and virtuous being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Glory</margin>
and because it is infinite, it is therefore an infinite and glorious being: it is therefore infinite glory, without which an infinite and eternal being could by no means be glorious; in which being *glorifying* and *eternizing* are infinite, without which the eternal being would have eternal pain: which is false and impossible. And such a being in which there is *eternizing* and *glorifying* we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Difference <note>original: "iss" likely for "differentia" or "distinctio"</note></margin>
and in it its co-essential reasons are clear and not confused: namely its concrete form which is "the eternal," and it is good through goodness, and great through magnitude, and powerful through power, etc. Not that they are different reasons in existing, but in acting: namely, in the eternal being itself, its goodness and magnitude are the same by essence, so that eternity is not good and great by accident, but by itself. Indeed, by reason of action they are clear: because eternity is the reason for the eternal [being] that it should act well, and it is the reason of magnitude that it should be an *eternized* product; from which it follows necessarily that in the essence of eternity there is a "good eternizer" and a "great producer," distinct from the "good and great eternized," and that they are distinct from *eternizing*, *bonifying*, and *magnifying* by an essential relation existing as one essence; otherwise the reasons would be

<column-break/>

confused. And such an eternal and absolute being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Concordance</margin>
and consequently the eternal being is: and in that eternal being its co-essential reasons concord in one and in many; namely, that just as eternity is infinite duration, so its goodness is infinite *bonifying*, and its magnitude is infinite *magnifying*, and its power is infinite *powering*, and its intellect is infinite *intellection*, and its will is infinite *volition*, etc. And that all are one good, great being, etc., which being indeed has through goodness an infinite *bonifying*, through magnitude an infinite *magnifying*, etc. And such a being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Contrariety</margin>
and consequently the eternal being is: and because eternity itself is infinite, etc., it follows that the eternal being is infinite: because the being itself is good. Indeed, no finite being can contradict the eternal and infinite being when it acts as the eternal and great good, etc., nor indeed can the eternal being itself. It could not be otherwise since the co-essential virtues and reasons are infinite and have infinite acts. And such a being we call God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Beginning</margin>
and it is itself; but eternity is infinite duration: time, however, cannot be infinite duration; the reason for this is because time cannot be without motion; eternity, however, is without motion; from which it follows that eternity is the first and last principle lying before time absolutely: and such an eternal being existing as the first and last principle we say is God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Middle</margin>
and because it is an absolutely infinite essence, it follows that in it is *eternizing*, which is the middle between the "eternizer" and the "eternized," without which eternity would be infinite as to existing, and finite as to acting, by reason of which its absolute infinity would be destroyed: which is impossible. And such an eternity in which there is co-essential *eternizing*, we say is God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>End</margin>
and because it is infinite in existing, likewise also in acting: so that its end is equal to its existence; namely, that just as it is infinite as to existence, so it relates to infinite acting, through the "eternizer," the "eternized," and "eternizing": and such an eternity which relates to the ultimate end, we say is God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Majority</margin>
and it is the greatest duration that can be, with the greatest goodness that can be: and with the greatest magnitude that can be: which "minority" <note>The state of being lesser</note> cannot contradict since they are infinite reasons in existing and acting. And such a greater duration is God.

### Eternity is:
<margin>Equality</margin>
and consequently the eternal being is. In which eternal being its co-essential goodness, magnitude, etc., are equal to eternity: so that its goodness, magnitude, etc., are thus infinite as to *bonifying*, just as eternity is as to duration: and such an eternal being we say is God.

# Ninth Part.

<margin>Minority <note>original: "Minoritas"; referring to the state of being finite or lesser.</note></margin>
Infinite duration is indeed infinitely distant from minority, which is finite: and consequently from the finite, which is less than eternity. And thus, whatever things exist can be spoken of in terms of lesser agency and existence. ¶ We have proved that God exists according to the "prolas" <note>A technical term in this system for a type of logical progression or demonstration.</note> through all principles; nevertheless, it can be proved through all principles by syllogism: no infinite being is without infinite power; eternity is infinite; therefore, etc. And such a being is not the heaven, nor anything contained beneath it; therefore, such a being is said to be God. And the question is resolved which asks whether God exists: because we have proved Him to exist with the principles and the rule of B. <note>Referring to "Rule B," a specific logical tool in the author's Art.</note> Regarding His existence and His intrinsic agency, knowledge can be had through the mediation of His grace; I say this, however, regarding apprehension <note>Grasping the concept.</note>, but not regarding comprehension <note>Fully exhausting the mystery.</note>: for God is infinite, but our intellect is finite.

### Concerning God, deduced through Rule C.

<margin>What</margin>
<margin>Concerning God, deduced through Rule C.</margin>
Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: what is God? So that we may have a clearer knowledge of God, we wish to define Him through His definitions. In these, the subject and predicate are convertible <note>Meaning the terms are interchangeable in a logical sentence.</note>: because one cannot be without the other, by reason of the natural conjunction which the subject and predicate possess. Just as if one asks: what is substance? And the answer is: that which is a being subsisting through itself. And to ask: what is a being subsisting through itself? It must be said that it is substance. ¶ God is the being in whom His reasons <note>Attributes or essential principles.</note> are convertible. Indeed, the being in whom His reasons are convertible is God. ¶ God is the being in whom the divine reasons have infinite acts: just as infinite goodness has infinite "bonifying" <note>The act of making or being good.</note>, and magnitude has infinite "magnifying," etc. But the being in whom there is goodness having an infinite act, etc., is God. ¶ God is the being for whom His coessential goodness is the reason why He acts as an infinite and eternal good: indeed, the being for whom His coessential goodness is the reason why He acts as an infinite and eternal good is God. ¶ God is the being who cannot exist without infinite reasons: but the being who cannot exist without infinite reasons is God. ¶ God is the "bonifying" being who cannot "bonify" without an infinite "bonified" <note>The object of the act of goodness.</note>: the infinite "bonified" and the "bonifying"—which could not exist without a "bonifier"—is God. ¶ God is the substance stripped of every accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality (like color); God is pure essence.</note>: indeed, the substance stripped of every accident is

<margin>Goodness</margin>
<margin>Magnitude</margin>
<margin>Eternity</margin>
<margin>Power</margin>

<column-break/>

God. ¶ God is the absolute being not depending on anything: the absolute being not depending on anything is God. ¶ God is the being who needs nothing outside of Himself: the being who needs nothing outside of Himself is God. ¶ God is the being who cannot be otherwise than He is. But the being who cannot be otherwise than He is, is God. ¶ God is the being who relates to His own end as much as He Himself is: the being who relates to His own end as much as He is, is God. ¶ God is the being who can do as much from Himself as He Himself is. But the being who can do as much of Himself and in Himself as He Himself is, is God. ¶ God is the being above whom there is no "majority" <note>No greater state of being.</note>: the being above whom there is no majority is God. ¶ God is the being who knows Himself as an agent as much as He Himself is. The being who knows Himself as an agent as much as He Himself is, is God. ¶ God is the being for whom it is impossible not to be. The being for whom it is impossible not to be is God. ¶ We have defined God through twenty reasons in which the subject and predicate are necessarily converted: as is evident through Rule B. ¶ And through such necessary definitions, the human intellect is greatly clarified for knowing the divine essence, and its intrinsic and natural acts. ¶ However, descriptions of God can be made through accidents in this way: God is the Creator, and Governor, and First Cause, and First Mover, and Savior, and such things. But through such descriptions, the intellect is not as greatly clarified as through the substantial definitions mentioned above. ¶ Through the second species of Rule C, it is asked: what does God have in Himself, coessentially and naturally? To this it must be answered that He has coessential, natural, and substantial relatives. Just as through His goodness He has the "bonifier," the "bonified," and the act of "bonifying." And through His magnitude, the "magnifier," the "magnified," and the act of "magnifying." And through His eternity, the "eternizer," the "eternized," and the act of "eternizing," etc. ¶ Without these correlatives, the aforementioned reasons could not be realized in God; nor could our intellect have knowledge of His essence. For without them, the reasons or "dignities" <note>The divine attributes like Power, Wisdom, and Love.</note> of God would be empty, idle, and imperfect; and each would be a privative habit <note>A state of lacking something.</note>. And consequently, God would need to be worthy after He lacked perfect reasons: because without such an intrinsic "having," the nature of the relation would be destroyed, as would the nature of the aforementioned reasons, which is impossible. ¶ Through the third species of Rule C, it is asked: what is God in another? To which it must be said that He is in His effect as the First Cause, First Mover, Ruler, and Governor, acting in His effect according to His pleasure.

### Concerning God, deduced through rule D.

<margin>Concerning God, deduced through rule D.
First:
Matter
Possibility</margin>
Through the first species of rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "Of what?" (De quo?)</note>, it is asked: of what is God made? And it must be answered that he is of himself. For thus, possessing infinite reasons <note>The "Dignities" or divine attributes like Goodness, Greatness, etc.</note> having infinite acts, he cannot be from any other pre-existing thing. But he himself is indeed pre-existent to all other beings that are distinct from him by essence: just as the divine goodness is the primary source for all other goodness. Just as an infinite being is the primary source for a finite being. And thus it can be said of divine greatness and eternity, etc. And in this step, the human intellect recognizes that God is pure act <note>Pure actuality without potentiality or change</note>.
¶ Through the second species of rule D, it is asked: of what is God made? And to this it must be answered that he is of his "correlatives" mentioned before: just as divine goodness is composed of that *through which* it acts, consisting of its "bonifier" <note>the actor</note>, the "bonified" <note>the object</note>, and the "to bonify" <note>the act of making good</note>: and all these three are of goodness itself: just as a concrete thing is of its essence: and as a man is of his humanity, and a lion of its lionness, etc. And in this step, our intellect recognizes that in God no malice, smallness, or novelty can exist.
¶ Through the third rule of D, it is asked: to whom does God belong? And to this it must be answered that he is subject to no one: for he is infinite and eternal; nevertheless, in paradise he is the "subject" <note>The object of focus</note> for all the saints who receive their presented glory from him.

### Concerning God, deduced through rule E.

<margin>Concerning God, deduced through rule E.
Form</margin>
Through the first species of rule E <note>Rule E usually asks "Why?" (Quare?)</note>, it is asked: why is God? And it must be answered that he is formally through his correlatives from which he is composed. And consequently through his co-essential reasons: and because in him the subject and predicate are interchangeable: as was proven above in his definition. Just as a substance exists through this: because it is composed of its matter, form, and their conjunction. And man of his body and soul and their con-

<column-break/>

-junction. And thus of a syllogism it can be said that its "middle term" is the connective with its major and minor terms. ¶ Furthermore, God exists through this: because his infinite reasons are interchangeable according to the identity of his essence. For all are one singular divine essence: and further because all his "dignities" <note>divine attributes</note> have infinite acts: and in his definition, the subject and predicate are essentially interchangeable, as was said above. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that God is immutable: and that his being cannot be otherwise.
¶ Through the second species of rule E, it is asked: why is God? And it must be answered that he is for the sake of his own absolute end; for an infinite and eternal end cannot exist for the sake of a finite end. ¶ This is further manifested: namely, that God exists for the sake of an absolute end, and not for another. For each correlative of his dignities exists for the sake of the other correlative: because each exists so that the other may be: otherwise none could have infinite goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ Furthermore, God exists so that his "agency" <note>the power to act</note> can be, and vice versa. ¶ Moreover, in God his co-essential reasons exist so that he himself, with them, can have intrinsic and infinite acts: so that his agency is as infinite as his existence. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the error of those who say that God has reasons so that he might act finitely with them externally, like an efficient cause in a foreign subject, by accident. Such an error is indeed evident. For God, without co-essential natural reasons having intrinsic and infinite acts, would not be the highest and infinite being: because he would not be supremely good, great, or eternal through himself, but through another: indeed, a man, or a rose, or a lion would have more regard for their end than God, because they have their own natural ends for which they exist to be what they are. And thus it is clear that the aforesaid error is exposed.

# Part Nine

<margin>Real</margin>
<margin>Numerical</margin>
<margin>Correlatives</margin>
<margin>The fourth number</margin>
<margin>The fourth number</margin>
<margin>Even odd</margin>

<margin>The middle subject in a proposition</margin>
continuous quantity; or numerical <note>discrete</note> quantity. God indeed does not have real <note>physical/material</note> quantity, because He does not have a body; for a corporeal being has quantity. But God Himself has continuous essence and goodness, etc. For in an infinite subject, quantity can in no way exist, just as in eternity, time and motion cannot have being. Numerical quantity can be in God by reason of His correlatives <note>The internal relationships within the Trinity</note>: as in the divine goodness, in which the **Bonifier** <note>The Father</note> knows Himself to be one distinct thing; and knows the **Bonified** <note>The Son</note> to be another distinct from Him. And in turn, the Bonifier and the Bonified know the **Bonifying** <note>The Holy Spirit</note> to be another distinct from themselves; and thus numerical quantity follows in them: namely, one, two, three. And at this step, the intellect doubts whether three correlatives or more are sufficient in the divine goodness. But it is reminded of the divine unity and singularity through which God is: one and singular; just as through His goodness He is good, and through His greatness He is great, etc. Therefore, one singular Bonifier (and not Bonified) is sufficient; and one singular Bonified (and also Bonifier); and another one singular Bonifying (and not Bonifier). If, however, there were a **fourth number** there, etc., there would already be a destruction of unity and singularity. Indeed, a fourth number would either be a Bonifier not Bonified, or Bonified and Bonifier, or Bonifying and not Bonifier; and thus there would be a superfluity there which would be evil, against the nature of infinite goodness, and a vice against the great and eternal virtue of divine goodness; and it would also act against the glory of divine goodness and would be an evil and privative habit: like deafness, ignorance, or privation; which is impossible. ¶ Further, the intellect considers numerical quantity, which is the principle of number: and the second unity arises from it; the third unity arises from them, like a conclusion from two propositions: and thus follows a **perfect number**, because every number is included in them: namely, even and odd. Two indeed are an even number; but three is odd. Whence it appears clearly that a fourth unity is superfluous; and also a fifth, etc. ¶ For now even and odd are possessed; and also because the fourth unity is disconnected from the second unity, which is a middle between the first unity and the third: just as in a mood of the first figure <note>A term from Aristotelian logic regarding syllogisms</note> in which the middle is the subject in which the predicate of the major proposition and the subject of the minor proposition are joined: so that the subject and predicate in the conclusion agree in nature, as is clear through this syllogism: *Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance.* ¶ Thence

<column-break/>

therefore the intellect knows that in the divine goodness a threefold number <note>The Trinity</note> suffices: and that neither a greater nor a lesser number is necessary. Nevertheless, in species there are more individuals than three. Just as there are one, two, three, and four men in the human species: and those must be numbered by more unities or numbers, as is self-evident.

### Concerning God, deduced through Rule G.
<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Quality</margin>
<margin>Concerning God deduced through Rule G</margin>
<margin>Properties</margin>
Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: **of what sort is He?** And to this it must be answered that God is such as are His properties or reasons, and their consubstantial acts: as through His goodness, because through it He is good; and through His greatness He is great; and through His eternity He is eternal; and so of the others. ¶ Furthermore, since goodness is the reason for a good thing that it should produce good, and it is great through greatness, and eternal through eternity; and it is goodness itself: therefore goodness is the reason for God that He should be of such a sort properly in producing an infinite and eternal good: just as heat—and much better—is the reason for fire that through it the fire should be of such a sort in heating a good, great, and durable heated thing. And this is signified in the correlatives which are through the second species of Rule C. For without such proper and consubstantial qualities, God could not have proper being, nor being through Himself, nor consequently would He have intrinsic, infinite, and eternal acts. ¶ Furthermore, He could not appropriately produce anything outside Himself in another subject; for a quality that is appropriated must be caused by a proper quality: just as air and water which are heated are so by the proper heat of fire. ¶ Through the second species of Rule G, it is asked: **what sort of God is He?** And it must be said that God is such through description: because He is Creator and Governor and Savior and suchlike; as God who disposes Himself to be just and merciful, pious and benign, as an efficient cause in His effect, which is distinct from Him by essence and nature.

<margin>C in the middle</margin>
<margin>Appropriated</margin>

### Concerning God, deduced through Rule H.
<margin>Concerning God deduced through Rule H</margin>
<margin>c d K</margin>
It is asked whether God is in time. To this it is answered that He is not properly, but by accident. For an eternal being having an eternal act cannot be in time.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Nine Subjects" within the author's philosophical system, specifically applying his logical rules (represented by letters like C, D, and K) to the nature of God.</meta>

# On the Nine Subjects
->Page 54<-

Just as an infinite being cannot exist within a finite quantity; and just as the number six cannot be contained within the number five; nor an evil essence within a good essence; nor seeing within a physical accident; nor hearing within seeing; nor understanding within ignorance, etc. And all these things are made manifest through the rule of C. D. K. <note>These letters refer to specific logical categories in Ramon Llull's "Art," where C often represents Greatness, D Duration, and K the rule of "How" or "With what."</note> to a man who looks closely, to whom we leave the explanation to avoid being overly wordy.

### Concerning God through the discourse of rule I.

<margin>Concerning God through the discourse of rule I. D. K.</margin>
It is asked: is God in a place? And it must be answered that God is not properly in a place, but only by "accident" <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature—like a person's hair color versus their humanity.</note>. For just as eternity cannot exist within time, nor goodness within malice, nor a truly understanding intellect within ignorance; so indeed God, by reason of His infinity and immensity, cannot be situated in any specific place. For infinity and immensity are that through which God encompasses and passes through every place. ¶ From this it is clearly evident that He is in every place, and yet outside of every place immeasurably; and He exists infinitely stripped of all physical quantity and surface. And the rules B. C. D. K. prove this.

### Concerning God through the discourse of the rule of Modality.

<margin>In what manner</margin>
<margin>Concerning God through the discourse of the rule of Modality.</margin>
Through rule K <note>The rule of "How" (Quomodo).</note> it is asked: how does God exist, and how does He act? ¶ To the first, it must be answered that God has a mode of being what He is through that manner which His essential and natural principles possess; and this is illustrated in the chapter on "Place" in which it is asked where God is, and how God produces within His "correlatives" <note>A technical term in Lullian logic referring to the active, passive, and verbal relationship within an essence (e.g., the Lover, the Beloved, and Loving).</note>, as was said above. ¶ Furthermore, it appears clearly to one who knows this Art that God has a manner of acting within His "relatives": just as His goodness is the reason for a good being to act goodly, and greatness to act greatly, and eternity the reason for it to be eternal; therefore goodness is the reason for a good being to produce what is good, great, and eternal, etc. And this happens intrinsically—namely, in His very own essence and nature without any external accident. ¶ Moreover, God has a manner of acting extrinsically by reason of the "conversion" of His dignities <note>The "Dignities" are God's primary attributes like Goodness, Greatness, Power, etc.</note>. For when God created the world, His intellect understood it, and His

<column-break/>

will willed it, and His power "possibilized" it <note>original: "possificauit" — a coined term meaning to give the power or possibility of being.</note>, and His goodness "bonified" it <note>original: "bonificauit" — to make good.</note>. For it was good to create the world, and this happened in an instant, without a sequence of His principles. And God has this same manner in performing miracles, and in judging, and in sparing, and in giving grace, and such things: because He wills to act upon an object, and He makes that action happen; and His power gives it possibility, and His truth makes it true. And the created subject is obedient to such an action. For a finite being cannot resist an infinite being.

### Concerning God through the discourse of the rule of Instrumentality.

<margin>Concerning God through the discourse of the rule of Instrumentality.</margin>
It is asked: with what is God existing and acting? And it must be answered that He is existing with His "correlative" co-essential principles, without which He cannot be what He is, nor would He be the Supreme Being—just as a man cannot be a man without a soul, a body, and a head. For if God were the Supreme without His goodness, He would no longer have a nature by which He was distinct from malice; and thus He would no longer be the Supreme, but rather the lowest, which is impossible. And if He were the Supreme without immensity, He would no longer have that by which He stood apart from physical quantity. And if He were not eternal, He could not be separated from time. And if He were not powerful through Himself, He would no longer be "of Himself"; and so on for the others. And because He is "of Himself"—as proved above—it is therefore clear that He exists with His co-essential principles, without which He would not be the Supreme. ¶ Furthermore, God acts intrinsically with His principles, as appears in His correlatives designated by the second type of rule C. ¶ Again, He acts with the aforementioned principles and relatives extrinsically as an "effecter" <note>As a cause producing an effect.</note>, but not by natural necessity. For He inclines Himself morally toward His effect: just as a just man inclines toward judging with justice, and a logician toward a syllogism with reason, and such like. ¶ We have spoken of God through the deduction of rule K; and through those things we have said of Him explicitly, the practitioner of this Art can speak of God through "implicit principles" reduced to "explicit principles," just as we have done. ¶ We have treated the first subject <note>God</note> at great length because its matter is very vast. Regarding the other subjects, however, we shall not speak in this way, because their matter is not so vast. And since knowledge can be had of those subjects through what we have said about the first subject; and this indeed is signified in the Fatherland <note>original: "patria" — a common medieval term for Heaven.</note>. For the saints, in beholding God as their object, know all things.

The author concludes the section on God, noting that understanding the Divine essence allows for the understanding of all other subjects.</summary>

### Concerning the second subject, namely the angel: and first deduced through the principles.

<margin>The deduction of the angel through the principles.
Goodness</margin>
The **Goodness** of an angel is the reason why it acts well; insofar as such a reason is great, it is the reason for it to perform a great good. And insofar as it is lasting, it is the reason for it to perform a lasting good, and so on. However, I do not say that an angel produces or generates another angel: because if it were so, it would empty itself by reason of its infinity, novelty, and indivisibility, which it possesses far removed from length and width <note>The author argues angels are spiritual points without physical dimensions</note>. Indeed, that which an angel possesses within itself is the goodness of understanding, loving, and recollecting natural principles. ¶ Furthermore, an angel shares good words with another. But the human intellect wonders 
<margin>Why angels do not have tongues.
Greatness</margin>
why angels do not have tongues, and organs, and such things by which speech can occur. Until the intellect remembers that their speech is nothing other than the goodness of understanding, loving, and recollecting one another: for through their goodness, all of this is good. ¶ The **Greatness** of an angel is the reason that its goodnesses are great. Whence it follows that goodness is great through its <term>correlatives</term> <note>In this philosophical system, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving</note> without which it would not be great. ¶ But here the intellect wonders what the angel "bonifies" <note>original: "bonificat"; to make good or act out goodness</note>, since it does not produce or generate another angel, until it remembers the action of other "bonifying" principles in their own "bonifiable" subject: just as the intellect, in its own "intelligible" subject, makes other intelligible or understood principles. 
<margin>Duration</margin>
¶ The **Duration** of an angel is the reason by which it lasts: and also its principles and acts last in an instant without succession <note>Angelic time is viewed as "aeviternity," a single moment rather than a linear flow</note>. But the intellect wonders what the cause of its sustenance is, since it receives no nourishment or growth from the outside, until it remembers the angelic nature: which is certainly not composed of contraries <note>Unlike physical bodies made of competing elements like hot and cold, angels are simple spirits and thus do not decay</note>. And if the sun, which is a bodily being, lasts without nourishment, then much more so does the angel, who is a spirit stripped of any physical surface. 
<margin>Power</margin>
¶ The **Power** of an angel is the reason that it can exist and act. ¶ But the intellect wonders, since the angel has no organs to serve as its instruments of acting: and then it remembers the correlatives of its power with which it acts, as if by way of "possifying" instruments <note>original: "possificando"; the act of making something possible or exercising power</note>. For just as heat, which is an <term>accident</term> <note>A non-essential quality</note>, is the instrument with which fire can act by heating, so—and much more so—the angel can exist and act through the correlatives of its power. For these correlatives are substantial to it. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes 

<column-break/>

that the <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Sharing the same essence or substance</note> principles of angels are to them like instruments. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes the reason why the angel is in a higher grade than lower beings. 
<margin>Wisdom/Intellect</margin>
¶ The **Intellect** of the angel is the reason by which it understands with its correlatives: for with its "intellective" part it is an "understander," namely it is active in understanding within its "intelligible" part, in which it understands other beings. Is it any wonder if it does this? For fire, which does not have as high a power as an angel, heats other elements within its own "ignitable" sphere. ¶ Furthermore, the intellect wonders by what means the angelic intellect understands things, since it does not create <term>species</term> <note>Mental images or representations of objects</note> through the senses or through imagination. ¶ But it remembers that the angelic intellect is like an instrument for understanding: although it is consubstantial to the angel, just as other principles are consubstantial to it, like the will of a man is for willing: and much more so, because man cannot will without a bodily organ; but the angel, who is a higher creature than man, can understand without an attached organ. 
<margin>Will</margin>
¶ The angel uses its **Will** as an instrument, although it is not truly a separate instrument; rather, a natural will belongs to the angel for the purpose of willing: so that with that will it may act upon the "lovability" assigned to it by the supreme order. ¶ But the intellect wonders what the cause is that an angel's will can love those things which are neither in the senses nor in the imagination: but it remembers its own rudeness and coarseness which it has: because it is joined with sense and imagination: but the angel's will is not so: and it can relate to an object without sense and imagination much more than a plant can relate to appetite without sense and imagination. 
<margin>Virtue</margin>
¶ The angel has **Virtue** with which it naturally acts in its principles, insofar as those principles are virtuous, and have virtuous acts, and are good through goodness, and great through greatness, etc. ¶ But the intellect wonders by what means the angel acquires accidental virtues, until it remembers that the angel has virtuous habits, by perceiving objects through virtuous understanding and loving: and also through acting justly, prudently, and charitably, by helping us against sins and evil angels, by bringing us announcements from the Supreme Principle, and by carrying our prayers to Him, and by praying for us. 
<margin>Truth</margin>
¶ The angel through its **Truth** is a true understander, lover, and recollector: just like a man, and much better, who through his soul truly understands, loves, and recollects: and through his imagination truly imagines: and through...

### Concerning the angel as deduced through Rule B.

Through Rule B, it is asked: whether there is an angel or whether angels exist? And it appears through Rule B itself that they do, as is evident in the <term>mixture of principles</term><note>A core concept in Lullian logic where basic attributes like Goodness and Greatness are combined to find truths</note>. But in this part, we intend to explain and prove this through the mixture of principles, by resuming certain things said in the chapter on Goodness. ¶ In the beginning of the chapter on Goodness, it is said in the first part of the second principal part of the distinction, that goodness is of itself the reason for a good thing to act or produce good; and because it is great through Greatness, it is a doubled reason for a good thing to produce a great good; and this is known by Divine Wisdom, which is good and great. And because the Divine Will is made equal to Divine Goodness, and Wisdom in its greatness wills that there be angels; and in willing, therefore, there are angels. ¶ It is said in the chapter on Wisdom—the chapter previously cited—that goodness is knowable through wisdom, etc. And therefore, Divine Goodness is knowable; and just as it is knowable and lovable, it is knowable and lovable with the greatness of its knowability and lovability. Therefore, its act is more knowable and lovable, and consequently its effect, because it is lovable. And if we did not have an unjoined spirit—namely the angel—the Divine Will would be hindering it from being; because if He did not want it to be, He would contradict the great action of Divine Goodness in that which is superior, and not in that which is inferior: which is impossible and contrary to the knowability of Divine Wisdom. Therefore, it is proved through superior causes that angels exist. ¶ We have proved that angels exist through the three reasons mentioned above; and because we avoid prolixity, let what has been said suffice. ¶ And in this passage, it is shown that the mixture of principles is the matter and subject in which the artist can find many things at his pleasure and apply them to his purpose.

<meta>This page continues the systematic investigation of the nature of angels using a logical framework of "rules" (questions). It follows a discussion on the definitions of subjects, now applying specific categories to the angelic essence.</meta>

# Concerning the nine subjects.

<margin>Angel</margin>
foreign intelligibilities <note>original: "intelligibilitates peregrinas"; likely referring to knowledge or concepts originating outside the angel's own nature</note>. ¶ Through the third species <note>a specific category of inquiry in this logical system</note> it is asked: what is an angel in another? And it must be answered that it is both active and passive: active as in lower things in which it acts by understanding and loving, etc. And its power fulfills that which its will desires, and that which its intellect understands, and what its memory recalls. And this happens without succession <note>meaning instantaneously, not step-by-step</note> and without phantasms <note>mental images derived from the senses</note>, yet with the help of divine goodness, greatness, etc. And by the presence of God, it receives the influences of causes by being passive; and this "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note> is its salvation and perfection. However, the evil angel receives passions from without when it cannot achieve its sins. And it has passions because God is absent from it through grace, and it is emptied of its true end. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does an angel have in another? And it must be answered that it has power over lower things, because it acts without touch, without sight, hearing, or imagination; and it has this power through the presence of God in which it exists, just as a joined soul has power in the lower faculties because it is joined with them. Furthermore, good angels have glory in God, and the evil angel has punishment, but it would be long to enumerate these.

# Concerning the angel, deduced through Rule D.

<margin>concerning the angel deduced through D.</margin>
<margin>First</margin>
<margin>Matter</margin>
Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: of what is an angel made? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is not derived from any other thing. The reason for this is so that its innate goodness, greatness, etc., may be its innate, primitive, dissimilar, and incorruptible principles, so that its essence can be permanent and incorruptible; nevertheless, we say that it is created by God. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is the angel composed? And it must be answered that it is of its innate principles, such as its true goodness, greatness, etc. And because each principle exists in it in a threefold way: such as goodness through the *bonified*, the *bonifiable*, and the *act of bonifying* <note>original: "bonificatum, bonificabile & bonificare"; these are technical terms for the object, the capacity, and the action of goodness</note>; and greatness through the *magnified*, the *magnifiable*, and the *act of magnifying*, etc. And because these principles differ essentially, the angel is composed of its goodness, greatness, etc. And from all its active principles <note>original: "tiuis," likely an abbreviation for "activis"</note> there is constituted in it one form in common with which it is active; and from all its passive principles <note>original: "bilibus," likely "passibilibus"</note>, namely the bonifiable and magnifiable, etc., there is constituted one matter with which it is passive; and from all its acts—namely bonifying, magnifying, etc.—there is constituted one act in common with which it causes extrinsic acts. Thus, from all the three aforementioned things, its substance is composed, united, and substantially separated from all corporeal <note>physical</note> matter. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does the angel belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to God with blessing, glory, and glorification; but the evil angel belongs to God with contradiction, punishment, and pain.

<column-break/>

# Concerning the angel, deduced through Rule E.

<margin>why</margin>
<margin>Possibility</margin>
Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: why is there an angel? And it must be answered that it is constituted from its natural principles, as we said above in the second species of Rule D. Since its principle is composed with another, a being composed of necessity must be given in common. Just as it is said that when the soul is joined with the body, a human follows of necessity. And when the "elemental power" is placed with the "vegetative power," a vegetative element follows of necessity.
¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is there an angel? And it must be answered with respect to its end <note>purpose</note> that the angel exists so that it may understand, love, and remember God, and do Him honor, and fill the universe; for if there were no angel in its place, the universe would be a vacuum, as was proven above.

It must be answered that an angel is of two modes: namely, of qualities that are innate and proper, and of qualities that are appropriated and not natural to it. We call its natural and substantial goodness, greatness, etc., from which it is constituted, its "proper" qualities. # Ninth Part.

<margin>When</margin>
It is asked concerning the time of an angel. And we say that an angel is in time: because it began in time, without which it would not have had a beginning. **The reason for this** is: because that which exists and once did not exist cannot be without time. Furthermore, an angel is in time with respect to its contrariety <note>The author likely refers to the angel's changing states or actions</note>: that is, without succession and without motion <note>Angels move instantaneously in scholastic thought</note>: but when it acts externally, it acts anew "now" in another place: just as when it acts on the Lord's day <note>Sunday</note> that which it was doing on the Sabbath day. And it is in one time when it is at Rome by day: and it is in another time when it is at Paris by night. Nevertheless, when it departs from Rome and is in Paris, its departure is not with motion, nor with succession. For just as it does not need eyes to see color, so it does not need motion nor succession in its departure: but it wills, and it is where it wills. ¶ **By rule .i.** <note>The letter 'i' refers to the question "Where?" (Ubi)</note> it is asked concerning the place of an angel: The answer is that an angel is in a place, because it was created in a place: but it is not in a place by occupying space: because a place cannot be occupied without a line, an angle, and a figure <note>geometric dimensions</note>, from which every angel is separate. And it is in a place because it is in one place and not in another where it is not: and it is in that place in which it acts, in which place it cannot act without its presence. **The reason for this** is because it acts with its essence and not with a physical organ. ¶ **By the first species of rule .k.** <note>The letter 'k' refers to the question "How?" (Quomodo)</note> it is asked, how is an angel and how does it act? And the answer is that an angel has a mode of being through the composition of its principles: as was illustrated in the second species of rule .d. mentioned above. And it has a mode of acting with its principles with which it causes external acts: just as with its goodness it produces good, and with its power it produces power, and so with the others. ¶ **By the second species of rule .k.** <note>The letter 'k' here refers to "With what?" (Cum quo)</note> it is asked, with what is an angel and with what does it act? And the answer is that it is with its innate and natural principles joined together, as was indicated in the second species of rule .d. And it acts with them; namely, with the intellect it understands, with the will it loves, with the memory it recollects: and if it is good, with its goodness it produces good, and with its power it exercises power. And if it is evil, it makes evil its understanding, recollecting, and loving: and so with the others: and it acts with its principles both intrinsically and extrinsically, i.e., by causing something externally with an act that is internal. Just as a man who causes in his mind the words which he brings forth with his mouth.

### Concerning the Heavens deduced through the principles.

<column-break/>

<margin>Concerning the Heavens deduced through the principles.</margin>
In this chapter we shall treat the Heavens <note>the celestial spheres/astronomy</note> joined with the principles from which they are made, and with which they relate to the lower principles effectively, like a cause to its effect. ¶ The Heaven is good through its innate goodness: and it is great through its natural greatness: and therefore its goodness and its greatness are the reasons for it to act well, greatly, and naturally upon these lower things by moving itself and others. And if it is said that sometimes it acts badly, such as Saturn which is "evil" <note>In astrology, Saturn was considered a 'greater malefic'</note>: I answer that this is by accident: because lower things do not receive [the influence] well due to the contrarieties of the elements, by reason of which Saturn sometimes causes monstrosities in lower things through excessive coldness and dryness. ¶ The Heaven is great and durable. Great as to its essence and agency: and it is durable because it is incorruptible and immaterial: and there is no being except God that can compel it, nor hinder its motion. ¶ The Heaven is durable of itself, because duration is its innate quality. ¶ The Heaven is powerful of itself, because its power is a quality innate to it; and just as its duration is great and good, so its power is good and great. And in this passage it appears that the Heaven can move itself, so that its goodness, greatness, and duration do not fail its power, nor power fail them. ¶ Just as the Heaven has a natural will coessential to itself, so it has a natural instinct coessential to itself with which it governs its order, its motion, and the acts of its principles, without which instinct it could not do this. Just as a lion, which has one instinct with Saturn through heat, dryness, cold, and through night-nature, masculinity, long-duration, malice, plurality, and "dyasobistatem" <note>original: "dyasobistatem" — likely a technical term in the author's Lullian system referring to a specific planetary influence</note>. But it has another with Jupiter through goodness, and "stagneitate" <note>original: "stagneitate" — likely referring to tin, the metal of Jupiter</note>, and "dyaioueitatem" <note>original: "dyaioueitatem" — another Lullian term for Jove-like quality</note>, and so with the others. ¶ The Heaven has instinct as was said above: and it has appetite, because with its appetite it moves itself and lower things, so that it has one appetite with one planet, and another with another, as was exemplified above through instinct. ¶ The Heaven has appetite: and it has virtue <note>power or inherent strength</note>. And just as its appetite is natural and coessential to it, so is its virtue: and just as its appetite is good through its goodness and great through its greatness, so is its virtue. # On the Nine Subjects
## On the Heavens

<margin>Virtue</margin>
one with the Virgin <note>likely referring to the constellation Virgo</note>, another with Saturn, another with Jupiter; so it is with virtue. ¶ The Heaven is virtuous, as has been said; and it is true in itself, for just as it is virtuous through an innate virtue, so it is true through an innate truth. Through this truth, it places desirable things in reality, and to this end, instinct, power, etc., concur. ¶ The Heaven is true, as has been said, and it possesses an innate delight. I do not mean a vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, or even a reasoning delight, but a motive one <note>a delight found in movement</note>. For just as a plant has a certain natural delight in growing, so the heaven has in moving itself and the lower things. And just as the delight of the vegetative power is not reached through the senses or the imagination, so it is with the heaven's delight; only the intellect can grasp this. ¶ The Heaven has delight, as has been said, and its delight is unconfused because of the "difference" <note>a technical term in this system for the principle of distinction</note> which is its innate principle in which it acts and causes many differences while delighting. This difference itself is imperceptible because it is a general principle. ¶ The Heaven is composed of many differences, just as a whole is composed of its many parts. And "concordance" is a principle co-essential to it, with which it causes many harmonies; thus it is one substance having many things within itself through difference and concordance. ¶ The Heaven has concordance, as has been said, and it possesses a "foreign contrariety" <note>an external opposition</note> that is not co-essential to it, so that it is not corruptible. Rather, it is the instrument by which it opposes lower things, such as through hot and cold, dry and moist, through day and night, and the like. With these, it causes menstruation, lightning, thunder, illnesses, misfortunes, and such. Contrariety is not a principle co-essential to the heaven, but concordance is its principle, as has been said. Thus, the heaven acts more upon lower things by harmonizing than by opposing; for this reason, there are more instances of health than illness, more good fortune than misfortune, and a human is more frequently born with two eyes than with one, and so on for other things. ¶ The Heaven has its innate principles, as has been said, with which it begins lower things effectively, mediated by lower natural beings, such as the qualities of the heavens and their properties. This is true of the elements, metals, plants, and sentient beings. To this concurs the magnitude of the heaven, which magnifies the power of the heaven and its instinct, appetite, virtue, and the like; from which follows the influence from higher things to lower things, and the reflux

<column-break/>

from lower things up to the moon; and this happens continually. The reason for this is that the heaven is always in continuous motion. ¶ In the heaven, there is a "medium" <note>a middle or mediating principle</note> co-essential to it, with which it causes lower mediums; just as celestial "good-making" causes eternal "good-making," and celestial moving causes earthly moving, and so on for others. ¶ The Heaven has a medium, as said above, through which and with which its principles pass to their ends, so that they may rest in it; which rest is to move itself and lower things. The reason for this is that it was created for this purpose. ¶ The end <note>purpose</note> of the heaven is with "majority" <note>greatness/superiority</note>, so that it may serve man, and man may serve God; for its end cannot be at a higher level—namely, beneath that greater end is its own major end: namely, to move, etc. Just as the major end of the vegetative power is to grow, and the major end of the sensitive power is to feel. ¶ We have spoken of the majority of the heaven; its "equality" is the equality of its principles which are co-essential to it. The equalities of the heaven participate in "minority" <note>lesser status</note> with respect to the soul, because the heaven does not possess intellect, memory, or will, nor can it receive merit.

### On the Heaven deduced through the rules.

<margin>On the heaven deduced through the rules.</margin>
**Q**uestion: Is the heaven from eternity? It must be answered that it is not, as is indicated by Rule B. But for the greater evidence of this science, or art and doctrine, we intend to explain in this chapter that which pertains to the heaven. Through what we say about the heaven, we shall give the practitioner a doctrine through which he will know how to act. Because we wish to avoid prolixity, we will apply only "B" to the other letters placed in the alphabet of this art up to "K." Just as we apply "B" to the other letters, so the other letters can be applied to one another in turn. ¶ If the heaven were from eternity, it would not be created from nothing, because it would have always been; nor would it be made from something, because there is no matter outside the heaven from which it could be made, nor within it, because its magnitude contains all things. And thus, the Divine Goodness would not be the reason for God to act upon a "good heaven" nor the "goodness of the heaven," because it would be eternal. The same would apply to the magnitude of God, which would not cause the magnitude of the heaven. It follows then that the world is not an effect as to its goodness and magnitude... <note>original: "ad sua bonitate & magnitudinez"</note>

# Ninth Part.

And therefore there is a difference between the goodness of God and the goodness of the heavens (or their harmony); and likewise concerning magnitude, which requires harmony according to justice between cause and effect. And therefore, if harmony is taken away, contrariety and injustice arise, and greed is caused. God's goodness would not be a greater reason for Him to perform a great good effect if God did not consent to the reason of His own goodness; and because all these things are impossible, it follows that the heaven was created and is new <note>original: "nouum"; in this context, it means "having a beginning in time" rather than existing from eternity</note>.

¶ B. d. If the heaven is eternal, there are multiple eternities: namely, the eternity of God and the eternity of the heaven. And with the eternity of the heaven, infinite eternities are implied, such as innate goodness, duration, etc., and likewise for its stars and revolutions. And thus injustice and gluttony would have existed as early as justice and malice; and contrariety would be as old as goodness and harmony among men. This is because there would never have been a first man, nor a second, nor will there be a last. And thus the divine goodness fails; and there is no reason for God that divine goodness should precede malice, or that the eternity of God should precede the eternity of the heaven. It also follows that there would be no other life <note>referring to the afterlife</note>, since all the matter contained within the heaven would not suffice for the resurrection of dead men—which is what we intend to prove. Thus the justice of God would be defective and hindered from rewarding the righteous and punishing the unrighteous for eternity; and injustice and malice would be the causes of such a state. God's strength would be weakened, and lust would be eternal. Because all these things would be impossible, it follows that the heaven is new and had a beginning.

¶ B. e. If the heaven is eternal of itself, it is able to be eternal because an eternal being was never in a state of potentiality to exist, nor is it in potentiality to not exist. Thus the power of God would not be the cause of the power of the heaven, nor God's goodness the cause of the heaven's goodness. Also, the power of God could not deprive the heaven of its power, because the heaven would govern itself by itself; and thus pride would be eternal, and consequently sin.

¶ Whence it follows that the heaven would have its end within itself, and God would not be its end <note>its ultimate purpose or goal</note>. Since if the cause is taken away, the effect is taken away. And because all these things are evil, unjust, and full of pride—and it has been shown against the rule of goodness that they are impossible—therefore the negative side of the question must be held.

¶ B. f. If the heaven is eternal, time is eternal. And thus the eternity of God does not precede time, which is against justice and faith. Sloth <term>acidia: a state of spiritual apathy or listlessness, one of the seven deadly sins</term> would be eternal, and eternal injustice would follow. This would be known by divine wisdom; and divine goodness is the reason for God to do good by destroying the aforementioned evils; yet [if the heaven were eternal] God would not consent to this; and

Thus He would be unjust and acting against His own charity and justice, which is impossible; and the opposite is necessary.

Because all these are against divine goodness, justice, and truth, it follows that the heaven is new. It is just that divine goodness and truth should precede the duration of the heaven by their eternity, just as they precede the goodness and truth of the heaven (which are limited and finite) by their immensity and infinity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "nine subjects" (subiectis), specifically focusing on the nature of the Heavens (the celestial sphere) through a series of logical inquiries based on a set of rules (labeled c, d, e, f, g, h, i).</meta>

# Concerning the Heavens, deduced through rule C.

<margin>Concerning the Heavens, deduced through rule C. 1. In itself</margin>
Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is the Heavens? And it must be answered that it is the "first movable" <note>original: *primum mobile*; in medieval cosmology, this is the outermost moving sphere that carries the others</note>: and it is a body having the greatest magnitude and the greatest motion. Beyond it, there is nothing movable. It is a body moving by itself, because no mobility is greater than its own; therefore, speaking naturally, motion begins from it and remains from it. It is the fountain from which motion is sometimes derived, just as streams flow from a fountain. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what do the Heavens have within themselves that is co-essential and natural to them? And it must be answered that they have their own motivity <note>the power to move</note>, mobility, and the act of moving. Through motivity, they have form; through mobility, they have matter; and through moving, they have the act with which they create external acts. They also have their innate goodness, magnitude, etc., as well as the stars, planets, and signs, and so with their other co-essential parts.

<margin>In another</margin>
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what are the Heavens in another thing? And it must be answered that the Heavens are in the elements as an agent, moving and influencing them, while having no passion <note>passive reception or suffering of change</note> within themselves. This is by reason of their great activity and motivity; also, the Heavens do not receive increase or decrease within themselves. The intellect marvels at this: since the Heavens possess such great motivity without any alteration or mutation of the subject. But the intellect strengthens itself by considering the divine and infinite power, which can create such an effect according to its pleasure.

<margin>In another</margin>
¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what do the Heavens have in another? And it must be answered that the Heavens naturally have dominion over the elements and the "elementated" things <note>things composed of elements, like plants or animals</note>, with which they cause natural mobilities in the lower regions: the four seasons, days, hours, thunder, lightning, wind, rain, snow, menstrual cycles, illnesses, and the like. This happens because the lower things receive their mobilities and influences from the Heavens, which act as the efficient cause.

<margin>D. From what (limits)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: from what are the Heavens made? It must be answered that they are from themselves, because they are not made from any pre-existing matter from which they were derived. And because they are primarily from themselves on account of their pre-eminent motivity, they are incorruptible; and through themselves, they are permanent in their motivity.

<margin>Matter</margin>
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what are the Heavens composed? And it must be answered that they are composed of their co-essential parts: such as their innate goodness, magnitude, etc. This is signified through the second species of rule D.

<column-break/>

<margin>Possession</margin>
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom do the Heavens belong? It must be answered that they belong to God, just as an effect belongs to its cause. And because they are possessed by God, they cause effects in lower things just as God wills.

<margin>E. Why (formal)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why are there Heavens? And it must be answered that the Heavens exist because they are constituted from their co-essential parts, such as innate goodness, magnitude, etc., excluding contrariety <note>the conflict of opposites like hot/cold</note>, which is not co-essential to them; for if it were, they would be corruptible. They also exist because their celestial matter and form are joined within them, by which they are necessitated; just as a human exists when the soul and body are joined within him.

<margin>Formal</margin>
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why are there Heavens? And it must be answered by reason of their end <note>purpose</note>: that the Heavens exist so that, as a caused thing, they may cause lower motivities, by which man may be disposed toward existing and serving God.

<margin>F. How much (Continuous/Discrete)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: concerning the quantity of the Heavens? And it must be answered that the Heavens have continuous quantity and discrete quantity. Continuous in a circular way, as is figured within them; discrete, as through the eighth sphere which is concave, and likewise for the sphere of Saturn, etc.

<margin>G. What kind (Proper/Appropriated)</margin>
¶ Through rule G, it is asked: what kind of thing are the Heavens? And it must be answered that they are "of a kind" through primary and appropriated qualities. Their proper qualities are their innate goodness, magnitude, etc., their motion and their shapes; and likewise regarding their quantity. Their appropriated qualities are heat and dryness, coldness and moisture, masculinity and femininity, and the like. It is said that these are their appropriated qualities because it is with these that they act upon lower things; just as the Sun is called "hot and dry" because it heats and dries.

<margin>H. When (c d k)</margin>
¶ Through rule H, it is asked: concerning the time of the Heavens. It must be answered that the essence of the eighth sphere is in that "now" in which it was caused; like a circle which exists without succession in regards to its essence. But by reason of its motion, it causes time in lower things; just as in Saturn, which moves successively from one "now" to another "now." And there is one day from the eighth sphere down to the sphere of fire; but from the sphere of fire down to the earth, there are many days, many nights, and hours, and so forth.

<margin>I. Where (c d k)</margin>
¶ Through rule I, it is asked: concerning the place of the Heavens. It must be answered that the eighth sphere is in that place in which it was created in regards to its essence; and likewise for Saturn, etc. But by reason of motion and the many circles—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the celestial spheres and transitions into the fourth subject: the nature of Man (Anthropology) according to the principles of Ramon Llull's Art. It specifically addresses the unity of the intellect against Averroist theories.</meta>

->First part. Whether there is one intellect in all men.<-

The positions of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> down to the sphere of fire, in respect to their alignment, occur in many places: just as Saturn is joined with Aries at one time, and with Taurus at another. And so it is with the sun, which is in one place of the heavens at one time, and in another at another time; and in one place it causes days artificially, and in another it causes nights. ¶ Through the first type of the rule "R" <note>In Llull's Art, Rule R often asks "How?" (Quomodo)</note> it is asked: *How* is the heaven? And it must be answered that the heaven is modal through the particular modalities that belong to its essence, which are its innate parts: such as goodness, greatness, etc. And likewise regarding its habit, position, and the like.
<margin>In what manner</margin>
¶ Through the second rule "R," it is asked: *With what* is the heaven? It must be answered that it is with its natural parts with which it is composed: such as its goodness, greatness, etc., with which it causes circularities, and mobile goodnesses, greatnesses, and so forth.
<margin>With what</margin>

### Concerning the fourth subject, which is about Man, through the discourse of the principles.

<margin>Concerning the fourth subject, which is about Man, through the discourse of the principles.</margin>
In man, his goodness is the reason why he performs specific good. Indeed, that which a man does according to his species, he does either naturally or morally. In man, spiritual and corporal goodness are joined by reason of his soul and body. And therefore, by this duality of reasons, he has the nature or reason for doing good: by objectifying, understanding, loving, and remembering; and corporally, such as by procreating a man, and sensing, and imagining. From both of these come forth good operations, as appears in the liberal and mechanical arts.
<margin>Greatness</margin>
¶ In man, his greatness is twofold, just as his goodness is. And therefore, when a man does good, he does it with greatness as something great. Just as with goodness he does that which is good.
<margin>Duration</margin>
¶ In man there is duration: and this is the reason for his goodness and greatness; and likewise for other things that endure. And this is twofold, as was said above: namely, morally and by choice.
<margin>Power</margin>
¶ In man, his power is twofold, as was said of goodness. And it is that by reason of which he is able to exist and act. From this, therefore, it is clear that he can exist and act through his species. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what manner it possesses specific freedom for acting.
<margin>Wisdom</margin>
¶ In man, his intellect is specified, with which he understands in a special way; not that his intellect descends from another intellect by way of generating it, nor

<column-break/>

is it the same cause with another intellect essentially: otherwise it would be something begotten; and also after the death of the man it would be annihilated or corrupted; and it would be situated, figured, punctuated, and lined in time, place, quantity, surface, division, succession, and motion: which is impossible. For all these things belong to the nature of corporeity or the body. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes how badly and falsely those spoke who thought and affirmed that in all men there was but one single intellect. <note>A refutation of "Monopsychism," the Averroist idea that all humans share one collective soul/intellect.</note> ¶ Furthermore, our intellect recognizes through what has been said that the natural instinct of the human body is joined with the intellect of the man, as was said regarding goodness. ¶ The intellect has a mode through which it creates an "intelligible species" <note>A mental representation or concept</note> through the sensing and imagining powers in its own proper intelligible [realm], from which intelligible species it creates knowledge.
<margin>Will</margin>
¶ In man, his will is a specific power with which he performs special acts of loving; indeed, this will does not descend from another general will. For otherwise it would be generable and corruptible in its essence, as was said of the intellect; and its freedom would be destroyed, because it would be necessitated to will by its general principle: just as a body has an appetite necessitated by that which is above it. For example, when it desires food, drink, or intercourse, or heat when it feels great cold; and so with others. ¶ Furthermore, if all people had one will, then all men would relate themselves to the same object in the same way; and also, when a man died, the rational soul would be dead. And thus there would be no other life; nor would the justice and mercy of God have a subject in which to act: which is impossible and a very absurd distinction. ¶ Moreover, the appetite of the body and the will are joined, as was said of goodness; by reason of which the will creates species through the sensing and imagining powers by willing, just as the intellect does by understanding; and the same can be said of the memory, which is a part of the soul, in its own way.
<margin>Virtue</margin>
¶ In man, corporal and spiritual virtue are joined: and because spiritual virtue is higher, it therefore forms and perfects the lower virtue. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which moral virtues arise from spiritual and corporal virtue, as if from form and matter; concerning which virtues we shall speak in the ninth subject.

# On the nine subjects.

<margin>Glory</margin> Just as the natural sense perceives through sight and hearing, and so with the others, so the soul truly reaches the essences of things by understanding, loving, and remembering. For otherwise, the lower part would act more with its power than the higher part with its own, which is absurd to the reason of the intellect. And in this step, the intellect rejoices greatly. ¶ In man, natural, spiritual, and corporal glory are joined: that is, natural delights are joined spiritually and corporally. From which it follows that the soul has delight in acting upon the body, and the body under it in receiving <note>original: "patiendo" - here meaning the passive reception of the soul's action</note>, and man with these aforementioned things. The body is under it in receiving, and man with these aforementioned things. And here the intellect recognizes the manner by which man has delight in moral behaviors. ¶ In man, spiritual and corporal differences are joined: by reason of which the intellect understands in one way with sight, and by another with hearing, and so with the others; similarly, the body also receives in one way under the intellect, and in another under the will, and by another under the memory. And thus, through the aforesaid, the intellect recognizes the manner by which it creates knowledge through discourse, the will creates loving, and the memory creates remembering. ¶ In man, the soul and body agree between themselves by composing him, the soul remaining in its own essence and the body similarly in its own. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which the soul and body agree, by directing themselves toward the same object: the body in seeing, hearing, and such things; the soul in understanding, loving, and remembering. ¶ The body of man is composed of the four elements. The soul, however, is not made of contraries, because it is incorruptible. And because the soul and body are joined in man, therefore man suffers direct and natural contrarieties on the part of the body, but on the part of the soul, oblique and accidental ones. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that all sin is by accident <note>meaning sin is not part of the soul's essential nature, but an "accidental" deviation</note>. ¶ Since in man the soul and body are joined, therefore man is an efficient cause, moving form in matter for the sake of an end: namely, he moves the soul in the body. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which man is an efficient, material, formal, and final principle. ¶ In man, the soul and body are joined, in which act the union signifies that there is a medium <note>a middle ground or bridge</note> influenced by the soul and the body. And this medium is connatural and substantial: to understand, to will, to remember, to elementate, to grow <note>term: "vegetare" - the biological function of growth and nutrition</note>, to feel, to imagine; without which man would not be substantially joined.

<column-break/>

And man lives as long as this material union lasts in him; when, however, it is dissolved, man dies immediately. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which the soul and body are joined, measuring their acts according to a method of dispensing and proportioning, with the soul flowing in its power and the body flowing back its own, man existing as the medium brought into a third number. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which there is in man a radical and a nutritional moisture. <margin>Radical and nutritional moisture</margin> The radical moisture <note>term: "humidum radicale" - the vital fluid thought to be the seat of life, consumed over a lifetime like oil in a lamp</note> is from the primitive principles and points and lines with which the soul is joined. And the nutritional moisture is its instrument, like a small shuttle <note>original: "nauicula" - a weaver's shuttle</note> in a fabric in which the points and lines are introduced through the movement of the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative powers, by flowing in and flowing out. And the radical moisture returns and augments itself from that which comes from outside, thus converting it into its own species through the vegetative power. Just as the vegetative power transubstantiates <note>transforms the substance of</note> food into flesh, nerves, and bones, and drink into blood; and it transubstantiates food and drink into marrow, and also into choler, phlegm, and melancholy <note>the four humors of medieval medicine</note>, and the brain; and it transforms it into the water of the eyes, and into spit, and also into sweat. ¶ In man, the spiritual end and the corporal end are joined naturally: by reason of which man relates to the aforementioned ends—to the spiritual end with the soul, and to the corporal end with the body. <margin>End</margin> And from the soul and body indeed arise or go forth moral ends, with which the soul and body find delights in which they rest. ¶ In man, the soul is the greater substantial image. But the body is the lesser image and the image of the soul. Again, in the body, the imagination is a greater image than the sensitive power, because it presents objects; and it also moves the sensitive power itself secondarily. And the sensitive power is a greater image than the vegetative, for it is inserted and founded upon it. And thereafter, the vegetative is greater than the elemental, for the vegetative is founded upon the elemental. <margin>Majority</margin> And therefore, in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as the substantial powers are greater and lesser, and similarly the accidental ones in man, the soul and body are not equal; for the soul has higher principles, but the body lower ones. Nevertheless, they are joined: the soul indeed is entirely in the body, and vice versa, so that man may be equally joined and composed. Since man is brought forth from nothing in respect to creation, he is therefore led into a state of minority <note>a lesser or humble status compared to God</note>.

### Concerning man as deduced through the rules.

<margin>The deduction of man through the rules.</margin>
Through rule **b.** it is asked: whether man is more knowable through affirmation than through negation? and it must be answered that he is: for to predicate a predicate of a subject by affirming is to define the subject of which the predicate speaks, a nature existing between the subject and the predicate: as when it is said, *man is a rational animal*. When, however, a predicate is predicated of man negatively, no certainty or knowledge of man is obtained: as when it is said, *man is not a stone* or *man is not a plant*. For a true affirmation places those things which are in the subject: but a true negation always removes them from the subject. A false one likewise has a manner of removing from the subject. ¶ Furthermore, since affirmation precedes negation, just as an antecedent precedes its consequence: it is therefore clear that man is more knowable through affirmation than through negation. To be a man and to be ignorant of what a man is, is to neglect the being of man. ¶ And therefore, so that we may know what man is and have great knowledge of him, we shall define him through thirty definitions taken in a broad sense, by which he might be defined through one definition taken in a strict sense. But we define man in this way: so that we may know him more clearly in our intellect. And these definitions will be abstracted from the twenty-eight principles of this art and from the ten categories <note>The "ten categories" or predicaments are Aristotle's classification of all possible things that can be said about a subject (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.).</note>, by predicating of the substance such a predicate that agrees with the subject in nature. ¶ And first, through the first species of rule **c.** it is asked: what is man? and it must be answered: that he is an animal of whom more goodnesses differing in species are predicated than of any other animal. ¶ Man is an animal in which one part of him is incorruptible <note>Referring to the immortal soul.</note>. ¶ Man is an animal in which there are more powers than in any other ani-
