# Part Nine

->**The Power of Imagination**<-

<margin>Power</margin> They present objects from the imagination. For just as spiritual objects endure in a rational animal <note>i.e., a human being</note> through memory outside of the imagination, so do sensible objects endure through the imagination outside of the senses in brute animals. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as the rational soul perfects the lower powers, so the imaginative power in brutes perfects their lower powers. ¶ The imagination has power over the sensitive faculty: indeed, the power of the imagination descends to the lower power so that it can act within itself with that power; just as the radical moisture <note>A medieval medical term for the vital fluid that sustains life</note> descends to the nutritional moisture so that it may live with it. ¶ The <margin>Wisdom</margin> imagination has a natural instinct, as is evident in brutes, which indeed through the imagination possess the industry for living and for evading evil, such as the goat evading the wolf. ¶ The <margin>Will</margin> imagination has an appetite with which it desires the thing imagined. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the imagination has an instrument so that it can exercise its act and reach its object. ¶ The <margin>Virtue/Power</margin> imagination has a virtue with which it attracts <term>species</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, "species" are the mental images or "likenesses" of external objects</note> from sensible things, placing them in its "imaginable" <note>the mental space where images are formed</note>, in which it characterizes them and imagines them. ¶ Truth is the instrument of the imagination, so that with it, it can truly reach the object; nevertheless, it sometimes fails, just as an agent fails in the thing to be done when the instrument is lacking, or because he does not know how to work <margin>Gloss</margin> with it. ¶ The imagination causes delight <margin>Difference</margin> or sadness in the subject in which it exists. ¶ The imagination has a "difference" <note>a distinguishing characteristic</note> with which and through which it acts in various ways upon the object, like a mirror which, through its own difference, receives diverse images. <margin>Concordance</margin> ¶ The imagination accords the object with the subject in which it is: like a mother who imagines her son, rejoicing with the image or likeness of him acquired <margin>Contrariety</margin> through her imagination. ¶ The imagination, through contrariety, contradicts or resists the subject in which it is by presenting a hateful or undesirable object: such as a mother imagining her son dead, with sadness. <margin>Principle</margin> ¶ The imagination is an efficient principle, transmitting nothing outside of itself and making matter out of sensitive things by abstracting from them the sensible species with their form: namely, with its "imaginative" which is the form of that species, so that by reason of it, it can rest in the object. <margin>Medium</margin> ¶ The imagination is a medium in man, existing between the sensitive and intellectual powers, so that the intellect can acquire sensible and imaginable species in the imagination. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the species which it acquires from sensible things, it then draws or abstracts from the

<column-break/>

imagination, outside of the sense or without the sense. ¶ However, the imagination is not a medium in a brute; rather, it is its highest extremity or form, with which its life is habituated and completed, just as <margin>End</margin> the rational soul is in the human body. ¶ The imagination has a nature with which it fails in its end, which is the imagined object; otherwise, its imagining would not be its own proper act. ¶ The <margin>Greatness</margin> imagination has greatness: for its substantial goodness is greater than its accidental goodness, and its intrinsic act is greater than its extrinsic act. Furthermore, it has greatness in presenting a lion in respect to a goat; and it has greatness in presenting a large man, or one larger than him, or the greatest of them. ¶ The <margin>Equality</margin> imagination has equality in its correlatives, designated by the second species of Rule C; for unless they were equal by essence, they could no longer relate equally to the object, which is impossible. ¶ The <margin>Smallness</margin> imagination, by reason of smallness, is directed toward that smallness when it presents the smallest object.

# On the Nine Subjects
->Folio 60<-

<margin>Definitions of Imagination according to the ten categories.</margin>
**Imagination** is active through the **imaginative power** <note>original: "imaginatiua"</note> existing under the rationale of a form moved by the animal, so that the object is moved within the internal "imaginable" space of the imagination itself. ¶ Imagination is passive in its "imaginable" just as in matter, so that within that "imaginable" the object is characterized and imagined. ¶ The **imaginative power** is an animal habit <note>A "habit" here refers to a stable disposition or quality of the soul.</note> with which it creates "imaginable species" <note>Mental images or representations.</note>. ¶ Imagination is a power situated in the middle of a certain membrane of the animal's skull, in which the imaginations of objects appear to its imaginative power, just as images appear to the eyes in a mirror. ¶ Imagination is a power existing in time through the subject in which it resides, without which it can neither exist nor use an object. ¶ Imagination is a power existing in a place for the purpose of imagining an object in that place. ¶ We have defined imagination through the ten categories <note>The Aristotelian categories: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and passion.</note>; and just as we have defined it through those, so can the other bodily powers be defined through the same categories in their own way. ¶ Through the second type of the rule "C" <note>A reference to the author's mnemonic system of inquiry.</note>, it is asked: **What does imagination have in itself?** And it must be answered that it has its own correlatives without which it cannot exist: namely, the **imaginer** <note>original: "imaginatiuum"</note>, the **imaginable**, and the **act of imagining**. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: **What is imagination in another?** To which it must be said that in man it is a disposition with which the intellect disposes itself to objectify lower things; and the sense disposes itself to perceive along with the imagination itself; and in a brute <note>A non-human animal.</note>, the imagination itself is the form and completion of that animal. ¶ Through the fourth type, it is asked: **What does it have in another?** And it must be answered that it has an object in the subject in which it is; and it has discovery in things perceived by the senses, so that it may abstract "species" from them with its own light—namely, with its imaginative power. The imaginative power is the investigator of species, and also their placer and clarifier within its own "imaginable" which is co-essential to it; just like a crystal which, with its transparency, colors itself with the color of whatever it is placed upon; and also like a mirror which takes on the character of the things presented to it. ¶ Through the first type of "D", it is asked: **Of what is imagination?** And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a specified species. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **Of what is imagination?** And it must be answered that it is of its own matter and form, so that with them it may be active and passive in the subject in which it is. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: **To what is imagination subject?** And it must be said: to man, and also to the soul of that man. In a brute, however, it is subject to it as a part

<column-break/>

<margin>Form, as the form of the end.</margin>
is to its whole. ¶ Through the first type of rule "E", it is asked: **Why is there imagination?** And it must be answered that it is constituted of its parts: namely, the imaginer, the imaginable, and the act of imagining. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **Why is it?** And it must be said: so that the animal can objectify its object by imagining in the absence of the senses; and the sense itself, with the imagination, disposes and proportions itself to perceive sensible things when the sense is present; just like a carpenter who imagines the shape of a chest so that he may bring it from potentiality into reality. And like a bird disposing itself to fly when it is necessary. ¶ Through the first type of rule "F", it is asked: **How great is imagination?** <note>Referring to quantity or extent.</note> And it must be answered that it is as great as its essence extended in its correlatives; or as great as the habit of the subject in which it is; just like a cloak which is as large as the person wearing it. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **How great is imagination?** And it must be said that it is as great as its distinct correlatives are. But here the intellect marvels: what is the cause why imagination increases or decreases its act? As when a man imagines a small stone, and then imagines the same stone as large as a mountain. Then he reflects upon himself, considering that in brutes, the imagination imagines an object in the same way that the sense perceives or apprehends the object, and not otherwise—like a goat that imagines a wolf just as its sense perceives or apprehends it. It cannot imagine the wolf as large as a mountain; for if it could so increase its imagining, it would already be creating "science" <note>Systematic knowledge or reasoning.</note>, which is impossible. But because the imagination is subject to the intellect, and the intellect is a higher power than it, the intellect uses it over the senses to such an extent that it makes it imagine a wolf as large as a mountain. And by this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which **geometry** measures the heavens and their heights. And also **arithmetic**, by which way it counts infinite units along with geometry, dividing one part into two, and thereafter into infinite parts. And it also recognizes the way in which the **logician** uses "secondary intentions" <note>Logical concepts about concepts, rather than about things.</note> joined to primary ones. ¶ Furthermore, it recognizes that something is in the intellect which was never in the senses: for a wolf as large as a mountain was never in the senses. And when the intellect has recognized all these things, it then understands that, totally and without doubt, it is itself another essence, remote from the others.

And afterwards, with the approach receding from the sensed thing to the imagination itself mediated by the sensitive faculty; and also with the nourishment of the forms; and so with other things that could be said, with which the imagination reaches its object. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as it is itself greatly occupied and burdened by its object, so also is the imagination by its own, in its own way.

The **Sensitive Power** <note>Latin: *sensitiua*; the faculty by which living beings perceive the world</note> is the power with which an animal feels; it is also the "perceived" within the animal in which the sensitive power acts as the **common sense** <note>The "common sense" (*sensus communis*) was believed to be the internal faculty that binds together data from the five individual senses</note>, and it possesses the particular senses. ¶ The Sensitive Power is a **good** power because it causes "good sensing" through its own goodness; and when **greatness** is added, it causes "great and good sensing." ¶ The Sensitive Power is a **great** power because it causes great sensation, as is evident in sexual intercourse and the touch of hot iron, or in the touch of boiling water. ¶ The Sensitive Power **endures** through the duration of the subject in which it exists, along with its innate goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ The Sensitive Power, through its **power**, is able to exist and to act. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that an animal perceives through its own "species" <note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" is the mental image or likeness of an object that travels to the senses</note>, just as a magnet attracts a likeness through its own. ¶ The Sensitive Power has an innate **instinct**, as is seen in a human who fears a snake they see, or similarly a goat fearing a wolf; and like a puppy who, though not yet seeing, has instinct, appetite, and touch, and finds the teat and imagines it. In this step, the intellect recognizes which principles dispose the **imagination** toward imagining. ¶ The Sensitive Power causes an **appetite** for sensing in the animal, so that through the animal in which it resides, it may exercise its act. ¶ The Sensitive Power has the **virtue** <note>Or "power/strength"</note> of sensing, as is evident in its particular parts; for just as sight cannot see without illuminated air, neither can it see unless it is habituated by innate virtue and situated within it. ¶ The Sensitive Power truly senses through **truth**, just as a hand touching hot iron truly feels the heat. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that it truly understands its own object. For otherwise, the sensitive power—which is inferior to the intellect in its action—would be superior, and the intellect—which is the superior power—would be inferior, which is impossible; the intellect greatly rejoices in the resolution of this impossibility. ¶ An animal, through the sensitive power, has the **delight** <note>Glory/Joy</note> of sensing, as is seen when it beholds beautiful figures or hears a beautiful song and the like. ¶ The Sensitive Power, through **difference**, possesses particular senses through the mediation of organs by which objects differ, such as color (the object of sight), sound (hearing), and so on. But the intellect wonders whether the judgment of an object is made by the common sense or the particular sense, until it remembers a spring of water having many streams: the water is essentially one in itself and in its streams, but it has one position and one shape in one stream, and another in another; similarly, the common

# Ninth Part: The Sensitive Power

toward the thing sensed with its instinct and appetite, and likewise concerning other innate principles. Just as a man, using his feet and his sight, moves himself to a place in which he desires to rest; in this step, the intellect recognizes that the sensitive power <note>The "sensitive power" refers to the faculty of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared by humans and animals.</note> acts with its own innate principles.

<margin>Superiority</margin>
¶ One sensitive power is greater than another sensitive power, but this occurs by accident <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like being tall or short.</note>. For just as some water from a certain spring is greater in coldness, flavor, or healthfulness by reason of the greater disposition of the quality of its location, so one sensitive power is greater than another by reason of the greater disposition of the quality of its location regarding the species of the subject in which it exists. For example, the eagle possesses a greater sensitive power through sight than other animals; the vulture through smell; the dog through hearing; and man through taste and touch. ¶ In the sensitive power, quality consists between the power, the object, and the act; and this is intrinsic regarding its correlatives: namely, the "senser," the "sensible," and the "sensing." However, I do not say this regarding an external object, such as the sensed flavor of an apple and the flavor caused by the act of sensing.

<margin>Equality</margin>
<margin>Inferiority</margin>
¶ One sensitive power is lesser than another sensitive power according to the subject in which it exists. For a bird that does not live by prey <note>i.e., a non-predatory bird.</note> does not sense as much through taste as a bird that lives by prey; and so it can be said of others in their own way, as was indicated in the chapter on superiority.

### Concerning the Sensitive Power conducted through the Rules.

<margin>On the sensitive power deduced through the rules.</margin>
<margin>A notable question.</margin>
<margin>C: It is in itself</margin>
<margin>What it has in itself</margin>
<margin>It is in another</margin>
It is asked whether the sensitive power comes from a generator <note>i.e., biological parents.</note> or from a creator <note>i.e., God.</note>. It must be answered that it comes from a generator. This is evident because an animal without the sensitive power cannot sense the corruptible conditions which it ought to sense, both in the imagination and not in itself, because it is not naturally inserted and founded in the vegetative power. ¶ Furthermore, [if it were not so], Martin would not be the son of John according to species, which is impossible. ¶ But the intellect wonders: when a man dies, where does the sensitive power go and where is it? It must be said that it goes to its universal principles in which it remains and stands in its number miraculously—provided, however, that there is a resurrection of men, so that the justice and mercy of God may have a subject upon which they can act. ¶ It is asked through the first species of Rule C: *What is the sensitive power?* To this, it must be answered that its definition has already been given above. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: *What does the sensitive power have in itself?* It must be answered that it has its correlatives from which the common sense is constituted.
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: *What

<column-break/>

is in another?* And it must be said that it is a being causing sensed beings with which it senses: just as sight, which senses a colored thing found by it, is seen; and just as smell, which causes a scent found by it, is smelled.

<margin>What it has in another</margin>
¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: *What does the sensitive power have in another?* It must be said that it has an object: just as sight has the colored and the shaped, and smell has the scented; and it has knowledge of that object, because it makes a judgment concerning it.

<margin>D: From what (Origin)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: *From what is the sensitive power?* It must be answered that it is from its principles: namely, from the first parents from whom it was derived and generated; for otherwise, one animal would not be the offspring of another, which is impossible.

<margin>Matter</margin>
¶ Through the second species, it is asked: *Of what is the sensitive power made?* It must be answered that it is made of its matter and form: because through its matter it is passive, and through its form it is active.

<margin>Possession</margin>
¶ Through the third species, it is asked: *Whose is the sensitive power?* It must be answered that it belongs to the animal in which it exists, just as an instrument belongs to the agent using it. For the animal senses, lives, and generates another animal with it.

<margin>E: Why (Form/End)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: *Why is the sensitive power?* <note>original: "quare est" - referring to its formal cause.</note> It must be answered that it is joined and constituted from its matter and form.

¶ Through the second species, it is asked: *Why is the sensitive power?* <note>Referring to its final cause or purpose.</note> It must be answered that it exists so that its instinct and appetite can have natural acts, so that the animal can have the industry <note>Skill or practical ability.</note> to live. Furthermore, it is so that the imaginative power can draw "species" <note>Mental images or sensory impressions.</note> from it, imagine the sensed object, and perform its own act.

<margin>F: How much (Quantity)</margin>
¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: *How great is the sensitive power?* It must be answered that it is as great as the subject that is sensed by it. ¶ But the intellect wonders in what way it can be continuous in the subject in which it exists, and in which there are hair, nails, and bones that do not feel—until it remembers its "discrete quantity" <note>A mathematical term for things that can be counted individually rather than measured continuously.</note> indicated by the second species. ¶ Furthermore, the intellect wonders, since the sensitive power is not made of points or lines, nor has a shape, in what way it has quantity—until it remembers a crystal placed over a colored object, which takes that color upon itself. Thus, the sensitive power is quantified and habituated by the quantity of the subject in which it exists. For the quantity of points and lines multiplies its "species" in the sensitive power, just as a colored thing in a crystal multiplies its color in the aforementioned crystal. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which one "habit" <note>A disposition or acquired quality.</note> is placed upon another. ¶ Through the first—

### On the seventh subject, namely the Vegetative, deduced through the principles. .106.

On the seventh subject, namely the Vegetative, deduced through the principles.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a floral or foliate pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>
THE VEGETATIVE <note>term: Vegetative - the faculty of life responsible for nutrition, growth, and reproduction in plants and animals</note> is good: as is evident in plants, which through goodness are good for themselves and for other things that live from them, which indeed could not live without them, nor could they have the kind of being they possess.
<margin>
Greatness
</margin>
¶ The vegetative is great: for it encompasses and comprehends every vegetative and planted thing in the world. Here the intellect asks: is the vegetative faculty that is in animals one and the same as that which is in plants? To which it must be answered that the vegetative is one and the same in its genus; but there are many differing in species in various subjects by reason of the subjects themselves, not by reason of itself. For whoever would say that by reason of itself the vegetative were many, would indeed be saying that one was many and many were one, which is impossible; therefore it is clear that it is one and the same in genus, but many differing in species in various subjects. ¶ The vegetative lasts through its specific duration; but the intellect asks from what it endures, since its subject in which it exists is corruptible. But it remembers the "elementated" <note>term: elementated - things composed of the four elements (earth, water, air, fire)</note> matter from which it endures, just as the flame of a fire in a lamp endures from the oil.

This appetite is general to all appetites that are in the genus of the vegetative. ¶ The vegetative is of a virtue that is habituated, quantified, qualified, positioned, etc., as is evident in a plant. Furthermore, the vegetative has a virtue in plants of which physicians have experience.

# Why the color green? Part Nine. Greenness.

<margin>Truth</margin>
¶ The **Vegetative** power <note>The "Vegetative Soul" or power was the medieval term for the basic level of life responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> truly nourishes by reason of truth and possesses true conditions: namely, true substance, quality, etc., without which it would not be planted in its own truth. ¶ The **Vegetative** power finds delight in preserving its own being and multiplying its species, as is apparent in plants that reproduce and thus are able to avoid non-existence. ¶ The **Vegetative** power is rooted and planted in difference, so that many species may exist within its genus; but the intellect asks: what is the cause that the color green is more general in plants than any other color? It then remembers the earth and water that compose the green color, in which the plant is most especially rooted and nourished. ¶ **Furthermore, the intellect wonders**: why the fig tree does not produce a hard surface for its fruit as the walnut does, and why the rose has a red color and the lily white; but it remembers greatness <note>original: "magnitudinem," referring to the scale or scope of natural diversity</note> by reason of which the difference is great. ¶ The **Vegetative** power possesses a concordance so that its species may agree among themselves in certain things; just as pepper and garlic agree in heat, while lettuce and gourd agree in coldness; and many things agree in the same color, position, and the like. This same thing can be said in its own way regarding the vegetative power in animals; for the vegetative power always follows the greater temperament <note>original: "complexionem," the balance of bodily humors</note> of the subject in which it exists. Contrariety is the subject in which the vegetative power is planted, such that contrariety is the cause of corruption, just as concordance is the cause of generation. But the intellect asks: what is the cause why arsenic <note>original: "realgal," red arsenic sulfide</note> kills an animal, while wheat gives it life? And why are garlic and gourds contrary? But it remembers the greatness in which the contrariety of vegetation is planted. ¶ The **Vegetative** power is a principle; in it, vegetation (or the composite) transmits one species into another. Form in this vegetative power is another principle in which the composite transforms a new form into its old one, and new matter into old matter; and this is for the sake of the end: namely, the vegetated thing in which the species is generated and multiplied. ¶ The **Vegetative** power is a general medium existing between the elemental <note>original: "elementatiuam," the power governing the four elements</note> and the sensitive <note>original: "sensitiuam," the power of perception found in animals</note>; like a line between two points. The vegetative is indeed inserted and planted in the elemental, while the sensitive is in the vegetative. And because the sensitive is the end, it is therefore above the vegetative and flows into it; and the vegetative flows back to the sensitive itself with its specific principles. And because the vegetative is above the elemental and flows into it, the elemental flows back to the vegetative. In this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which plants and animals live, are nourished, and grow through the vegeta-

This could not be unless the vegetative power were planted and rooted in equality. ¶ **Concerning the minority** <note>original: "minoritate," the opposite of greatness/majority</note> of the vegetative power, it can be spoken of just as its majority was; for they relate to one another. The vegetative power is reducible through minority to non-existence, because it is, and was not before it was created.

<margin>On the vegetative power through the rules of the subjects.</margin>
Through **Rule B** <note>Rule B in Llull’s system usually asks "Whether it is?"</note>, it is asked whether the vegetative power is a sensed power. And it must be answered that it is so, in a certain way: namely, according to the conjunction or composition which the vegetative has with the sensitive power in the subject in which it exists. And in another way through the voice, such as **speech** <note>original: "affatus" — a technical term in Llull's philosophy for a "sixth sense" of vocal expression</note> which names it, and through hearing which hears its name. Truly, the other senses cannot perceive it. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that speech is a sense after it perceives its object and gives to the hearing something audible. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C asks "What is it?"</note>, it is asked: what is the vegetative power? And it must be answered that it is a power transforming one species into another: as in animals, in which it transforms food into flesh; and in plants, transforming the elemental matter into themselves. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does the vegetative have in itself? And it must be answered that it has its own **correlatives** <note>Llull’s theory that every essence has three parts: the doer, the object of the action, and the act itself</note> from which it is composed, and with which it performs its operations: namely, the *vegetative* [the power], the *vegetable* [the object], and *to vegetate* [the act]. For in its vegetable, it vegetates all foreign vegetable matter, just as the sensitive power in its sensible object perceives all foreign sensible things, and as a heater in its heatable object heats all heatable things. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is the vegetative in another? And it must be answered that it is a foundation in the sensitive power; however, it is itself founded in the elemental power. In the **categories** <note>The Aristotelian Predicaments or Categories of being</note>, it is the same as what it is: namely, it is a substantial part of the very substance in which it exists. In terms of **quantity**, the vegetative exists above the quantity of the elemental; and thus it can be spoken of regarding its quantity and relation, etc. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the vegetative is a higher power than the elemental; but the intellect doubts whether its relation is an **accident** <note>A non-essential quality</note> until it remembers its substantial relation, which has an accidental relation serving as its instrument and the "habit" with which it acts in the subject in which it is—just as a substance acts by means of its accident. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does the vegetative have in another? And it must be answered that it has its substance in the substance of the elemental, and its quantity in the quantity of the elemental, and so on for the other categories. In this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the vegetative is situated and placed within the elemental. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D asks "From what?" or "Of what?"</note>, it is asked: of what is the vegetative made? And it must be answered that it is made of its specific principles with which it acts. ¶ Through

the second species, it is asked: of what is the vegetative composed? And it must be said it is of its correlatives. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does the vegetative belong? For the vegetative is a part of the animal with which it acts and lives. To which it must be answered: that it vegetates within its own intrinsic and co-substantial "vegetable" <note>The internal essence of the plant</note>, outside of which and without which it cannot vegetate; just as a heating power cannot heat outside of its own heatable subject. The place of the vegetative power is indeed knowable through rule c. d. K. This vegetative power itself reaches the substance, because it participates with it through contact. ¶ Through the first rule of K. it is asked: by what means does the vegetative power vegetate that which is vegetated? And it must be said that it vegetates through that mode which it possesses in relation to its correlatives: for the "vegetative" places form and matter into its intrinsic "vegetable," which come to it from the **elementative power** <note>The power that governs the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>. And within that vegetable, it changes its substance into another, with the vegetative power stripping the form and matter from the elementative power as it comes from it. And from those, the vegetative power itself clothes the new vegetated thing. ¶ But many modes concur in this process, namely the mode of proportion, the motion of generation, of corruption, of privation, and of augmentation, and the like, by placing part in part, and parts in the whole, and vice versa; and with the whole transmitting its likeness to that which is assimilated to it. ¶ Through the second species of K. it is asked: with what does the vegetative power vegetate? And it must be answered that it vegetates it with its own proper correlatives, namely: the *vegetative*, the *vegetable*, and the *act of vegetating*, which are co-essential to it. For the vegetative, in its intrinsic vegetable, vegetates all foreign vegetable matter by means of the act of vegetating. Furthermore, it vegetates with the principles of this Art, namely with **goodness** and **greatness**. ¶ And let these things which have been said of the vegetative power suffice; although many things could be said of it, nevertheless whatever can be said of it is implied in the aforementioned things.

# Ninth Part: The Elemental Power

<margin>C. What is it?</margin>
For it is composed of those things, and not from one alone. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: **What is the elemental power?** <note>Latin: *elementativa*. In Lullian philosophy, this is the power or faculty that governs the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) within a physical body.</note> And it must be answered that its definition has already been given above. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **What does the elemental power have in itself essentially and substantially?** And it must be said that it has its own correlatives from which it is made, and with which it acts in "elementated" things <note>Things composed of elements, such as physical objects or living beings.</note>: namely in stone, flame, plants, and animals. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **What is it in another?** And it must be said that it is an instrument in the elements with which the elements themselves act upon elementated things. ¶ Furthermore, it is that which exists in the ten categories <note>The Aristotelian Predicaments (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.).</note>, and it is the foundation in the vegetative power. ¶ Furthermore, the elemental power in the potentiality of fire is an image of the infinity and eternity of God insofar as it is fire: if it had infinite wood, it would burn infinitely and eternally; but because it does not, that power remains only in disposition, and is finite because the matter is finite. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: **What does it have in another?** And it must be said that it has in the subject in which it exists its own matter, its form, its quantity, its quality, its motion, and such things, as in a plant or an animal. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: **From what is the elemental power made?** And it must be said that it is made from its own primitive principles placed within elementated things: from those principles as if from universal matter and universal form, just like the elements. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **Of what is the elemental power composed?** And it must be said that it is of its own specific form and matter, or that it acts with them through its own species by "elementing" <note>The process of combining elements into a complex form.</note> elementated things. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: **To what does the elemental power belong?** And it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it is, just as a part belongs to its whole; as is evident in a plant which, by generating, "elements" another plant. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: **Why does the elemental power exist?** To which it must be said that it exists because it is composed of the elements. ¶ Through the second species of Rule E, it is asked: **Why does the elemental power exist?** To which it must be said: so that through it, elementated things may exist. Furthermore, so that the vegetative, sensitive, and imaginative powers may be founded, nourished, and generated by it. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: **Whether the elemental power has continuous quantity?** And it must be answered: yes, so that its continuous quantity may be the genus for the quantity of individuals which are outlined and sustained in them. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: **Whether it has discrete**

For the destruction of the universal leads to the destruction of the particular. Likewise, if fire, which is hot by itself in its sphere and dry through the earth, were dry by itself; and if air, which is moist by itself and hot through fire, were hot by itself; and further, if water, which is cold by itself in its sphere and moist through the air, were moist by itself; and similarly if earth, which is dry by itself in its sphere and cold through the water, were cold by itself: then there would be two qualities of each element in its genus. # On the Nine Subjects. Justice.

two drynesses, two fierinesses, two airinesses, two waterinesses, and two earthinesses; and consequently eight elements just as there are eight qualities mentioned above. This is absurd to say, just as it is absurd to say there are two "whitenesses" in a single genus, or two types of vegetation, or two types of sensation. <note>The author argues against the redundancy of elements; nature is unified.</note> Furthermore, natural appetite would be destroyed because it would have no object; for one fire would not desire another fire, nor would fire desire earth, since it would be dry in itself. The same could be said of the other elements in their own way. Thus, the appropriate quality would be destroyed, as would the second species of Rule G <note>original: "regule .g."</note> signifying that quality. Again, motion would be destroyed—both the appetite for upward motion and downward motion—and consequently nature itself would be destroyed, because it would have no subject in which it could be sustained. The "elementative" power <term>elementatiua: the formative power that organizes elements into bodies</term> would be destroyed, and consequently the "elementated" things <term>elementata: physical objects composed of elements</term>, the vegetative things, and the sensitive things. Moreover, every body existing beneath the moon would be composed in a void of purpose, to the extent that the end of nature would be a privative state, like blindness is to sight or deafness to hearing. Since all these things are clearly impossible, it is evident through Rule H and the definition of truth that all elementated things are mixed in their spheres and in their masses likewise. In elementated things, they are even more mixed and composed, as in plants where they are composed with the vegetative power, and in animals with the sensitive and imaginative powers; and this occurs by means of the elementative power composed with them.

But here the intellect wonders: how can earth, which is below, ascend to the heights, namely into the sphere of fire, since air is in the middle opposing the earth? And similarly, how can fire descend to the depths below, since water is contrary to it? This is understood once one remembers the "Ladder of Concordance" designated in the Second Figure. For fire descends by giving its heat to the air, and it agrees with it in descending; and air, by giving its moisture to the water, agrees with it in descending. Thus fire passes into water through heated moisture. Water descends to the earth by giving it its heated and moistened coldness; and earth ascends to the fire by giving it its heated, moistened, and cooled dryness. And because qualities do not leave their own proper subject, they ascend and descend with the qualities that are ascending and descending. Thus follows circular motion and mixing.

Through the first Rule K, it is asked: how is the elementative power mixed and composed of the four elements? But the intellect remembers the paragraph on "Place"

The ninth subject concerns craftsmanship (artifice), and it has three species. The first concerns **Morals**. The second concerns the **Liberal Arts**. The third concerns the **Mechanical Arts**. We shall treat the first here, namely morals. We shall treat the second and third in the eleventh part of this book, namely in the "Application." It should be known that morality can be treated in two ways: according to **virtues** and according to **vices**. And first, we shall treat **Justice**, which is in the genus of virtue. 107

### Justice deduced through the Principles

<margin>
On Justice deduced through the principles.

<margin>

Since justice is applicable to its genus—namely to **Virtue**, which is one principle of this Art—and the same can be said of **Equality**, therefore, just as these two principles are deduced through the principles and rules (as appears in the eighth part of this book concerning the mixture of principles), so justice is applicable to virtue and equality according to how they themselves are deduced through the principles and rules. For the particular is applicable to its universal according to the conditions of that universal. But for the greater evidence of justice, we wish to run it through the principles and rules of this Art.

**Justice** is the habit with which the just person acts justly. Since **Goodness** is the reason for a good person to do good, it is therefore just that the good person does good. Wherefore, when he does good, he acts justly.

# Ninth Part

<margin>Greatness and Duration</margin>
It acts: from which it is clear that justice arises from the nature of goodness. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that justice arises when its act begins, and that goodness is what disposes justice itself, insofar as it is the reason for a good person to do good. Since greatness is that by which duration etc. are great, therefore greatness is the disposition of great justice, goodness, and duration: as when a good man does a great and lasting good deed, then such justice will be a great <term>habit</term><note>In medieval philosophy, a 'habit' (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality of the soul, like a virtue.</note> gathered from goodness, greatness, duration, etc. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as great justice is connected with the principles and derived from them—just as goodness and greatness last through duration—so justice lasts through it, provided that no injury <note>original: "iniuria," meaning injustice or legal wrong</note> intervenes. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the habit of justice lasts, even if a person is using another virtue or is asleep. In this step, the intellect is both moral and practical.

<margin>Power</margin>
Since goodness is the reason for a good man to do good, and greatness disposes that good to be great, and duration disposes it to be lasting: and power is the reason that the good can exist and act well, justice disposes it so that it is brought forth through that acting. And when a good man does good, then justice arises and is brought from potential into act.

<margin>Will</margin>
Justice is intelligible through the intellect and lovable through the will. And therefore the intellect and the will themselves present it as an object; after justice is born, the acts of justice remain in potential. For justice itself is governed in duration and power, etc. Justice is disposed through goodness, greatness, etc., and therefore it is lovable through the will. For every good thing is lovable: and therefore when it is loved with the disposition of goodness, greatness, etc., then justice is brought from potential into act.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
Justice is a virtue, and this virtue is its own genus, because many virtues exist under the heading of "virtue." Therefore, just as virtue in general arises from goodness, greatness, etc., so justice arises in the same way that a moral virtue arises. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the particular is ruled and directed with its universal. And in this step, jurists <note>legal scholars and lawyers</note> ought to rejoice greatly, because this step is a general, infallible rule for all laws.

<margin>Truth</margin>
Justice cannot exist without truth: and therefore when it is with truth, it follows that justice is knowable in the same way that truth is knowable in the discourse of principles and rules. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that justice is easy to know when the discourse of truth is placed within the mixture of the regular principles.

<column-break/>

<margin>Glory</margin>
In glory, goodness, greatness, etc., find delight and rest; however, they could not have this without justice. And therefore, when they are in delight, the conscience does not bite <note>original: "conscientia non mordet," the 'remorse' or 'sting' of conscience</note>, because justice is present in that delight. From this it follows that the rest of the conscience signifies and declares the presence of justice in that delight.

<margin>Difference</margin>
Justice, by reason of "difference," has two parts: namely, weight and proportion. Regarding weight, it is intensive; but regarding proportion, it is extensive. Therefore, in legal cases, sometimes an intensive judgment is required, and sometimes an extensive one, according to how the subject of the judgment is disposed and ordered to receive the judgment.

<margin>Concordance</margin>
Justice arises and lives through the concordance of principles; and therefore, in recognizing the concordance of principles toward a single judgment, one recognizes justice with its conditions. For when the cause is known, the effect is known.

<margin>Contrariety</margin>
Injury <note>Injustice</note> is the enemy of justice, because injury is a privative habit <note>a habit defined by the absence of a good</note>; and because concordance is the friend of the principles, justice is a positive habit. For one contrary is known through the other.

<margin>Power and Prime</margin>
"Justice" speaks of or signifies essence, but "Law" <note>original: "ius"</note> signifies the *being* of justice. And because an essence is sustained in its being, therefore justice is sustained in law. From the aforesaid, it is clear that the judge, in the absolute principle, is the efficient cause; justice is the formal principle and law is the material principle, because it is formed through justice. Judgment, however, is the final principle, because in it there is rest.

<margin>Medium</margin>
Justice is the medium between the plaintiff <note>original: "actor"</note> and the defendant <note>original: "reus"</note>, by which the judge gives to each his own right. For just as justice cannot be a medium without judging, neither can it be so without "good-making," "great-making," etc., so that its judging is thus mixed with goodness, greatness, etc.

<margin>End</margin>
The end <note>goal or purpose</note> of justice is the rest of the principles, because without justice they cannot be at rest. From this it follows that justice is the final subject in which the principles have peace between the plaintiff and the defendant, by rendering to each what is his own.

<margin>Majority</margin>
Justice is "greater" through substance and through accident. It follows that its greater "majority" is substantial, and its greater "minority" is accidental. That greater majority exists with greater goodness, greatness, etc., and the greater minority exists with lesser goodness and greatness, etc. Therefore, in legal cases, a judge must recognize when justice is greater or lesser by recognizing substantial and accidental justice. This knowledge is very necessary in cases: for justice sometimes stands for the plaintiff substantially and for the defendant accidentally, and vice versa; as is clear through "being" and "well-being": for being in a case...

Through rule B <note>Rule B usually refers to "Whether it exists."</note>, it is asked: if justice is corrupted in a person, does that same numerical justice return when the injury is undone? The answer is no. For just as matter is naturally disposed and proportioned successively for a form that is introduced into it in an instant, so a moral habit is successively disposed and proportioned and is perfected in an instant; therefore, when a habit is corrupted, it is corrupted in an instant. ¶ Through the first species of rule C <note>Rule C: "What is it?"</note>, it is asked: what is justice? The answer is that it is that form to which the power of judging properly belongs. ¶ Through the second species of rule C, it is asked: what does justice have in itself, essentially and substantially? The answer is that it has its moral correlatives, namely: the *justifier*, the *justifiable*, and the *act of justifying*, with which it exists as a habit. But here the intellect doubts: does justice remain a habit when a person is not using it, or is sleeping, or is practicing another virtue? The answer is yes; for justice is not corrupted unless an injury is introduced. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is justice in another? The answer is that in legal causes it is the "cause," and in other virtues it is their connection—such as humility and patience, which agree with one another justly. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does justice have in another? The answer is that it has objects in legal causes which are justly "objectified"; it also has the impressions of the principles, the rules, and the ten categories. <note>The "Ten Categories" refer to Aristotle's Predicaments (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.).</note>

First.
Matter.

¶ Through the first species of rule D <note>Rule D: "Of what?" or "From what?"</note>, it is asked: of what does justice consist? It must be said that it consists of the disposition of the regular principles and the ten categories, because it falls under them. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is justice made? It must be said that it consists of its own specific matter and form, which descend through "difference" and "property" from general virtue, so that a just man may act through justice in judgment. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does justice belong? The answer is that it belongs to the just man, just as a cloak belongs to the cloaked man.

The answer is that it is collected from the various principles, namely from the *justifier*, the *bonifier* <note>One who makes good.</note>, etc., and the *justifiable*, the *bonifiable*, and the acts of *justifying*, *bonifying*, and *magnifying*, etc. It is situated in the rules by its own property, and is brought forth by improper and specific matter and form. For just as the same quality—that is, the same meaning—is expressed through one specific form in a rose and through another in a violet, so the same virtue exists through specific form and matter in justice, and through others in prudence. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there justice? The answer is: so that the principles from which it descends may have right actions in legal cases. Furthermore, it is so that the city may have peace and the public good.

The answer is that it is "continuously great" or has continuous quantity, because it is a continuous habit. It is not, however, made of points or lines, since it is not a physical body; it neither grows nor decreases, although its act may sometimes be great and sometimes small—just as the same hammer sometimes gives a great blow and sometimes a small one, according to the will of the agent using it at his pleasure.

For justice has one quantity in a judge, another in a plaintiff, and another in a defendant; just as the same water takes one shape in a circular vessel and another in a triangular vessel.

To which it must be answered that insofar as prudence is a <term>habit</term> <note>A stable disposition of the mind or character.</note>, it possesses continuous quantity just as a hooded cloak belongs to the one wearing it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of prudence: and it must be answered that it possesses discrete quantity by reason of the difference of its <term>correlatives</term> <note>The internal components of a principle, such as the "power to act" and the "act" itself.</note>. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked concerning the prudence which is its own proper passion and quality: to which it must be answered that it is prudence itself. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of prudence? And it must be answered that it is goodness in good things and malice in evil things. ¶ Through rule H, it is asked concerning the time of prudence: and it must be answered through rules C, D, and K. For those signify the manner in which prudence exists in time through that which it is: both through the things it concerns, and through the manner it holds in time when the prudent person uses prudence in time. ¶ It is asked through rule I: where is prudence? And it must be answered that it is in rules C, D, and K, outside of which it can in no way exist in a subject. ¶ Furthermore, it is in the deeds of the prudent person with which he acts prudently. ¶ Through the first rule K, it is asked: how does prudence exist? And it must be answered that it exists through that manner which the prudent person possesses by causing it, and by gathering the similarities of the principles and rules from which it is made. ¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked: with what does prudence exist? To which it must be answered that it exists with providence, diligence, knowledge or belief, disposition, and proportion, without which it cannot exist.

**Fortitude** <note>Strength of mind or courage.</note> is nourished, colored, and disposed, proportioned and conditioned under the rationale of **goodness**. ¶ Fortitude, when joined with the greatness of goodness, magnitude, duration, etc.—excepting contrariety and minority—is both able to be attacked and able to be defended. ¶ Fortitude made ancient through the duration of goodness and greatness submits new fortitudes to itself. ¶ Fortitude with the power of goodness, greatness, etc., can do all things. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with understanding and with believing. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with love and with fear: without fortitude, no virtue is strong. ¶ Fortitude with truth causes boldness and victory. ¶ Fortitude with delight makes a person magnanimous. ¶ Fortitude with other virtues diversifies its acts. ¶ Fortitude with greater virtue possesses a greater memory. ¶ Fortitude in sins is a <term>privative habit</term> <note>A "habit" defined by the absence of a good quality.</note>. ¶ Fortitude has specific principles so that it can have specific acts. ¶ Fortitude is a medium existing between virtue and virtue. ¶ Fortitude, when without an end, causes boldness and victory. ¶ Fortitude is greater through those things which are substantial than through those which are accidental. ¶ Fortitude is stronger with equal causes than with unequal ones. ¶ Fortitude is lesser with a greater vice, and is also vulnerable and conquerable with it.

### On Faith deduced through principles.

<margin>On Faith deduced through principles.</margin>
<margin>vmt</margin>
<margin>Nong</margin>
We must traverse this chapter by means of <term>analogy</term>: so that we may see in what manner Faith is superior and the Intellect is inferior. First, through **Goodness**: since the intellect cannot grasp God as an object as much as He is capable of being grasped, therefore Divine Goodness is the reason why God presents Himself to the human intellect through "objectifying" and "believing." Indeed, this understanding is good; and at that time, the intellect grasps God by believing Him to be one, infinite, and eternal Creator, Savior, and the like. This the intellect does above its own nature; and let us say that such a grasping is holy, admirable, and good Faith. ¶ God is a great object, and according to His greatness, the intellect cannot naturally grasp Him; therefore, God magnifies the intellect so that it may act magnificently above its nature by simply believing. Thus, Faith ascends above the intellect, just as oil rises above water. For when the intellect reaches the fact that God is One through Faith, it believes Him to be One more than it understands Him to be One through the act of understanding. For the intellect is higher through greatness when believing without labor than when understanding with labor. ¶ Faith lasts through a duration given by God, whereas understanding lasts through acquired knowledge. From this it is clear that Faith is superior, but the intellect is inferior. And when a person <insert>habituated</insert> in Faith sins through greed or lust, etc., Faith remains in the subject in part, but with deformity. For the subject is not disposed with justice, prudence, etc. ¶ Just like a donkey who is not fit to be clothed in silk. ¶ The <term>First Cause</term><note>God, as the ultimate source of all existence.</note> can do more than the secondary cause, and when the secondary can act with the First, then it can act above itself. Therefore, the intellect can, through the First Cause, believe in it; but what it can do by itself is to understand God—yet with believing assisting its understanding. As Isaiah said: *Unless you believe, you shall not understand* <note>original: "nisi credideritis, non intelligetis" - Isaiah 7:9</note>. Just as a man who was not a philosopher, and later became a philosopher: when he was not a philosopher, he believed God existed; but when he was a philosopher, he understood God existed. And then the intellect ascended to that level by understanding where it previously was by believing. However, I do not say that Faith is destroyed because of this, but that it ascends to a higher level of grasping, believing more that God exists than understanding that He exists—just like oil in a vessel where it is above the water. And if one were to add more water to the said vessel, the water would indeed rise to the place where the oil was, and then the oil would ascend to a higher place where it was not before. ¶ God is intelligible by His nature. And He causes the human intellect to understand much by nature, with God providing the habit of Faith so that Faith itself may help it to understand. For the intellect can ascend more toward the "First Intelligible"—namely God—with two habits than with only one; just as it can do more with prudence and fortitude than with prudence alone. When the intellect understands the First Object, Faith disposes the intellect for understanding. Just as Charity disposes the Will to love the First Object. And just as the Will could not love the First Object without Charity, so the intellect cannot understand the First Object without Faith. From this it is clear that just as Charity is not corrupted when the Will loves the First Object, so Faith is not destroyed when the intellect understands the First Object. For a power does not contradict its own common disposition; rather, through it, it ascends and is strengthened. ¶ Faith is

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the relationship between faith and the intellect, likely following a discussion on the theological virtues. The author uses scholastic metaphors, such as climbing a ladder or a mountain, to explain how faith elevates human understanding.</meta>

# First Part.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
Virtue is a <term>habit</term><note>Latin: *habitus*; a stable disposition or quality of the mind</note> existing in the intellect; otherwise, faith could not be a virtue, nor a habit, just as charity could not be a habit unless the will were its subject. And therefore, just as charity makes the will ascend to loving an object virtuously, so faith makes the intellect ascend to understanding an object virtuously. ¶ Faith, along with truth, is a habit of the intellect; and when the intellect understands the First Object <note>God</note> with truth, it understands by means of this habit. For without truth, it cannot understand Him. Therefore, truth is a principle common to both faith and the intellect; nevertheless, faith in truth is higher in the act of believing, while the intellect is lower in the act of understanding. Thus, when the intellect ascends to a higher degree in truth, faith similarly ascends to a higher degree in that same truth. For the habit is above, but the one possessed of the habit is below—just as a man wearing a cape <note>Latin: *cappatus*</note> ascending a mountain has a body that is lower, while his cape is higher upon him. The intellect cannot understand God except with labor, just as a man ascending a mountain cannot reach the top without effort; but when the intellect ascends to God with faith, it does not labor, but rather delights itself in Him by believing. And because a higher power operates without labor compared to one with labor, the intellect is higher by believing in divine glory than by understanding it. The intellect does not distinguish by believing in a <term>modal</term><note>specific ways or modes of being</note> or necessary way, but broadly and confusedly; however, when the intellect understands truly, it understands necessarily and without confusion. Therefore, the intellect is instantaneous in believing, but successive in understanding; wherefore it is clear that the intellect is higher in believing than in understanding, the reason being that its act of believing is above its own nature, just as water is above its nature when it is being heated. ¶ Faith is a habit given by God, and is thus governed by God just as it is created by God. From this it is clear that the intellect cannot govern such a habit, for it is above its own nature; nevertheless, the intellect disposes itself to submit to it, fearing to offend God by not believing in Him. And thus a concordance arises between understanding and believing. Whatever law exists through faith must be true. Just as through goodness it must be good, and through greatness, great, etc. Therefore, that law must be true if faith is higher in truth and more opposed to sins; and in this step, the intellect recognizes which law must be true: whether the law of the Christians, or of the Saracens <note>Muslims</note>, or of the Jews. ¶ In the beginning, faith disposes the intellect toward understanding, as is clear through rule B. And when the intellect is at a certain degree in understanding, faith disposes it at that degree in believing, so that it may ascend to another degree in understanding; and so from degree to degree, until the intellect ascends to the First Object and rests in Him by understanding—but most especially, while on this journey, by believing.

<column-break/>

<margin>Merit</margin>
¶ Faith is the medium with which the intellect acquires merit and ascends to the First Object; indeed, faith flows into the intellect so that it may be like a foot for the intellect to climb with. The intellect has another foot from its own nature, namely understanding, just as a man climbs a ladder with two feet. And on the first rung, the foot of faith is placed first. Then the foot of the intellect is placed on that same rung, ascending step by step. On the second rung, the foot of faith is placed first, and then the foot of the intellect, ascending step by step with the priority of faith and the posteriority of the intellect. It is similar to a disputation: first the doubt is posed, then the affirmation or negation. Believing is not the final end of the intellect, but understanding is; nevertheless, faith is its instrument for elevating its understanding through believing. Therefore, just as an instrument stands between the cause and the effect, so faith stands between the intellect and God—faith having flowed from God into the subject so that through it, the subject may find rest in the First Object.

<margin>The End</margin>
<margin>Greater</margin>
¶ That faith which is greater in goodness, greatness, etc., and also in hope, charity, etc., must be true; but the faith contrary to it must be lesser and false. Otherwise, positive principles would succumb to privative <note>negative or lacking</note> principles, which is impossible. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which faith is greater and truer by observing which one possesses greater virtue and a greater object.

<margin>Equality</margin>
¶ That faith which believes more that there is equality in the reasons of God must be true. But that which posits inequality in them must be false. For in God there is neither "before" nor "after"; because divine goodness, greatness, etc., must have their equal correlates, just as the intellect and the will have equal powers. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which faith is true.

<margin>Lesser</margin>
¶ With a lesser faith, the intellect cannot elevate its understanding, but it can with a greater one. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that its greater understanding is not against its greater believing, just as in climbing a ladder one foot is not against the other; even in running, one foot is not against the other.

Supposing that the intellect could understand concerning God those things which it can believe through faith: faith would indeed be destroyed, and consequently **merit**; as it is said: *faith has no merit where human reason provides proof.* <note>original: "fides non habet meritū / cui hūana ratio prebet experimentum" — a famous quote from St. Gregory the Great.</note> To which it must be answered that this is not so. The reason for this is: because faith indeed ascends above the intellect, as has already been shown; for the merit of faith consists first. The merit of the intellect, however, comes later; but if they were on the same level, what you say would indeed follow. ¶ Through the first species of rule **C**, it is asked: **what is faith?** To which it must be answered that it is a virtue given by God, so that through it we may believe that which we cannot understand through the intellect. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what does faith have in itself co-essentially?** And it must be answered that it has its own <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Llullian logic, "correlatives" refer to the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the loving).</note> with which it is a <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality of the soul.</note>. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **what is faith in another?** To which it must be said that it is a habit in the intellect, existing above the habit which the intellect itself possesses through science; as appears by a taster tasting wine from a jar, by which he judges what the tasted wine is like. But because it is possible for the wine to be altered at another time, therefore the intellect does not have certain science through understanding, but through faith it believes that it is such. ¶ Furthermore, faith is good in **goodness**, and great in **greatness**, etc. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: **what does faith have in another?** And it must be answered that it has intelligibility in the intellect; and it has lovability in the will, for it is loved by it; and recollectability in the memory, because it is recollected by it. ¶ Through the first species of rule **D**, it is asked: **of what is faith?** And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a creature. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **of what is faith?** And it must be answered that it is of its own active and passive principles with which it is a special virtue. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: **whose is faith?** And it must be said that it belongs to the subject in which it is, just as a cloak belongs to the one cloaked. ¶ Through the first species of rule **E**, it is asked: **why is there faith?** And it must be answered that it is because it is its own cause. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **why is there faith?** And it must be answered that it exists so that the intellect, through it, can believe that which it cannot understand by itself. Just as imagination exists so that a man may imagine that which he cannot perceive through the senses. ¶ Through the first species of rule **F**, it is asked: **how great is faith continuously?** And it must be answered that it is as great as a man can, with it, direct himself toward objects. ¶ Furthermore, it is continuous because it is an indivisible habit. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **how great is faith discretely?** To which it must be answered that it is as great as are its correlatives, by which its act increases or decreases. ¶ Through the first species of rule **G**, it is asked: **what is the proper quality of faith?** And it must be answered: **belief**. For this belongs to no other virtue. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: **what is the appropriated quality of faith?** And it must be answered: your goodness and greatness; these and other reasons belong to other virtues, just as they do to this one. ¶ Through rule **H**, it asks concerning the **time** of faith. To which it must be answered through the third species of rule **C**, that it is in time because it is new within it. And through the fourth species of **C**, it has corruption in time when a man does not believe concerning God those things which he used to believe of Him; and it is in reviving in time when a man rises again by believing concerning God those things which they used to believe of Him. ¶ Furthermore, it is in time: for sometimes it has a great act, sometimes a small one. ¶ Likewise, it is in time because sometimes it targets one object, sometimes another. And thus it can be said of rules **D** through **R** in its own way. ¶ Through rule **I**, it asks: **where is faith?** To which it must be answered by the second species of rule **C**, that it is in its correlatives; and by the third species of **C**, it must be answered that it is in the intellect, like a habit in its subject; and thus it can be said of rules **D** through **R** in its own way. ¶ Through the first species of rule **K**, it is asked: **how is faith?** To which it must be answered that it is through that mode which the first object has in presenting itself as an object to the intellect; and by believing, the intellect itself targets it above its own understanding. ¶ Through the second rule **K**, it is asked: **with what is faith?** And it must be answered that it is with power, object, and act. Through the intellect indeed it is with power, which effectively and morally uses faith; and it is with the object, namely with God, without whom it cannot exist; and with the act, namely with believing. But here the intellect itself doubts, asking: when it does not believe but understands, where is faith? To which it must be answered that faith is in the intellect itself, because it is its own habit. And at that time, believing is in it in potential, but it is reduced to act when the intellect believes.

# Ninth Part

<margin>Memory</margin>
Memory, by reason of its own goodness, and memory thus presents God as an object above its own powers through hoping, just as the will with charity <note>Charity here refers to *caritas*, or divine love.</note> ascends to God by loving. And this is a great good for the memory. ¶ Memory is greater through two acts than through one alone: namely, that it should hope to recollect, rather than through recollecting alone. Therefore, the greatness of God magnifies the memory of man when man magnificently disposes himself to recollect God with the habit of hope: so that when memory cannot recollect Him, it may be able to hope for Him. And this is a great thing for the memory.

<margin>Endurance</margin>
¶ Hope endures in a subject <note>The "subject" is the person or the soul in which the virtue resides.</note> along with the disposition of that subject: namely, by recollecting God by reason of His goodness, greatness, eternity, etc. But when the memory does not dispose itself to recollection, and sin is its habit, then hope has no subject in which it can endure, and thus it fails.

<margin>Power</margin>
¶ Memory with its own power can recollect; and similarly, with the power of God mediating through hope, it can hope in God. And thus, speaking analogically, the power of hope is superior, while the power of memory is inferior; by reason of which, the power existing below ascends to the object with the power existing above, just as the power of understanding ascends with the power of believing.

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
¶ A man who is a sinner, understanding in the hour of his death his great sins and the great justice of God, is near to desperation in his understanding and recollecting. But hope, which is the habit of the memory, ascends to the divine mercy, with God presenting Himself as an object to the sinner who possesses hope. And then the sinner withdraws himself from desperation; however, he could not do this unless hope were a habit of the memory.

<margin>Will</margin>
¶ When a man is in war or at sea with great misfortune, or has a great need for some thing, at that time his will is so weakened and broken on account of excessive fear that it cannot lift its loving up to God; but memory, presenting God as an object with hope, excites the will to love Him with charity. And then the will is comforted and consoled through the memory. And the same can be said of the intellect, which finds no other remedy except to hope in God.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
¶ Memory with hope is virtuous, just as the will is with charity. And just as the will is vicious without charity, so is the memory without hope. Since memory and will are mutually helping one another, therefore memory with hope helps the will, and the will with charity helps the memory, so that they themselves may be virtuous. Hope with truth is true, and with falsehood it is false. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that a sinner, when he can flee from sin and will not, but yet proposes to leave it, then believes himself to have hope, yet he does not have it.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
<margin>Glory</margin>
¶ For hope with sin cannot participate in the subject. ¶ A sinner with hope has de-

<column-break/>

-light; but without hope, he has sadness and grief. For with hope he has loving; but without hope he has hating. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the sinner with hope ascends to loving; without hope, he descends to hating and despairing, turning loving and hoping into hating and despairing, and into the sadness and grief which are in such a sinner, which one might estimate.

<margin>Difference</margin>
¶ There is a difference between recollecting and hoping, just as there is between understanding and believing. The reason for this is that hoping is superior, but recollecting is inferior; recollecting is a natural act, but hoping is a supernatural act. Hoping and recollecting agree with one another. For recollecting disposes one to hope, provided that the hoping is with goodness, greatness, etc. And it makes the hoping ascend, and the recollecting ascend by degrees, so that the hoping may ascend through the ascent of the recollecting. Just as a hooded cloak <note>original: "cappa"</note> ascends a mountain through the ascent of the one wearing the cloak <note>original: "cappati". This is a classic Lullian analogy regarding how a quality moves with its subject.</note>.

<margin>Comparison</margin>
<margin>Contrariety</margin>
¶ Legitimate hope and spurious hope are opposed, to the extent that they cannot stand in the same subject. For otherwise, there would be an opposition in the object. ¶ Legitimate hope is that which is with goodness and truth and the like, and is against malice and falsehood. But spurious hope is that which is with malice and falsehood, and is against goodness, truth, etc. And in this step, the memory grieves that it recollects so many sinners habituated in spurious and deformed hope.

<margin>Principle</margin>
¶ In the beginning, the man hoping in God is the efficient cause, and hope is the form. And those things which the man recollects are the matter, and the highest object is the end, with recollecting subsisting for the sake of hoping.

<margin>Means</margin>
¶ Hope is the medium existing between the sinner and God, because it is the messenger of both: God flowing hope into the sinner, and the sinner reflecting his good and great recollection back to God. When a sinner or a man in need recollects God without hope, he finds no rest in his recollecting. The reason for this is that his recollecting is not in that degree in which rest is found. But when hope is joined, then recollecting ascends with hope to that degree in which rest is found.

<margin>Fear</margin>
<margin>Greater</margin>
¶ That hope which is greater by reason of goodness and greatness is a sign and light of true faith or law. For a lesser faith or law cannot stand in a greater hope. But a greater hope stands in a greater faith or law; otherwise, there would be an opposition in the object. And in this step, the intellect recognizes which people persist in the true law.

<margin>Equal</margin>
¶ Hoping and recollecting can be together in the highest object at the same time, but not equally: because hoping is prior, while recollecting is posterior. Just as willing and loving can be in one and the same subject at the same time. Loving, however, is prior as a habit; willing is posterior, because it is habituated by charity; just as at the height of a mountain, the cloak is upon the one wearing the cloak.
