It is asked whether hope is a <term>habit</term> <note>A "habit" (habitus) in medieval philosophy is a stable disposition or quality of the soul that allows one to act easily and well.</note> of the memory? And it must be answered that it is: because in a time of necessity, the memory, by hoping, strengthens and consoles the intellect and the will. And thus "recalling" ascends to the highest object through "hoping," just as "understanding" does through "believing," and "willing" through "loving." Likewise, hoping is not of the category of certainty, which belongs to the category of knowledge; nor is it of the category of the will. For the will desires many things for which it does not hope; from which it follows that since hope is neither of the category of the intellect nor of the category of the will, it must be of the category of the memory. And since in the soul there are no other powers than those aforementioned, hope is furthermore not of the category of the imaginative nor the sensitive faculties. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, it is asked: what is hope? And it must be answered that it is the virtue to which "hoping" properly belongs. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does hope have in itself co-essentially? To which it must be said that it has its own special correlatives with which it acts through its own species. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is hope in another? And it must be answered that it is a special virtue within other virtues, and also a messenger consoling, strengthening, advising, and the like. Furthermore, it is good within goodness, and great within greatness, etc.; and in the imaginative faculty it is unimaginable, and in the sensitive faculty it is insensible, and in its subject it is indivisible. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does hope have in another? And it must be said that it has "hoping" within "recalling," just as charity has "loving" within "willing," and faith has "believing" within "understanding." Furthermore, it has a good act in goodness, and a great one in greatness, etc., and a just one in justice, etc. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D, it is asked: of what is hope? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is a created habit. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is hope? To which it must be said that it is of its own specific likenesses derived from the relatives of the memory, of which it is a habit. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is hope? And it must be answered that it belongs to the memory, like the instrument of an agent. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E, it is asked: why is there hope? To which it must be answered that it exists because its cause exists; just as an artificial day exists because the sun is above the earth. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there hope? And it must be answered that it exists so that the memory can lift up its "recalling" in a time of necessity, by advising, helping, and strengthening. By advising the intellect in its "understanding," and the will in its "willing," so that they may be able to ascend to the highest object. ¶ Through the first species of Rule F, it is asked: how great is hope continuously? And it must be answered that it has a great and continuous quantity. For it has a great office in consoling, strengthening, and elevating the other powers to the highest object; its quantity is indeed indivisible, since it is neither a point nor a line. ¶ Through the second species of Rule F, it is asked: concerning the discrete quantity of hope? To which it must be answered that it has a discrete quantity with respect to its correlatives with which it has differences, and with which it increases or decreases its acts at will. ¶ Through the first species of Rule G, it is asked: what is the proper quality of hope? And it must be answered that it is "hoping." For "hoping" belongs to hope alone. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of hope? To which it must be said: goodness, greatness, and the like. ¶ Through Rule H, it is asked concerning the time of hope? And it must be answered that it is in time: for it is a new habit and depends on things past. And it is in the present time, because it exists; furthermore, because it has its act and encompasses future time, for it hopes for that. And this is designated through Rules C, D, and K. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that hope is a very great habit within time. ¶ Through Rule I, it is asked: where does hope have its act? And it must be answered that it has it in the "recallability" of the memory, outside of which it cannot have it. For outside the recallability of the memory, forgetfulness is a privative habit. And this is designated through Rules C, D, and K. ¶ Through the first rule of K, it is asked: how does hope exist, and how is it corrupted? To which it must be said that it exists through the manner which the memory has, disposing its act with principles and with other virtues; just as a person in a time of necessity, when they cannot help themselves with their own virtues, helps themselves with goodness thereafter. And similarly with mercy and with the charity of God, and the like. Its destruction, however, occurs when sin happens in the subject in which it resides

Charity is a habit of the will; and charity, by reason of its goodness, elevates the will to love the divine goodness more than itself. ¶ Charity, by reason of its greatness, makes all good things common. ¶ Charity, with its duration, causes one to endure in loving with goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ The will, with the power of charity, conquers all things. ¶ Charity, with great duration, disposes the intellect to understand the Supreme Intelligible <note>God</note>. Since God is supremely lovable, therefore the will with charity elevates its loving to prize God more than itself. Since God is lovable in Himself, and not [merely] believable or hope-able in Himself insofar as He is of Himself, therefore charity is a higher virtue than the other virtues. ¶ Charity lives with truth, and also conquers things imaginable and sensible. ¶ Charity finds delight in all things. ¶ Charity does not distinguish between what is one's own and what is common. ¶ Charity leads all things back to a true good and a concordant end. ¶ Charity finds no contrary. ¶ The will through charity is prior in love, and through the act of willing is posterior in it. ¶ Charity is the medium existing between the friend and his beloved. ¶ Charity rests in all things. That law with which charity is greater is also truer than any other law. ¶ Charity makes all good things equal. ¶ Charity with minority <note>smallness or deficiency</note> is weak.

And it must be answered that charity is that virtue with which the will ascends to love

### On patience drawn through the principles. 110

<margin>
patience drawn through the principles.
</margin>
Since patience is a habit of the will: that is, the will with the goodness of its patience overcomes its own malice. ¶ The will with the greatness of patience overcomes anger. ¶ Patience with duration lasts against impatience. ¶ Patience with the power of charity and humility overcomes all things. ¶ Patience with the deliberation of the intellect preserves and nourishes. ¶ Patience with charity is of the genus of humility. ¶ Patience under charity is a greater virtue than under any other virtue. ¶ Against true patience, no anger can stand. ¶ Patience with suffering <note>original: "passione"</note> acquires joy and delight. ¶ Patience does not distinguish between the one who reproaches and the one reproached. ¶ Patience is connected with charity, piety, and humility. ¶ Patience does not care for vengeance. ¶ Patience in the beginning has suffering, but in the end, action and victory. ¶ Patience is a medium existing between labor and rest. ¶ A person habituated in patience is always at rest. ¶ Patience with greater labor is a greater virtue. ¶ Patience makes prosperities and adversities equal.

### A person with a minority of patience is in danger.

<margin>
a person with a minority of patience is in danger.
C.
</margin>
Whether patience is a stronger virtue absolutely than the vice of impatience: and the answer is yes, because patience is a positive habit, while impatience is a privative one <note>a "privative" vice is defined by the absence of a good, rather than being a thing in itself</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which a person sins. ¶ Through the first species of rule C <note>Rule C usually asks "What" (Quid)</note>, it is asked: what is patience? To which it must be said that it is the virtue by which the will is moved to choose sufferings beyond its own strength. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does patience have in itself essentially? To which it must be said that it has the passive likenesses of the principles with which it suffers. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is patience in another? And the answer is that it is the habit overcoming and pacifying two people quarreling between themselves. And it is consoled in prudence when a deed cannot be handled otherwise. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does patience have in another? And the answer is that it has action in the will primarily, and the will has it in itself secondarily. ¶ Through the first species of rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "From what" (De quo)</note>, it is asked: of what is patience made? And the answer is that it is made of its specific possibilities <note>original: "bilibus," likely referring to the "principles" or "capacities" of the soul</note> with which it is a specific virtue. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does patience belong? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the will, which with it submits itself to sufferings. ¶ Through the first species of rule E <note>Rule E usually asks "Why" (Quare)</note>, it is asked: why does patience exist? And the answer is that it exists because charity, prudence, justice, fortitude, and humility cause it in a disposed and proportioned will, by submitting it to another's will. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there patience? To which it must be said: so that the intellect and will may have continuous deliberation, choosing useful things. ¶ Through the first species of rule F <note>Rule F usually asks "How much" (Quantum)</note>, it is asked: concerning the continuous quantity of patience? And the answer is that it has continuous quantity, because it is not a habit of a single point, nor a line, nor is it divisible. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the discrete quantity of patience? To which it must be answered that it has discrete quantity, for it is composed of many sufferings. ¶ Through the first species of rule G <note>Rule G usually asks "Of what kind" (Quale)</note>, it is asked: what is the proper quality of patience? And the answer is passibility <note>the capacity to feel or suffer</note>. For this belongs properly to patience alone; for through the suffering of patience, the sufferer endures. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of patience? And the answer is goodness, greatness, etc., victory, justice, etc. ¶ Through rule H <note>Rule H usually asks "When" (Quando)</note>, it is asked: concerning the time of patience? To which it must be answered through the third species of rule C that it is new in time. ### On Piety derived through principles.

<margin>

The will, with the goodness of piety, disposes itself to have sorrow for the weakness of one's neighbor. ¶ The greatness of piety moves the will to have great sorrow for the adversities of one's friend and even one's enemy. ¶ Piety lasts with charity, humility, patience, and gentleness. ¶ The will, with the power of piety, can cause sighs in the heart, tears and weeping in the eyes, and sadness in the soul. ¶ The intellect understands that the signs of piety are charity, humility, patience, gentleness, sighs, and weeping. ¶ Piety is lovable because with it the will destroys its own cruelty. ¶ Piety with charity, humility, etc., shows itself to be a virtue. ¶ True piety is the true medicine of the will. The will with piety thinks that its own weakness and its own sadness are its glory and its delight. ¶ Piety, by means of the habit of charity, does not distinguish between what is one's own and what is common. ¶ A pious man, with piety, accords and pacifies enemies. ¶ Piety with charity, humility, patience, and gentleness contradicts impiety, which is its enemy. ¶ Piety is the formal and humble principle; sighs and weeping are its matter; and the act is its end. ¶ Piety stands in the midst of charity. ¶ Piety without the act does not fail. And in this step the intellect knows that the will with piety delights itself when the pious man grieves, weeps, and sighs. ¶ That law with which greater piety can be had must be true. ¶ A pious man equates his own weaknesses with the weaknesses of his neighbor. ¶ Piety with lesser signs shows itself to be lesser.

### On Piety derived through rules.

<margin>
On Piety derived through rules.

Whether charity is the habit of piety? And it must be answered that it is. The reason for this is that charity, by reason of the highest object <note>i.e., God</note>, is prior; but piety, by reason of the lower object <note>i.e., one's neighbor</note>, is posterior. ¶ Through the first species of rule **c**, it is asked: what is piety? To which it must be said that it is the virtue with which the will moves itself to have sorrow for the weaknesses of one's neighbor. ¶ Through the second species of **c**, it is asked: what does piety have in itself co-essentially? And it must be said that it has its correlatives with which it is a special virtue. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is piety in another? And it must be answered that it is the virtue signified in its signifiers: namely in charity, humility, patience, gentleness, sighs, weeping, and the like; just as wine is signified by the ivy branch existing before the tavern <note>A common medieval reference to a "bush" or branch hung outside a tavern to indicate wine was for sale.</note>. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does piety have in another? And it must be answered that it has its signs in a pious man just as impiety has its signs in an impious man. ¶ Through the first species of rule **d**, it is asked: of what is piety? And it must be answered that it is of itself, because it is an acquired habit. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is piety? And it must be answered that it is from that matter signified by its signs. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: whose is piety? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it is, like the instrument of an agent. ¶ Through the first species of rule **f**, it is asked: how great is piety continuously? And it must be answered that it is as great as it is signified through its signs. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what is the discrete quantity of piety? And it must be answered that it has a discrete quantity with which it increases and decreases its act without the increase or diminution of the continuous quantity of its essence. ¶ Through the first species of rule **g**, it is asked: what is the proper quality of piety? And it must be answered: the compassion which it has for the weakness of one's neighbor. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of piety? And it must be said: sadness. For sadness is a common form; and likewise of charity, humility, and so of its other signs. ¶ Through rule **h**, it is asked: concerning the time of piety? And it is answered through the third rule **c**, that it is in time when it is signified by its signs, and so of the others signified by **c.d.R.** ¶ Through rule **i**, it is asked: concerning the place of piety? And it must be answered that piety is in the pious man, and is in all those signs with which it is signified. ¶ Through the first rule **K**, it is asked: how is piety? To which it must be said that it is through that mode which a pious man has for acquiring it with charity, humility, patience, and gentleness, etc. ¶ Through the second rule **K**: with what is piety? To which it is answered that it is with its signs, just as a blacksmith is with his instruments: namely with the furnace, anvil, hammer, tongs, etc. ¶ We have spoken of nine virtues: and just as we have spoken of them through principles and rules;

### Principles derived concerning avarice

<margin>Principles deduced concerning avarice.</margin>

Avarice, with its malice, hinders goodness so that there is no good reason for it to do good with its goods. ¶ Avarice, with its greatness, magnifies malice, duration, and power through its own act. As long as avarice lasts, so long does its insatiable act last: and because of this, the greedy man, by increasing his riches, believes he is decreasing <note>likely meaning decreasing his want or poverty</note>, but he cannot. ¶ The power of avarice is a <term>privative habit|A "privative habit" is the presence of a lack, like darkness being the absence of light</term> of the power of generosity, just as deafness is a privative habit of the power of hearing. Wherefore the greedy man does not have a resting power. Just as faith elevates the intellect to believe truths beyond its own strengths, so avarice elevates the intellect to believe falsehood beyond its strengths; and just as the greedy man believes himself to be generous, so charity exalts the will to love beyond its strengths. Thus avarice elevates the will to love the future, and it does not rest in those things which it already possesses. ¶ The more a greedy man has, the more he believes himself to be virtuous. ¶ The greedy man believes that which is true to be false, and vice versa, just like an unfaithful person. For falsehood and avarice agree, just as generosity and truth agree in their own way. ¶ The greedy man does not take delight in the things he has, for he still believes himself to be in need; nor in the things he hopes for, for he does not yet have them. ¶ The greedy man does not distinguish between generosity and avarice, because he believes that which is avarice to be generosity. ¶ A greedy man, by reason of his avarice, can have no harmony with any virtuous man, for avarice contradicts all virtues. ¶ The more a man is wealthy, the more he contradicts his first principle, because he is contrary to the Good End. ¶ The greedy man turns positive principles into privative ones: and thus the more he believes he is decreasing his want, the more he labors; just like a man believing he sees better with blinded eyes than with seeing ones. ¶ The greedy man joins and measures all things with his avarice. ¶ The greedy man rests in the end of privation, like a man suffering from hunger who is pleased to suffer it. ¶ The greedy man is more greedy with greater riches; whence it is clear that the more he has, the more he desires to have. ¶ The greedy man does not observe equality, for avarice consists in extremes. ¶ Lesser avarice has lesser signs, just as greater avarice has greater ones.

Whether avarice is a more general sin objectively? And it must be answered that it is, because it targets and desires many and diverse objects. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is avarice? And it must be answered that avarice is a sin that diverts goods from the end for which they exist. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does avarice have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it has privative correlates, just as generosity has its positive ones. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is avarice in another? And it must be answered that it is a privative habit in the greedy man, with which he causes for himself poverty, sadness, and labor; just as a man wearing a cloak <note>original: "cappatus"; a common Lullian metaphor comparing accidents or habits to clothing</note> that is too large and heavy causes for himself weariness and labor. ¶ The greedy man, habituated by this privative habit, has rest neither in his riches nor in other things, but rather labor and anguish. ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: of what is avarice? And it must be answered that it is of itself: for it has no nature, nor is it a creature, because it is a sin; nor is it a virtue. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: from what is avarice? And it must be answered that it arises from the moral defect of man, just as deafness arises from a defect of nature: for just as deafness is a privative habit against the positive habit of hearing, so the greedy man is against the positive habit of generosity; and in this step the intellect recognizes from what sin is made. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is avarice? And it must be answered that it belongs to the greedy man, like a cloak to the one wearing it. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why is there avarice? And it must be answered that it exists because man does not wish to have generosity; just as a man's nakedness exists because the man is not clothed. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: for what purpose is avarice? And it must be answered: so that man may have neither generosity nor rest in his goods. ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked concerning the continuous quantity of avarice? And it must be answered that it has continuous quantity, for the habit is continuous, like the cloak on the one wearing it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of avarice? To which it must be said that it has discrete quantity, so that it can increase and diminish its acts at will. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked: what is the proper quality of avarice? To which it must be said that it is insatiability; and in this step the intellect recognizes that the more the greedy man has, the more he desires to have. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of avarice? And it must be answered that it is poverty, labor, and sadness.

...the glutton: just as a cloak is defined by the cloak-maker. ¶ Through the second species of the rule, it is asked *why* gluttony exists: And the answer is so that through it, one is not made a laughingstock, or lazy, or poor, or sick, and sometimes dead and placed in hell. Through the first species of rule **F**, it is asked *how great* gluttony is: And the answer is that it possesses such a great continuous quantity that it is indivisible; the glutton can never be satisfied by it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked *how great* gluttony is discretely <note>referring to "discrete quantity," or things that can be counted</note>: To which it must be answered that it is as great as the number of vices the glutton employs, increasing or decreasing his acts according to his own pleasure. ¶ Through the first species of rule **G**, it is asked *what* is the proper quality of gluttony: And the answer is the insatiability of the soul through the sense of taste beyond its own powers. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which gluttony raises the appetite of the intellect above its natural strength: just as fire raises water by heating it beyond its own power. ¶ Through the second species of **G**, it is asked *what* is the appropriated quality of gluttony: and to this it must be answered that it is neglect, mockery, poverty, drunkenness, and the like. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the first species belongs to the appetite of the soul, but the second to the body, by reason of which gluttony acts more effectively in the soul and thereafter in the body. ¶ Through rule **H**, it is asked concerning the *time* of gluttony: And the answer is that it is a new habit within that time. ¶ Furthermore, regarding time: it makes use of past time. For the glutton grieves that he can no longer drink and eat [as he once did]. And similarly, he uses the present, because he possesses the practice of it through that medium. And similarly, he uses the future: when he desires to eat and drink. ¶ Likewise, in the internal sense, he uses that time in which he will suffer inestimable and eternal hunger and thirst. Through rule **I**, it is asked *where* gluttony is: And the answer is that it is a privative habit <note>a "privative habit" is the absence of a required virtue, like darkness is the absence of light</note> in its correlatives and in those things in which it exists. And this is signified through the rule of the principles. ¶ Through the first rule **K**, it is asked *how* gluttony is. And the answer is that just as temperance exists in a positive manner, so gluttony exists in a privative manner. For the glutton has neither manner nor measure in eating or drinking. ¶ Through the second rule **K**, it is asked *with what* gluttony exists: To which it must be said that it is with its cause, just as a cloak is with its wearer, for it is made or crafted through him.

## On Lust through derived principles

<margin>On Lust through derived principles. Master.</margin>
<insert>L</insert> <note>The decorative initial L begins the section on Lust (Luxuria)</note>
Lust, by reason of tactile "goodness" <note>The author uses "goodness" ironically here to mean the perceived pleasure of the sense of touch</note>, acts wickedly and blames the goodness of chastity. ¶ Lust, by reason of great tactile sweetness, magnifies the magnitude and the penalty in the reasoning mind. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the conscience arises. ¶ Lust, by reason of the duration of bodily delight, causes lasting pains in hell. ¶ Lust submits spiritual power to bodily power. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which the lustful man is bound. ¶ Lust perverts the intellect into believing that it is not a sin: just as greed perverts it into believing that it is not a sin. And in this step, the intellect recognizes what the obstinacy of the sinner is. ¶ Lust, by reason of the beauty of a woman's face, "thread-captures" <note>original: "filocapit," a Lullian term meaning to ensnare as if with a string or thread</note> the lustful man into loving the baseness and foulness that lie beneath, which the woman has within herself. And a man greatly ensnared by lust believes himself to be very virtuous. And at such a belief, the intellect wonders greatly. ¶ Lust is a lying habit, because it begins with beauty and comes to rest in baseness. And that which is evil, it holds as good. ¶ The lustful man, through the delight he has in seeing, hearing, imagining, thinking, and touching, loses the glory of paradise on his journey: and acquires eternal pains for all his powers in hell. ¶ The lustful man does not distinguish between the baseness and the beauties of a woman. For from these, he makes one end, one resting place. ¶ The lustful man accords beauties and baseness toward a single end. ¶ The lustful man contradicts chastity through lust: so that through chastity he might not have happiness. Nevertheless, he does not believe he is doing this. ¶ Lust begins with the sensory power: and multiplies its effect with the imaginative power, until it becomes a sin in the reasoning power. ¶ The end of lust flows into the sensory; and the sensory flows back to the end. And this is mediated by the imaginative power, until it is a sin in the perverted reasoning power. ¶ The lustful man first rests in beauties: then in baseness and foulness. ¶ Greater lust shows and demonstrates itself with greater signs. ¶ Man and woman sin equally through lust: yet they do not love each other equally. ¶ Lust is lesser through the body: but greater through the soul. For through the body it is in the process of becoming; but through the soul, it is in its completed state of being.

Whether lust begins first through the imagination or through the senses? And the answer is that it does. For the imaginative faculty is closer to the reasoning faculty than the sensory faculty is. ¶ Through the first species of rule **.c.** it is asked: what is lust? And the answer is that it is the sin to which "to lust" properly belongs. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: how does lust exist co-essentially in itself? And the answer is that it has its own correlatives <note>In this philosophical system, correlatives are the active, passive, and verbal components of a concept</note> with which it constitutes a specific sin. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is lust in another? And the answer is that it is an intended sin in the soul, but an extended one in the body. And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which lust is in the soul without succession <note>i.e., instantaneous</note> and in the body with succession <note>i.e., occurring over time</note>. ¶ Through the fourth species it is asked: what does lust have in another? And the answer is that it has height through domination in the person in whom it resides, just as a cloak exists in a cloaked man as an ornament. ¶ Through the first species of rule **.d.** it is asked: of what is lust made? And the answer is that it is of itself: because it is a sin that is not made of anything; for sin is nothing <note>A reference to the Augustinian view of evil as a privation of good, rather than a substance</note>. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is lust made? And the answer is that it is made of moral monstrosity: because it is a privative habit in moral matters, just as deafness is in natural matters. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does lust belong? And the answer is that it belongs to the subject in whom it resides, like the cloak of the cloaked man. ¶ Through the first species of rule **.e.** it is asked: why is there lust? And the answer is that it exists because it is an acquired habit. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is there lust? And the answer is that it exists so that there may not be chastity: just as deafness exists so that there may not be hearing, and just as hot water exists so that it may not be cold. ¶ Through the first species of rule **.f.** it is asked: how great is continuous lust? And the answer is that it has continuous quantity because it is an indivisible habit. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: how great is discrete lust? To which it must be said that it is as great as the degree to which lust can increase or diminish its acts; and in this step the intellect recognizes that in the same essence and habit, discrete quantity consists of several acts differing in number. ¶ Through the first species of rule **.g.** it is asked: what is the proper quality of lust? And it must be said that it is that through which it is a specific vice. Just as heat is the proper quality of fire. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of lust? And the answer is that it is the "heating" with which the flesh of the lustful man grows. ¶ Through rule **.h.** it is asked concerning the time of lust? And the answer is that lust is in one time through aptitude by reason of the sensory and imaginative faculties, and in another time through the completed act by reason of the soul's conception.

<column-break/>

And this is signified through the rule **.c.d.k.** ¶ Through rule **.i.** it is asked: where is lust? And the answer is that it is in the sensory and imaginative faculties as an instrument; but in the soul, it is there by essence and habit. And this is signified through the rule **.c.d.k.** ¶ Through the first rule **.k.** it is asked: by what means is lust? To which it must be said that it is by the manner of seeing, hearing, touching, and imagining, and by the manner of the soul conceiving and commanding. ¶ Through the second rule **.k.** it is asked: with what does lust exist? And the answer is that it exists with perverse movements: just as hot water exists with its perverse and contrary nature (namely, with heat). And just as the intellect exists with ignorance and hearing with deafness.

Pride, by reason of its malice, makes the subject in which it resides descend: just as humility makes the subject in which it resides ascend. ¶ The greatness of pride makes its subject small, just as humility magnifies its own. ¶ The duration of pride disposes the subject so that it holds everlasting punishments in Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. ¶ The power of pride cannot stand against the power of humility. ¶ That man is proud who believes he has his natural goods and his riches from himself. ¶ A man loving himself more than God is proud. ¶ When a proud man is corrected, he believes himself to be virtuous and the one correcting him to be vicious. ¶ Pride is a lying habit: for it believes it is ascending when it is descending; and even when it believes it is speaking the truth, it speaks a falsehood. ¶ A proud man does not rest with anyone, nor does anyone rest with him. ¶ The proud man does not distinguish between his own pride and the humility of another. ¶ Pride has concordance with all vices. ¶ Pride contradicts all virtues. ¶ Pride is a "principle" <note>In the sense of a starting point or source</note> because it makes that which is higher descend, and that which is lower ascend. ¶ Pride impedes the "middle" existing between the beginning and the end. For this reason, it descends and does not ascend. ¶ The proud man never finds rest. ¶ Greater pride has greater signs. ¶ The proud man finds no equal for himself, nor does he want a companion. Lesser pride is through the body; greater pride, however, is through the soul.

Whether pride exists more through the intellect than through the will. And it must be answered that it is through the intellect; for the intellect is first in presenting the object, but the will follows in choosing it. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule C** <note>Rule C usually asks "What is it?" in this logical system</note> it is asked: what is pride? To which it must be said that it is a sin which, the more it believes it is ascending, the more it descends. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: what does pride have in itself essentially? And it must be answered that it has its own privative <note>terms indicating the absence of a quality</note> and opposite correlates to the positive relatives of humility. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: what is pride in another? To which it must be said that it is indicative in the intellect, elective in the will, and conservative in the memory; and it is the empress over all sins. ¶ It is asked through the fourth species: what does pride have in another? And it must be answered that it has a descent in the subject in which it exists, just as the soul has motion in a running body. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule D** <note>Rule D usually asks "Of what is it?"</note> it is asked: of what is pride? And it must be answered that it is of its own existing privative correlates to the positive relatives of humility. Just as night is the absence of day, and deafness is the absence of hearing. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: of what is pride? And it must be answered that it is of its own specific correlates from which it is a specific sin. And in this step the intellect recognizes that the first species has respect to the defect of its contrary, but the second to itself alone. ¶ Through the third species it is asked: to whom does pride belong? To which it must be said that it belongs to its own subject, for it is its own habit <note>a settled disposition or state of being</note>. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule E** <note>Rule E usually asks "Why is it?"</note> it is asked: why is pride? And it must be answered because it is absent from the subject in which humility exists; just as blindness is in a subject because visibility is absent from it. ¶ Through the second species it is asked: why is pride? And it must be answered that it is so that humility cannot exist; just as the end of fire is in a choleric person so that the end of water may not be in him. ¶ Through the first species of **Rule F** <note>Rule F usually asks "How great is it?"</note> it is asked concerning the continuous quantity of pride? And it must be answered that pride has this, for it is an invisible habit; for when it is generated, it is generated in an instant. And when it is destroyed, it is destroyed in an instant. ¶ Through the second species it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of pride? And it must be answered that it has this. For it is composed of several privative principles:

And it must be answered that it is with the privation of humility, obedience, justice, and the like; and also with all other things which are predicated of it.

# Sloth, Part One. Envy.
## 113

<margin>Comor <note>Likely a reference to a specific authority or a mnemonic contraction.</note></margin>
Sloth <note>original: "Accidia" - a spiritual apathy or "no-care" regarding one's duties to God.</note> in the pursuit of knowledge does not clarify it, but rather confounds it. ¶ The slothful person aligns their higher and lower powers in all their capacities [toward idleness]. For with sloth, one is lazy in acquiring virtues. ¶ The slothful person opposes the diligence of virtues with the preoccupation of vices. ¶ Sloth perverts positive principles into privative <note>Privative: defined by the absence of something, like darkness is the absence of light.</note> ones. Wherefore the slothful person murmurs and feigns to be a prophet; they give counsel when it is not necessary, they find fault in good things, and they are an enemy to the end goal. Furthermore, it binds the form and corrupts the matter, so that the agent themselves becomes habituated in laziness. ¶ Sloth obstructs the middle path, so that the rightful beginning does not find the end in which it should rest. ¶ The slothful person rests against the end, but labors at the very end. For sloth is the enemy of the perfection of the end. ¶ Greater sloth is the fountain of all vices. ¶ The slothful person, through their sloth, is the source of all vices. ¶ The slothful person with their sloth balances the acts of vices, so that sloth becomes strong against the diligence of virtues. ¶ Minor sloth concerns minor diligence, or greater diligence, or none at all.

It is asked: whether sloth is a mortal sin? And it must be answered that it is; for it hinders all acts of the virtues. ¶ But here the intellect marvels: since sloth is a mortal sin and is marked and figured by many signs, why is it so little recognized by men? Until one remembers that the greater part of men are habituated to sloth. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is sloth? And it must be answered that sloth is a sin with which the slothful person grieves over the good of their neighbor, but rejoices in their misfortunes. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does sloth have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it has its own correlatives which are among the privative correlatives of charity. For a charitable person rejoices in the good of their neighbor and grieves at their misfortunes. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is sloth in another? And it must be answered that it is lazy and malevolent toward good things, but swift, anxious, and selective toward evil things. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does sloth have in another? To which it must be said that it has its acts in all sins. ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: of what does sloth consist? To which it must be said that it consists of the absence of charity in a subject in which charity once was; just as a consequence does not exist because its antecedent does not exist. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what

<column-break/>

does sloth consist? To which it must be said that it consists of its specific privative correlatives with which it is a specific sin. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: to whom does sloth belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in whom it exists, just as deafness belongs to the deaf person. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why does sloth exist? And it must be answered that it is because a habit has been acquired; just as it is day because the sun is shining upon the earth. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why does sloth exist? And it must be answered: so that charity may not have a subject in which it can exist; for it is a privative habit against the positive habit of charity, hindering its end. ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: concerning the continuous quantity of sloth? And it must be answered that it possesses this in all the vices caused by it. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: concerning the discrete quantity of sloth? And it must be answered that it has discrete quantities by reason of the difference of the vices in which it has different acts. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked: what is the proper quality of sloth? To which it must be said that it is laziness <note>original: "pigricia"</note>, for without it, sloth cannot act. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of sloth? And it must be answered: malevolence and iniquity; for through these, the slothful person rejoices in evils and grieves at goods. ¶ Through rule H, it is asked concerning the time of sloth? And it must be answered through rule C that it is lazy in that time, so that the subject in which it exists does nothing useful while they have the time. ¶ Through rule I, it is asked: where is sloth? To which it must be said that it is in the laziness of the soul, the imagination, and the senses, which indeed neglect to do good but love to do evil. ¶ Through the first rule K, it is asked: how does sloth exist? And it must be answered that it exists in a manner contrary to the manner of charity. For just as charity has a way of being in loving the good of one's neighbor and in hating the evil of their misfortunes, so sloth exists in the contrary manner. ¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked: with what does sloth exist? To which it must be said that it exists with the privative habits of the virtues: namely with injustice, imprudence, etc. Furthermore, it exists with laziness, anger, and the like.

### Concerning Envy deduced through the principles.

<summary>This page provides a scholastic analysis of Sloth (Accidia), defining it as a mortal sin that acts as the opposite of Charity and the fountain of other vices. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "nine subjects," focusing here on the vice of Envy. The author uses a scholastic method, analyzing the vice through its principles and logical rules (the "Art").</meta>

# On the nine subjects.
-> fo. lxxv. <-
-> L iij <-

<margin>On envy conducted through the principles.</margin>
The envious person desires to have the goods of another against reason, wherefore evil follows him in spiritual matters. And if the envious person truly recognized this often, he would no longer possess envy. ¶ The magnitude of envy exists alongside the magnitudes of other vices; and therefore, it cannot be overcome by a single magnitude of virtue <note>The author suggests that because envy is "large" and interconnected with other sins, it requires a broad application of multiple virtues to defeat it</note>. ¶ Envy lasts as long as other vices last; wherefore it cannot be overcome without the duration of other virtues. ¶ The power of envy is rooted in the powers of other vices. And therefore, it cannot be overcome without the power of charity <term>charitas: the highest form of love/grace</term> within the powers of other virtues. ¶ The envious intellect is perverse and altered by envy. For it does not know itself; the cure for which consists in this: namely, that the intellect should understand the envy itself. ¶ Envy turns the will away from the highest good; nevertheless, it can be cured by frequently returning the will to the highest object <note>i.e., God</note> and focusing upon it. ¶ The envious person does not have virtues but vices; therefore, if he wishes to have virtues, let him exchange those things which he has for those which he does not have. ¶ The envious person does not have truth, but falsehood; therefore he deceives himself. A cure can be applied to this: namely, that he should not deceive himself. ¶ When the envious person has those things which he envied, he still does not find rest in them. For his foreknowledge gnaws at him. ¶ The envious person has as many diverse acts through envy as there are acts of other vices; nevertheless, he can be cured by frequently counting them. ¶ Envy has no harmony with any virtue; the cure lies in recognizing this. Envy contradicts the virtues with privative habits <note>A "privative habit" is the absence of a good quality that should be there, like blindness is the absence of sight</note>; its cure is achieved through the opposition of positive habits. ¶ Envy begins with things perceived by the senses; it is arranged with things imagined; and it is perfected with spiritual things, by destroying the imaginable and the sensible. ¶ Envy is the measure with which the envious person measures injury, imprudence, and the like. But the cure consists in the measure of justice, prudence, and the like. ¶ The envious person does not rest in the things he focuses on. For he desires them with labor; yet a cure is given when that labor is avoided until he arrives at rest. ¶ The envious person has greater labors with greater envy; nevertheless, with greater charity he can be cured so that he may perform greater actions. ¶ Envy, through its act, makes all the acts of others equal <note>likely meaning it reduces all others' achievements to a single point of resentment</note>. And the cure for this consists in the act of charity, by which all other acts of the virtues are made equal. ¶ The envious person believes the things he possesses to be smaller, and those things he envies to be greater; but the cure is through justice, by seeking what is the utility and the end of that thing.

### On envy deduced through the rules.

<margin>On envy deduced through the rules.</margin>
Is envy a more general sin objectively than avarice? And it must be answered that it is. For the avaricious man does not focus on as much as the envious man. For the avaricious man believes he can have that which he focuses on; but the envious man focuses on many things that are impossible for him to have. ¶ Through the first species of rule C, it is asked: what is envy? To which it must be said that it is a sin with which the envious person desires to have the things of another without reason. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: what does envy have in itself co-essentially? And it must be answered that it has its own privative correlatives <note>terms that define each other by their absence</note> with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: what is envy in another? And it must be answered that it is a habit in the envious person with which the envious one always labors with sadness and pain. ¶ Through the fourth species, it is asked: what does it have in another? To which it must be said that it has height and precedence in the envious person, just as a cloak is in a cloaked man. ¶ Through the first species of rule D, it is asked: of what is envy? To which it must be answered that it is of its own privative and specific correlatives with which it is a specific sin; just as deafness is of its own parts, and hearing of its own. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: of what is envy? To which it must be answered that it is of its own specific relatives; just as blindness is of its own. ¶ Through the third species, it is asked: whose is envy? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in whom the habit exists; just as malevolence belongs to the will, and forgetfulness to the memory, and ignorance to the intellect. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked: why is there envy? And it must be answered that it exists because it is an effect caused by the envious person; just as deafness is an effect caused by a defect of hearing. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked: why is there envy? And it must be answered that it exists so that the subject in whom envy resides may suffer labor; and in hell, perpetual pain and sadness. ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked: concerning the continuous quantity of envy? And it must be answered that it has such a quantity that with it the envious person can measure avarice, lust, gluttony, and the like. ¶ Through the second species, it is asked concerning the discrete quantity of envy? The **Will** moves itself with wrath to hate the good without deliberation. And therefore the remedy consists in deliberation. ¶ **Wrath** with great fury overcomes all things; but the remedy provides for this with great abstinence and deliberation. ¶ **Wrath** lasts a long time, as long as its act lasts. The remedy consists in presenting a foreign object <note>i.e., a distraction or a different focus</note> and persevering in it. ¶ The **Power** of wrath is conquered by the power of patience, abstinence, and also deliberation. ¶ **Wrath** confounds the **Intellect**, in that it takes away understanding from it; the remedy, however, is to restore its understanding to the intellect. ¶ **Wrath** perverts the **Will** into hating what it ought to love; its remedy is abstinence until it rises again through loving. ¶ The **Will** with wrath is in vice; its remedy is that through abstinence it may be in virtue. ¶ The **Intellect** with wrath does not understand virtue; but the remedy consists in this: namely, that through patience it may recognize it. ¶ An angry man, while hating, suffers that which he knows, but through loving he is cured. ¶ An angry man does not distinguish between his own evil and the evil of another; the remedy consists in

For it is a new habit <note>original: "habitus" - a settled disposition of character</note>; and in that time it multiplies its act. ¶ Through rule I, it is asked: where is anger? And it must be answered: it is in the **will** by hating, and in **injury** by injuring, and the like. It is also in motion: for the more it is moved, the more it multiplies its act. ¶ Through the first rule K, it is asked: in what manner does anger exist? To which it must be said: it exists in a perverse mode of the intellect, the will, the memory, and the imagination; the perversion existing under the rationale of the cause of fury, and without deliberation. ¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked: with what does anger exist? And it must be answered: it exists with sensible and imaginable things; and also with a perverse soul, and with habits that deprive one of principles: namely with malice and the like.

### On falsehood deduced through principles.

<margin>
On falsehood deduced through principles.
Greatness
Soul
Power
</margin>
A false man, in deceiving another, deceives himself: the knowledge of which is gained through the definition of goodness. ¶ Falsehood is not recognized by its own greatness; rather, it is recognized by the greatness of **legality** <note>original: "legalitas" - here meaning lawfulness or integrity</note>. ¶ Falsehood lasts as long as it is not recognized; for when it is recognized, it is destroyed. ¶ Falsehood has no power against **understanding**, but against **belief**; indeed, **prudence** is its enemy. ¶ Falsehood, when joined with belief, deceives the understanding. ¶ Falsehood, under the shadow of legality, makes itself loved: but the end <note>The "end" refers to the final outcome or purpose.</note> of legality reveals and proves it. ¶ Falsehood, with hypocrisy, feigns itself to be a virtue: but prudence destroys it and manifests it for what it is. ¶ Falsehood does not act alongside the act of truth; hence it follows that it is recognized by the act of truth. ¶ Falsehood promises delights, but gives punishments: and through this it is recognized. ¶ Falsehood does not distinguish, but confuses. Therefore, it is recognized by distinction. ¶ A false man brings sensible things and their signs into agreement so that he may deceive the imagination and the intellect; which, with its own power of harmony, shells <note>original: "enucleat" - to lay bare or extract the kernel of an argument.</note> the aforementioned falsehood. ¶ Falsehood contradicts the end, by which falsehood itself is contradicted. ¶ Falsehood delights in the beginning, but in the end it is saddened; by which reasoning it is recognized. ¶ Falsehood withdraws the "middle" <note>The "mean" or balanced path between extremes.</note> existing between the beginning and the end. And therefore, it is recognized by this. ¶ A false man is at rest in the beginning, but labors in the end; by which reason the falsehood itself is known. ¶ Greater falsehood is recognized by greater legality. ¶ A false man equates like with like; by which reason falsehood is known. ¶ Falsehood is recognized by a lesser virtue.

¶ Through the second type of rule, it is asked: of what is falsehood made? To which it must be answered that it is made of its own specific privative principles <note>original: "principiis specificis privativis"; referring to the absence of truth</note> with which it is a special sin; just as deafness is made of its own principles with which it is a special monstrosity. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: to whom does falsehood belong? And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in whom it exists, just as a habit does. ¶ Through the first type of rule E, it is asked: why is there falsehood? And it must be answered that it exists because there is no legality <note>or "lawfulness/uprightness"</note> in its subject. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: for what purpose is there falsehood? And it must be answered that it exists so that a human may be deceived; just as a tool exists so that an effect may be produced by someone through its mediation. ¶ Through the first type of rule F, it is asked: how great is continuous falsehood? And it must be answered that it is as great as the subject can act concerning it. ¶ Through the second type of F, it is asked: how great is discrete falsehood? To which it must be said that it has a discrete quantity caused by privative principles. ¶ Through the first type of rule G, it is asked: what is the proper quality of falsehood? To which it must be said that it is deception; for that is its special act. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: what is the appropriated quality of falsehood? To which it must be said that it is lying, hypocrisy, and the like. ¶ Through rule H, it is asked concerning the time of falsehood: And it must be answered that it is in time, because it is a new habit, and in time it has its actions. ¶ Through rule I, it is asked: where is falsehood? And it must be answered that it is in lying men, hypocrites, and deceivers. ¶ Through the first rule K, it is asked: in what manner is there falsehood? And it must be answered that it is by way of a fiction for deceiving and lying and the like. ¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked: with what does falsehood exist? And it must be answered that it exists with dissimulation and deception and the like; as has been signified by what has been said.

### On inconstancy deduced through principles. 114

<margin>
On inconstancy deduced through principles.
Magnitude.
Duration.
Power.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a floral or foliate motif within a square frame.</image-desc>
Constancy is a <term>habitus</term> <note>A settled disposition or character trait</note> in which goodness is the reason for a good person to do good; and inconstancy hinders this, therefore it is a sin. ¶ Inconstancy is overcome by the magnitude of constancy. ¶ As long as inconstancy lasts, for that long constancy is in a state of privation. ¶ The power of inconstancy has no power against the power of constancy. ¶ The intellect joined with inconstancy does not have strong understanding. ¶ Constancy with inconstancy is not lovable. ¶ Constancy with inconstancy is not a virtue. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy cannot exist together in truth. ¶ Inconstancy is not of the genus of delight, but of the genus of labor. ¶ Constancy opens and distinguishes differences; inconstancy, however, closes and obscures them. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy do not agree in genus nor in species. ¶ It is of the nature of inconstancy that it must be resisted in the beginning. ¶ For afterwards it is difficult to resist it. Since constancy is prior, therefore all inconstancy is posterior. ¶ Constancy joins together; but inconstancy disjoins. ¶ A constant man rests with constancy; however, the inconstant man labors with inconstancy. ¶ Greater inconstancy cannot be above greater constancy, nor can it hold a rank above it. ¶ Constancy and inconstancy are equally eligible by reason of free will; but they are not equally measurable. ¶ Minor inconstancy is easily conquered by major constancy.

Whether inconstancy is more a habit of the will or of the intellect? And it must be answered that it is so <note>i.e., it is a habit of the will</note>. Indeed, the will is more changeable than the intellect. The reason for this is: because the intellect is discursive <note>moving step-by-step through reasoning</note>, but the will is suddenly changeable. Therefore, the intellect knows that the remedy against inconstancy is to take away the suddenness of the will by placing it in discourse with the intellect. ¶ Through the first type of rule C, it is asked: what is inconstancy? And it must be answered that it is a stream diverted from the end <note>goal/purpose</note> of constancy. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: what does inconstancy have in itself that is co-essential? To which it must be answered that it has its correlatives with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: what is inconstancy in another? And it must be answered that it is an empress in the will, disobedient in the intellect, bashful in the imagination, and unstable in sensible things. ¶ Through the fourth type, it is asked: what does it have in another? And it must be answered that it has a defect of fortitude in the will, and deception in its promises. ¶ Through the first type of rule D, it is asked—

Regarding what Inconstancy is: it must be said that it is of itself, insofar as it is a sin. ¶ Through the second species it is asked, from what does inconstancy arise? And it must be said that it arises from its own privative and specific principles with which it is what it is. ¶ Through the third species it is asked, to whom does inconstancy belong? To which it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in whom its habit resides. ¶ Through the first species of rule E, it is asked, why is there inconstancy? And it must be answered that it exists because in the subject in which it resides, constancy is not present: just as heat which is in hot water exists because coldness is not in it. The intellect does not recognize by what mode natural habits are similar to moral habits. ¶ Through the second species of rule E, it is asked, for what purpose is inconstancy? To which it must be said that it exists so that constancy may not have being. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that sin is nothing: because it is contrary to being. <note>A common medieval philosophical argument: evil/sin has no independent existence but is a "privation" or lack of good.</note> ¶ Through the first species of rule F, it is asked, how great is inconstancy? To which it must be said that it possesses this because the will is often changeable in practice. ¶ Through the first species of rule G, it is asked, what is the proper quality of inconstancy? and it must be answered that it is the alteration of the will. ¶ Through the second species of rule G, it is asked, what is the appropriated quality of inconstancy? And to this it must be answered that it is the weakness of the heart's fortitude. ¶ Through rule H, it is asked concerning the time of inconstancy: and it must be answered that it exists in that time in which the will is changeable and habituated by it. Furthermore, it exists in the time in which the will acts with inconstancy against constancy. ¶ Through rule I, it is asked, where is inconstancy? and it must be answered that it is in the weakness of the will and also in the privation of perseverance and in its aforementioned places. ¶ Through the first rule K, it is asked, by what means is inconstancy? and it must be answered that it is through the contrary mode by which constancy exists: which indeed exists through the mode of discourse, deliberation, and choice with prudence, and especially with fortitude. ¶ Through the second rule K, it is asked, with what does inconstancy exist? and to this it must be answered that it exists with sudden alteration: and it is with its cause of which it is the effect: and with the privation of constancy, just as a shadow exists with the privation of light. ¶ We have spoken of the nine subjects of discourse or those deduced through the principles and rules of this art: and through those things which we have said of them, the artist <note>The practitioner of this logical system.</note> will be able to speak skillfully in a similar way about other foreign things attributed to them.

## Concerning application through the implicit and the explicit. 114

The first part of the tenth principal [division] concerning application through the implicit and explicit.

Let the application which is made through the implicit and explicit be done thus: namely, that the terms which are in the question be received: as if it is asked whether God exists. In this question, the letter **P** (whether) is applied to **B**. In **B**, goodness and difference are applied: and thus the artist ought to help himself with those terms which are under **B**, and at the same time help himself by applying those terms implied in the question itself which are explained in the art: such as greatness, eternity, etc. For if God exists, He exists through infinite greatness and eternity. And if there are no infinite greatness and eternity, it follows that God does not exist: and thus he will have the chamber **B.C.D.** <note>Refers to the "chambers" or combinations in the author's combinatorial logic wheels.</note> ¶ Next, let him discourse through these terms to prove that God exists or to disprove it, just as three terms are discursive through principles and rules. <meta>This page continues the "Tenth Part" of the treatise, focusing on the practical application of the Art's logical figures and terms to specific questions. It follows the previous discussion on the definitions of the principles.</meta>

<header>Tenth Part.</header>

<margin>Whether God is more "act" through his intelligence.</margin>
<note>The author is demonstrating how to use the "chambers" or combinations of terms from the Lullian wheels to solve theological problems.</note>
...according to goodness, difference, and "whether" <note>original: "utrum"</note>; and in the chamber of greatness, concordance, and "what is it"; and in the chamber of duration, contrariety, and "of what." In these terms are implied the definitions and species of the rules. And thus the entire chamber may be applied to the proposition—that is, to the conclusion. And just as we have explained in the aforementioned cases, so it can be explained in others. ¶ Furthermore, if it is asked **whether God is more in act through his understanding than through his eternity**, let "greater" be applied to majority and "lesser" to minority. For "less" belongs to the genus of minority, while "greater" belongs to the genus of majority. And if it is asked whether he is as powerful through his power as through his will, let one recur to equality, in which comparison is implied (just as "greater" is in majority and "less" is in minority). And if it is asked whether God is just, let one recur to virtue, for "just" belongs to the genus of virtue; and let one recur to goodness, since it is a good thing that God is just; and so with others in their own way.

### .2. On application through the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>
1.
abstract
substance

2.
abstract
accidental

abstract substance
concrete accidental

4. abstract accidental
concrete substance
</margin>
<margin>The second part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application through the abstract and the concrete.</margin>
This application is to be described in four ways. ¶ The **first way** is when the terms placed in the question have a substantial abstraction, such as the terms "abstract" and "concrete"—for example, *fire-ness* <note>original: "igneitas"</note> and *fire*. Fire-ness is indeed a substantial essence, while fire is a concrete and substantial term. ¶ The **second** is when there is an abstract and accidental thing (or accident) and its concrete equivalent likewise; such as "quantity" and "how much" <note>original: "titas & tū" (quantitas et quantum)</note>; I say "how much" insofar as it is a habit <note>term: habit (habitus) — here meaning a state of being or an acquired quality</note>, and thus it is accidental or an accident. ¶ The **third** is when the abstract is a substance and the concrete is an accident, such as *fire-ness* and *the hot*. I say "the hot" insofar as it is a habit, for in that way it is an accident. ¶ The **fourth** is when the abstract is an accident and its concrete is a substance, such as *whiteness* and *the white*; and I say "the white" by reason of a body that is characterized by whiteness, and thus it is a substance and not an accident. All these four modes are implied in the terms of the question and vice versa; and thus they ought to be explained in the conclusion according to these four modes, so that the intellect is not deceived by a variation of the middle term.

<margin>The third part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through the first figure.</margin>
### .3. On application through the first figure.

According to what has been said, let it be done by affirming or denying: namely, circularly through the conversion of the subject and predicate, such as "great goodness" and "good greatness." And if they are not convertible, such as "eternity" and "greatness" (for some greatness is not eternity and vice versa), nor is every goodness great (because some goodness is small), and so with others in their own way.

<column-break/>

### .4. On application through the second figure.

<margin>The fourth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application through the second figure.</margin>
Application through the second figure itself is done through the triangles themselves, and through the "ladders" <note>term: ladders (scalae) — Lull's diagrams showing the hierarchy of concepts from general to specific</note> placed upon the angles. In these ladders are implied the most general principle, the most specific principle, and the subalternate principle. A **most general principle** is like "difference" having nothing above itself. A **most specific principle** is like the "difference" existing between this stone and this plant. A **subalternate** is like the "difference" existing between one sensible thing and another sensible thing, etc. ¶ And also in this ladder is implied the ascent and descent of the intellect; and outside of these ladders, the ascent and descent of the intellect can in no way be implied. ¶ We say, however, that the terms of the second figure are explainable according to how they lie in the figure itself, according to what we say about it. ¶ Furthermore, we say that the second figure is applicable to the first, such as placing a difference between goodness and goodness, etc., and placing a concordance between goodness and goodness, as is marked in the third figure.

### .5. On application to the third figure.

<margin>The fifth part of the tenth principal part, which is on application to the third figure.</margin>
Let the application of a question to the third figure be done thus: namely, if the matter of the question concerns **B**, apply **C** to **B**; and if **C** is not sufficient for **B**, apply **D** to **B**. And so on until the chamber **B. K.** <note>note: These letters refer to the Lullian alphabet where B=Goodness, C=Greatness, etc.</note> And let one look at the meanings of the chambers, affirming or denying, in such a way that the letter remains with its conditions and its meanings. Nevertheless, if the matter of the question fits **C**, let the other letters be applied to **C**, just as we said regarding **B**. And this same thing can be said of **D**, **E**, etc. And such an application is infallible and very general.

# On Application

<margin>The sixth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application to the fourth figure.</margin>

The application of the fourth figure <note>The "Fourth Figure" in Lullian logic is a circular device used to combine terms to find middle terms for syllogisms.</note> is done as follows: namely, if the matter of the question fits the "chamber" <note>A "chamber" (camera) refers to a specific combination of letters/concepts on the Lullian wheel.</note> **b.c.d.**, let it be applied to that chamber. And if the matter fits **b.c.e.**, then with **d.** let the smaller circle be turned and let **e.** be placed under **c.**, and let the chamber **b.c.e.** be made. Then let the meanings of the letters be received, with which the question may be solved. And as we have said concerning these, so it can be said concerning others.

<margin>Note an application more general than the others.</margin>

¶ This application is more general than that of the third figure, because the chamber consists of three letters; and it is general to the extent that it contains within itself all the chambers of the table.

### 7 On application through definitions.

<margin>The seventh part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application through definitions.</margin>

According to the second mode of this Art, the artist <note>The "artist" refers to the practitioner of Ramon Lull's Great Art (Ars Magna).</note> ought to define the terms that are in the question, whether they be explicit or implicit. For example, if it is asked whether God is infinite: then the respondent must define "God" and "finiteness," saying thus: God is a being so perfect that outside of Himself He needs nothing else; and infinity is a being to which infinite correlatives <note>Correlatives are a key Lullian concept: the active power, the passive object, and the act itself (e.g., Loving, Lovable, and Loving).</note> belong, without which it can least of all exist. ¶ Furthermore, just as it is said: "goodness is a being by reason of which a good [agent] acts good," so it can be said that "greatness is that by reason of which a great [agent] acts great," and so on for others in their own way. ¶ Furthermore, a term placed in a question can indeed be defined in multiple ways by running through the species of the Rules. ¶ And first, through the species of Rule C <note>Rule C usually asks "What?" (Quid).</note> thus: man is a rational animal—and this is through the first species. Through the second species: man is an animal having his own proper correlatives, namely: the "man-ifying" [power], the "man-ifiable" [subject], and "to man-ify" <note>original: "hominificantem, hominificabile: et hominificare." Lull creates new Latin verbs to describe the essential functions of a thing's nature.</note>. ¶ And through the third species: man is an animal acting in the mechanical arts, such as writing in a manuscript, riding on a horse, and the like. ¶ And through the fourth species of the same rule: man is a being having greater possession over brutes and plants. ¶ Through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D usually asks "From what?" (De quo).</note>: man is a primitive being in the nobility of sensitivity. ¶ Through the second species: man is a being constituted of soul and body. ¶ Through the third species: man is a being to whom brutes, plants, and the like are subject. ¶ Through the first species of Rule E <note>Rule E usually asks "Why?" (Quare).</note>: man is a substance through his humanity. ¶ Through the second species: man is a being created to serve God along with vegetative and sensitive [beings]. ¶ Through Rule F <note>Rule F usually asks "How much?" (Quantum).</note>: man is a quantitative and continuous being through his elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and reasoning [powers] from which he is composed. And these

<column-break/>

five powers are his discrete parts, because they are different. ¶ Through Rule G <note>Rule G usually asks "Of what kind?" (Quale).</note>: man is a being to whom "man-ifying" properly belongs; and a being capable of laughter; and he is a being who writes and rides, and such things. ¶ Through Rule H <note>Rule H usually asks "When?" (Quando).</note>: man is a being understanding and reading in time, etc. ¶ Through Rule I <note>Rule I usually asks "Where?" (Ubi).</note>: man is a being digging in a vineyard, and in a church he is one praying to God. ¶ Through the rule of Modality: man is a being having a mode of working mechanically and of generating another man. ¶ Through the rule of Instrumentality: man is a substance generating another man with a woman; and with a hammer, he is a being driving a nail, and things of this sort. ¶ And just as we have given the example of man, so it can be given for others in their own way. ¶ And in this step, a doctrine is given through which a person may know how to make definitions in diverse ways for one and the same thing, so that the thing itself—which was previously unknown—is known through all these thoughts or definitions. And therefore the artist must define in such a way that the definitions remain uncorrupted.

### 8 On application to the rules.

<margin>The eighth part of the tenth principal part, which concerns application to the rules.</margin>

When a question is asked about some doubt, the artist ought to apply that doubt to the rules successively. For just as a crystal placed in a red color takes that color upon itself, and also if it is placed in green, it takes that color upon itself, and so with others; so when an unknown thing is run through the rules and the species of the rules, then the unknown is "colored" or declared through the species of the rules in which it is placed subjectively and objectively. Then the intellect knows through the species of the rules that which was previously unknown. And just as we gave the example of man defined through the rules, for the sake of greater clarification we wish to exemplify "nature" as derived through the rules. ¶ Through the first species of Rule C, we say that nature is an essence sustained in its natural concrete form and moved through a natural act, in which act it is at rest. ¶ Through the second species, it is an essence having conatural correlatives: namely, the "naturizing" [power], the "naturizable" [subject], and "to naturize" <note>original: "naturatiuum, naturabile et naturare."</note>, without which it cannot exist. ¶ Through the third species, nature is in the subject in which it is active and capable of "conaturizing." ¶ Through the fourth species, nature has in the subject in which it is, action and passion and act; and this through a natural agent and through natural form, matter, and

### On the application by the Table.

<margin>
The ninth part of the tenth principal part. On the application by the table.
</margin>
The application of the table is when the terms of questions are applied to the table itself. For if the terms of a question agree with the first column, namely **b.c.d.** which is the first column: as if it were asked, whether it would be a great good for the world to have existed from eternity. Or if it were asked, whether there is an infinite act: assuming that goodness is the reason why it acts for the good; and that greatness is the reason for that act being great; and that eternity makes that act endure from eternity to eternity, it follows that the same infinite act must endure.

<column-break/>

<margin>
8
b.c.d.
</margin>
¶ Furthermore, if the terms of the question fit the second column: as if it were asked, why is there a greatness of goodness and power? And the answer must be that it is through the correlatives of goodness, greatness, and power; and so of others in their own way.
¶ Moreover, any column is applicable to another: just as the second column is applicable with the first and with the third, because it contains elements of the first (**b.c.**) and likewise of the third; and so with the others, since they are chained together. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that all columns can be applied to the same conclusion. And thus it knows itself to be very general through the application itself, which is very general.
<margin>
b.c.t.b.
</margin>
¶ Likewise: when it is asked, whether the world is eternal? Then the second chamber, which is **b.c.t.b.**, is applied to the upper chamber. And so with the chamber which is **b.c.t.c.**, and so with the others up to **t.b.c.d.** The reason for this is that eternity is the term explained in the question. ¶ Again, if it is asked, whether the power of the world is infinite? Let the response be applied to column **b.c.d.** just as the question regarding the eternity of the world was applied; and let the negative be held. For just as a great inconvenience <note>In scholastic logic, an "inconvenience" is a logical absurdity or contradiction</note> would follow if the world were from eternity, so a great inconvenience would follow if the world had infinite power. And as we say of the world, so it can be said of those things which it contains within itself.
¶ Furthermore, if it is asked, whether one angel produces another angel? Let the response be applied to **b.c.d.** because between the essence of an angel and a human or a rose, there is a great difference. For the body of a human exists under the general matter of the elements, by reason of which one human can produce or generate another human, and one rose another. Concerning an angel, however, it is not so. For one angel does not have that from which he might produce another angel, since he is not derived from one and the same general angelic matter, as he is finite in his primitivity.
¶ Just as we have given an example through those things we said about the table, so it can be said of many other things in their own way.
¶ The application which is made through the table requires that the species and rules of the chambers be preserved, and that those things which they signify be applied to the proposition: namely to the conclusion, by affirming or denying conveniently or inconveniently, as is clear through the example mentioned above.
