<margin>The eleventh part of the tenth principal part: on application through the evacuation of the third figure.</margin>

### On application through the evacuation of the third figure.

Application which is performed through the third figure <note>The Third Figure in Lull’s Art consists of a series of compartments (cameras) representing combinations of principles like Goodness and Greatness.</note> is done in this manner: namely, that the terms explained in the question are applied to the "evacuation" <note>original: "evacuationem"; in Lullian logic, this refers to the exhaustive analysis of all possible meanings or combinations within a specific compartment.</note> of the third figure, specifically to that compartment with which the terms most agree. For example, if it is asked whether it is a great good that goodness and greatness have substantial correlatives, and whether those correlatives are in good and great concord. Then such a question should be applied to compartment **B.C.** <note>The compartment combining Goodness (B) and Greatness (C).</note> And through those things which we said in the chapter on evacuation regarding that compartment, the question will indeed be solved. The same applies to other questions, according to how their terms can enter the compartment, either by affirming or denying, and either agreeably or disagreeably. Furthermore, if the question is asked whether contrariety of goodness can exist in eternity from eternity. Let that question be applied to compartment **B.C.**, and to compartment **C.D.**, and to compartment **D.E.** And according to what has been said in those compartments, the question will indeed be solved; and so with other questions, according to how their terms can enter the compartments: affirming or denying agreeably or disagreeably. Furthermore, let a subalternate question be applied to a particular question, and vice versa: as if it were asked whether there are great correlatives in goodness? And let this question be applied to this one: whether there are great correlatives in the goodness of Socrates or of this rose. And then let these questions be applied to compartment **B.C.** Then the answer will be found already solved by the things that have been said. Furthermore, if it is asked: of what are the correlatives of greatness? and of what are the correlatives of Socrates? Let these questions be applied to compartment **C.D.** and let the subalternate question be applied to the particular question: and then the conclusion will be found declared and designated by the time <note>original: "temporis"; likely a reference to the temporal duration or the specific instance of the logical operation.</note> through those things we have already said in that compartment; and so for the other compartments. We shall give an example of this in the treatise on questions.

<margin>The eleventh part of the tenth principal part: on application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.</margin>

### On application through the multiplication of the fourth figure.

We have said that the multiplication of the fourth figure <note>The Fourth Figure is a circular device used for generating complex syllogisms and combinations.</note> consists of five modes: namely, in multiplication, in the finding of the middle term, in the proof of the major and minor propositions, in solving fallacies, and in the teaching through which other arts can easily be learned. And therefore, if the artist <note>The practitioner of Lull's Art.</note> wishes to multiply many reasons for the same conclusion, to find many middle terms, to prove the major and minor propositions, to solve fallacies, and to easily and briefly teach other sciences with this General Art: let him apply the mode which we held in the multiplication of the fourth figure. For that mode is universal, and through that mode, the particular mode will be regulated and brought to light. For the particular shines back in the universal and vice versa; and let these things suffice, for it is sufficiently declared.

### On the application of the mixture of principles and rules.

This Art is divided into two parts. In the first, we shall speak of the principles explained. In the second, of the implication <note>original: "implicatione"; the folding together or practical application of rules to principles.</note> in which we shall apply the places of the rules of this Art to the explained principles. These principles themselves shall be called the "hundred forms"; we do this so that the Art may be more material <note>More tangible or accessible.</note> to the intellect for finding many conclusions. We intend to say little about them because we avoid prolixity. But through what we shall say of them, the artist can know the process of any form through all the rules: just as we did in the deduction of the explained principles, and also the rules. And first, we shall speak of the first part thus:

<margin>The twelfth part of the tenth principal part, which is on the application of the mixture of principles and rules, divided into two small sections.</margin>

#### First part.

If a question contains within itself explained terms—as if it were asked whether a being is good, great, and eternal—let one recur to the chapter on goodness, greatness, and eternity. And also let him see by what mode goodness is discoursed through the principles and rules, and so for the other principles. And then let him conclude by affirming or denying according to how the principles are in such a way that the principles and rules remain unharmed. And then the intellect will find the truth concerning that which it seeks. This truth will be brought to light through that discourse. And just as we gave an example of goodness, greatness, and eternity, so it can be given for other principles. And let these things suffice as far as the first part is concerned.

# Tenth Part.

<margin>
The thirteenth section of the tenth part of the principle concerning the application of the nine subjects.
</margin>

We have spoken of the nine subjects: therefore, if a question arises concerning God, let it be applied to the first subject; and let the discourse run through it just as God is discussed in such a way that the affirmative or negative aligns with the text. ¶ If the question is about an angel, let it be applied to the second subject in which the angel is the discourse: and let that which agrees with the text be held concerning the question. And so with the other subjects in their own manner.

### On the application to the hundred forms.

<margin>
The fourteenth section of the tenth part of the principle which is about the application to the hundred forms.
</margin>

We call these the hundred forms. For we consider them in the abstract. Some will be most general; others will be subordinate: and to each form we assign its own concrete <note>In scholastic logic, the "abstract" is the quality (e.g., Whiteness) and the "concrete" is the thing possessing it (e.g., a white thing).</note>, so that each form may shine more clearly to the intellect: especially since whatever exists is either abstract or concrete. For outside of these no being can exist: and first we must speak of the first part.

#### 1 On Entity.

<margin>
The first form: on entity.
</margin>

<margin>
Being converts <note>original: "convrtit" - meaning the terms are interchangeable in logic.</note> D. First E. form. C. contains in itself.
</margin>

Entity in this Art is an implicit term: and its definition can be made just as the definitions of the other explained principles of this Art are made; therefore let the artist apply it to the definition of goodness, greatness, etc. For just as goodness is the cause why someone good performs a good act, so entity is the cause why some being causes another being. And just as greatness is the cause why goodness is great, so entity is the cause why goodness is a being: and so of the others. Its concrete, however, is "being," implied in the second species of D and in the first of E. And those things from which it is implied are in the second species of C: and therefore whatever is asked concerning entity and being, let it be applied to the explained principles; and let such judgment be made of it according to the rules, just as was done for goodness, greatness, etc.

#### 2 On Essence.

<margin>
The second form: on essence.
</margin>

Since entity and essence are interchangeable, it follows that "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note> and "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> are interchangeable: and therefore just as we spoke of entity and being, so we can speak of essence and "to be." ¶ If it is asked whether there is a difference between essence and "to be," then at that time let one recur to "Difference," which is an

<column-break/>

explained term; and let judgment be made according to how Difference is discussed through all principles and through all rules: and then without doubt it will appear that the affirmative is to be held in the question. ¶ For Difference is essence, and its correlatives <note>A technical term in Lullian philosophy referring to the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the loving).</note> are in the reckoning of height by abstracting: and its concretes are in the reckoning of infinity by containing: and thus it is clear that difference exists between essence and "to be." And to this, rule B consents.

#### 3 On Unity.

<margin>
The third form: unity.
</margin>

Unity is the form to which "uniting" properly belongs. And it is indeed applicable to goodness, greatness, etc., since it is good, great, and so forth. Just as unity is good through goodness, and great through greatness, so goodness is one through unity, and greatness is another, one creature through that same unity, and so of the others. And in this step the intellect recognizes that Difference distinguishes between goodness and greatness: so that, like the principle of Difference, every principle may have its own proper truth. And therefore if there is an explained term in the question, let one recur to what was said in the discourse on goodness, greatness, and difference, and let the response be made according to what was said of them. ¶ The concrete of unity is indeed implied in the concrete of goodness, greatness, etc. For the good is one, and the great is another one. That "one" has its own correlatives from which it is composed. This is applicable to the second species of D and the first of E. And those correlatives are applicable to the second species of rule C and the first of D.

#### 4 On Plurality.

<margin>
The fourth form: plurality.
</margin>

Plurality is a form aggregated from many things differing in number, as is clear through the second species of rule C, which is its source. It is indeed applicable to the explained principles, because it is good, great, and eternal. And just as it is good through goodness, and great through greatness, etc., so goodness and greatness are plural through plurality itself. And there are also many goodnesses differing in species. And likewise of greatness: as is clear through the second species of rule C, which is its source.

# On Application.

## On Application.

<margin>A hundred forms</margin>
¶ Indeed, the primary causes of plurality assist through difference, concordance, and equality; and so it is with other correlatives <note>In Llull’s system, "correlatives" refer to the active, passive, and verbal relationship within a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving.</note> and plurality. This is applicable to the principles themselves and vice versa. Its concrete form <note>The "concrete" refers to the embodied or specific instance of an abstract quality, like "a good thing" versus "Goodness."</note> is applicable to the concrete form of goodness, magnitude, etc. This is evident in a compound element <note>original: "elementato"</note> which is "greatly good" and is one constituted from many, so that plurality is sustained within it.

### 5 On Nature.

<margin>The fifth form: On Nature.</margin>
Nature is the form to which "to nature" <note>Llull often turns nouns into verbs to show their active essence; "naturare" means the act of being or producing nature.</note> properly belongs. And because the principles are natural through nature, nature is applicable to natural goodness and natural magnitude. Thus, nature can be known through the discourse of principles and rules, as we have said above in a broad manner. ¶ Furthermore, nature is applicable to the natural correlatives of goodness, magnitude, etc., because those natural correlatives cannot exist without concrete things. ¶ Indeed, the natural concrete is applicable to natural concretes, as is evident through the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E. <note>These refer to specific logical keys in Llull's "Ars Brevis" for answering questions about "What" and "From what."</note> ¶ Furthermore, since one nature of goodness exists with magnitude, another with duration, etc., and vice versa, it is applicable to "mixture," where we spoke of derived goodness, magnitude, and duration.

### 6 On Genus.

<margin>The sixth form: On Genus.</margin>
Genus is a being considered as highly diffused, which is predicated of many things differing in species. We have said enough regarding genus in the *New Logic* <note>original: "logica noua," referring to Llull's own treatise on logic.</note> which we composed. It is indeed applicable to the explained principles, because through it they are general; just as a genus is good through goodness, and great through magnitude, etc. It is also applicable to the explained correlatives, because those correlatives are general through it, and also their correlatives are known through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Furthermore, its concrete is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E, by which we know that genus is a real being, existing in itself. For if it were not, the correlatives of the explained principles could not be general, nor consequently could the explained principles themselves be general.

### 7 On Species.

<column-break/>

<margin>Goodness does not generate in their order here when it runs <note>This marginal note appears to be a mnemonic or a correction regarding the sequence of the principles.</note></margin>
<margin>The seventh form: On Species.</margin>
Species in this Art is an explained principle, and its definition is this: Species is a being that is predicated of many things differing in number. Species is also applicable to the "places in mixture" where we say "great goodness," etc. For the goodness which was most general is not entirely general when it is called "great goodness," because it has been contracted to the specific nature of magnitude; and so it is with the others. ¶ Furthermore, it is applicable to correlatives, because each of the explained principles has specific correlatives and its own numerical differences through "Difference" <note>Difference is one of Llull's primary principles.</note>. Thus, species is applicable to Difference, which is an explained principle in this Art; this Difference distinguishes a genus into many species differing in number, just as "man" is one species and "lion" is another. ¶ Likewise, species is applicable to the "Middle" <note>The principle of Medium or Middle.</note>; for just as the middle stands between the beginning and the end, so species stands between the genus and the individual. In this step, the intellect recognizes that species is necessarily a real being; for just as the beginning and end would not exist at the extremities of a middle unless the middle were a real being, so consequently neither the genus nor the individual would be real beings. ¶ The concrete of species is the "specific," which is applicable to the second species of Rule D and the first of Rule E, through which it is knowable; it is, however, both beyond the senses and imaginable. ¶ Furthermore, there are other species which are natural, such as "visibility" through the visual power and the like, which consist of sight and power, such as colors and shapes which are perceived in a subject through sight. ¶ Furthermore, there are other species which consist in power through the moral virtues, such as "justifiabilities" through justice, "prudentialities" through prudence, "credibilities" through faith, and "hope-abilities" through hope. Such species are "phantasms" <note>Mental images or representations.</note> as the imaginables of the imagination, the intelligibles of the intellect, the lovables of the will, and the memorables of the memory. Nevertheless, the species of the virtues are secondary.

### 8 On Individuality.

<margin>The eighth form: On Individuality.</margin>
Individuality is definable through the first species of Rule C. For just as goodness is the reason for a good thing to act goodly, so individuality is the reason for an individual to produce an individual. And just as individuality is good through goodness, etc., so goodness is individuated through individuality; and so it is with their concretes and relatives with which the essence is indivisible. These correlatives of goodness and correlatives of individuality are applicable so that the intellect may have knowledge of them...

# Part Ten

<margin>Corrected</margin> Truly, the correlatives <note>In Llull's system, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal functions of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving.</note> cannot be perceived by the senses nor imagined, since they are placed and contained in essence beyond physical shape. ¶ The concrete form of individuality is the individual. And this is demonstrable through the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E. In elemental things, however, it is sensible and imaginable, as is evident through "this rose" and "this lion."

### 9 On Property.

<margin>g.</margin>
<margin>The ninth form: On Property.</margin>
<margin>c.</margin>
<margin>Corrected</margin>
<margin>D. E.</margin>
Property <note>original: "Proprietas"; here meaning the specific quality that makes something what it is, or "ownership" in a legal sense.</note> is an explicit principle, as is evident through rule G. But in other principles and rules, it is an implicit principle. And its definition is applicable to the first type of rule C. ¶ For just as goodness is the reason why a good person acts well, so property is the reason why that which is "proper" acts in its own way. And just as goodness has its own correlatives through property, so property has its good correlatives through goodness. Property is also applicable to "Difference." For just as difference is the cause of differing, so property is the cause of appropriating; and so it is with the others. ¶ Furthermore: the concrete form of property is the "proper," constituted from concrete correlatives; and this is signified through the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E: such as "this man" who is a proper animal, and "this lion" which is another proper animal, and "this horse," and "this rose" which is another proper body. And so it is in moral matters: such as Socrates who has his own proper horse, and Plato likewise, as is evident through the third type of rule D. And in this passage, the intellect recognizes from which principles the science of law arises, and in which principles it consists, and which principles a jurist ought to use; and it also recognizes that laws are applicable to the mixture of principles and rules.

### 10 On Simplicity.

<margin>The tenth form: On Simplicity.</margin>
Simplicity is applicable to the principles of this Art, because through simplicity the principles are simple; just as simplicity is good through goodness, and great through greatness. And just as the explicit principles are discussed in the mixture of principles and rules, so simplicity can be discussed through all principles and rules. Its definition is indeed through the first type of rule C, for it is the form by which principles are simple. ¶ Simplicity, through the second type of rule C, has its own simple correlatives: just as goodness has the simple "bonificative" <note>the power to make good</note>, the "bonificable" <note>that which can be made good</note>, and "to bonify" <note>the act of making good</note>. With simplicity and its correlatives, there consists one simple essence having simple and primitive principles through the first type of rule D. Its concrete form or its being is "the simple." And this is signified through the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E.

<margin>c.</margin>
<margin>Corrected</margin>

### 11 On Composition.

<margin>The eleventh form: On Composition.</margin>
Composition is a form aggregated from several essences. It is indeed applicable to the contraction and meeting of explicit principles, as is evident in the chapter on goodness applied to the principles: where it is said that "great goodness" is doubled, and "great and durable goodness" is tripled, etc., constituting a composite from several explicit principles. And in this passage, the intellect recognizes where composition arises; and rule K agrees with this. ¶ Furthermore, composition has its own composite correlatives, as is evident through the second type of rule C. And so in created things, the "bonificative" and "magnificative" <note>the power to make great</note> etc., compose the "magnificable" and "bonificable"; and also "to bonify" and "to magnify" are simply composed, etc., and together they constitute one essence, which essence we call "composition." Its being or its concrete form is "the composite" to an intellect enlightened through the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E.

### 12 On Form.

<margin>The twelfth form: On Form.</margin>
Form is applicable to the twelve principles: therefore, just as a principle runs through the explicit principles and rules, similarly "form" can be run through in its own way. However, we say this concerning "composite form" in created things, because the "bonificable" <note>the passive/material element</note> is of the nature of matter; but in God, it is not. ¶ Form is that essence with which an agent acts upon matter naturally. This composite form indeed has its own composite correlatives, as was said above. But a "simple form" in caused things does not have correlatives, because it is one simple part of a substance: namely, the "formifying" or the agent, considered according to the first type of rule E; and the same can be said of accidental form. ### 13 On Matter.

<margin>Thirteenth form: on matter.</margin>
<margin>Commentary C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Matter is a simple passive essence; it is applicable to the "passion" <note>In medieval philosophy, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive a quality.</note> of the explained principles, such as that which can be made good, that which can be made great, etc. These indeed belong to the category of matter by reason of passion. ¶ Matter truly does not have concrete forms <note>original: "concreta"</note>; and this is through the second type of rule C, because simplicity posits that its passion is one simple part of its substance. And its primitive principle is designated through the first type of rule D. ¶ The **concrete** or the "materialized" is composed of many passions, such as that which is made good, made great, etc. ¶ This materialized thing is declared through the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E. ¶ Indeed, this materialized thing is the fountain from which all particular matters are derived, just as the "formed" is that from which all particular forms descend when they are brought from potentiality into act.

### 14 On Substance.

<margin>Fourteenth form: on substance.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
Substance is applicable to the contracted triangle <note>A reference to Lull's combinatorial diagrams</note> insofar as it says that "majority" <note>original: "maioritas," meaning greatness or superiority in scale</note> exists between substance and substance; therefore, the discourse of substance is implied in the discourse of majority through all principles and rules. The definition, however, is applicable to the definition of goodness, etc. For just as goodness is the reason for a good thing to produce good, so substance, as to its genus, is the reason for it to produce a "substantiated" thing. ¶ Substance indeed has its substantial correlatives through the second type of rule C: namely, the substantiated, the substantiable, and the act of substantiating. <note>original: "substantiatum, substantiabile et substantiare"</note> The "substantiating" is applicable to the "bonifying" and "magnifying"; the "substantiable" is applicable to the "bonifiable" and "magnifiable"; and "to substantiate" to "to bonify" and "to magnify." And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way sub-

### 15 On Accident.

<margin>Fifteenth form: on accident.</margin>
<margin>Commentary r r m</margin>
Accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature, like the color of a shirt.</note> is implied in the yellow triangle, where it is said that "majority" exists between accident and accident. And therefore its discourse is applicable through all principles and rules in the aforementioned triangle; the aforementioned discourse is implied. ¶ An accident is indeed a form not existing by itself, unless it relates principally to its own end; but it relates to the ends of the substance. However, accident does not have correlatives properly, but only by accident, because substance is characterized by it as having quantity, position, etc. ¶ In the chapter on goodness where it is said "goodness is great," etc., accident arises because there is a multiplication of the composite. It is "how much" <note>original: "quanta"</note> through the quantity arising by accident. And because it is situated in a subject, "position" <note>original: "situs"</note> is indeed an arising by accident; and so it is for the other categories, and also for motion and the like. ¶ The **concrete** is the "accident" and the "accidental," which is applicable to the second type of rule D and the first type of rule E, just as a chest is an accidental subject because it has an accidental shape through craftsmanship. And just as with a logician who is accidentally a master. And so it is for others in their own way.

Quantity is a term explained in this art, namely in rule F, but its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, etc. For just as goodness is a being by reason of which a good thing acts well, so quantity is a being by reason of which a "quantified" thing acts. Its primitives and origins are applicable to the chapter on goodness deduced through the principles: that it is one essence and another magnitude. And when they are contracted, multiplication follows; and consequently quantity, without which multiplication in creatures cannot occur. And this is seen through the first type of rule D. And in this step, the intellect recognizes where quantity arises. ¶ Likewise, quantity is applicable to the substantial correlatives through the second type of rule C. ### 17 On Quality.

<margin>Explanation: The seventeenth form, on Quality.</margin>
Quality is an explicit term, as is clear through Rule G. <note>A reference to the author's mnemonic system of rules and principles</note> Indeed, by its own definition, it is applicable to the definition of Goodness, etc. For just as Goodness is the being by reason of which a good thing does good, so Quality is the form that establishes that the "bonifier" <note>The active principle of making something good</note> is of a certain quality in acting, and the "bonified" <note>The recipient of goodness</note> is of a certain quality in being acted upon. ¶ This Quality is applicable to the substantial correlatives <note>Pairs of terms that imply one another, like father/son or acting/being acted upon</note> as seen in the second type of Rule C, because those correlatives are "habituated" <note>Clothed or characterized</note> by quality. And Quality itself is situated by those same correlatives. Furthermore, through the third type of Rule C, it places the "qualified subject" in which it exists, which qualified subject is its own concrete form. ¶ Furthermore, Quality is applicable to the second type of Rule D in the chapter on Goodness, running through the principles and rules, and likewise for Magnitude, etc. For Goodness, which is a most general principle, is not "of a quality" until it is contracted <note>Limited or specified from a general concept to a specific instance</note>; as when it is asked: "Of what quality is the goodness?" and it is answered that it is great and durable, etc. And then Quality has arisen accidentally through the contraction of the principles.

### 18 On Relation.

<margin>The eighteenth form, on Relation.</margin>
Relation is an implicit term, and its definition is applicable to the definition of Goodness, etc. For just as a good person creates a good thing through goodness, so a relative person creates a relative thing through relation. For if there is a "relating" thing, it follows there is a "related" thing. And vice versa. If there is an antecedent, it follows there is a consequent, and vice versa. And if there is concordance, it follows there is plurality, and so with the others. The "related" is indeed its own concrete form of that relation, and is habituated in it, and so forth. ¶ Furthermore, Relation, being an accident, is applicable to the contraction and mixture of principles with the first type of Rule D and the second of Rule C. For if Goodness is great, it follows that it has correlatives that are good and great, without which Goodness could in no way be great. And so with others in their own way.

### 19 On Action.

<column-break/>

<margin>The nineteenth form, on Action.</margin>
Action is a term implied in correlatives, and it is applicable to those correlatives—namely to the "bonifier," the "magnifier," etc. And its definition is applicable to the definition of Goodness, etc. For just as Goodness is the being by reason of which a good thing does good, so Action is the reason in the agent for acting in its own concrete form; however, it is not a name imposed in a straight line. <note>Likely meaning it is not a primary substance but a derivative category</note> Moreover, the concrete form is designated through the second type of Rule D. ¶ Further, Action is declared through the first type of Rule D in the correlatives through the second type of Rule C, and this by the definition of the "middle" <note>The mean or mediating link</note>; and so with others in their own way.

### 20 On Passion.

<margin>The twentieth form, on Passion <note>In this context, "Passion" means being the recipient of an action, or "undergoing."</note></margin>
Passion is an implicit term. ¶ And it is applicable to correlatives. ¶ Through the second type of Rule C, namely to the "bonifiable," the "magnifiable," etc. Therefore, just as passive correlatives exist through the mixture of principles, so Passion, which is a general principle, can be deduced through the mixture of principles and rules. ¶ Furthermore, the "sufferer" <note>Latin: *passus*; the one undergoing the action</note> is its own concrete form which is situated in the passion and habituated by it. Indeed, Passion itself arises in the contraction and mixture of principles: just as Goodness is a passion insofar as it is habituated by Magnitude, and vice versa. And this is clear through the first type of Rule D, and Rule B agrees with this.

### 21 On Habit.

<margin>The twenty-first form, on Habit <note>Latin: *habitus*; refers to a state of being, a disposition, or "having" something (like clothing or a virtue).</note></margin>
Habit is a principle, and it is implicit; but it is applicable to explicit principles. For just as a good man does good by habituating himself with good moral virtue, so the "habituator" habituates himself with a moral habit by reason of Habit; and so it is with Goodness habituated by Magnitude. ¶ The "habituated" is its own concrete form. For just as a white thing is habituated by whiteness, and a cloaked man by a cloak, and fire by heat, and a just man by justice, so is the habituated by habit. ¶ Furthermore, through the first type of Rule D and in the mixture of principles and rules, the intellect recognizes whence Habit arises and in which subjects it is diffused. ## On Position

<margin>The twenty-second form: On Position.</margin>
Position <note>original: "Situs"</note> is an implicit term, but it is applicable to correlatives <note>interrelated terms like "the lover" and "the beloved"</note> through the second species of Rule C and D, and the first of E, and also to the definition of Goodness, etc. Indeed, its own definition is applicable. For since Goodness is the reason for a good thing—why a good thing acts as good in the essence of Goodness—it follows therefore that the correlatives of Goodness are "positioned" <note>assituata</note> and vice versa. And thus Position is an accident causing the state of being positioned within the Principles. ¶ Furthermore, through the first species of Rule D and through the contraction and mixing of the Principles and Rules, the intellect recognizes where Position originates, and where it leads from potentiality into act: such as a great Goodness which is positioned, and vice versa. And the correlatives of Goodness are positioned within the correlatives of Magnitude; Rule B consents to this.

## On Time

<margin>Explanation of the twenty-third form: On Time.</margin>
Time is a principle explained in the Art; but for the sake of explanation, we wish to show in what way it is applicable to all Principles and Rules, just as its definition is applicable to the definition of a Principle. For Time is that principle with which all created things were made new. And its definition is also applicable to the Tenth Rule, because Time is the instrument by which there are days and nights, hours, motions, and the like. ¶ Furthermore, Time is applicable to correlatives through the second species of Rule C, by which it is led from potentiality into act: when an agent acts upon that which can be acted upon <note>the "agible"</note> within time, multiplying days, hours, nights, and so on. Its concrete form <note>the physical manifestation</note> is "that which is timed" <note>temporificatum</note>.

## On Place

<margin>Explanation of the twenty-fourth form: On Place.</margin>
Place is an explained principle derived through the Principles and Rules, and its definition is applicable to the definition of a Principle. For Place is the principle by which all beings are containing and contained. It is applicable to the Tenth Rule, because Place is the instrument by which all movable things are moved from a new place to a new place. ¶ Place itself is also applicable to the correlatives from which it arises: when those substantial correlatives situate "foreign" correlatives within themselves. Just as fire in the "fire-able" <note>ignibit</note> also colors heated water with heat. And a generator, in its internal "generatable" part, generates the thing generated, and so on. Its concrete form is "that which is placed" <note>collocatum</note>.

<column-break/>

## On Motion

<margin>The twenty-fifth form: On Motion.</margin>
Motion is an implicit principle and its definition is applicable to the definition of a Principle, and also to the Tenth Rule, and so on. For Motion is that principle by which all movable things are moved; and its correlatives emerge from substantial correlatives, just as an accident emerges from a substance. ¶ Motion is indeed the instrument with which a substance moves itself locally, augmentatively, and alteratively. Locally, such as the heavens which move themselves circularly with their own appetite <note>desire or natural inclination</note> which is in the genus of motion. Augmentatively, such as a plant by growing and generating. Alteratively, such as wine which changes into vinegar, or water from coldness into heat, or a human from health into sickness, or justice into injury, and the like. Its concrete form is the "moving thing." The essence of Motion is indeed insensible and unimaginable; but in the subject in which it exists, it is sensible and imaginable: just as sight reaches the mover and the moved when a hammer moves a nail. And touch reaches the impulse of motion. I do not say that it reaches motion as to the essence of motion itself, but only the figure; and so on in its own way, just as sight reaches a falling stone, but does not reach the essence of motion, nor of the stone, but only the color and figure.

## On Immobility

<margin>The twenty-sixth form: On Immobility.</margin>
Immobility is an implicit principle; but its definition is applicable to the definition of a Principle. For just as a Principle is the cause why beings are "principled" <note>capable of being traced to a beginning</note>, so Immobility is the principle by which immobile things are immobile or permanent. Immobility itself is applicable to its internal correlatives, from which it can in no way be separated. Just as form from action, and matter from passion <note>being acted upon</note>, and the hot from heat, and the good from goodness, and a human from their species, etc. ¶ The concrete form of Immobility is the "immobile thing"; the correlatives of Immobility are the "unmoving" and the "immobile."

### 27 On Instinct.

<margin>28. The form of instinct. Related to wisdom.</margin>
Instinct is an implied principle: and it is applicable to wisdom, which is an explicit principle: and consequently, it is applicable to the definition of wisdom along with the tenth rule. For just as wisdom is the being by reason of which the wise person understands: so natural instinct is the being by reason of which the subject in which nature exists acts naturally according to its entire species: as in a plant. For its instinct applies itself to generating flowers, leaves, fruits, and flavors, and such things. And so it is with brute animals, which have instinct and industry for living through the second type of Rule C. ¶ The correlatives <note>terms that exist in relation to one another, like "lover" and "beloved"</note> of instinct are applicable to the correlatives of the explicit principles: and so with the other types in their own way. Its concrete form is the "instincted thing": as designated by the second type of Rule C and the first of Rule E: and its end <note>purpose or goal</note> consists in the second type of Rule E.
<margin>Common</margin>

### 28 On the Appetite of Nature.

<margin>28. The form of the appetite of nature. Related to the will.</margin>
The appetite of nature is an implied principle: and its definition is applicable to the definitions of the will. For just as the will hungers for an object: and establishes it as a thing desired and has concupiscence <note>strong desire</note> for it: so appetite relates to an object, so that it may rest in it: just as the elements have an appetite for the "elementated" <note>the compound body made of elements</note>: and the plant for vegetating: and for generating flowers, leaves, and fruits: and for multiplying its species into individuals. And the explicit principles concur in this: just as the goodness of an animal which is in a subject has an appetite: so that it may have its own act, "bonifying" <note>the act of making or being good</note>: and this is designated through the second type of Rule C. Appetite has its correlatives applicable to the correlatives of the will. It is the appetite having its own concrete form: as designated through the second type of Rule D and the first of Rule E: with which it moves itself toward the second type of Rule C so that it may rest, just as a human moves himself with his will toward loves or toward the beloved and such things.

<column-break/>

### 29 On Attraction.

<margin>29. The form of attraction. Related to the end.</margin>
Attraction is an implied principle: and it is applicable to the definition of the "end" <note>the final purpose</note> and of goodness. For the end attracts to itself that which is at rest, just as the "bonifying" attracts the "bonified," and the will the beloved, and the breath the thing breathed, and sight the colored thing, and taste the flavorful thing, and such. ¶ The correlatives of attraction are applicable to the correlatives of the explicit principles through the second type of Rule C. For the "attractor" attracts the "attracted" in the passion <note>the state of being acted upon</note> of its essence: just as fire attracts air in its heating, so that the air itself is heated: and the breath attracts air, so that the air itself is breathed. And the power attracts the object, so that it becomes "objectified": and so with others in their own way. Its concrete form is the "attracted thing": for it attracts species and natural operations to itself: so that it may be an agent: and so that through it the explicit principles can have their acts: and may rest in the second type of Rule E: and such things: just as the magnet, which by its whole species attracts iron: so that the dryness and coldness existing in the iron may artificially rest in the dryness and coldness of the magnet, which is a natural subject: and in this step the intellect recognizes the manner by which those things that exist artificially are attracted by those things that exist naturally.
<margin>Common E</margin>

But I say that the "recipient" receives the foreign "receivable" in the passion of its essence, just as sight receives color in its visible object, and the intellect receives foreign species in its intelligible object, and such things. ¶ And in this step the intellect recognizes that the object does not move the power, but the power moves itself with the object. ### 31 On the Phantasm.

<margin>The thirty-first form: on the phantasm.</margin>
The phantasm <note>original: "fantasma"; refers to a mental image or sensory representation stored in the mind.</note> or species is applicable to the definition of species and of the will along with the fourth instrumental species: because they do not act except with phantasms. Indeed, the phantasm is applicable to the first type of rule D and to the definition of a principle, and in this way: A man seeing a horse does not [merely] imagine it; but when he closes his eyes, or the horse is absent, then he imagines it. The phantasm is thus led from the power of the subject into act: and it is received in the imagination, in which the intellect collects it; and it places it in its "intelligible" <note>The realm of pure thought or understanding.</note> so that knowledge may be had; and it also places it in the memory in which it is preserved; and thereafter another phantasm is acquired, and likewise for the will through the concupiscible and irascible powers <note>The "concupiscible" power desires good; the "irascible" power resists obstacles to that good.</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes by what mode knowledge or "mode" is generated; and to this end all the explained principles and rules concur. For it is very difficult to generate a phantasm by reason of the smallness of the being in which it exists. ¶ The concrete form of the phantasm is the "phantasized thing," constituted of several likenesses. In brute animals, however, it does not pass beyond the imagination. For if it did pass beyond, brutes would then possess science. But it is permanent in the imagination, so that they may have industry for living; and this is manifest through rule B.

### 32 On Fullness.

<margin>The thirty-second form: on fullness.</margin>
Fullness is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, greatness, etc. For the fullness of goodness is the reason why good is not diminished. And the fullness of greatness is the reason why goodness is full of it, and vice versa. And thus it is marked concerning others in the mixture of principles and rules. ¶ Furthermore, the correlatives of fullness are applicable to the correlatives of goodness, which are full of the correlatives of fullness. Its concrete form is "the full": and this is manifest through the second type of D and through the first, etc. And especially when it finds rest through the second type of rule E. ¶ Emptiness, however, is its opposite. And its definition is applicable to its contrary terms. And let these things suffice regarding what was previously said about evacuation.

### 33 On Diffusion.

<margin>emptiness</margin>
<margin>The thirty-third form: on diffusion</margin>
Diffusion is an implicit principle: and its definition is applicable to the definition of goodness, difference, etc. For goodness is the reason producing good: and it is diffusive; and it dilates itself in the subject in which it is, contracting itself to greatness and duration, etc., with difference distinguishing the diffusion with its correlatives marked by the second type. ¶ The concrete form of diffusion is "the diffused": and it is habituated by diffusion, and situated within it, etc., as is manifest through the second type of D and the first of E. The opposite of diffusion is restriction, which is applicable to the definition of concordance; with this, indeed, the greedy man causes greed.

### 34 On Digestion.

<margin>The thirty-fourth form: on digestion.</margin>
Digestion is an implicit principle. And its definition is applicable to the definition of virtue and majority <note>original: "maioritas"; refers to the state of being greater or superior.</note>. For innate virtue digests foreign virtues into its own species with its majority: just as in a plant in which the elements are digested into its own species; so it is in an animal through drink and food. ¶ The correlatives of this digestion are applicable to the correlatives of virtue and majority. Its concrete form is "the digested," habituated by digestion.

# Tenth Part

### 36 On Signification.

<margin>The thirty-sixth form: On Signification.</margin>
<margin>Concealment</margin>
Signification is an implicit principle: its definition is applicable to all explicit principles and rules. For since goodness is the reason why a good thing is produced, goodness joined to greatness signifies that a great good person produces a great good. And so it is with the others. ¶ The correlatives <note>Lullian technical term for the active, passive, and verbal relationship within a principle (e.g., the signifier, the signified, and the act of signifying).</note> of signification are applicable to the correlatives of goodness, greatness, etc. With these correlatives of signification, goodness signifies that which it is and those things which it contains within itself; its concrete form is the "signified," which is characterized by the sign itself. Concealment, however, is the opposite of signification, and its definition is applicable to the terms opposite to signification itself.

### 37 On Beauty.

<margin>The thirty-seventh form: On Beauty.</margin>
<margin>C <note>Refers to a specific compartment or rule in the Lullian combinatorial wheel.</note></margin>
Beauty is an implicit principle, and its definition is applicable to the definitions of the explicit principles. For goodness and greatness, etc., are beauties—excepting contrariety and smallness. Nevertheless, a smallness that is proportioned within the subject in which it exists is beautiful, as is evident in a small child. The correlatives of beauty consist of the second species of Rule C, such as a beautiful cause which naturally causes a beautiful effect. And just as the intellect in the imagination causes a beautiful figure with love by reason of the end <note>The "final cause" or purpose.</note> designated by the second species of Rule C; and also through Rule G, through which a beautiful and most proper quality consists through appropriation. And likewise, beauty consists more through greatness than through smallness, as is evident in rhetoric, in which the rhetorician colors his words more with a greater end than with a lesser one.

### 38 On Novelty.

<margin>The thirty-eighth form: On Novelty. D</margin>
Novelty is the first form whose subject is characterized by new habits, just as the heaven is characterized by place, time, and motion; and the same can be said of all individual things composed of the elements. And this is signified through the first species of Rule D: that first novelty had to be such as were the first motion, time, and place. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that outside

<column-break/>

of time, place, and motion, no novelty can exist, because it is necessary that they exist simultaneously and at once. And to this, Rules B, H, and I agree.

### 39 On the Idea.

<margin>The thirty-ninth form: On the Idea.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
In eternity, the Idea is God; but in novelty <note>i.e., in the created world of time.</note> it is the creature, like the figure of an ark which was new in the meditation of the carpenter, but once brought from potentiality into act, it became old. And this is manifested clearly enough in the divine correlatives signified by the second species of Rule C. ¶ For the Divine Knower, in His own infinite and eternal Intelligible, attracts all novelties stripped of their created subject; these novelties are the Divine Ideas. But through the third species of the same rule, they are new, finite, and terminated creatures.

### 40 On Mathematics.

<margin>40th form: On Mathematics.</margin>
Mathematics is the form with which the human intellect strips a substance of the accidents <note>Non-essential qualities like color or size.</note> that underlie them, so that it can create genus and species with which it may acquire and produce science. This mathematical form is modeled and stripped by means of the Idea stripped of all creatures, so that the Idea may be known with the mathematical form. And this is evident through the first species of Rule D, the second species of Rule E, and the fourth species of Rule K. Such a form is the genus in all forms which are brought from potentiality into act, as is evident in the ninth subject.

### 41 On Being existing in Potentiality.

<margin>41st form: On Being existing in potentiality.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Being existing in potentiality is a form existing in a subject which is [removed] from all motion, surface, quantity, quality, and the like, as is seen in a piece of wood in which a tree exists in potentiality. And when that form is brought from potentiality into act, its accidents accompany it in such a leading-out or generation. And when the aforesaid form has arisen with the aforementioned accidents, they have already arisen from the accidents existing in act in the subject in which the previously mentioned form was in potentiality. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes how one substance arises from another substance, and accidents from other accidents naturally. And to this, Rule D agrees, along with the definition of goodness and power.

### 42 On Pointness. 118
<margin>42. The form of pointness.</margin>
<margin>.6.</margin>
Pointness <note>original: "Puncteitas"; the essence or state of being a point</note> is the essence of a natural point, which is the smallest part of a body. Indeed, a point exists only through its smallness and is indivisible to such an extent that it cannot be reached by the senses or the imagination. ¶ And at this step, the intellect marvels at how it can have knowledge of a natural point, since it is imperceptible and unimaginable; but it assists itself with a "moral" point <note>a conceptual or visible representation used for teaching</note> presented through sight and imagination. And through this, it also ascends to the knowledge of the natural point, about which it creates science. And to this, rule B and the first type of rule D agree. And the same can be said of rules F and I.

### 43 On the Line. 119
<margin>43. The form of the line.</margin>
<margin>F.</margin>
<margin>.k.</margin>
A natural line is a length composed of several continuous points, the extremities of which are two points; it is the second part of a body. And you should know: it is composed of several points, as is indicated in rule K and rule F. A point signifies discrete quantity, while length signifies continuous quantity. ¶ And in this, it is clear that a point signifies discrete quantity. For a line is divisible by points; width arises and is caused by several continuous lines; and consequently, a surface arises from length and width existing together in the subject in which they are. Depth, however, arises from the roundness of the points. For a point is more round in nature than it is long or wide, as is evident in the leafy branches of a tree. ¶ Furthermore, the reason for this is that a circle—by reason of the heavens which it resembles—is of a stronger figure in the motion of nature than any other figure. ¶ And at this step, the intellect recognizes what the primary principles of a body are: namely, the point, the line, length, width, surface, and depth.

### 44 On the Triangle. 118
<margin>44. The form of the triangle.</margin>
A triangle is a form having three angles contained by three lines, as is evident in the elements, in which every element has its own triangle. For example, fire has one acute angle through the hot and dry; another through the hot and moist; and another through the dry and cold. Such a triangle is attributed

<column-break/>

to fire; for it reigns over other triangles through the hot and the dry. Similarly, air has another triangle through the moist and the hot. ¶ Furthermore, water through the cold and the moist; and again, earth has another through the dry and the cold. ¶ And at this step, the intellect recognizes the essences of which an elemental body is full, by reason of which the elements relate to one another in a composite through difference, concordance, and contrariety. ¶ But the intellect marvels at how it can have science of such triangles, since they have never been in the senses. But it remembers the triangle of a plane figure, which is perceptible, with which it imagines and knows the natural triangle, by means of rule K and the second type of rules D and C.
<margin>.k.</margin>

### 45 On the Quadrangle. 118
<margin>45. The form of the quadrangle.</margin>
<margin>g. i.</margin>
A natural quadrangle is a figure having four right angles; and in every angle of a triangle, two right angles are implied, because they are of the genus of the triangle. For every element has two qualities: namely, one proper and another appropriated, as is clear in rule G. In the quadrangle, fire has one angle like a king, and similarly for the others, etc. And it is clear because a quadrangle is divisible into four equal triangles with diagonal lines. ¶ And at this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the quadrangle is multiplied through four triangles, and the triangle through three lines, and the line through continuous points.

### 46 On the Circle. 118
<margin>46. The form of the circle.</margin>
<margin>D. k.</margin>
The circle is the ultimate and strongest figure, and it is more perfect than any other figure. For it contains within itself all other figures; it descends from them and is constituted by them, as is clear through the second type of rule D and the fourth type of K. For the circle is caused by the triangle, the quadrangle, and the circular line point-by-point, in the likeness of the heavens, which is the greatest figure; and rule B agrees with this.

### 47 On the Body. 118
<margin>47. The form of the body.</margin>
A body is a substance full of points, lines, and angles, situated by length, width, and depth, and shaped by a surface. The body itself has co-essential parts: namely, points and lines, etc.

### 48 On Figure.

<margin>
48. The form of figure.
</margin>

Figure <note>In this context, "figure" refers to the geometric shape or outward form of an object.</note> is an accident constituted from position and shape: which, according to the second species of Rule C, are its parts; according to the third species of the same, it is the shape within a body; and according to the fourth, it possesses straight and curved lines. Indeed, figure combined with color is the object of sight; however, with lines and angles but without color, it is the object of touch; and with all the aforementioned, it is the object of the imagination. In this step, the intellect recognizes that the imagination is a more general power than sight; for figure is not an object of the intellect without the imagination. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that when a person dies, the soul retains the "species" <note>Mental images or impressions.</note> which it acquired through the imagination, so that it may have a memory of this life and the body in which it dwelt.

### 49 On General Rectitudes.

<margin>
49. The form of general rectitudes.
</margin>

General rectitudes <note>Refers to the six principal directions or dimensions of physical orientation.</note> are the six by which a body is centered through diametrical lines, so that through them a body can be in motion: namely, toward the up, down, front, back, right, and left. These six rectitudes are co-essential to motion. ¶ But the intellect wonders why there are six and not more or fewer; but it remembers that motion cannot be perfect without them; if there were more or fewer, it would indeed be imperfect, as is evident through the third and fourth species of Rule C. And by the second species of the same, it is indicated that the six aforementioned rectitudes are co-essentially parts of the motion in which a body is accustomed and shaped. But the intellect wonders why a spherical body does not have such rectitudes as mentioned above—such as a human head, an eye, an apple, and the like. But it remembers the world <note>The universe or cosmos.</note>, which is a spherical body; this world does not subsist by those rectitudes because it is the ultimate body which causes its likenesses in the aforementioned spherical bodies, so that the intellect can have knowledge of it; and to this, Rules B and K agree.

### 50 On Monstrosity.

<margin>
50. The form of monstrosity.
</margin>

Monstrosity <note>In medieval science, a "monster" was any biological deviation from the natural norm.</note> is a deviation of the motion of nature from the starting point to the end point within a subject, caused by an excessive influence or a deficiency in the power of the bodies above, below, to the right, to the left, and also those existing in front and behind. Such motions cause privative states: namely blindness, deafness, and the like. The reason for this is that it falls outside the second species of Rule C. And in the third species, the motion itself is imperfect, and in the fourth species, it possesses those imperfections because the second species of Rule C is lacking.

### 51 On Derivation.

<margin>
51. The form of derivation.
</margin>

Derivation is the general subject through which a particular descends from a universal, just as a stream from a spring; a line from points; a triangle from lines; a son from parents through general instruments; a conclusion from its premises; and consequently, a result from its antecedent, and knowledge from things—mediated, however, by the intellect. ¶ And the intellect, thus considering derivation, recognizes by the second species of Rule C that derivation contains within itself essential correlatives by which many particulars are derived: just as many sons from those parents, and many elemental things from the four general elements; and many sciences are discovered by one intellect. Indeed, the intellect itself contains within it essential and general relatives with which it inquires and creates many sciences derived by the intellect from the same form or species. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the relatives of the intellect itself are superior, and the sciences are inferior, and the species are in the middle, just as between cause and effect; and in this step, it recognizes from what and how the sciences are derived.

And the intellect considers that the air is transparent <term>diaphanous: a medium that allows light to pass through</term>: because outside of the shadow it receives the color of the sun and fire—namely, brightness—and in the place where the shadow exists, it receives the color of the earth. This is just as a crystal <note>original: "cristallus"</note> in a yellow setting takes on a yellow quality, and when placed in a black setting, takes on a black quality. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that light is the color of the sun and fire; blackness is the color of the earth and the transparency of the air; and whiteness is the quality of water which causes whiteness. Indeed, crystal is nothing other than frozen water. ¶ Furthermore, the shape of a shadow is the boundary where light and shadow terminate; the definition of the "middle" and the second and fourth types of Rule C agree with this. ¶ But the intellect asks: what is the cause of the moon's shadow? And it remains in doubt until it considers that the moon is a transparent body in which the shadow of the earth appears. But it wonders why a shadow does not appear in the sun, which is also a transparent body. It remains in doubt until it remembers that the sun is colored by its own proper light. The light of the moon comes from the sun just as the heat of the air comes from the heat of fire; and this is proven by Rules G and B.

### 53 On the Mirror.

<margin>54th form: on the mirror.</margin>
A mirror is a transparent body disposed to receive all shapes presented to it. But the intellect wonders: since glass is a transparent body, why does it not receive shapes like a mirror, which is also glass? But it remembers the chapter on shadows, which clears up the doubt. For glass or lead <note>The author likely refers to the metallic backing of a mirror</note> is a transparent body receiving transparency on both sides, passing through the six straight lines of which we have already spoken. But in a mirror, it is not so: for the lead resists certain straight lines by reason of the thickness of its matter and its great density; indeed, the parts of lead are very tightly packed together. And therefore, just as a tree causes a shadow because it stands in the midst of light, so the glass—existing between the lead, the air, and the shape or color presented to it—generates within itself a shadow similar to the shape presented to it through similar qualities and colors. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the principles of the mirror's shadow, as is evident through Rules B and G.

### 54 On Color and the Colored Object.

<column-break/>

<margin>54th form: on color and the colored.</margin>
Color is a quality existing as the object of sight. In a colored thing, it is a quality <note>original: "habitus"</note>; and the shape of the colored thing is the quality of the color. ¶ The "colored" is the substance in which the color is sustained. ¶ Color indeed has substantial correlatives <note>Lullian terminology referring to the internal structure of a thing: the actor, the object, and the action</note>; but color is the quality of the substantial correlatives. And through the first species of Rule D, it is of itself; and through the third species of the same rule, it belongs to the colored thing. ¶ Color, through the first species of Rule G, is a "proper" quality <note>essential to the thing</note>; in a true man or a true plant it is appropriate; but it is also in a painted man or a painted plant, etc. ¶ However, the "totality" of color is not proper to it, but rather is appropriated to it; nevertheless, it belongs to the colored thing. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which one accident is situated in another by reason of Rule G. Just as has been said of color and the colored, so it can be said of heat and the heated.

### 55 On Proportion and the Proportioned.

<margin>55th form: on proportion and the proportioned.</margin>
Substantial proportion consists of co-substantial relatives: as is evident through infinity, to which its co-substantial correlatives are proportioned, without which infinity could not exist in being and acting. Indeed, the finite is not proportioned to the infinite by means of the infinite which is proportioned to it; and this same thing can be said of the "eternizer," the "eternized," and the "act of eternizing" <note>Lullian active/passive/verbal triads for Divine attributes</note>; and so with other divine reasons. Similarly, it can be said of substantial correlatives in created substances: as in the intellect, in which the "understander," the "understandable," and the "act of understanding" are correlatives naturally proportioned to it. However, knowledge cannot be [perfectly] proportioned to it; for it cannot suffice for it, just as wood cannot suffice for fire. For the fire can burn more wood than the wood can overwhelm the fire. Nevertheless, accidental proportion can well exist among correlatives, such as between the "heated" and the "act of heating." ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that no accident can be proportioned to a substance in terms of weight <note>metaphorical "weight" or importance</note>. For substance possesses more, while the accident possesses less. And this is clear through the definition of "majority" and "minority." However, according to efficiency, proportion can be given between substance and accident, and between one accident and another. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the members of the soul...

### 56 On Disposition and the Disposed.

<margin>56. The form of disposition and the disposed.</margin>
<margin>C <note>Refers to "Rule C" in the author's logical system.</note></margin>
Substantial disposition is a form in which substantial correlatives <note>Lullian term for the active, passive, and verbal components of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving.</note> are equally disposed through object, power, and act. This is like the divine goodness, infinite and eternal, which is the disposed reason of the infinite and eternal good, so that it may produce an infinite and eternal good, which is disposed to the "bonifier" <note>original: "bonificanti" - the active principle of goodness.</note>. And thus, regarding the act of "bonifying," it can be said that it is disposed to it through infinite and eternal goodness. However, there is another disposition by accident, which is evident through the third species of Rule C: like God, who disposes Himself to judge and proceed according to how a human disposes themselves to receive judgment or mercy. I do not say this in terms of weight <note>i.e., physical quantity</note>, but in terms of justice. For God disposes Himself more toward the human by reason of His goodness than the human does toward Him; just as fire is more disposed to burning wood than the wood is to being sufficient for its combustion. The same can be said of the human intellect. Indeed, the intellect is more disposed to understanding an accidental object than the object itself is to being understood by it. For example, the intelligibility of a stone is not proportioned to the intellect; the intellect can understand something higher, such as a sensing sensibility, or the heavens, or an angel, etc., which are higher intelligibilities than those of a stone. And so it can be said of man: for a man can run more than he actually runs. For he does not always will to run as much as he is able; and so it can be said of other things in their own way.

### 57 On Creation and the Created.

<margin>57. The form of creation and the created.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>c</margin>
Creation is an Idea <note>original: "ydea" - the divine archetype or blueprint in the mind of God.</note> in eternity according to the second species of Rule C; wherefore from eternity and in eternity it is known through divine wisdom and loved through divine will. But in the created being, it is a habit <note>term: habitus - a stable quality or disposition of a being.</note> and an action with respect to the third species of Rule C and through the fourth species of the same rule. Creation, which is an Idea, possesses the creation which is the creature, with which it has the "newly created" thing—the recipient of action <note>original: "passionatum"</note> under that very action, and endowed with a habit under the new creation. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which the Idea passes into the "Ideated" <note>original: "ydeatum" - the physical manifestation of the divine Idea</note>, multiplying its likeness with respect to the fourth species of Rule K.

### 58 On Predestination and the Predestined.

<margin>58. The form of predestination and the predestined.</margin>
Predestination is an Idea in the wisdom of God in eternity; thus it is from eternity as it is in eternity. This is by reason of the correlatives according to the species of Rule C. For one who understands the eternal in his own eternal intelligible understands all things past and new. Future and new things are "from the part before," that is, from eternity; but past and ancient things are "from the part after," that is, in eternity. Therefore, the predestined person, existing by accident in the middle of these two aforementioned terms, is endowed with a habit of "new predestination," just as a man wearing a cloak <note>original: "cappatus"</note> is endowed with a new cloak. Therefore, one predestination exists through the second species of Rule C, while another exists through the third species of the same. For with respect to that second species, it is an Idea; but with respect to the third, it is a created habit. To this habit, the predestined person freely disposes themselves to do good, like the man who is clothed in a new cloak, or like a judge who disposes himself to judge through the habit of justice. Otherwise, the predestination which is an Idea would not have a way of creating a new predestination as an object from eternity and in eternity—which is false, as is clear through the fourth Rule K. ¶ And in this step, the intellect rejoices because it has a great clarification concerning predestination; but it grieves that such a clarification is little known in the world. For the clouding of predestination leads many people into error and doubt.

### 59 On Mercy and the Mercied.

<margin>59. The form of mercy and the "mercied" <note>original: "misericordiato" - the recipient of mercy.</note>.</margin>
Mercy is an Idea in eternity according to the respect of Rule C; and with respect to the third species, it is a habit existing in the newly predestined person who disposes themselves toward contrition, confession, and satisfaction for things committed, so that they may be endowed with the habit of mercy. This is just as the predestined is endowed with predestination through good works loved with their own free will. Otherwise, unless the sinner disposes himself to receive pardon, he could not be endowed with the habit of mercy; just as an evil man doing evil cannot have the habit of goodness. ¶ And in this step, let the sinners rejoice who act...

### On Necessity and the Necessitated.

<margin>60th form: on necessity and the necessitated.</margin>
Necessity is the form by which a thing cannot be otherwise: and this is evident through the second type of rule C <note>In Llull’s system, "Rule C" typically asks "What is it?" and its second species concerns the essence of a thing.</note>. And because it cannot exist without necessity, it follows that necessity is the antecedent and the necessitated is the consequent. For example, the infinite and eternal divine goodness is the infinite reason for the good and eternal to produce an eternal and infinite good; and therefore, that which is produced is necessitated by reason of goodness. Consequently, both the produced and the act of producing are necessitated. This is clear in the second type of rule C. ¶ Furthermore, another necessity and necessitated follow: namely, if a man is good, he is necessitated toward the good. But if he is evil, toward evil. For the justice of God necessitates judgment by judging, just as the mercy of God necessitates pardon by forgiving. In this step, the intellect recognizes that when a sinner disposes himself to receive judgment by judging himself, he disposes himself to penance in order to receive pardon. ¶ Further, the intellect recognizes the manner in which the mercy and justice of God necessitate their own acts in a new subject; the intellect is greatly rejoiced by the knowledge of this.

### On Fortune and the Fortunate.

<margin>61st form: on fortune and the fortunate.</margin>
Fortune is an act outside the second type of C in M <note>Likely referring to the "Middle" or "Medium" in the Art's combinatorial logic.</note>. It is a habit <term>habit: a stable disposition or quality of the soul</term> with which the fortunate person disposes himself toward that good fortune which happens. For example, a traveler going on a pilgrimage who finds gold by chance. Fortune itself exists through the second type of rule D, and it has being in the subject in which it exists through the fourth type of rule C, and it is that which exists through the third type of D. It is outside of beginning, middle, and end, and outside of concordance and contrariety; however, it is not outside of majority and minority. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that fortune has little "being" in regard to itself, but in regard to the fortunate person, it has great being.

### On Ordination and the Ordained.

<margin>62nd form: on ordination and the ordained.</margin>
Ordination <note>The act of ordering or arranging</note> is the aggregation of many principles, so that one principle may serve another toward a single end. The "ordained" is its concrete expression, and is habituated by its own ordination. ¶ Ordination is first begun through the second type of rule C, so that it may be a habit in the subject in which it exists; and it has its rest through the fourth type of C. Indeed, ordination has its own primitive principles, as is clear through the first type of rule D and through the definition of "principle"; and it is a consequence through the definition of "concordance," whose enemy is "contrariety," failing in the manner designated by rule K.

<column-break/>

### On Counsel and the Consulted.

<margin>63rd form: on counsel and the consulted.</margin>
Counsel is a doubtful proposition; the "consulted" is its end and rest. ¶ A counselor ought to look upon that doubtful proposition by running through the second type of C and rule B, testing the manner in which the consulted is shaped with the definitions of the principles. Through the "new subject" in the third type of C, he should be habituated in the virtues in the fourth type of C, and this habit should be removed from vices not in the subject, by means of rules D, E, F, G, H, I, and K.

### On Grace and the Graced.

<margin>64th form: on grace and the graced.</margin>
Grace is a primitive form placed in the graced person without the merits of the one receiving it: as is clear through the first type of D, and through the "majority" of the giver of grace and the "minority" of the receiver of it, and also through the habit of charity. ¶ Furthermore, grace is in the graced person through the definition of goodness and through the magnificence of the will habituated in liberality. Because of this, in this step the intellect recognizes the manner in which grace is diffusive in the subject in which it exists; and when it is produced, it is not hindered by superior principles but by inferior ones: namely, when a person considers himself worthy of receiving grace by reason of his own merit, rather than by reason of the largesse and kindness of the giver of grace.

### On Perfection and the Perfect.

<margin>65th form: on perfection and the perfect.</margin>
Perfection is a form at rest in a perfect subject, with which the perfect subject quiets itself, becoming habituated by that which is habituated in the perfect subject: as is clear through the third type of C. And such perfection is derived from the second type of C through many streams: namely, through many principles and rules of this Art. And such perfection is especially moral, as... <note>The text cuts off here.</note>
