Tenth part.

[The text begins mid-sentence] ...appears in the ninth subject. Nevertheless, it is a natural perfection and a most perfect essence, both essentially and naturally, infinitely and eternally. Indeed, it is most perfect through its own co-substantial <note>original: "consubstantialis"; meaning sharing the same substance</note> relatives designated by the second species of [the rule] C. For the "perfecting" agent, out of its own co-substantial and natural perfection, produces the "perfected" result, and not from any other being; this perfected result is indeed co-essential with it, and both together—namely the perfecting agent and the perfected result—complete the act, which is "to perfect," which is essential and substantial.

## On declaration and the declared.

<margin>Sixty-seventh form: on declaration and the declared.</margin>
<margin>C.</margin>
Declaration is the form in which the intellect, by making distinctions, comes to rest immediately, with the definition of "concordance" being entirely separated from the definition of "contrariety." ¶ The "declared" is its own subject in which declaration exists as a habit <note>term: habit (habitus); a stable disposition or state of being</note>, as is evident through the third species of C. Its essence, however, consists in the second species of C, in which the "understander" declares the "understood" to be passive from itself, and this occurs through the act of "understanding." And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner in which a habit arises from a substance by accident: so that a declaration can be made from knowledge, though only by means of the principles and rules of this Art.

## On transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.

<margin>Sixty-seventh <note>The text repeats "67th" in error; it should be 68th.</note> form: on transubstantiation and the transubstantiated.</margin>
<margin>62</margin>
Transubstantiation is an act of nature in the "transubstantiated" thing when it is stripped of an old form. It puts on a new form so that its act can exist in successive motion within things that are generated and corrupted <note>i.e., the physical world of birth and decay</note>. For without such transubstantiation, nature would indeed be bound regarding its substantial act, and also regarding the act of its accidents; its habit would be unchangeable in a state of privation, and consequently the definitions of its principles would be destroyed, which is impossible. The artist can have knowledge of this in a broad sense in the seventh subject, in which the vegetative power is led through the principles and rules of this Art.

## On alteration and the altered.

<margin>Sixty-eighth <note>The text numbers this 68th, though the previous was also 67th.</note> form: on alteration and the altered.</margin>
<margin>C.</margin>
Alteration is a form born in the "altered" thing, as is evident through the third species of C. And this kind of alteration arises from the alteration existing in the second species of C, just as a stream flows from a spring. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the paths of natural and moral motion. In generation, it recognizes the natural path of that motion: namely, in the generation of the form and matter of the thing altering. For the "alterer," in its own "alterable" subject, alters the things that come to it, so that motion exists in the process of becoming and in the completed state, mediated by the definition of the "middle." Moral alteration, however, is when a person changes themselves from one habit to another, such as from justice to injury, from anger to patience, from logic to medicine, from sadness to joy, and the like.

<column-break/>

## On infinity and the infinitated.

<margin>Sixty-ninth form: on infinity and the infinitated.</margin>
<margin>C.</margin>
<margin>leads to another</margin>
Infinity is a form having an infinite act, far removed from everything finite; this form can in no way exist without the "infinitated" <note>term: infinitated (infinitatum); that which is made infinite or acted upon by infinity</note>. The reason for this is that its rest cannot exist in a finite subject. Infinity itself has its own correlatives through the second species of C, which it cannot have without infinite goodness, greatness, eternity, etc. For otherwise it would involve a contradiction: namely, that it would be both infinite and not infinite, and that it would be hindered and not hindered, which is impossible. Infinity itself is the cause of finiteness or the finite, as is evident through the third species of C, with infinity having action in the infinite and in the finite being. ¶ Through the fourth species of C, the finite is thus habituated with "passion" <note>meaning the capacity to be acted upon</note> just as it is habituated with "newness." For otherwise it would have one infinite habit and another finite one, which is impossible. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that just as the finite has co-essential correlatives—the "finisher," the "finished," and "to finish"—so, and much more perfectly, does infinity have them: namely, the "infiniter," the "infinited," and "to infinite." Otherwise, the nature of finiteness would have a greater range, and the nature of infinity a lesser range, which is impossible.

## On deception and the deceived.

<margin>Seventieth form: on deception and the deceived.</margin>
Deception is a positive habit of the "deceiver" and a privative habit of the "deceived." And therefore, through the second species of rule C, you shall understand the cause in its intelligible object through reception... <note>text here is slightly compressed</note> and through the third species of rule C. And the deceiver is in the deceived, in whom he causes the deception; the deceived, however, does not deceive through his second species of rule C, but in the third he is deceived, and in the fourth he possesses the habit of deception, by which he deviates from the end <note>goal or purpose</note> for which he exists. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes where sin arises and where it remains.

### 71 On honor and the honored.

<margin>71. The form of honor and the honored.</margin>
Honor is an active habit <note>In this context, a "habit" refers to a stable quality or disposition of the mind or soul.</note> in the one who honors, but a passive one in the person being honored. Therefore, the one who honors possesses more than the one honored: this is because, according to the second type of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull’s Art usually asks "Of what?" and deals with origin and composition.</note>, he causes the habit of honor; in the third type, he is the act of honoring; and in the fourth, he possesses the habit of honor. Meanwhile, the honored person merely receives it; in the third type he receives it, and in the fourth he possesses the habit of honor. ¶ And in this step, the intellect understands how this habit is situated within many living beings. ¶ Furthermore, it understands how the one who insults is more characterized by the habit of insulting than the one who is insulted. The intellect rejoices greatly in such knowledge discovered through this Art.

### 72 On capacity and incapacity.

<margin>72. The form of capacity and incapacity. C.</margin>
Capacity is the form by which a capable thing can contain and observe as much as can come to it. Incapacity is the opposite. ¶ Capacity consists of the second type of Rule C, through which it is a positive habit existing in the third and fourth types of that same rule. This is achieved through the definitions of the Principles <note>The "Principles" are Llull's fundamental divine attributes like Goodness, Greatness, and Power.</note> and the types of Rules. ¶ Incapacity, however, is not caused in the second type; for it is a privative habit <note>A "privative" habit is defined by the absence of a quality, like darkness is the absence of light.</note> and is removed from every benefit of the Principles and Rules. Nevertheless, incapacity is closely related to the definitions of contrariety and minority. ¶ And in this step, the intellect understands the cause of intellectual dullness, as well as cruelty and the impiety of the will.

### 73 On existence and agency.

<margin>73. The form of existence and agency. C. E.</margin>
Existence is the form by which an existing thing exists as what it is; agency is the form moving that existing thing toward its intended end. This is evident through the second type of Rule C, through Rule E <note>Rule E asks "Why?" and deals with purpose and necessity.</note>, and through the definitions of Goodness, Power, and the Medium. If the definitions are added, it follows by necessity that existence is as great as agency. ¶ And in this step, the intellect understands that God is the ultimate Agent through the second type of Rule C, and through the first type of Rule E. He is the Existent of whom knowledge of existence and agency can be found in the "First Subject" in the chapter where God is defined.

<column-break/>

### 74 On comprehension and apprehension.

<margin>74. The form of comprehension and apprehension.</margin>
Comprehension is a likeness of infinity; therefore, the agent of comprehension comprehends, and with apprehension, he apprehends. He comprehends by virtue of the grace of infinity. Here the intellect enters, which is the reason why the agent, through comprehension, makes the thing to be apprehended an object. He remembers a man tasting a drop of wine: I comprehend its quantity in the throat, with which I apprehend the quality of the wine in the cask; just as the intellect, through the senses, apprehends the essence of the thing sensed, but does not comprehend the essence of the thing sensed when it is stripped away from the senses. ¶ And in this step, the intellect understands how it is both comprehending and apprehending. Through the discourse of the types of Rule E and the first type of Rule C, it comprehends by defining; and through the second type, it apprehends. It cannot comprehend itself because it is the thing apprehending, yet through the first type of C, it is comprehending. ¶ Furthermore, in the third type of C, it is comprehending, but in the fourth type of that same rule, it is habituated in both comprehension and apprehension. ¶ And in this step, the intellect is very high and subtle. <margin>C.</margin>

### 75 On invention and the invented.

<margin>75. The form of invention and the invented. C.</margin>
Invention <note>original: "inventio" - in a medieval context, this means "discovery" or "finding" rather than creating something new.</note> is the form by which the intellect finds the thing discovered. As the second type of Rule C indicates, the discoverer, within his own discovery, finds "foreign" discoveries; just as the intellect, within its own intelligible nature, makes incoming species <note>Mental images or sensory data.</note> intelligible. In the third type, it is the cause of discovery in the act of finding; in the fourth type, the thing discovered becomes its habit. ¶ And in this step, the intellect understands how it creates knowledge and what its subject is—namely, this Art—because with the Principles and Rules, it finds what is to be discovered.

### 76 On likeness and the assimilated.

<margin>76. The form of likeness and the assimilated. C.</margin>
Likeness is the form by which the assimilator makes the thing assimilated like itself. Likeness itself arises through the Principles, such as through Goodness, because every thing is good. Another likeness arises through the second type of Rule C, as an assimilator who makes the assimilated like himself—for example, a human father makes his son like himself.

# Tenth Part

### On the Antecedent and the Consequent

<margin>77. The form of the antecedent and the consequent.</margin>
The antecedent is the form causing the consequent. The consequent, however, is the subject in which the antecedent rests: the antecedent indeed consists of the principles and rules of this Art, and the consequent indeed arises from them. For if an agent acts with goodness and greatness, it follows that his act is good and great, and consequently that it is "possified" <note>original: "possificatus"; a Lullian term meaning "made possible" or "brought into the realm of power"</note>. And if goodness is great through greatness, it follows from this that greatness is good through goodness. ¶ Furthermore, if greatness is infinite duration through eternity, it follows that eternity is infinite immensity through greatness; and if power is infinite duration through eternity, it follows that eternity is infinite "possification" through power; and so with the others. ¶ Further, through the second species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Lull's Art usually asks "Of what?" or "From what?"</note>, there is an antecedent to the third species of C, and it is an antecedent to the fourth species of Rule C, just as goodness with its "bonifier," "bonifiable," and "to bonify" is a habit attained in man. And if a man is habituated in goodness, it follows that he has merit through his goodness. And so with other antecedents and consequents: just as if "man" is, it follows that "animal" is; and if two premises are present, it follows that the conclusion is in nature.

### On Power, Object, and Act

<margin>78. The form of power, object, and act.</margin>
Power is the form with which the intellect reaches the object. The object, however, is the subject in which the intellect rests: but the act is the connection of power and object. And all three consist through the second species of C, just as in the correlatives of goodness in which there is indeed a "bonifier" [active] and a "bonifiable" [passive]: "to bonify," however, is the act proceeding from both. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that those who say the object moves the power assert what is false; and those who say the power moves itself to the object along with the object itself in the third species of C assert what is true. Power is active and the object is in the same step: but in the fourth species, power has action, and in the same species, the object has passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon</note>. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the naturally moving thing does not desire to be immobile, nor vice versa. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes who is capable of receiving a great declaration of philosophy.

<column-break/>

### On Generation and Corruption

<margin>79. The form of generation and corruption.</margin>
Generation in created things is the form with which an agent causes new forms. But corruption is the form with which it deprives old forms. And privation is the form existing in the middle of them. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way these three forms consist in the subject in which they are: and the generative and privative are one form and the same power which generates new forms positively and corrupts old forms privatively with one and the same constituted act; [however] "to generate" and "to corrupt," the "generatable" and the "corruptible," are not the same. For they have different ends from one another. For the generatable concerns *being*; the corruptible, however, concerns *non-being*: although they are from one and the same agent and in the same subject: just as fire which is the agent, and from one and the same heat, has different acts: as appears in drying a <unclear>ruler</unclear>, and in dissolving [it], and in softening wax. Generation in the third species of C is active. ¶ Corruption, however, in the same is passive with the same natural motion. The reason for this is: because through the fourth species, the subject has action through generation and passion through corruption, in the subject itself habituated with a privative and positive habit. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the way in which generation, corruption, and privation are natural principles in elemental things. ¶ We have spoken of the 80 forms which are the explicit principles of this Art to which the implicit principles can be applied: such as whatever may be said of generation, corruption, and privation, let it be applied to the chapter on generation, corruption, and privation in such a way that those things which were said in the chapter itself are not harmed: for they are known through themselves. Now, however, we intend to apply this general Art to particular arts so that it may be declared in what way this Art is general to all other arts, and so that those knowing this Art may more easily be able to learn and possess other arts: and first we shall speak of theology.

# On Application

<margin>80th Form: On Theology. 47</margin>
Theology is the science in which one speaks of God. And for that reason, the first subject designated by **B** <note>In Lullian art, 'B' often represents Goodness or the first subject, God</note> is the place in which one speaks of God artificially <note>original: "artificialiter" — meaning according to the rules of this specific Art or system</note>: because it proceeds through principles and rules. Therefore, those wishing to speak of God naturally or artificially should recur to the aforementioned subject and say of God those things which are found within it. If, however, they wish to multiply the words that are in it, let them apply them to the explained words which are in the aforementioned subject, in such a way that the explained words remain unharmed <note>i.e., the fundamental definitions are not contradicted</note>, saying thus: "Whether God can not-be." And let him recur to those things which are said of Him by **B. C.** etc. And if he asks why God cannot not-be, let him recur to the rule in which it is asked, "Why is God?" And if it is asked whether God can be evil, or whether there are many gods, let him recur to the place in which it is said that goodness is the reason that produces infinite and eternal good, and also to that place in which God is defined. ¶ Likewise, if it is asked which law is true—whether the law of the Christians, or the Jews, or the Saracens <note>Muslims</note>—let him recur to the subject in which one speaks of God, and look into that in which the law is implied. And if a preacher wishes to preach about God, let him extract the matter of his sermon from that subject, which is a great and very wide path for the lost, and a very diffuse matter; and so with others. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what way the first subject is a very great object for it, in which it greatly rejoices.

### On Philosophy

<margin>81st Form: On Philosophy.</margin>
Philosophy is the subject in which the intellect contracts itself to all arts and sciences; and therefore the philosopher, through this Art, can have a great subject for understanding. For he can philosophize through the subjects of substance designated by **C. D. E. F. G. H. I.** and also through the *hundred forms* <note>original: "centum formas" — likely referring to Lull's 'Book of the Hundred Forms'</note>; for the philosopher treats naturally of angels, the heavens, man, the imaginative, sensitive, vegetative, and elementary powers. Concerning miracles, however, he does not; for they are above nature. Wherefore, if anyone asks philosophically, let him recur to the aforementioned subjects, applying that which he seeks to them. In such a way, let him respond so that the essence of what he seeks remains unharmed, holding to the affirmative or negative of the question; for those things which are treated in the aforementioned subjects are clear and manifest to an intellect that understands subtly. If, however, that which is sought is implicit or foreign, let it be applied to the aforementioned explained things, and with them let the aforementioned question be answered

<column-break/>

in such a way that the explained and implied words agree reasonably in the proposed conclusion. And in this step, the intellect recognizes that this Art is a wonderful and very general subject for the intellect of the philosopher.

### On Geometry

<margin>82nd Form: On Geometry. Quantities.</margin>
Geometry is the art invented for measuring lines, angles, and figures. And because in this art one treats of quantity, designated by **F**, and through the medium of measurement which is designated by **F** itself, one runs through **B. C. D. E. F. G. I.** and **K.** Therefore, quantity itself is the subject of geometry, just as superior measures cause inferior ones; for goodness is one measure according to its own reason, and magnitude another, etc. And this is signified by the ladders of the second figure and by the species of the rules. And therefore, goodness, in as much as it is, measures the good and the great, so that the good and the great may produce the good and the great. And this is signified in the place where we spoke of the point, line, triangle, and quadrangle, circle and figure. ¶ Furthermore, measures begin through the correlatives of the second species of rule **C**, and are derived into the third in which are the habits of the *measurer*, the *measured*, and *to measure*. In the fourth species, however, the *measured* has the habit insofar as it is figured, just as the colored has color. And we shall signify this through these two following figures:

¶ I suppose that this quadrangle <note>a square or four-sided figure</note> is worth 4 spans: and it is divided into two equal parts by a diagonal line: and one part is divided into two. Let the largest part be called **a**, the second **b**, and the third **c**. Now it is asked: how does the intellect begin to find geometry? To which one must answer through the definition of the "beginning" and through the rule of **f, h, i,** and **k**, and also through the subjects marked by **e, f, g**. For the intellect, through sight, reaches nine angles in that figure. For **a** would have three; **b** three; and **c** three. But the intellect, together with the imagination, reaches twelve angles. For if **a** is worth as much as **b** and **c** combined, it has as many angles through the intellect with the imagination as **b** and **c** have through the senses. But **b** and **c** have six; therefore **a** has six: of which three are "in act" <note>actually visible</note> according to sight; but the other three are "in potency" <note>existing as a logical possibility</note> which the intellect with the imagination reaches beyond the senses. Because they were never in the senses, geometry creates knowledge <term>scientia</term> regarding quantity existing in potency; once that quantity is brought into the senses through likeness and through experience, such knowledge remains in the intellect and in the imagination beyond the senses. The second species of rule **c** is the subject of this knowledge, and the third and fourth are the experiences of said knowledge. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the method by which geometry creates knowledge: namely, that with the quantity which is in potency, it measures the quantity which is in the senses. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that this proposition is false: *nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.* <note>original: "nihil est in intellectu quin prius fuerit in sensu" — a famous Aristotelian maxim which the author here disputes.</note> For the line which is in the intellect was never in the senses; just as the three angles in potency which are in **a** were never in the senses. ¶ Furthermore, since the intellect cannot measure a circular line with a compass, how can it know how many spans a circular line would have if it were stretched out? Then the intellect ascends to the higher measures which are beyond the senses, of which we have already spoken. And after this manner, it descends to the measures which are in the senses: and through the definition of the "middle," and through rule **f**—namely through ebb and flow—and through discrete and continuous quantity, it measures the circular [line] beyond the senses, considering how many spans it can have. And first, it makes this figure in which there are three quadrangles and one circle, as is evident.

### The second figure follows.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large square containing a circle, which in turn contains a smaller square rotated 45 degrees (diamond shape).</image-desc>

¶ I suppose that the smaller quadrangle is equivalent to four equal spans: and the larger quadrangle is worth six spans: and thus I say that whatever stands between four and six is equivalent to five spans. But the circle stands between the larger and smaller quadrangle, as is evident to the senses: because it is contained by the larger, and the circle itself contains the smaller arrangement of lines: therefore it is necessarily evident that if the circle were stretched out, it would be equivalent to five spans existing between six and four: just as in a number where the second unit exists equally between the first unit and the third. And this same thing can be said of three units existing equally in the number nine, which stand equally between the three units placed before and after. ¶ Furthermore, the intellect performs another demonstration: namely, it places one red quadrangle equally between the larger and smaller quadrangle, with which it squares the circle according to the measure of the container and the contained. For if the circle contains the red quadrangle and vice versa, as is revealed at their extremities: the line of the circle is worth as much as the line of the quadrangle. But the red quadrangle is equivalent to five spans, because it stands equally between the smaller and larger quadrangle. And this can be held through experience: if the red quadrangle were stretched out with a compass: therefore the circular line would be equivalent to five, if it were stretched out. ¶ Again, through this demonstration, the red quadrangle and the circle seem to be equivalent: if four are worth 12 houses. And similarly six...

### On Astronomy <insert>83</insert> <insert>121</insert>

<margin>33rd form: On Astronomy</margin>
Astronomy is the part with which astrologers <note>In this period, "astronomer" and "astrologer" were often used interchangeably</note> recognize the powers and motions which the heavens have effectively over lower things. In this art, the heavens are designated by the letter **b**. Therefore, if any doubt arises concerning the heavens, one should return to the third subject and answer the doubt according to what is explained in the subject of the heavens. This should be done in such a way that what is said of the heavens remains unharmed. For example, if it is asked whether there is any other heaven except the heaven of this world: let the answer be negative through the definition of "concordance." For if there were another heaven, both would agree in corporeality and figure without a common subject for both, and they would imply a contradiction, which is impossible. For species cannot exist without a genus, nor can distance and proximity exist between them, as is apparent.

### The Third Figure Follows

<image-desc>A square diagram containing two circles. The upper circle is labeled with the letter 'a' and the lower circle is labeled with the letter 'b'.</image-desc>

¶ Through these two figures, one of which is called **a** and the other **b**, which are distant from each other at their upper and lower parts but not at their middle parts, as is clear by the three lines. For two are long and one is short. It would have to be granted that a vacuum was the subject of the long lines and the short line, and thus distance and proximity would be given in a vacuum as a subject, which is impossible. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that another starry heaven is not capable of existing, so that the aforementioned inconvenience does not follow, nor is the definition of concordance destroyed. Nevertheless, I say that it is possible for a second heaven to exist because the power of God <note>original: "potestas dei"</note> is infinite; and if it did exist, the distances and proximities would indeed exist in potential and in disposition, but outside the heavens they would not exist in actuality, for lack of a subject—namely, a vacuum existing as a place between the heavens. ¶ But here the intellect wonders: since the sun is not inherently hot, what is the reason why it heats the air? But it considers that the sun causes heat through its presence just as it causes darkness through its absence, so that days and nights may exist.

### On Arithmetic <insert>121</insert> <insert>84</insert>

<margin>84th form: On Arithmetic</margin>
Arithmetic is the art invented for counting many units. The principles of arithmetic are the principles of this Art <note>Referring to the author's "Great Art" of logical combinations</note>. For the primitive principles, insofar as they are primitive, are numerical. Just as Goodness is one principle in its genus, and Greatness is another, etc. And because the principles are mixed with one another, they therefore compose a number. This numbered sum has two species: namely, an even number (like two principles) and an odd number (like three or five principles, etc.). And in these two species, every number is counted. ¶ There are other principles of number considered through the "correlatives" of the second species of Rule C: such as in the essence of Goodness, in which one correlative is the "bonifier" <note>the one doing good</note>, another is the "bonified" <note>the object of the good</note>, and the third is the "to bonify" <note>the act of goodness itself</note>. And in these three, the number is perfected regarding the essence of Goodness. ¶ Goodness in number signifies the first unity; the "bonified" signifies the second unity arising from the first; and "to bonify" signifies the third arising from the aforementioned. And because these three unities exist through even and odd numbers, the number is multiplied by even and odd. Just as three times three are nine unities, and through the composition of an even and odd number, the fifth unity is found. For two and three are five unities. And thus...

### On Music.

<margin>84. The form of music.</margin>
<margin>Through Concord</margin>
<margin>ut re mi fa sol la <note>The traditional hexachord syllables used in medieval music theory</note></margin>
Music is an art invented for the purpose of ordering many voices concordant in one song, just as many principles lead to one end: and this definition signifies through the definition of concordance and the principle of definition. ¶ Again, it is received through relation to the correlatives of music: for just as a carpenter conceives the form of a chest in his mind and he leads it from potentiality into act, so indeed the musician conceives an ordered voice in the mind: and leads it into the third species of rule **c**, in which music is a habit <note>A learned disposition or skill</note> with which the musician is a practitioner. ¶ The musician is a practitioner through six degrees, ascending and descending, by saying: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. But here the intellect wonders why there are six degrees, and neither more nor fewer. But it remembers the chapter on "rectitudes" treated above. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which it ought to help itself with the hundred forms treated above by applying doubtful questions to them. But the intellect still wonders about the five voices <note>Referring here to the five vowels</note>, why there are five and neither more nor fewer. But it remembers the four spheres of the elements and the "fifth essence" <note>The quintessence or ether</note> which are signified through the third and seventh subjects. And because they consist in motion, and because motion generates sound, and the musician extracts the voice from sound, the intellect therefore recognizes that the ordered primitive voice is through five simple voices from which are derived the

<column-break/>

consonant or composite letters. And thus it knows why there are five vowels, and neither more nor fewer. ¶ Again, the intellect wonders why this **e** is more capable of being composed with other letters in the alphabet than **a**, and **a** more than **u**, and why **i** and **o** do not cause consonants as **a** and **u** do. But it remembers the triangle composed of "majority" and "minority" which the vowel letters enter. For **e** has more matter than **a**. Indeed, **e** causes **b, c, d, f, g, l, m, n, p, r, s, t,** and **x**. In the alphabet, however, **a** causes **h** and **k**; indeed **a** is greater than **u** because it causes the two aforementioned consonant letters: but **u** causes only **q**. And just as majority and minority are in the vowels, consequently equality is in **o** and **i**, for they cause no consonants. The intellect, thus considering **e** to be greater by reason of matter, recognizes that **e** corresponds with the motion of the Earth; and **a** with the motion of Water. The reason for this is because Earth has more matter than Water. But **u** corresponds with the motion of Air, because it has less matter than Water; **o**, however, corresponds with the motion of the Heaven, because it is shaped in the mouth for the voice in the likeness of a circular figure. But **i** corresponds with Fire by reason of its thinness and sharpness, because it has the least matter.

### On Rhetoric.

<margin>86. The form of rhetoric.</margin>
Rhetoric is an art invented with which the rhetorician colors and adorns his words. And because this art is general, therefore the rhetorician has a general subject for ordering his words: namely, as with **b**, "Goodness is great" and "Goodness is eternal"; and now he adorns them more when they are joined, saying thus: "Goodness is great and eternal." And therefore the rhetorician adorns his words when he colors a beautiful subject with a beautiful predicate. Just as in Figure **A**, all principles are predicated of one and the same subject. ¶ There is another way of adorning or coloring: namely, to adorn a principle with its correlatives. Just as adorning "goodness" with "the beautifier," "the beautified," and "to beautify" <note>The author uses Lullian "correlatives": the agent, the object, and the action</note>. ¶ Furthermore, to adorn any relative with other relatives by saying thus: "The good, great, and eternal [agent] produces a beautified, magnified, and eternalized [object]." ¶ Moreover, there is another way of adorning: namely, to adorn a principle with its definition, and with the definitions of other principles: as when it is said: "Good, great, and eternal goodness is the reason for the good [agent] that he may produce the good, great, and eternal [object]." Just as the logician finds natural conjunctions between the subject and predicate so that there may be a true conclusion in a syllogism, so the rhetorician inquires into natural conjunctions between the subject and pre-

# On Application

<margin>83. Logic. Predicables. Predicaments <note>These are technical terms in Aristotelian logic: Predicables are types of relationships between a subject and predicate; Predicaments are the ten categories of being.</note></margin>

The predicate: so that a beautiful subject can be adorned by its essential predicate by speaking thus: "The lady queen has a beautiful face, beautiful hair, beautiful hands," and the like. ¶ There is yet another way of adorning a subject through accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like wearing a crown.</note>: as when it is said, "The lady queen has a beautiful crown," and "she speaks beautiful words," and "the lady queen is good"; and this is evident through rule G. ¶ Again, the rhetorician adorns with meaningful speech: as when it is said with fitting and greater words which are more beautiful; rather than when one says "October" and "November," because they <insert>the former</insert> signify flowers, and leaves, and the song of birds, and the renewal of time, and of things that can be generated. October and November, however, do not. This same thing can be said of springs, rivers, streams, meadows, trees, shadows, and the like, which are beautiful words according to the senses and the imagination; and this is evident through rule E. ¶ Just as the rhetorician praises his friend with beautiful words applied to a good end, so he vituperates and scorns an enemy with beautiful words that are removed and diverted from their proper end: as when one says to a dishonest monk, "If I had been a monk, I would have had beautiful, honest words"; and this is evident through the definition of end, concordance, and contrariety. ¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns his words according to the office of the people: as when a man speaks of science, of generosity, and chastity, and the like. And similarly, there is rhetoric in knighthood: when it is said, "the man speaks of audacity, of probity, nobility, of the horse, of the sword," etc. And in the art of trade, to speak of silver, of gold, of precious merchandise, and the like. And in agriculture, to speak of the field, the iron <note>original: "ferro" - likely referring to the plow or tools.</note>, the garden, and plants and animals. For just as it is a beautiful word for a merchant to speak of gold, etc., so it is a beautiful word for a peasant to speak of the field or iron, and the like. ¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns with three degrees: namely the positive, comparative, and superlative. But he adorns more with the comparative than with the positive, and more with the superlative than with the comparative: as when he says, "the rose is beautiful"; but he adorns more when he says, "the rose is a more beautiful flower than the violet." And even more when it is said, "the rose is the most beautiful of all flowers." And this is evident through the definition of majority and minority. ¶ Likewise, the rhetorician adorns when he colors a beautiful subject with a beautiful adjective, or dishonors a beautiful subject with a beautiful adjective: as when it is said, "the queen is good," or "the queen is dishonest." For "dishonest" is a more beautiful word than "malice." ¶ The rhetorician colors matter with a beautiful form, and colors form with beautiful matter,

<column-break/>

as when it is said: "The human body has a rational soul," and "the rational soul has a body well-disposed to doing good with vigor," and the like. And this is manifest through the scale of the principle and its definition. ¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns the middle with a beautiful principle, and adorns the end with a beautiful middle; just as in love, in which a good lover loves to love the good out of his own goodness; and the beloved is adorned and colored by his loving, just like a good man who is habituated by a good habit. And this is evident through the definition of the beginning, the middle, and the end. ¶ Further, the rhetorician can adorn his words more with substantial and necessary principles than with accidental or contingent ones, even in facts: because existence is more than appearance. The reason for this is: that a necessary principle rests more in the end than an accidental or contingent one. And this is evident through the triangle of majority and minority, and through the definition of the beginning and the end. ¶ Furthermore, the rhetorician adorns his words by declaring through the possible and the impossible, and through the easy and the difficult, and through the useful and the useless, and through the frequent and the rare, and the like; and this is evident through rules B, C, D, etc. ¶ Additionally, the rhetorician adorns his words with beautiful proverbs applied to the purpose, as is evident in the *New Rhetoric* which we have composed.

## 87 On Logic. 121

<margin>83. Logic.</margin>
Logic is the art with which the logician finds the natural conjunction between the subject and the predicate, which is the "middle" <note>The "middle term" in a syllogism that links the subject and predicate.</note> with which he knows how to make necessary conclusions. The logician, through the definition of the middle, finds the contiguous middle: both through the agreements existing between the subject and the predicate; and an example of this is given in the multiplication of the fourth figure <note>A reference to the fourth figure of the syllogism in formal logic.</note>. ¶ Furthermore, the logician treats the five predicables and the ten predicaments; and an example of this is in the *Treatise of a Hundred Forms*. ¶ Likewise, the logician treats the syllogism, and the figures, and the fallacies; and examples of all these have already been given above. And therefore, if any doubt or strange question arises concerning logic, let it be reduced to those things which are said about logic, holding the affirmation or negation of the question in such a way that those things said about logic in this art remain unharmed. ¶ Furthermore, the logician makes a superior predicate from an inferior one: just as "animal" is predicated of "man," and "body" of "animal," and "substance" of...

# Tenth Part. On Grammar.

And similarly, it posits a multiplicity of species: for it posits subaltern species, such as all those things that exist between substance and man in a direct line. Just as goodness is the most general principle when it is not restricted; but when it is restricted in the middle, it is a subaltern genus or principle, as when saying: "goodness is great." From the intellect, a conclusion is concluded for him with the stability and immutability of the principles, species, and rules; and immediately he will not know how he may escape.

The logician treats secondary intentions <note>In medieval logic, "secondary intentions" are concepts about concepts, like 'genus' or 'species', rather than things themselves.</note> joined to primary ones; but the general Artist treats primary things through the second species of Rule C, and through the first and fourth species treats secondary things just as the logician does. 

¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that logic is an unstable or fleeting science; this General Art, however, is permanent and stable. Item: the logician makes a conclusion with two premises; but the general Artist of this Art does so with a mixture of principles and rules. ¶ Furthermore, the logician cannot find the true law with logic; but the general Artist finds it with this Art. For that law is true which the principles and rules of this Art can enter. ¶ Moreover, logic is a difficult art to learn; this Art, however, is very easy by reason of the mixing and concatenation <note>The "chaining together" of ideas.</note> of the principles and rules. And therefore, an Artist can learn more of this Art in one month than a logician can learn of logic in one year.

Grammar is the art for finding the way of speaking correctly and writing correctly through the definition of difference. ¶ Grammar is divided into nine modes.
¶ The first mode is about grammar and the number of the eight parts of speech. ¶ The second about case. ¶ The third about conjugation. ¶ The fourth about declension. ¶ The fifth about gender. ¶ Sixth about government <note>The grammatical "ruling" of one word over another.</note>. ¶ Seventh about construction. ¶ Eighth about orthography <note>Correct spelling.</note>. ¶ Ninth about figure. 

¶ Grammar is applicable or to be applied to this Art. For just as grammar teaches the way of speaking correctly and writing correctly, so this Art teaches how to find other arts. Therefore, we apply grammar to this Art so that it may be more certain and clarified in our intellect. 

¶ There are eight parts of speech, namely: noun, pronoun, participle, verb, conjunction, preposition, adverb, and interjection. 
¶ The noun is applicable to the principles of this Art, such as to goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ For nouns are the pronoun which is applicable or to be applied to them; for the pronoun is placed in stead of a proper noun. For the principles of this Art are nouns, as has already been said above; and they have "property" because they are proper names by reason of the generality they possess. For they can be applied to every faculty. The principles of another faculty or science, however, cannot be applied to other sciences; for they do not have a property so general as the principles of this Art have. 

¶ The verb is to be applied to the second species of Rule C, namely: to make good <note>original: "bonificare"</note>, to make great <note>original: "magnificare"</note>, etc. For they signify action just as a verb does. 
¶ The participle is applicable in the same species of C, as is evident through the meanings of "making good" and "having been made good," "making great" and "having been made great," and so forth. 
¶ The conjunction is implied in the same species of C, i.e., in "to make good." For "to make good" joins the "maker-good" and the "thing-made-good" to be one perfect concrete thing, just as a conjunction joins different words to be one perfect sentence. 
¶ Furthermore, the adverb is implied in the same species: as when it is said, "the maker-good makes-good his thing-made-good *well*." For every agent intends to bring forth its effect from itself *well*; therefore the adverb is implied in it. 
¶ The preposition is applicable to the fourth species of Rule C, or to the rule of instrumentality. For the grammarian [treats] of it...

¶ We must speak concerning the Case.
¶ The **Nominative** case is implied in the second species of Rule C, namely in the "bonifying" <note>The author uses "bonifying" (making good) as a placeholder for any active verb or agent</note>. For the bonifying agent exists through itself and does not descend from any other insofar as it is the nominative; and it is the principle of the other cases descending from it. ¶ Similarly, the **Genitive** is implied in the second species of Rule C, namely in the "bonified" and "to bonify." For the bonified and the act of bonifying descend from the bonifier, just as the genitive descends from its nominative. It can also be applied to the third species of Rule D, for that signifies possession, just as the genitive does. ¶ Furthermore, the **Dative** is implied in the second species of Rule C, in the bonified and the act of bonifying. For the bonifier gives being to it; and both—namely the bonifier and the bonified—give being to the act of bonifying. ¶ Furthermore, the **Accusative** is implied in the same rule, namely in the third species. For in it, the act of the agent is terminated, as if in the patient <note>The "patient" is the person or thing receiving the action</note>. For the accusative is that case in which the act of the agent terminates, as if in its doable object or patient. ¶ Moreover, the **Vocative** is implied in the fourth species of the same rule. For in it, the vocative has its "called" object objectively. It can also be applied in Rule B, as is clear to one looking closely at the nature of the aforesaid rule. ¶ The **Ablative** is implied in the second species of Rule C, in the essence of the bonifier, the bonified, and the act of bonifying. For the essence itself is the principle and cause of these three essential and natural correlatives. ¶ **Conjugation** is implied in the second species of Rule C, in its correlative essences, as in "Goodness" and its correlatives. For Goodness is the principle and cause of its correlatives descending from it, which differ from one another according to their diverse properties; just as in conjugation there is a certain principle from which many words are derived, differing from one another by person, time, mood, and so forth. ¶ **Declension** is implied in the second species of Rule C; for "to bonify" and "the bonified" descend from "the bonifier" by generation, just as one case descends from another by declension. ¶ **Gender** is implied in the correlatives of the second species of Rule C. For in them, every gender is implied. For the "bonifier" signifies the masculine gender by reason of action; the "bonified" signifies the feminine by reason of passion <note>In the sense of being acted upon</note>; and "to bonify" signifies the neuter by reason of neutrality. ¶ **Governance** <note>Latin: *Regimen*; the way one word controls the case of another</note> is implied in the greater power and virtue with respect to the ruler; and also in the lesser power and virtue with respect to the ruled or governable.

<column-break/>

For it is fitting for one having greater power and virtue to rule and not be ruled. But for one having lesser power and virtue, it is fitting to be ruled and not to rule. Indeed, it is fitting for a Count to rule his simple soldier, and not the other way around. ¶ **Construction** <note>Syntax</note> is implied in the triangle of Beginning, Middle, and End by reason of due order. For the Beginning is prior to the Middle and the End according to the way of nature, and this is clear through its definition. And also the Middle is prior to the End itself, as is also clear through its definition. And the End is last, as is clear by the same reasoning. For in the End the Beginning rests, and this happens through right and due order. Thus, even in construction, the subject is placed before and the predicate is placed after, as when one says: "Peter runs." For he does not order well who wishes to place the roof before the building of the house, or the foundation and the wall after the building; for that is impossible. ¶ **Orthography** <note>Correct spelling/writing</note> is implied in the rule of Modality. For the rule itself teaches how a part is a part, and how one part is in another part, or joins with another part. ¶ Furthermore, how parts are in the whole, and the whole in its parts; and afterwards how the whole transmits its likeness outside itself; so it is in orthography, in which it is taught how a letter is what it is, and how one letter is joined with another letter, and one phrase with another phrase, and one accent with another accent, etc. ¶ **Figure** <note>Rhetorical figures or grammatical irregularities</note> is implied in the definition of Contrariety and Concordance. It is applied to the definition of contrariety insofar as a figure is a fault made against right grammar, and thus is contrary to grammar. But because the figure itself can exist in grammar through some reason which it contains in itself, it is therefore applied to the definition of concordance. For by that reason which the figure possesses, it accords with grammar and is placed within grammar; otherwise, it would not be placed in it at all.

### 89 On Morality 71/121

<margin>89. Form of morality.</margin>
Morality is a habit for doing good or evil. ¶ We have treated **Morals** in the ninth subject; and therefore, if a question is asked about any morality that is explicitly stated in that subject, let one return to the subject itself. If, however, it is implied, let one return to those things which are explicit in the subject: just as if one asks about injury, let him return to justice. And if one asks about generosity, let him return to avarice. For one contrary [is known by the other...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Ninth Subject (Morality) and introduces the Tenth Subject (Politics). It maintains the instructional tone of a logical-theological manual, likely Ramon Llull’s "Ars Brevis" or a related work in the Lullian tradition.</meta>

# Part Ten

...is known through the rest. Whoever makes a subject out of a single virtue and predicates the principles of this Art upon it, that virtue is multiplied and strengthened—not in its essence, but in its action. For example, when it is said: "Charity is good," "Charity is great," "Charity is lasting," and so on. In this way, one disposes Charity so that it becomes a <term>habit</term><note>A "habit" (habitus) in medieval philosophy is a stable disposition or skill acquired through practice.</note> with which a person may act charitably well, masterfully, and enduringly.

<margin>Instruction for avoiding vices</margin>
However, whoever wishes to destroy a vice should make a subject of it, and let the principles of this Art be predicated of it by saying: "Cruelty is evil," "Cruelty is as evil as it is great," "As long as it lasts, it is evil and dangerous," and so forth.

<margin>The Third Figure</margin>
¶ Whoever wishes to use a virtue well and masterfully should run it through the "evacuation" of the Third Figure <note>The Third Figure in Lullian logic involves combining terms from the Second Figure to find middle terms.</note>: for example, using the letters *l.c.u.z.* and *b.r.* One says: "Charity is good and great." Then let them ask: "What is good and great charity?" and so on for the other combinations contained in chamber *b.c.* Afterward, let them descend to chamber *b.d.* and so on for the others. Let them ask: "From what does the goodness of charity endure?" Then let them answer in the same manner that questions are answered in that chamber, so that no contradiction follows between what is said in the chamber and what is said about charity. This same process can be done in its own way for cruelty. By this method, charity will receive nourishment, but cruelty will not. For the Good is lovable in itself when it is known with greatness and duration through what was said above.

<margin>The Fourth Figure</margin>
¶ In the multiplication of the Fourth Figure, the moralist can use virtues against vices by running the virtue or vice through the Table, seeking an "artificial middle" <note>A logical middle term used to connect a subject and predicate.</note> just as a logician does according to his art. By this method, the moralist can clothe themselves in virtue and strip themselves of vice—as with charity and goodness, which are in harmony with moral nature, because charity cannot exist without goodness. Just as a human being cannot exist without being an animal. The intellect greatly rejoices in such artistry and doctrine.

¶ Every vice and every virtue can be found through the species of the Rules. A vice or virtue is discoverable in one way according to one species, and in another way according to another. Just as the senses find color in an apple in one way, flavor in another, and weight in another. Similarly, Charity, when run through the four species of Rule C, is found in different ways. The same can be said and found regarding Cruelty.

¶ Whoever wishes to possess virtues and avoid vices, or wishes to multiply virtue and diminish vice, should turn to the Fourth Subject, which concerns Man. And according to how they find Man run through

<column-break/>

the principles and rules, let them help themselves to acquire virtues and avoid vices. If they are hindered in this, let them turn to the subject of the Imagination and the subject of the Senses; then they will be better disposed to acquire virtues and avoid vices. If all these are not enough, let them turn to the First Subject <note>The First Subject in this system is God.</note> by praying; then let them see how God is run through the principles and rules, habituating themselves in Hope. This is the final remedy. If they reach the goal, it is well indeed. If they do not reach it, they fail because they do not know how to act skillfully with this Art.

### On Politics. 90

<margin>90. The form of politics.</margin>
**P**olitics is the art with which the <term>burgesses</term><note>Citizens or city officials, typically of the merchant class.</note> look after the public utility of the city. It is derived from morality; therefore, politics is manageable through the Ninth Subject by acquiring virtues against vices, so that the public utility may be established with those virtues. This is done by running Politics through the principles and rules of this Art in its own way, just as virtues and vices are run in the Ninth Subject. Politics is known through its definition and through its <term>correlatives</term><note>Lullian "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal forms of a principle (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving).</note> marked by the second species of Rule C. Through the third species, it is the habit of peoples. Through the fourth species, peoples possess the political habit. Thus, Politics can be run through the other species of the Rules in its own way.

¶ Politics is the order placed in the senses along with the virtues, as in a city where a marketplace is established for things a person uses out of necessity, such as food and other similar things.

¶ Furthermore, Politics is the order regarding "well-being," such as the beautiful layout of streets, squares, and other places, the adornment of clothing, and such things.

¶ Moreover, Politics requires walls, trenches, and weaponry in a city, so that with all these, the city can defend itself from its enemies.

<margin>First principles</margin>
¶ Between a city and its lordship, there ought to be privileges existing by way of a "middle term," just as a logician places a middle between a subject and a predicate with the definition of Concordance and End. Those privileges ought to be guarded by the consuls and burgesses, so that there is a balance and determined law between the lord and the city.

¶ Politics in a city is the "general form" with respect to the city. In every house of the city, however, there is a "special form"; and this is joined by a middle in which the general and special forms are united. This is done through the definition of Concordance and through the mixing of principles, yet with the middle term kept away from all con—

### On Law.

<margin>92. The form of Law.</margin>
Law is an act regulated in a person accustomed to justice through the first species of Rule C <note>Rule C in Llull’s Art usually refers to the questions "Whose?" or "From what?"</note>. ¶ There are four primitive principles of law: namely, **divine law**, **the law of nations**, **natural law**, and **positive law**. ¶ **Divine law** consists of the definition of the majority, minority, and the concord existing between God and man. ¶ **The law of nations** <note>Latin: "ius gentium"; the common law shared by all peoples.</note> consists of the definition of the concord and equality existing between man and man. ¶ But **natural law** consists of the necessary definition of reason, goodness, greatness, etc. ¶ However, **positive law** <note>Man-made law, such as statutes or decrees.</note> consists of the voluntary reason of man, by his finding it and establishing the definition of goodness, greatness, etc. And in these terms or principles, every kind of law is contained through the second species of Rule C. ¶ Through the third species, law is in another. And through the fourth species of the same, it has action in the thing judged. ¶ Again, law has form and matter in the second species of D, Rule 1 of E, from which things it is made. In the second species of E, **justice** is the subject of law in judgment; it follows that justice is the subject about which the principles of this Art are predicated along with their definitions: as when it is said, "Justice is good," "Justice is great," etc. ¶ From which it follows that justice is the good and great reason of the judge, so that he himself may make a good and great judgment, etc. And by this it is clear that the principles of this Art are the forms of justice itself, without which justice cannot be perfect. ¶ Justice itself is indeed the subject of those things which are sustained in it. Nevertheless, justice itself is the form in respect to a judge who is accustomed to it. ¶ Again, it is the form by reason of the action which the judge has with it in the thing judged; and consequently it is clear that the thing judged is its matter, considering it in this way. For the judgment itself is made by the one judging, just as an act is made in the thing to be done by the agent. And this is clearly evident through the third species of Rule C. ¶ In a right and perfect judgment, it follows that the judge should discourse upon justice through the principles and rules of this Art, just as it was discoursed

<column-break/>

upon in the ninth subject. And if he does this, justice with judgment in the thing judged is a perfect and necessary form; and without any doubting conscience, the judge can use it in his judgment. ¶ But if the judge does not discourse upon it through the aforesaid—as was said above—he uses the said justice poorly, contingently, and even with a doubting conscience, which is a great and terrible danger to his soul. For he who gives a great judgment without prudence and discretion is worthy of a painful judgment. ¶ Written law is true if the principles and rules of this Art can be within it. But if they cannot be within it, such law is indeed fantastic, feigned, and out of harmony. For the principles and rules of this Art are true and necessary without any defect. For each thing is true and necessary because that which is cannot be otherwise. Just as a crystal placed over various colors is colored by them, so laws or canons, when they are placed or applied to these principles and rules of this Art, are "colored"—that is, they are strengthened by various necessary reasons. And quickly, by this method, the judge sees the truth of both parties, which he cannot do without the aforesaid; rather, with a great length of time and laborious study, he has to see the truth, and even then there is doubt. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that law is not an art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to a systematic, scientific body of knowledge.</note>, and that it cannot be reduced to an art except by reducing it through the aforesaid principles and rules. Since law is not an art, it is no wonder if it is confused and prolix, and the intellect is hindered by it. The subject of law consists mostly in the soul, as much through memory as through intellect, which is contrary to the proper order of the powers of the soul itself. For the intellect is primary for investigating and finding laws, and the will follows it in choosing, and then the memory in preserving the species. And because the universal is more than the particular, and because memory is the particular subject of particulars from which there is no science, therefore for many people law is not well-disposed nor well-ordered in the soul. And from this it is clear that when principles are lacking, the art fails. ¶ The form of law cannot act outside its own proper matter through the designated Rule G, nor vice versa. And therefore it is necessary for the jurist to know what are the matter and form of law. The form in respect to the principles of this Art is the aggregation of your aforesaid principles: namely, the justifying, the bonifying, the magnifying, etc., which by reason of concord meet in one form.

# Tenth Part.

That which is justifiable, that which is beneficial, and that which is magnifiable, etc., are the matter of law; however, the form and matter of discourse proceed through the straight line of the rules with the definitions of the principles. ¶ And in this paragraph, whatever can be said concerning law has been applied. ¶ In law, the intellect is stronger when combined with the imagination than with the senses, because the imaginative power is a higher power than the senses; and since the intellect is a higher power than the imagination, it is stronger in itself than it is in the imagination. ¶ And let the jurist <note>original: "iurista"</note> know how to act concerning any power according to whether it is more high or less high: I advise the jurist to have knowledge of the subjects designated by **e. f. g.** ¶ I advise that the jurist discourse through the species of the rules before he gives a judgment. For some judgment is competent with one species which is not competent with another: just as appears in the second species of rule **c.** For in that second species, laws arise from necessity; but in the third species of the same rule, they proceed from contingency: and this is manifest through the definition of majority and minority.

Medicine is the habit <note>A "habit" in this context refers to a stable disposition or learned skill.</note> with which the physician procures the health of the patient. ¶ The physician must have recourse to the mixture of the principles and rules of this art. For by that method through which they are mixed, the physician will habituate himself to possessing the habit with which he knows how to make the mixture of medicines—in making decoctions, ointments, plasters, syrups, and grading herbs against a disease. ¶ In the subject designated by **d.**, the heavens are discoursed upon through principles and rules: and because the superior principles and rules act upon the inferior ones, therefore the physician must have recourse to the aforementioned subjects: so that he himself may see under which constellation the sick person suffers: with which and according to which he ought to act, or practice upon the patient. ¶ Again, the physician ought to habituate himself regarding the subject designated by **f.**, so that he knows how to use the imagination, so that the intellect—which creates science from sensory things in the aforementioned imagination—may know how to use them outside of the senses: and with it descend to the senses objectively, and with the senses ascend to the imagination, in such a way that the imagination is a medium existing rightly and orderly between the senses and the intellect: and this with the definition of the medium. ¶ Furthermore, let the physician have recourse to the subject marked by **d.**, so that he knows how to use the senses, by seeing the color of the sick person and of his urine: and by inspecting his feces, smelling the breath, and hearing the wailing

To rule and govern him <note>referring to the Prince's subject or himself</note>. ¶ Likewise, let him return to other subjects: such as to subject **B** <note>Goodness</note> by knowing and loving it: for through the knowledge of it, he directs himself toward reigning and governing. ¶ Furthermore, let him return to subject **E** <note>Power</note>. For when a prince knows the manner by which a man is skillfully guided in principles and rules, he indeed makes use of the man, either by judging him or by advancing him. ¶ Moreover, let him have knowledge of the subject designated by **F** <note>Wisdom/Intellect</note>, so that he may know how to use his imagination in the city, in war, in judgment, in counsel, and the like. For just as a peasant does not know how to manage a horse or how to run it, so a prince without an ordered imagination does not know how to reign. Indeed, the intellect does not know how to use sensible things without an ordered imagination. ¶ Furthermore, a prince ought to have knowledge of the subject designated by **G** <note>Will</note>, so that he may know how to use his own sense regarding himself and his officials, and so that he may lead those things which are sensible from the imagination to the intellect, and from the intellect to the ninth subject <note>The Divine</note>. But if the prince should say that these things are difficult for him, let it be answered to him that he should do this according to his power; and beyond his own power, he should have his wise men who know how to do this and give him counsel. This should be done in such a way that the principles and rules remain without injury, and the prince may be in harmony with the highest subject <note>God</note> and removed from all contrariety. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes by what movement the governance of a prince can be reduced to an **Art** <term>Ars: a systematic method or science</term>, and how to treat it as a science. And would that a prince be found who reduces his governance to an Art, for which he might prepare his son and teach it to him, or cause him to be taught. Consequently, I grant to all princes on behalf of their sons that they should learn it.

<margin>What fortitude is.</margin>
For an Art is an unassailable habit. ¶ A soldier who possesses it has victory against one who does not know how to use the Art. ¶ **Fortitude** is the virtue strengthening the heart of man, and especially when he knows how to have knowledge of it; therefore, the more he knows it, the more it causes boldness. ¶ Whence it follows that if a soldier wishes to know fortitude perfectly, he should return to the ninth subject in which it is perfectly treated. ¶ A soldier without faith, hope, and charity is not fortified in war; and therefore, let the soldier clothe himself in the aforementioned virtues, with God helping, however, through that manner by which they are discussed in the ninth subject. ¶ A soldier through goodness wishes to be good, and through greatness wishes to have great victory, honors, and the like. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes in what manner **Knighthood** <note>original: *militia*</note> can be reduced to an Art. And it also recognizes that the greater armors are the virtues in the soul, rather than the armors of the body with which he is fortified. For the Art does not consist in the body, but in the soul alone. ¶ It is fitting for a soldier to be noble by birth; indeed, **Nobility** is a great habit in the heart, from which arises great boldness of face and of the right hand, which cause victory, the boldness of the heart existing with them. ¶ In war, a great imagination and a great sense are necessary. ¶ The greatness of the aforementioned things is through the discourse of the virtues of the ninth subject. For just as one sword with a stronger arm overcomes another sword in a weaker arm, so one soldier with greater sense and imagination overcomes another soldier in war. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that sometimes a few soldiers overcome many.

### On Knighthood.

<margin>93rd form: On Knighthood.</margin>
**Knighthood** is a habit with which a soldier helps the prince so that he may be able to uphold justice. For the soldier was invented so that through him, justice might be sustained. And therefore, the soldier ought to habituate himself to justice through that manner by which justice is discussed through the principles and rules of this Art in the ninth subject, so that the soldier may have perfect knowledge of it. ¶ Since a soldier needs **Prudence** in war, he ought to have it as a habit, so that with it he may be stronger against his enemy; therefore, the soldier must know it according to how it is discussed in the ninth subject, so that with it he may skillfully defend himself from his enemies.

### On Commerce.

<margin>95th form: On Commerce.</margin>
**Commerce** <note>original: *mercantia*</note> is a habit invented by which a merchant knows how to buy and sell, so that he may multiply his money, just as is known in the treatise of principles and rules: namely, the manner in which one principle relates to another. Just as in trading, the buyer relates to the seller with his principles and rules, and the seller likewise relates to the buyer with his own, so that each may be able to have that which is greater through that which is lesser. ¶ Whence it follows that the merchant who knows how to direct his intellect, imagination, and sense through the principles and rules of this Art possesses superiority.

With these, buying and selling are conducted in the marketplace. Therefore, so that the merchant may know how to act skillfully, he should place his imagination and his senses into his trade <term>mercatura: the art or business of trade</term>, without which buying and selling do not happen. And he will know how to do this if he knows how to habituate himself to the subjects designated by the letters C, F, and G. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes the manner by which one merchant multiplies money more than another. ¶ In the subject concerning E, he treats of man, and consequently of his body, for it is a part of him. And because buying and selling occur due to the necessity of the body, therefore a good merchant should run his intellect through subject E, so that he can have knowledge of the things necessary for the body. ¶ The third and fourth species of rule C are great subjects for the merchant by means of rules H and I. For the same trade-good or thing is of low price or high price according to the diversity of place and time. For things or trade-goods have more value in one time than in another, and more in one place than in another. And also more for one man because of necessity and utility, while for another man it is for the sake of goodness and honor. ¶ Furthermore, the second species of rule C, by means of rule G, causes profit in buying and selling. For that which is "proper" <note>essential or specific</note> relates to a higher end than that which is "appropriated" <note>accidental or assigned</note>. And for that reason, a thing which is properly necessary for a man is further removed from contingency than a thing which is necessary by accident. ¶ Trade in a faithful and virtuous man is a perfect habit; but in a deceptive and sinful man, it is an imperfect habit. Therefore, he who wishes to be a good merchant should habituate himself in the virtues through that method by which they are treated in the ninth subject. For in trade, a well-formed habit establishes community and society among men; but a deformed one causes the privation of community and society. ¶ Many other things could be said about trade, but let those which have been said suffice for the sake of brevity.

### On Navigation.

<margin>
The 16th form: on navigation.
</margin>
Navigation is the art by which sailors know how to travel by sea. ¶ Navigation indeed descends and arises from geometry, and from motion, time, and place, which mediate toward their correlatives designated by the second species of rule C: which are the mover, the movable, and the act of moving, with time and place mediating. ¶ A ship is in one place at one time, and in another place at another time. ¶ Since geometry and arithmetic descend from this art <note>referring to the author's "Great Art"</note>, as was proven above in their respective places, it follows therefore that the art of navigation descends primarily from this art, and secondarily from geometry and arithmetic, as is clear from the aforesaid. ¶ And to declare this, I have made here this figure divided into four triangles, as is clear in it; and it is constituted of right, acute, and obtuse angles.

# On Application

A triangle is formed through twelve miles / three times four; a quadrangle is caused four times three. And thus it is shown by what method a triangle and a quadrangle are composed in the motion of a ship. By the method we have given concerning the motion of a ship through twelve miles / a sailor can know that by traveling via the *Sirocco* <note>original: "exaloch"; the SE wind</note> for one hundred miles, the ship deviates from the East by 25 miles / the ship losing one mile in four toward the *Sirocco* relative to the East / the motion of the ship existing first through a point, then through a line: and afterwards through a triangle: and then through a quadrangle. If a ship departs from a port and wishes to go toward the East: but instead travels through the South: it indeed deviates by double from the East compared to the deviation it makes when it goes toward the *Sirocco*. The reason for this is: because the *Sirocco* stands in the middle of the East and the South. ¶ And if the ship goes via the *Libeccio* <note>original: "lebeich"; the SW wind</note> but still wishes to go toward the East / a triple deviation is caused. And if it goes via the West / it is caused fourfold. ¶ We have shown the method by which sailors can estimate the deviation of the place to which they intend to go; and the motion of that art which we gave for knowing deviation / by showing the general principles without which a ship cannot be in motion. Which principles are these: namely the point / the line / the triangle and the quadrangle. And the loss of one mile in four toward the *Sirocco* and two in eight miles toward the South: and so on for the others. ¶ Now we intend to give the teaching and art by which sailors may know how to recognize in what place of the sea the ship is: and this we intend to exemplify / by showing how far one mountain stands from another. ¶ I suppose that there is one mountain toward the East far from the port in which the ship sits by 4 miles, which shall be called mountain **L**: and that there is another mountain at the *Sirocco* / distant from the port by 4 miles: and let that mountain be called **M**. And let there be another mountain toward the South distant from the port by 4 miles and let it be called **N**. ¶ Further, I suppose there is another mountain toward the South distant from the port by 8 miles: and let it be called **O**. Now it is asked how far **L** is from **M** and from **N**.
