### On Conscience.

<margin>The ninety-seventh form: on conscience.</margin>
Conscience is the form with which the intellect afflicts the soul concerning things committed, according to what is marked in the fourth subject <note>referring to the soul in the author's logical system</note>: because conscience is an active form through the intellect; as to the will, it is elective; as to the memory, it is preservative. Therefore, he who wishes to use conscience well should lead it through the ninth subject. ¶ A great conscience is caused by the definition of majority; a small one, however, from the definition of minority; but a temperate and virtuous one from the definition of equality and virtue. ¶ Conscience, moreover, comes from the possible and from understanding, but not from the impossible and from ignorance. And therefore it is manageable with the definition of power and intellect. ¶ Conscience led through principles and rules is known, and especially if it is led through the mixture of principles. For any principle declares it according to itself and according to other principles, by reason of which conscience is clearly caused. And it gives as counsel that <term>contrition</term> <note>sincere sorrow for sin</note>, <term>confession</term>, and <term>satisfaction</term> <note>acts of penance to repair harm</note> be made for things committed. ¶ Conscience arises from the correlative principles with love, and it is in the third species with fear and sadness. In the fourth species of the subject in which it exists, it has passion with it by means of the second species of rule 'e'. Conscience, before a sin is committed, disposes one toward justice, prudence, and fortitude; but after a sin, toward sadness and languor. And therefore it is to be reduced to the definition of the beginning and rule 'h'. ¶ Conscience lives with goodness, greatness, and perseverance. But it dies with malice, smallness, and inconstancy. Wherefore it is to be reduced to the definition of goodness, greatness, and duration. ¶ Conscience is strengthened with the first subject by objecting to it according to its discourse through principles and rules. And thus it increases its act, from which arise contrition, confession, and satisfaction. ¶ Furthermore, through conscience itself, sighs arise from the heart, tears from the eyes, and many prayers from the mouth; and this is marked by rule 'i'. ¶ Conscience with divine justice performs acts of mercy; and with greatness and eternity, it multiplies them. With goodness, greatness, and divine mercy as mediators, along with hope and penance, it gives consolation to men. ¶ Conscience does not sleep, nor does it permit a man to sleep, by reason of the loss of time and penance. And therefore wakefulness, prayer, and diligence with fear are its blood-relations or neighbors. ¶ The intellect, considering in this way, recognizes conscience thus discoursed; for conscience thus discoursed through principles and rules is unassailable and infallible, in the knowledge of which the intellect is greatly gladdened.

### On Preaching.

<margin>The ninety-eighth form: on preaching.</margin>
Preaching is the form with which a preacher informs the people to follow good morals and avoid evil ones; and especially if that mode of discourse is through the principles and rules of this art, and also through the nine subjects, so that the intellect of the preacher and of the listeners may abound in great matter. Such preaching is very useful and very easy, just as it is very skillfully crafted and built and placed upon a great subject. ¶ Just as the preacher skillfully crafts his understanding for the purpose of leading, so he ought to skillfully craft his will to love the will of the listeners, so that the sermon may be as valuable in its essence as it is in its appearance. And this is through the definition of the equality of the intellect and the will, so that in the sermon the intellect and the will may descend equally; otherwise, the preacher in his sermon is sometimes habituated toward vainglory. ¶ The preacher ought to skillfully craft the memory of the listeners with the artifice of his crafted sermon: if the preacher preaches concerning the subject things joined in nature through the subject, such as "the justice of God is great." ¶ The mercy of God is...

And by such a method, the intellect of the preacher and the listeners will have great rest. Since God is intelligible, lovable, and rememberable with greatness; therefore, the preacher ought to give great knowledge of God, so that He may be greatly understood, loved, and remembered: and this he can do with a mixture of principles and rules, and also with the first subject. If, however, he does not do this, his sermon will indeed be imperfect and fleeting.

<column-break/>

<margin>Three places</margin>
There are three places, one of which is in every way perfect without any imperfection: and that is eternal and infinite glory. The second is totally imperfect: and that is hell, in which there is everlasting punishment. The third, however, is partly perfect and partly imperfect: and such a place is this world. Therefore, the preacher ought to recite and declare these three places, and say what they are, what they have within them, why they exist, and what utility they have in themselves. For the place that is perfect in every way is totally lovable; the one that is imperfect is utterly hateful. But that which is partly perfect and partly imperfect is indeed lovable in part by reason of its perfection, and hateful in part by reason of its imperfection. ¶ While the intellect considers in this way, it recognizes the method by which the sermonizer can reduce his sermon to the "art of preaching," so that he may know how to make sermons more skillfully and easily; just as we have made one part of sermonizing in which one hundred and eight sermons are organized or constructed skillfully.

### On Memory, deduced through the Principles.

<margin>100</margin>
<margin>The hundredth form: on Memory deduced through the principles.</margin>
<margin>Goodness</margin>
<margin>Greatness</margin>
Since memory is as perfect a power as the intellect and the will—which we have treated perfectly in the mixing of the principles—we wish to treat it perfectly here, discoursing upon it through the principles and rules, so that we may know it perfectly. We also do this to provide a doctrine: namely, that just as we discourse upon memory through the principles and rules, so every form of the hundred forms can be discoursed upon through principles and rules. ¶ Just as memory is good naturally through Goodness, so morally its goodness is the reason why it recollects a good, recollectable object. ¶ Memory is great by reason of Greatness, by which its magnitude is the reason for it to perform a "great recollecting," with which it recollects a great recollectable thing (or object, which is the same thing). Just as a cloaked man has one habit <note>note: a play on 'habitus' meaning both a garment and a mental disposition</note> by his cloak, and another by the tunic with which he is clothed, so memory has one condition through Duration and another through Power. For through Duration, it makes its recollecting endure and treats of the past; and through Power, it has another condition: namely, through the intellect and the possible. ¶ Memory has one condition with the intellect and another with the will. For through the intellect, it receives the species <note>term: species (mental images or impressions of things)</note> that are desired or hated; and in the same way it receives species from the will, it returns them to it. ¶ Memory is a virtuous habit naturally, because it naturally recollects an object virtuously; morally, it possesses a virtuous habit. When, however, it recollects a vicious habit, it possesses a vicious habit by accident. ¶ Memory is true through Truth; and through it, it truly reaches the object by recollecting. When it reaches the object in respect to the End, it is a just and true habit; but when it reaches the object against the ultimate End, it is an unjust and false habit. ¶ And by this step, the intellect knows in what manner virtues and vices are caused. ¶ Memory with Glory has delight in recollecting, and with Pain, it has sadness. Likewise, when it desires to recollect and cannot, it has pain, with which it is a passive and privative habit. ¶ Memory with Difference recollects objects in diverse ways; for just as the intellect knows the differences of objects, so the memory recollects them. The reason for this is that Difference is as general a principle or instrument for the memory as it is for the intellect. ¶ Memory, by reason of Concordance, accords in the object with the intellect and the will, by recollecting the object, the thing understood, and the thing loved or hated, so that the object is acted upon by these powers at the same time. ¶ Memory with Contrariety sometimes contradicts the intellect and the will by not returning to them the species they desire to recover, because it is not disposed to return the species; or the intellect and will do not desire to recover them because the memory does not return them in the manner in which the intellect and will delivered them to it; or the intellect is slow and the will too prompt, and vice versa; or the intellect desires one species and the will another. ¶ Memory acts in the Beginning by recollecting, and memory is its own form or instrument with which it recollects the object; and the object itself is the subject or matter; the one recollecting, however, is its end. And when the recollecting itself is impeded, the memory indeed suffers, and consequently becomes the acted-upon <note>note: original: "agens" vs "patitur," referring to the Aristotelian distinction between active and passive</note>. ¶ In memory, "to remember" is the medium between the rememberer and the remembered, with which the rememberer...

# Part Ten.

<margin>
The end <note>original: "finis"</note>
</margin>
...memorable things are joined together: assuming that the measurement is made by a straight line equally bounded between the one remembering and the thing remembered. ¶ There are three terms of memory: namely, **power**, **object**, and **act**. Outside of these, memory has no capability. And by the end of privation <note>Privation refers to the absence of a quality that should normally be present.</note>, memory is a deprived habit, just as when the act and object are lacking for them—much like when light and color are lacking for the eyes. However, the ultimate end of memory is to recall what is recallable. ¶ By reason of greatness, one memory is greater than another by essence or by quantity. For one memory has a greater act than another. ¶ Furthermore, since memory has a greater act, it is indeed a greater habit; I do not say that its essence increases or decreases, because it is neither divisible nor corruptible, being a spiritual power. But since man acts with memory at his pleasure, he sometimes recalls much and sometimes little. ¶ Memory naturally and equally exists between the **intellect** and the **will**, so that it may equally receive and return the species <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" are the mental images or forms of things perceived.</note> that are understood and loved. Nevertheless, it sometimes receives loved species that are not understood. This happens when one believes and does not understand by reason of the pleasure of the agent, who desires to believe more than to understand. ¶ Memory with "smallness" is concerned with nothing: namely, that when it forgets, it is a privative habit by reason of smallness.

It is asked whether memory receives species more quickly from the intellect than from the will? And the answer is yes. The reason for this is that the intellect produces knowledge, while the will holds its reason by virtue of its freedom. ¶ Through the first type of rule C, it is asked: **What is memory?** And it must be said that it is the power to which recalling properly belongs. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **What does memory have in itself co-essentially?** To which it must be said that it has its correlatives: namely, the *rememberer*, the *rememberable*, and the *act of remembering*. ¶ Through the third type, it is asked: **What is memory in another?** And it must be said that it is good in goodness objectively, assuming that the intellect and will rest in that object. And it is evil in malice, assuming that the will loves that evil. ¶ Furthermore, memory is in the subject as a habit with which it guards knowledge. ¶ Through the fourth type, it is asked: **What does memory have in another?** To which it must be answered that it has goodness in a good object, and greatness in a great one, etc., when it has an act

in the subject and in the object. ¶ Through the first type of rule D, it is asked: **Of what is memory made?** And it must be answered that it is of itself: for it was created. And it is indeed not begotten, nor made from anything pre-existing. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **Of what is memory made?** To which it must be said that it is made of its specific matter and form, since it acts through its own species. ¶ Through the third type of the same rule, it is asked: **To whom does memory belong?** And it must be answered that it belongs to the subject in which it exists: just as a part belongs to its whole naturally or morally, like a cloak belongs to the one cloaked. ¶ Through the first type of rule E, it is asked: **Why is there memory?** To which it must be answered that it is constituted from its form and matter. ¶ Through the second type of the same rule, it is asked: **Why is there memory?** To which it must be said that it exists so that beings may be recalled. ¶ Furthermore, it exists so that man may have knowledge of past things. ¶ Through the first type of rule F, it is asked: **Does memory have continuous quantity, since it is not linear?** To which it must be answered yes. For a spiritual power is both finite and indivisible. Everything that is a finite being has quantity. And if any spiritual being is finite, it is also a quantity; therefore it is clear that memory has continuous quantity. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **Does memory have discrete quantity?** And it must be answered yes: so that it may have its aforementioned correlatives through difference. For through the *rememberer* it has one correlative; through the *rememberable* it has another; and through the *act of remembering* it has another. Anyone who says memory does not have these correlatives says that it is empty and lacking in its own nature, which is impossible; therefore it is clear that memory has discrete quantity by reason of its correlatives. ¶ Through the first type of rule G, it is asked: **What is the proper quality of memory?** And it must be answered that it is its "recallability," just as "risibility" <note>The ability to laugh, often used in logic as a property unique to humans.</note> is in man. ¶ Through the second type, it is asked: **What is the appropriated quality of memory?** To which it must be answered that it is a moral habit: namely justice, hope, etc., or injury, etc., or grammar, etc., or soldiery, etc., or agriculture, etc. ¶ Through rule H, it is asked: **Is memory in time?** And it must be answered yes: because it is new, mediated by the motion of the subject in which it is, just as the soul is moved in a mobile body. And thus it can be said of the other types of rule H in their own way, which it has designated through C, D, and K; the declaration of which we leave to the skilled artist for the sake of brevity. Since memory does not have a surface, it is asked: **Is it in a place?** And it must be answered yes: like a part in its whole without physical contact, as in an elemental body...

And it must be answered that the method consists in "B" <note>The letter B in this Art often represents Goodness or the first degree of inquiry.</note>: namely, that a person should apply the definitions of the principles and the species of the rules to the likenesses which they desire to recall. For just as the intellect reaches a likeness through a likeness, so the memory recalls the desired object through a likeness. For if someone sees a man similar to their own son, they immediately recall their son through <margin>K</margin> the likeness of that man. ¶ Through the second species of K, it is asked: with what does the memory forget? To which it must be answered: with the "minority" <note>Minority (parvitas) refers to a lack of intensity or presence in the logical structure.</note> coursing through all the principles and species of the rules. For just as "majority" causes a positive habit, so minority causes a privative one in its own way. ¶ We have spoken of the hundred forms, and the doctrine has been given through which the artist may know how to run any form through the principles and rules of this Art. And at the end of the forms, it was shown in what way the liberal arts can be easily learned through this Art.

### The Eleventh Principal Part.

### Regarding the eleventh principal part, which concerns questions.

<margin>Heading of the eleventh principal art.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'H' containing a figure of a scholar or saint sitting at a desk with a book, framed by an arch.</image-desc>
This part is divided into six parts or places. ¶ The first part is about the questions we shall make through the Table. ¶ The second part is that which we shall make regarding questions through the "evacuation" <note>A technical term for exhausting all logical combinations.</note> of the Third Figure. ¶ The third part is that which we shall make regarding questions through the multiplication of the Fourth Figure. ¶ The fourth is about questions we shall make through the mixing of principles. ¶ The fifth is about questions we shall make through the Nine Subjects. ¶ The sixth is about the questions of the Hundred Forms. However, some questions we shall solve here, and others we shall refer to the places in this book where their solutions are folded in and marked; and in those which we solve, we shall teach the practice of this Art, and we shall give the doctrine for solving other "foreign" questions <note>Questions not explicitly listed in the text.</note> which can be solved according to the manner by which we solve the others. ¶ The reason why we refer some questions to their own places is to avoid prolixity, and because those who know this Art will be able to solve them through the places in which their solutions are implied. ¶ Likewise, we say that through the questions we make, we shall give the doctrine for forming questions by abstracting them from the meanings of the rules.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
In the Table, there are 84 columns; and because we avoid prolixity, we do not wish to make questions about all the columns, but only about seven columns, through which we shall give the doctrine for making and solving questions through all the columns of the Table.

### Regarding the questions of the first column: B. C. D. T.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' containing a human face in profile.</image-desc>
Through this column we have already made questions, as is evident in the Table, in which we prove that the world is not eternal. But so that it may be seen that the column is general, we wish to repeat it, abstracting some questions from it. And just as this column is general, so the other columns are general. ¶ Through the chamber B-C-D, it is asked: whether there is any infinite and immense Goodness through "bonification" <note>The act of making good or the essence of goodness in action.</note>, just as there is Eternity through duration? And it must be answered that there is: otherwise Eternity would not be totally good, nor totally great, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked: what is infinite and immense Goodness? And it must be answered that it is an essence having in itself many infinite and immense "correlatives" <note>Llull's term for the internal relations of a principle, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving.</note> marked by the second species of C. ¶ It is asked: of what is infinite and immense duration? And it must be answered through the first and second species of Rule D, and through the second of Rule C. And to this, Rule B bears witness: that it concerns the eternal correlatives of Goodness and Greatness, without which Eternity cannot be infinite and immense (B.C.T.B.). ¶ Whether Goodness can be great without Distinction? And it must be answered that it cannot: because there would not naturally be a reason for the Good to act upon the good, since in every action it is necessary for there to be distinction. It is asked: what is the great distinction of Goodness? And it must be answered that it is that of its correlatives in which it is sustained, and with which it has its nature, and is a perfect essence (B.C.T.C.). ¶ Whether Goodness can be great without Concordance? # Eleventh Part.

The answer is no. For just as contrariety <note>original: "contrarietas"; the state of being opposite or in conflict</note> relates to non-being, so does concordance <note>original: "concordantia"; harmony or agreement</note> relate to being. It is asked: what is the great magnitude of goodness? And the answer is that it consists in goodness having its own natural correlatives <note>technical term in Llull’s system referring to the active, passive, and verbal components of an essence, e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving</note> b. c. t. d. ¶ It is asked: is an angel greater than the heavens? And the answer is yes. The reason for this is that an angel possesses correlatives with which he perceives God as an object, whereas the heavens do not. ¶ It is asked: what is the great contrariety of the heavens? And the answer is that it is the immobility it possesses, assuming it does not move itself. Just as fire would have great contrariety if, through its lightness, it were unable to move itself. ¶ It is asked: from what does the great motion of the heavens arise? And the answer is that it arises from its correlatives according to the second species of rule C, designated b. d. t. b. ¶ Whether there is difference in eternity? And the answer is yes: so that eternity itself can have its correlatives, without which it would have neither a nature nor infinite goodness. ¶ It is asked: from what does the goodness of the motion of the heavens arise? And the answer is that it arises from itself, as signified through its correlatives b. d. t. c. ¶ Whether divine goodness and divine magnitude agree? And the answer is yes: for without concordance, divine goodness would not have infinite "magnification" <note>the act of making great</note> nor would divine magnitude have infinite "bonification" <note>the act of making good</note>. ¶ It is asked: what is the great concordance of divine eternity and divine goodness? And to this it must be said that it is the essence of their correlatives: namely, the "bonifier" <note>that which makes good</note> and the "eternifier" <note>that which makes eternal</note> which meet in one number; and the "bonifiable" and "eternable" in another; and the acts of "bonifying" and "eternizing" in a third. And these three meet essentially in one essence of goodness and eternity b. d. t. d. ¶ Whether there is contrariety <note>The scribe uses "proprietas" here, likely a slip for "contrarietas" given the context of the answer</note> between divine goodness and eternity? And the answer is yes, assuming that eternity could hinder goodness in its act, and vice versa—which is impossible. ¶ Assuming that there were contrariety between divine goodness and eternity, it is asked: from what would that contrariety arise? And the answer is that it would arise from privative principles existing against the positive correlatives of goodness and eternity—which is impossible and a manifest contradiction b. t. b. c. ¶ Whether difference and concordance can exist in the simple essence of goodness? And the answer is yes, assuming that goodness itself has its correlatives signified through the second species of C; which are indeed many through difference, but are the same through essence by way of concordance. ¶ It is asked: what are difference and concordance in the essence of goodness? And the answer must be given through the third species of rule C: that they are what they are, and yet they are goodness itself b. t. b. d.

¶ Assuming that the world were eternal: could difference and contrariety exist together in its goodness? And the answer is no: for no good difference could stand in the face of eternal contrariety. It is asked: from what does good difference arise? And the answer is that it arises from the correlatives designated through the second species of D, b. t. c. d. ¶ Assuming that the world were eternal: could concordance and contrariety exist together in its eternal goodness? And the answer is no: otherwise concordance would have a good act of "concordancing" and "contrarying" from eternity and in eternity—and likewise for contrariety—which is impossible. It is asked: what is the great contrariety of goodness? And the answer is: namely, when goodness is in a natural subject that is habituated with moral malice, as in a sinful man c. d. t. b. It is asked: what is the great difference of eternity? And the answer is that it is that which eternity possesses through its correlatives. It is asked: from what does the great difference of eternity arise? And the answer is, through the first species of rule D, that it arises from itself. For no cause can be prior to eternity c. d. t. c. It is asked: what is the great concordance of the heavens? And the answer is: its correlatives, with which it is what it is, and by which it moves itself. It is asked: from what does the great concordance of the heavens arise? And the answer is that it arises from its correlatives, with which it has motion and nature, and by which it moves and gives nature to all inferior bodies c. d. t. d. It is asked: what is the great contrariety of prudence and lust? And the answer is that it is a moral contrariety. It is asked: from what does moral contrariety endure? And the answer is that it endures from positive and privative habits resisting one another in a subject in which they cannot stand together c. t. b. c. ¶ Whether justice and prudence have great difference and concordance? And the answer is yes: because they cause great acts through great merits. ¶ It is asked: what is the great difference and concordance of justice and prudence? And the answer is: the great relatives with which they differ and agree c. t. b. d. ¶ Whether in a great essence there can be difference and contrariety? And the answer is yes: assuming the essence is composite, such as the essence of man and of the elements. But in a simple essence, by no means c. t. c. d. ¶ Assuming that in a simple magnitude there were concordance and contrariety: it is asked, what would that magnitude be? And the answer is that it would be an impossible essence.

It is asked concerning Great Concordance and Contrariety: from what do they originate? To this it must be said, through the first species of Rule D <note>Rule D in Llull's system usually asks "Of what?" (De quo?)</note>, that it is of themselves. For above Magnitude, no being lies prior to B.T.B.C. ¶ Whether in Eternity there are Difference and Concordance: and the answer is yes; for otherwise, in Eternity, Goodness would not be the reason why it acts for the good. For Eternity without Concordance would have something by which it would stand apart from Contrariety and idleness, which is impossible. It is asked: the differences of Concordance existing in Eternity, from what do they originate? And the answer is that they are from their own <term>correlatives</term> <note>In Llull's philosophy, "correlatives" are the active, passive, and verbal components of an essence (e.g., the lover, the beloved, and the act of loving)</note> through the first and second species of Rule D. ¶ It is asked: what are Difference and Concordance in Eternity? And the answer is that they are Eternity itself, B.T.B.D. ¶ Whether in Eternity there can be mutual Difference and Contrariety: And the answer is no; because if so, Eternity would be composed of many contrary and corruptible essences, as is evident in <term>elementated things</term> <note>Physical things made of the four elements, which are subject to decay</note>. ¶ Suppose that the Heavens were made of many contrary essences: it is asked from what would its duration originate? To which it must be said that it would be from positive and privative habits, which is impossible, D.T.C.D. ¶ Suppose that in the essence of an Angel there were Concordance and Contrariety: it is asked from what would the angelic duration originate? And the answer is that it would be from its own contraries, which is impossible. It is asked: what is the duration of an Angel? And the answer is that it is Concordance removed from all Contrariety, T.B.C.D. ¶ It is asked whether Difference can be the subject of Concordance and Contrariety: and the answer is no; because Concordance relates to *being*, while Contrariety relates to *non-being* in the subject in which they exist. It is asked: what is Difference in Concordance and Contrariety? And the answer is that Difference in Concordance is a positive principle, and in Contrariety, it is a privative one. ¶ It is asked: from what does Difference endure? And the answer is that it endures from its own concordant correlatives through an essence removed from all contrarieties.

### Concerning the questions of the second column: C. D. E. T.

<margin>Concerning the questions of the second column: C. D. E. T. C D R T</margin>
It is asked: what is the Great Power of Eternity? And the answer is that it is an infinite and eternal power, as signified through its correlatives. It is asked: from what is the Great Power of Eternity? And the answer is that it is from eternal correlatives. Why is there Great Power of Eternity? And the answer is that it is because Eternity can have infinite and eternal correlatives, C.D.T.C. ¶ It is asked: what is the Infinite Concordance of Eternity? And the answer is that it is an infinite eternal essence. It is asked: from what is the infinite and eternal essence? And the answer is that it is from infinite and eternal correlatives, without which it could not be infinite and eternal, C.D.T.D. ¶ Assuming that in Eternity there were Contrariety: it is asked what that Contrariety would be? And the answer is that it would be an infinite and immense essence, constituted of infinite and eternal contraries. It is asked: from what is the Magnitude of Eternity? And the answer is that it is an eternal and infinite essence. It is asked: from what is the Great Principle of Eternity? And the answer is that it is from its infinite and eternal correlatives. Why is there an infinite and eternal Principle? And the answer is that it is because Eternity has infinite correlatives separated from all idleness, C.E.T.C. ¶ It is asked: what is Infinite Power? And the answer is that it is Infinite Concordance. ¶ It is asked: why is there Infinite Power? And the answer is because it has infinite correlatives, C.E.T.D. It is asked: from what is Infinite Power? And the answer is that it is from its correlatives removed from all contrariety. It is asked: why is there Power without contrariety? And the answer is that it is an infinite essence separated from all contrariety, C.E.T.E. ¶ It is asked: why is there an Infinite Principle? And the answer is that it is because in itself it has its infinite correlatives in which it rests. It is asked: why is there Infinite Power? To this it must be said that it is because it cannot exist without an infinite subject, C.T.C.D. It is asked: what is Great Concordance? And the answer is that it is a great essence removed from all contrariety. It is asked: from what is Great Concordance? And the answer is that it is from its great correlatives, primitives, etc. It is asked: what is a Great Principle? And the answer is that it is a Great Concordance removed from all contrariety. It is asked: why is there a Great Principle? And the answer is that it is because it has great correlatives, C.D.T.E. It is asked: what is the Great Contrariety of a principle? And the answer is that it is an essence emptying a principle of its correlatives. It is asked: from what is a Great Principle? And the answer is that it is from its correlatives removed from contrariety. Or it is from its correlatives which contrariety can least of all contradict or resist.

# Part Eleven

<margin>d e t e</margin> **d.e.t.e.** <note>These letter combinations refer to Llull's "Alphabet of the Art," where specific letters represent principles like God, Eternity, Power, etc.</note> ¶ Why do Eternity and Power accord with one another? The answer is that they accord so that they may exist and act from eternity and in eternity. ¶ It is asked: what is the concordance of eternity and power? The answer is that it is an eternally powerful essence. ¶ It is asked: from what does the concordance of eternity and power arise? To this it must be said that it arises from the *eternizing* <note>original: "eternatiuo"</note> and the *power-making* <note>original: "possificatiuo"</note>, the *eternizable* and the *power-able*, and the acts of *eternizing* and *power-making*. ¶ It is asked: why can contrary ends not exist from eternity? The answer is because in eternity there is rest. ¶ It is asked: from what does the rest of eternity arise? The answer is that it arises from its own correlatives <note>The "correlatives" are Llull's specific term for the internal components of an attribute: the active agent, the passive object, and the act itself (e.g., the Lover, the Beloved, and Loving).</note> when all contraries have been removed.
<margin>d e t d</margin>
<margin>d e t e</margin> **t.e.** ¶ Why is eternal Power able to act from eternity and in eternity? The answer is that it is eternal primitivity <note>The state of being first or the ultimate source.</note>. ¶ Why is eternal Power an eternal principle? The answer is: because it is able to act from eternity and in eternity.
<margin>d t e d</margin> **t.e.d.** ¶ Assuming the heavens were eternal: it is asked, what would be their eternal concordance and contrariety? The answer is that their concordance would be one active and passive eternity, and their contrariety would be another eternity that is active and passive—which is impossible. For eternity cannot be composed of contraries, since it is infinite. ¶ From what does eternal contrariety arise? The answer is that it arises from a natural subject and a moral habit, as if a man wearing a cape were dressed in a cape of fire. <note>A metaphor for an external or accidental quality rather than an essential one.</note>
<margin>d t c e</margin> ¶ It is asked: what is the principle of eternity? To which it must be answered: namely, that it is the concordance of its correlatives. ¶ It is asked: from what does the concordance of eternity arise? The answer is that it is from the correlatives of eternity. **e.t.c.d.** ¶ It is asked: why can concordance and contrariety not be a single power? To this it must be said: because concordance tends toward *being*, while contrariety tends toward *non-being*. ¶ It is asked: what is the contrariety of body and soul in man? The answer is that it arises from contrary ends or contrary correlatives. **e.t.c.e.** ¶ It is asked: what is the power of prudence and the power of pride? The answer is that the power of pride is a privative habit <note>A "privative" habit is one defined by the absence of a good, like darkness is the absence of light.</note>, while prudence is a positive one. ¶ It is asked: why are the power of pride and the power of prudence not one single power? To which it must be said: because the definition of concordance cannot bring them into accord in a single end, since they are contrary principles. **e.t.d.e.** ¶ It is asked: why can power not consist of contrary principles? To this it must be said: for power possesses relative principles that are separated from contrariety through concordance. ¶ It is asked: from what do contrary principles arise? The answer is that they arise from contrary ends. **t.c.d.e.** ¶ It is asked:
<margin>e t c d</margin>
<margin>e t t e</margin>
<margin>e t d e</margin>
<margin>t c d e</margin>

<column-break/>

why is concordance a primitive principle, while contrariety is a consecutive one? The answer is that concordance is a positive principle, while contrariety is a privative one. ¶ It is asked: what is the primitivity of concordance and the posteriority of contrariety? The answer is that the primitivity of concordance is when many things relate to one; the posteriority of contrariety is when many things do not relate to one. ¶ It is asked: whether concordance and contrariety arise from one and the same principle? The answer is no, because they do not relate to a single end.

### Concerning the questions of the third column: D.E.F.T.

<margin>Concerning the questions of the third column: D.E.F.T.</margin>
It is asked: why is God as powerful through His eternity as He is through His intellect? The answer is because His eternity and His intellect are one and the same power. ¶ It is asked: from what does the power of eternity arise? The answer is that it arises from its correlatives, so that through them it can exist and act from eternity and in eternity. ¶ It is asked: how great is the power of eternity? The answer is that it is as great through its *power-making* <note>original: "possificationē"</note> as it is through its duration. **d.e.t.d.** ¶ It is asked: why can contrariety not exist in eternal power? It must be said that eternal power is as infinite through its power-making as it is through its duration. ¶ It is asked: from what does eternal power arise? The answer is that it arises from itself, as is clear through the first and second species of the Rule. **d.t.e.d.e.t.e.** ¶ It is asked: why does God have no beginning? The answer is because He possesses eternal power, before which no other power exists. ¶ It is asked: from what does the power of the heavens arise? It must be said that it arises from itself, because it is not derived from any principle existing before it. <note>In medieval cosmology, the "heavens" or celestial spheres were often considered incorruptible and distinct from earthly matter.</note> **d.e.t.f.** ¶ It is asked: how great is the power of the heavens? The answer is that it is as great as its correlatives are. ¶ It is asked: why are the heavens mobile? The answer is that they are mobile through their correlatives, as is clear through the first species of the Rule; and through the second species of the same, they are mobile so that there might be motions in the lower things <note>The "lower things" refers to the sublunary or earthly realm.</note>. ¶ It is asked: from what does the motion of the heavens arise? The answer is that it arises from its correlatives, without which it would have no motion naturally within itself or outside itself. **d.f.t.d.** ¶ It is asked: what are the correlatives of eternity? The answer is that they are as many as the correlatives of the divine intellect; otherwise, divine eternity would be hindered by eternal contrariety, which is impossible. ¶ It is asked—

**What can the middle be?** And to this it must be added that it is as much as is most intelligible through the divine intellect. <note>The letter combinations like f.t.r.g. refer to Llull's combinatorial system where letters represent specific principles like Goodness, Greatness, etc.</note> It is asked: why does the divine intellect understand a greater beginning? ### Concerning the questions of the multiplication of the Fourth Figure.

<margin>26.</margin>
<margin>The third part of the tenth principal part concerning questions.</margin>
The multiplication <note>In this context, "multiplication" refers to the expansion or systematic application of logical forms.</note> of the Fourth Figure occurs in five ways, as has been said. And just as the multiplication happens in five ways, so questions can be made in five ways. And so we shall say something about the first way and the others. ¶ The first way is subdivided into four parts. ¶ The first is: when it proves that the world is "new" <note>meaning "created in time" rather than eternal</note> through twenty arguments. And this is done through the column **b.c.d.** And just as it is said of the world, so it can be said of those things which are signified by **b.c.e.** in the alphabet, making solutions for each signified thing in its own way. Such as **b.**, which signifies God in goodness, difference, justice, and avarice <note>The system uses letters to represent both virtues and their opposing vices for the sake of logical contrast.</note>. And so for **c.**, which signifies an angel, greatness, etc. And **d.**, which signifies heaven, eternity, etc. And thus every particular question has its own involved solution. This solution can be reduced to the Art by holding to the method of this Art. And just as we have spoken of the first way, so it can be said of the others in their own way. ¶ And let these things suffice concerning the multiplication of the Fourth Figure for the sake of brevity.

### Concerning questions on the mixing of principles and rules.

<margin>30</margin>
<margin>The fourth part of the tenth principal part concerning questions.</margin>
In the mixing of principles and rules, it is shown when any principle runs through other principles and rules, making a predicate out of a subject and vice versa: such as "great goodness," "eternal goodness," "powerful goodness," etc.; "good greatness," "eternal greatness," "powerful greatness," etc. Therefore, if a question arises concerning goodness and greatness, or concerning goodness and eternity, etc., let one recur to the chapter on goodness and the paragraph on goodness and greatness. And if the question is about goodness and eternity, let one recur to the paragraph on goodness and eternity; and so for the others. And let them extract the solutions from those places in which the solutions are marked; and this is how: ¶ It says in the first paragraph in the chapter on goodness that goodness is, of itself, the reason for a good thing to act well or to produce. But because it is a "great reason"—doubled for the good through greatness—that it should produce a great good: therefore, if it is asked whether goodness is the reason for God to produce a great good, let it be granted through those things which were said above. ¶ Further, it is said in the fourth paragraph in the chapter on goodness that goodness is durable through duration; and thus through duration, it is a "tripled reason" so that the good may act well, greatly, and durably, as is evident. So if a question arises whether divine goodness is the reason for God himself to produce an eternal or durable good, let one recur to the chapter on goodness in the third paragraph. And let the solution be drawn from the text by the mixing of the definitions of goodness and duration; and so for the others. ¶ Further: what is that great good which God produces? Let one recur to the chapter on goodness and the rules through which goodness is deduced: such as when it is asked, "What is goodness?" And then let him respond through that text to the question according to the definition of goodness. If it is asked, "From what does God produce good?" Let one recur to the chapter on goodness and to the paragraph of Rule **D** <note>Rule D usually refers to "Where?" or "From what?" in the Lullian system.</note> in which it is asked "From what is goodness?" and from that text let the solution be extracted; and so for the others. ¶ Just as we gave the example of the goodness of God, so it can be said of the goodness of an angel in its own way; and of the goodness of justice; and of the goodness of prudence; and of the malice of avarice and gluttony; and so for others in their own specific way. ¶ And let these things suffice for the sake of brevity regarding the questions of mixing. And this is because the Art is sufficient for making and solving other questions. ¶ And in this step, the intellect recognizes that the mixing of principles is a very general subject for making many questions. And that in the text, the solutions are involved and marked.

<margin>6.</margin>

¶ And this concludes the fourth part of the tenth principal part.

# On Questions.

### On the questions of the nine subjects: and first concerning the first subject, which is God. And first through the principles.

<margin>
The fifth part of the eleventh principal part concerns the questions of the nine subjects: and first concerning the first subject, which is God. And first through the principles.
</margin>
<margin>46</margin>
To avoid prolixity <note>original: "prolixitatem"; meaning wordiness or excessive length</note>, we propose to pose certain questions concerning God: both to extract them from the text and to solve them through the text. This is to provide instruction on how the artist <note>The "Artist" refers to a practitioner of Ramon Llull's "Art," a system of logic and philosophy.</note> may know how to extract questions from a text and solve them by using that same text from which they were drawn. ¶ We intend to pose other questions and extract them from the text, but not solve them for the sake of brevity; rather, we will refer them to the appropriate text to provide instruction on the manner by which the artist may know how to solve questions through the appropriate text. This text is indeed general to many questions. We propose to maintain this manner and order in the other subjects. ¶ Whether by any mode it is necessary that God produces good? It is asked: by what means is it proven that angels exist? The solution is found in the first rule. It is asked: how is an angel defined? It is asked concerning the actions and passions <note>In medieval philosophy, "passions" refers to being acted upon or receiving an impression, rather than just emotion.</note> of angels. ¶ Since an angel does not possess imagination, by what means does it understand imaginable things? ¶ All these questions are solved by the aforementioned second rule. ¶ It is asked: what are the innate principles of an angel? The solutions are in the sixth rule. ¶ It is asked concerning the succession and continuation of angels: since an angel is not corporeal, does it have measures of time? The solutions are in the seventh rule. ¶ Whether an angel is located in a place. ¶ Whether an angel passes through a medium? The solutions are in the eighth rule. The solutions are in the tenth rule, marked by the letter K. ¶ Whether an angel suffers by fire? We say that it does, as is evident through the first [rule] and through the first species of *e*, and through the second of *g*, and by the definition of divine power. For if God wills that an angel can move stones without a body, likewise by divine power it can suffer by fire. It is asked: whether angels are our messengers and helpers? And it must be answered that they are. ¶ For just as the heaven with its innate principles is effectively and naturally a co-helper to the principles of the elements so that they may have their actions, so do angels help—not so that we may have moral virtues [alone]—and this can be proven by rules *b* and *c*.

**Q**ueried: Why are the heavens not from eternity <note>i.e., why did they have a beginning in time?</note> since they are not corruptible? Go to the rule of the second letter, *b*, of the third subject. ¶ Given that the heavens do not move themselves: it is asked whether they would be the "first moved" <term>primum mobile: the outermost sphere in geocentric astronomy that moves all others</term> by nature? The solution is in rule *c*. ¶ It is asked whether the heavens have formally and naturally innate correlatives <note>interdependent qualities</note> without which they could not cause lower correlatives? The solution is in the second species of *c*. ¶ It is asked whether the heavens receive "the more and the less" <note>degrees of intensity</note>? The solution is in the third species of *c*. ¶ It is asked what the heavens possess in lower things? The solution is in the fourth species of *c*. ¶ It is asked why the heavens are incorruptible. The solution is in the first species of *d*. ¶ Whether the heavens have specific principles with which they act specifically? The solution is in the second species of *d*. ¶ It is asked whether the motion of the heavens can resist miracles? The solution is in the third species of *d*. ¶ It is asked whether the heavens are necessary? The solution is in the first species of *e*. ¶ Whether lower mobilities <note>movements on Earth</note> could exist naturally without the motion of the heavens? And it must be answered that they cannot. For just as the will without charity <note>divine love</note> could not have the power to love God above itself, nor to love its enemy; so fire, etc., could not naturally move water without the motion of the heavens. For the heavens are prior, while fire is posterior. And go to the second species of *e*. ¶ It is asked why the heavens act with oblique quantity within themselves, but with straight quantity outside themselves? ¶ It is asked whether the heavens have discrete quantities, since they are in continuous motion? The solutions are in rule *f*. ¶ It is asked why the heavens act through a specific species? ¶ It is asked whether heat and dryness are qualities appropriated to the sun? The solutions are in rule *g*. ¶ It is asked in what way the time of the heavens has the logic of cause and effect, with the heavens being subject to it? The solution is in rule *h*. ¶ Whether the heavens are in a place? The solution is in rule *i*. ¶ It is asked in what way the heavens act upon lower things? And it must be answered that they act through their own mode in a lower mode; just as the prior acts in the posteriority through its own mode. ¶ It is asked: with what do the heavens act upon lower things? And it must be answered: with their innate principles, just as a cause which, with its own causes, causes other causes.

# On Questions.

Whether the proper quality of a sense causes the appropriated quality of the thing sensed? The solution is in the first species of G. It is asked: from where does the sensibility of a stone come? And it must be answered that it comes from the habit of the sense. And go to the second species of G. ¶ Whether the sensibility of a stone remains in time when the eyes are closed? And it must be answered that it does not: just as the second vision of the eyes does not remain when the eyes are closed. And go to rule H. ¶ It is asked: where does the sense perceive the thing sensed? The solution is in rule I. ¶ Whether the sense reaches the substance? And it must be said that it does: insofar as it is joined with it; but not insofar as it is separated from it. Just as sight does not reach the substance of a stone because it is not joined with it. ¶ It is asked: by what mode does the sensitive faculty perceive the thing sensed? The solution is in the species of rule K. ¶ It is asked whether the sensitive faculty perceives the thing sensed with the likeness which it sensed, which likeness is the habit of the thing sensed—just as a cloak is to the one cloaked? And go to the second rule K. ¶ Whether sensitive things are joined with their own proper subject? To which it must be said that they are: as is clear through the first definition of "concordance" and "the medium"; and so that the principle may have a medium through which it can pass to its end. ¶ Whether the sense is joined with the thing sensed: for example, with a stone or an audible thing, etc.? And it must be answered that it is not: because the habit is appropriated and new; just as a cloak is to the one cloaked: for the cloak is not joined <note>i.e., not essentially part of</note> with the one cloaked, but is applied to him by contact.

### On questions of the vegetative faculty through principles.

<margin>On questions of the vegetative faculty through principles.</margin>
Whether the vegetative faculty <term>vegetativa: the biological power of growth and nutrition</term> is good without the act of goodness? And whether it is good through its specific goodness? ### On the questions of the ninth subject, which concerns virtues and vices.

<margin>On the questions of the ninth subject, which concerns virtues and vices.</margin>
Just as the common sense, along with its particular senses, perceives sensible things, so the soul, with its powers, justifies justifiable things and vitiates <note>corrupts or makes faulty</note> vitiable things. And because it does this by means of the principles of this Art—virtues and vices—in a systematic way, just as the logician uses syllogisms with the principles of logic. Therefore, according to the aforementioned method, we intend to pose questions, and by that same method, the solutions are indicated; and first, we shall speak of justice.

# Part Eleven

Why justice exists: the solution is in the second species of E. ### Concerning the questions of gluttony: and first through principles.

<margin>Concerning the questions of gluttony: first through principles.</margin>
Whether gluttony causes "gluttonousness"—namely its own species—just as temperance causes "temperateness"? And we say that it is so: because if not, gluttony would not have that by which it would be a specific sin, just as temperance has that by which it is a specific virtue. It is asked: does a gluttonous man know that excessive eating does him harm, yet believe that it does him good? And it must be answered that the habit of gluttony makes him believe that which is beyond his understanding; and see in the first paragraph of the ninth subject in the chapter on gluttony. Why does a gluttonous man believe that excessive drinking is not an evil? And it must be answered that great gluttony magnifies believing and provokes understanding; and see in the 2nd. It is asked: why is a man gluttonous when the delights he has through gluttony do not last as long as the pains he suffers because of them? And it must be said that it is because he supposes and does not understand; and see in the third.

The solution is in the eleventh. ¶ It is asked: to what is sloth contrary? The solution is in the twelfth. It is asked: how does laziness behave regarding causes? The solution is in the thirteenth.

¶ It is asked: by what means does sloth impede the good? The solution is in the fourteenth. Why is the slothful person always in labor? The solution is in the fifteenth. It is asked: what is the fountain of vices? The solution is in the sixteenth. ¶ It is asked: by what means is sloth strong? The solution is in the seventeenth. ¶ It is asked: to what is "lesser sloth" close? The solution is in the eighteenth.

### On questions regarding sloth through rules.

<margin>On questions regarding sloth through rules.</margin>
It is asked: why is sloth less recognized than any other sin? The solution is in rule b. ¶ It is asked: what is sloth? The solution is in the first species, section c. ¶ From what do the correlatives of sloth come? The solution is in the second species, section c. ¶ What is sloth in other vices? The solution is in the third species, section c. It is asked: what does laziness have in good things, and what does it have in evil things? The solution is in the fourth species, section c. ¶ It is asked: why is sloth a privative habit? The solution is in the first species, section d. ¶ Concerning what things is sloth? The solution is in the second species, section d. ¶ Whether sloth is a bond of the slothful person for doing evil? The solution is in the third species, section d. ¶ Why does sloth act through its own species? The solution is in the first species, section e. ¶ It is asked: why does sloth exist? The solution is in the second species, section e. ¶ Whether sloth can be mixed with other vices without continuous quantity? The solution is in the first species, section f. Why does sloth have acts of succession since it is neither punctual nor linear? The solution is in the second species, section f. ¶ It is asked: what is the proper quality of sloth? The solution is in the first species, section g. It is asked: what are the appropriate passions? The solution is in the second species, section g. ¶ When does the slothful person use time? The solution is in rule h. It is asked: where is sloth? The solution is in rule i. ¶ How is sloth begotten? The solution is in the first rule, k. ¶ With what things is sloth brought about? The solution is in the second rule, k. It is asked: by what is sloth caused more—by the intellect or by the will? And it must be answered by making a distinction: namely, that it is caused by the intellect through laziness, and by the will more through anxiety <note>original: "sollicitudinez"</note>. The reason for this is: because the intellect labors in acquiring species <note>mental representations or concepts</note>, but the will does not. ¶ Why are idleness and anxiety species of sloth? And it must be answered that because the intellect has no inherence to the truth on account of laziness, and therefore it causes idleness; the will, however, on account of the inherence it has toward evil, causes anxiety.

### On questions through the explicit and the implicit.

<margin>On questions through the explicit and the implicit.</margin>
It is asked: in what manner are applications made through the explicit and the implicit? <note>The "explicit" refers to clearly stated logic, while the "implicit" refers to truths contained within a premise that must be drawn out.</note> How are these terms applied to the question: *whether God exists*? How do they apply to the question: *whether God is eternal*? How does it apply to this question: namely, *whether it is good that God is as infinite through His greatness as He is through His eternity*? How is it applied to the proposition: namely, *whether God is more active through His intellect than through His eternity*? How are these principles applied to the proposition: namely, *whether God is just*? Go to the tenth part of this book, to the rubric "through the explicit and the implicit," in which the solutions to these questions are implied.

### On questions through the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>On questions through the abstract and the concrete.</margin>
It is asked: how is the application of principles done through the abstract and the concrete? <note>In scholastic logic, "abstract" refers to a quality itself (e.g., Whiteness), while "concrete" refers to the thing possessing the quality (e.g., a white wall).</note> And it must be answered that it is through the four modes named in the tenth part of this book and in the aforementioned rubric. Through the first mode: as if it were asked *whether fire and "fire-ness" differ*; let them be applied to goodness and greatness, etc., with their correlatives, and the difference between the abstract and the concrete will appear. Through the second: *whether there is a difference between quantity and a "quantified thing"*; let accidental goodness be applied through the abstract, and moral good as the concrete which is constituted. Through the third: *whether there is a difference between heat and a "hot thing"*; to this, let substantial goodness be applied to the hot thing, and let accidental good be applied. Through the fourth: *whether there is a difference between whiteness and a "white thing"*; let accidental goodness be applied to whiteness, and substantial good to the white thing, such as to a white man who is a substance. And go to the tenth part, to the rubric marked above.

### On questions of the application of the first figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the first figure.</margin>

To this question, let eternity, power, etc., be applied with their definitions and with their correlatives signified through rule C, so that a "circulation" of the subject and predicate may occur; and go to the application of the first figure.

### On questions of the application of the second figure.

<margin>On questions of the application of the second figure.</margin>

Furthermore, if it is asked *which principles are the most general, the intermediate, and the most specific*. Also, if it is asked in what way the second figure is applicable to or serves the first figure: go to the application of the second figure.

# On Questions

### On questions regarding the application of definitions. 78
<margin>On questions regarding the application of definitions.</margin>
If something is asked concerning any subject: let that which is being asked be applied to the definition; namely, define it, and draw a conclusion about it through its own definition. For example, if it is asked: *Whether God has infinite action.* <note>original: "Utrum deus habeat actum infinitum."</note> God is an infinite being; therefore, God is not infinite without infinite action. And likewise for others. And go to the application of definitions.

### On questions regarding application through the rules. 78
<margin>On questions regarding application through the rules.</margin>
If any doubt is asked: let it be applied to the rules along with its definition, and let it run through all the rules; and then such a doubt will be clarified through the rules and their species <note>The "species" are sub-categories of Llull's ten general rules/questions.</note>, and its clarification will cause such a doubt to pass into either affirmation or negation. And this rule is infallible, just as a sign truly and infallibly signifies that of which it is a sign. The same example is given in the nine subjects; and go to the application of the rules.

### On questions regarding the application of the table. 78
<margin>On questions regarding the application of the table.</margin>
If it is asked: *Whether there is an infinite and eternal action:* let it be applied to the first column; and let it be asked through Rule C <note>Rule C usually corresponds to "What?" (Quid?)</note>: What is infinite action? And what is it in goodness through the definition of goodness? And what is it in greatness through the definition of greatness? And what is it in eternity through the definition of eternity? And this is signified through the third species of Rule C; afterwards, a conclusion is made according to what the letters signify. And likewise for others. And go to the application of the table.

### On questions regarding the application and exhaustion of the third figure. 79
<margin>On questions regarding the application and exhaustion of the third figure.</margin>
The application of the "exhaustion" <note>Llull uses "exhaustion" (evacuatio) to mean systematically working through every possible combination of terms in a figure.</note> of the third figure is done in this way: namely, if in a question "Goodness" is one term and "Greatness" is the other term; or if "Goodness" is one term and "Concordance" is the other term; and so on for others: let the question be applied to chamber B-C, and let that chamber be exhausted according to the method given in the exhaustion of the third figure; and let those things which are drawn from that chamber be applied to the proposed matter; and go to the application of the exhaustion of the third figure.

### On questions of essence.

<margin>On questions of essence.</margin>
Whether entity and essence are interchangeable? And it must be answered that they are: otherwise "being" and "that which is" <note>original: "esse et ens"</note> would not be interchangeable. ¶ Whether there is a difference between essence and being: go to the *Hundred Forms*, to the chapter on essence.

### On questions of goodness.

<margin>On questions of goodness.</margin>
It is asked, what is unity? Why is this goodness one? Why is this magnitude one? Whether in created things goodness and magnitude, etc., differ? And if they differ, it is asked why they differ: to which it must be answered that unity is joined to many unities, just as difference is joined to many things differing in number. ¶ What is the concrete form of unity? <note>In this context, "concrete" refers to the physical or specific manifestation of an abstract quality like "Unity."</note> And if it is said to be "the one": I ask why it is its concrete form. I answer so that unity may have a subject in which it is sustained, and so that difference can enter between unity and "the one," just as it does between essence and being: and go to the third chapter, which is on unity.

### On questions of plurality.

<margin>On questions of plurality.</margin>
It is asked, what is plurality? ¶ What is the source of plurality? What is the cause of the difference between goodness and magnitude, etc.? ¶ What is the concrete form of plurality? Go to the fourth chapter, which is on plurality.

### On questions of nature.

<margin>On questions of nature.</margin>
It is asked, what is nature? ¶ Whether any substantial principles are natural? And it must be answered that they are: as is clear through the second type of rule C, which is the concrete form of nature. ¶ With what things is nature mixed? Go to the fifth chapter, which is on nature.

### On questions of genus.

<margin>On questions of genus.</margin>
It is asked, what is genus? <note>A "genus" is a general class or category of things, such as "animal."</note> To which principles is genus applicable? ¶ Whether absolute good is a genus? And likewise for greatness, etc. ¶ Whether good-

<column-break/>

ness is more general substantially than accidentally: and it must be answered that it is. For goodness through substance is prior, but through accident it is posterior. ¶ Whether genus is a real being outside the soul? <note>A central debate in medieval philosophy: do categories like "humanity" exist in the world, or only in our minds?</note> And it must be answered that it is: for otherwise the soul would create the difference between species and species, which is impossible. ¶ Whether a brute animal can imagine a genus? And it must be answered that it cannot: for otherwise it would create science. ¶ Furthermore, because the imagination does not reach an abstract object with line, figure, or color, and so with other imaginings: but it reaches the concrete itself; but it reaches the concrete itself with those [qualities]: and go to the sixth chapter, which is on genus.

### On questions of species.

<margin>On questions of species.</margin>
It is asked, what is species? <note>A "species" is a specific category within a genus, such as "human" within the genus "animal."</note> To which places of this art is species applicable? Through the form, by what mode does it act through its species? ¶ Whether species is a real being outside the soul? ¶ Whether a genus without a species can participate with an individual? What is the concrete form of species? What is the difference between a natural species and a moral species, which are the species of virtues and vices? Go to the seventh chapter, which is on species.

### On questions of individuality.

<margin>On questions of individuality.</margin>
It is asked, what is individuality? How is individuality definable? ¶ What are the correlatives of individuality? Why is the individual indivisible? ¶ Whether the individual would exist outside the soul, assuming that the species were not outside the soul? Why are the correlatives of individuality not sensible? What is the concrete form of individuality, from the fact that individuality has indivisible concrete things? Go to the eighth chapter, which is on individuality.

### On questions of property.

<margin>On questions of property.</margin>
It is asked, what is property? <note>In logic, a "property" is a characteristic that belongs to all members of a species, like "the ability to laugh" for humans.</note> In what way is property an implicit principle in this art? ¶ To which rule is the definition of property applicable? Why is property the reason for the "proper," since it produces the proper itself? ¶ Whether property is the cause of appropriating, just as difference is the cause of differing? From what things is the concrete form of property made? ¶ How does property behave in natural and moral matters? ¶ In what way is property a cause of science? And likewise for the mechanical arts: go to the ninth chapter, which is on property.

# On Questions.

<margin>8th: On questions of simplicity.</margin>
### On questions of simplicity.

<margin>On questions of simplicity.</margin>
It is asked: what is simplicity? ¶ For what is simplicity a cause? To what things is simplicity applicable? What are the correlatives <note>Terms that exist in a mutual relationship, like "father" and "son."</note> of simplicity? Go to chapter 10, which is about simplicity.

<margin>8th: On questions of composition.</margin>
### On questions of composition.

<margin>On questions of composition.</margin>
It is asked: what is composition? ¶ To what extent is composition applicable? It is asked: from where does composition arise? What are the composite correlatives? Whether composition can exist in a composite thing, given that its simple principles are not essentially in the subject? And the answer is no, because the composite would have nothing from which it could exist; and the correlatives of composition and the second species of *d.* and the first of *e.* <note>These letters likely refer to specific diagrams or categories in the author's logical system.</note> would not exist in the world. Go to chapter 11, which is about composition.

<margin>8th: On questions of form.</margin>
### On questions of form.

<margin>On questions of form.</margin>
It is asked: what is form? ¶ To what principles is form applicable? ¶ What is the difference between created and uncreated form? Whether form has correlatives? Why is action part of the definition of form? Whether form can act outside of its correlatives? Why is form beyond the reach of the senses? ¶ What is the concrete <note>The physical or specific instance of an abstract concept.</note> of form? Which sensible things are signs of form? Go to chapter 12, which is about form.

<margin>8th: On questions of matter.</margin>
### On questions of matter.

<margin>On questions of matter.</margin>
It is asked: what is matter? ¶ To what principles of this art is matter applicable? ¶ Whether matter has correlatives? To which it must be said: no, for it would then already be composed of the things from which it is made. [On the matter] of action. The concrete of matter regarding genus. What is the universal source of matter? Go to chapter 13, which is about matter.

<margin>8th: On questions of substance.</margin>
### On questions of substance.

<margin>On questions of substance.</margin>
It is asked: what is substance? ¶ To what principles is substance applicable? Whether substance has correlatives? Whether every created substance is composed of form and matter? What is the concrete of substance? Why is substance existing through itself? And the answer is: because through form it is an agent, and through matter it is a patient <note>The thing being acted upon.</note>, and through their conjunction it is a composite. Why does substance stand under <term>accidents<gloss>non-essential properties like color or size</gloss></term> and why can it not exist or act without them? Whether substance is perceptible to the senses? And we say no, for the senses cannot perceive as much through accidents as the substance actually is. And go to chapter 14 on questions of substance.

<column-break/>

<margin>8. On questions of accident.</margin>
### On questions of accident.

<margin>On questions of accident.</margin>
It is asked: what is an accident? ¶ Where is an accident applicable? Whether an accident relates to its own end principally or to another? From what does an accident arise? ¶ What is the concrete of an accident? It is asked: whether an accident is twofold—namely, one intrinsic and the other extrinsic? Whether the senses reach the intrinsic accident? Whether the imagination can imagine an intrinsic accident without an extrinsic or sensible accident? Whether the intellect can produce knowledge without an intrinsic and extrinsic accident? And go to chapter 15, which is about accidents.

<margin>8. On questions of quantity.</margin>
### On questions of quantity.

<margin>On questions of quantity.</margin>
It is asked: what is quantity? Go to the definition of goodness, and define quantity according to the manner of the definition of goodness, saying thus: "Quantity is the being by reason of which a quantified thing quantifies the quantity." From what things does quantity arise? Whether the cause of quantity is consequence? What are the primary measures of quantity? What is the concrete of quantity? Go to chapter 16, which is about quantity.

<margin>8. On questions of quality.</margin>
### On questions of quality.

<margin>On questions of quality.</margin>
In what way can the definition of quality be found? Go to the definition of goodness, and define it according to the manner of goodness, saying thus: "Quality is the being by reason of which a qualified thing acts as a quality." Of what is quality an applied habit? In what things is quality situated? What is the concrete of quality? From what does quality arise? And why is it an accident? Go to the seventeenth chapter, which is about quality.

# On Questions.

<margin>On questions of natural appetite.</margin>
In what way can natural appetite <note>original: "appetitus naturalis"; refers to the inherent tendency or "drive" in all things to reach their perfection or purpose</note> be defined? To which principles can natural appetite be applied? Why do general principles precede appetite? What are the causes of concrete appetite? Does appetite rest outside of the thing desired? From what does appetite endure? From what does appetite grow? Is appetite both the mover and the moved? Go to the 28th chapter, which is on natural appetite.

### On questions of attraction.

<margin>On questions of attraction.</margin>
It is asked: how can the definition of attraction be made? To which principles is attraction applicable? Is attraction in any way part of the category of passion <note>In medieval philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon by an external force</note>? Does the attractor draw the attractable thing outside of its own essence? From what does the attractor draw the attractable? What is the concrete form of attraction? Is it the habit <note>A stable disposition or quality</note> of the attractable? Why is there attraction? Does the attractor draw by means of its own species <note>The "form" or "likeness" of a thing</note>? From which attractions are moral attractions derived? Go to the 29th chapter, which is on attractions.

### On questions of reception.

<margin>On questions of reception.</margin>
What is reception? To which principles is reception applicable? Is reception, in respect to its correlatives <note>Terms that exist in relation to one another, like "parent" and "child"</note>, in the category of action or passion? It is asked: where does reception receive the receivable? From what does it receive it? Why does it receive it? Is the receiver in the category of power <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to do or receive something</note>? Is the corruptible in the category of the object? Does the power move itself with the object, or does the object move the power? What is the concrete form of reception? Is it the most general genus, and is the receivable a subaltern? And does the receivable have species? Go to the 30th chapter, which is on reception.

### On questions of the phantasm.

Are phantasms in the process of becoming through sense and imagination

<column-break/>

without the intellect being in the finished state? In what way is knowledge or character generated? In what way is the same phantasm received in a different manner in the soul? Why is the phantasm more general in man than in beasts? Is the phantasm the subject or the concrete form of the imagination? Is the "imagined" constituted from the likenesses of the principles? Is the phantasm in the sense? Go to the 31st chapter, which is on the phantasm.

### On questions of fullness.

Is a thing composed of elements full without the essences of the elements? Is idleness the emptiness of a power, which is the concrete form of fullness? Can the full be filled with things that are not full? Are the correlatives of the principles the genera of fullness? Does "full" signify being, and "not full" signify non-being? Is a positive habit in the category of fullness, and a privative habit in the category of emptiness? Does generation tend toward the full, and corruption toward the not-full? Go to the 32nd chapter, which is on fullness.

Is diffusion the cause of generosity, and restriction the cause of greed? Go to the 33rd chapter, which is on diffusion.

### On questions of expulsion.

<margin>On questions of expulsion.</margin>
What is expulsion? And to which principles is its definition applicable? What are the signs of expulsion, and in which subjects do these signs consist? Does one <term>phantasm</term><note>A mental image or representation produced by the imagination.</note> expel another phantasm, just as in the vegetative faculty a new leaf expels an old leaf? ### On questions of novelty.

<margin>On questions of novelty.</margin>
What is novelty? Can an effect exist without novelty? Can time and place exist without novelty, and vice versa? Why does a second novelty make an earlier novelty old? Are infinity and eternity within the category of novelty? Why does nobility consist more in antiquity than in novelty? Why do new things please men? Because we are "on the way" <note>A reference to the "homo viator," the human being as a pilgrim or traveler through life toward eternity.</note>. Can motion exist without novelty? <margin>On questions of mathematics.</margin>

Why is a body infinitely divisible? Is it because mathematics is the instrument of the infinity of division? Why is mathematics a sign of infinity? Is mathematics like a habit of the intellect regarding infinite things that can be understood, just as faith is regarding infinite things that can be believed? Go to chapter 34, which concerns mathematics.

### On questions of general rectitudes. 84

<margin>On questions of general rectitudes.</margin>

### On questions of monstrosity. 89

<margin>On questions of monstrosity.</margin>
What is **monstrosity** <note>In medieval philosophy, a "monster" or monstrosity refers to any natural birth or event that deviates from the typical species-pattern</note>?
