### On questions of disposition and the disposed. 85

<margin>On questions of disposition and the disposed.</margin>
What is <term>disposition</term> <note>The state of being prepared or arranged for a specific function or quality</note>? What is a substantial disposition, and what is an accidental one? Is a stone disposed only so far as to be sensed, and then the sense is disposed toward sensing? ¶ Is the sense disposed only so far as to be imagined, and then the imagination is disposed toward imagining? Is the imagination disposed only so far as to be understood, and then the intellect toward understanding? Is God more disposed than the intellect is, and the human intellect toward understanding? Is the intellect more disposed toward believing in God than toward understanding Him? And it must be answered that it is so: provided, however, that faith mediates. ¶ Is God more disposed to be remembered than the memory is to remember Him? And it must be answered that it is so: otherwise hope would be in vain. Is God more disposed to be loved than the human will is to love Him? And it must be answered that it is so: otherwise charity <note>original: "charitas"; divine love</note> would be in vain. ¶ Is God more disposed toward creating the world than the world is toward being created? And it must be answered that it is not so. For an effect is not as capable through its passive nature as a cause is through its active power. For otherwise the heavens would be as capable of being great extensively and infinitely as they are of being created from eternity: which is impossible. Because of this, the intellect recognizes that it is impossible for the heavens to exist from eternity, and the will rejoices greatly in this knowledge. Go to chapter 56, which is concerning disposition. ¶ It is further asked: is God disposed only toward acting infinitely through His infinity and eternity, and then toward understanding and willing through His intellect and will? And it must be answered that it is not so: for in God there is neither "before" nor "after." ¶ Is God more disposed toward creating a greater creature than a lesser one? To which it must be said that it is so: just as a greater agent is more disposed toward making a greater thing than a lesser one. ¶ All these things having been thus considered, the intellect and the will are greatly disposed toward rejoicing.

### On questions of fortune and the fortunate.

<margin>On questions of fortune and the fortunate.</margin>
What is fortune? Where is the subject <note>The "subject" refers to the underlying entity or person in which fortune resides.</note> of fortune? What are the principles of fortune? Whether fortune has more of its "being" through its effect than through its seed <note>original: "semen"; likely referring to the causal origin or potentiality</note>: whether fortune makes one fortunate, or does the fortunate person make themselves fortunate along with fortune, just as a knowing person makes themselves knowing through the intellect? And the answer is no: because a knowing person makes themselves knowing through understanding, but a fortunate person makes themselves fortunate through ignorance. Regarding how fortune is: go to chapter 61, which is about fortune.

### On questions of ordination and the ordained.

<margin>On questions of ordination and the ordained.</margin>
What is ordination <note>The act of arranging or the state of being ordered toward a goal.</note>? Where does ordination begin? Where does it rest? What are the primary principles of ordination? Whether predestination and the heavens can destroy the ordination of man, and of plants, and of animals, and of the elements? Go to chapter 62, which is about ordination.

### On questions of counsel and the consulted.

<margin>On questions of counsel and the consulted.</margin>
What is counsel? To which principles is counsel applicable? Whether counsel has general principles with which it may be general? Whether counsel formed by discourse through principles and rules is well-formed, and that which does not discourse through them is deformed? Whether counsel discoursing through principles and rules is assertive, and that which does not discourse through them is doubtful and dangerous? Whether counsel concerning contingencies is dangerous? Why does counsel stand more by what is prior than by what is posterior? Whether ignorance and sin are enemies of counsel? Go to chapter 63.

### On questions of grace and the graced.

<margin>On questions of grace and the graced.</margin>
What is grace? With which principles may grace be known? Whether grace can exist in an undisposed subject? Whether grace can exist without charity? Whether hope is formed with grace? Whether faith without grace is in vain? Which virtues govern the greater disposition for receiving grace: the cardinal or the theological? Why is there grace, from what does it come, and how great is it? And whether it is a proper passion <note>In scholastic logic, a "proper passion" is a characteristic that belongs uniquely and necessarily to a specific subject.</note>. How is grace, where is it, and with what is it? And go to chapter 64.

Whether moral perfection is a sign of natural perfection? Go to chapter 65.

# On Questions
<page-num>folio 120</page-num>
<header>On Questions</header>

<margin>On questions of infinity and the infinite.</margin>
What is infinity? Does infinity have correlatives <note>terms that exist only in relation to one another</note> that are co-essential and natural to it? With what conditions is infinity associated? Can infinity be hindered? ¶ Does it belong more to an infinite being to act infinitely than to a finite being to act finitely? Is the power which fire possesses to burn infinite wood—if it were provided with it—a sign of divine infinity and of the divine act of "infiniting" <note>original: "infinire"; a technical term in Lullian philosophy referring to the active exercise of infinity</note>? Is the power possessed by the human intellect, lasting into eternity and having a sufficiency of objects, multiplying an infinite number through understanding and through the will in loving, a sign of infinity and of its own act of "infiniting"? ¶ Given that the heavens possessed an innate memory and, moving into eternity, numbered and recollected infinite days: it is asked whether that memory would be a sign of infinity and eternity and of their acts: namely, "infiniting" and "eternizing"? And it must be answered that it is so: as is evident through the argument from the lesser <note>a logical move: if it is true for a smaller thing, it is even truer for a greater thing</note>; and Rule B <note>a reference to the author's specific logical system</note> cannot deny this; and go to chapter 69.

### On questions of deception and the deceived.

<margin>On questions of deception and the deceived.</margin>
What is deception? In what way do the positive and privative <note>the presence of a quality versus the absence of one</note> habits differ in deception? Does the deceiver deceive himself, and likewise for the deceived? From what does deception arise, how does it happen, and how is it recognized? With what does it occur, and with what is it known? And go to chapter 70.

### On questions of honor and the honored.

<margin>On questions of honor and the honored.</margin>
What is honor? Why is the one who honors prior, and the one honored posterior? Why is the one who slanders more slandered than the one upon whom the slander is inflicted? Why can the one seeking honor for himself never be satisfied by it? And it must be answered that it is because honor is owed to God alone by all. It is asked: does the one seeking honor more for himself than for God sin more than another who sins through avarice or through some other sin? Does God require anything else from men except honor for Himself? Which is a greater sign of God's honor: the honor of the one honoring, or the honor of the one honored? Go to chapter 71.

<column-break/>

### On questions of capacity and incapacity.

<margin>On questions of capacity and incapacity.</margin>
What is capacity? In what do capacity and incapacity differ? What is the cause of a dull intellect? Why is the intellect more capable of numbering infinite units in number—assuming objects were sufficient to it—than fire is of burning all bodies, if it had a sufficiency of wood? Is the intellect by its nature more capable of understanding than of being ignorant? Go to chapter 72.

### On questions of existence and agency.

<margin>On questions of existence and agency.</margin>
What is existence? What is agency <note>original: "agentia"; the active power of doing</note>? Can any existence contain within itself as much agency as it itself is? Can the principles of the First Figure <note>a reference to the Lullian "Art," a system of logic using diagrams</note> exist in any essence without agency? Can a separate intellect <note>an intellect existing without a physical body, like an angel</note> understand as much as it exists? Can principles be in a subject without the power of potency? Go to chapter 73, which is on existence.

### On questions of comprehension and apprehension.

<margin>On questions of comprehension and apprehension.</margin>
What is comprehension? And what is apprehension? In what way is the intellect "comprehending" and "apprehending"? Why can the senses not comprehend a sensible thing through sensing as much as the intellect can through understanding? Can the intellect comprehend "intelligible" things more than fire can "ignitable" things? Why are the powers hindered by apprehension and not by comprehension? ¶ If the heavens moved for eternity, would they comprehend more days than fire would wood for burning? To which it must be said: yes, because the heavens would cause the days in their own essence, whereas fire would not cause the wood in itself nor in another. ¶ Through the comprehension and apprehension of the intellect, are the heavens and fire similar signs of the infinity of God's creation of the world? Go to chapter 74.

### On questions of discovery and the discovered. 87

<margin>On questions of discovery and the discovered.</margin>

<margin>On questions of the antecedent and the consequent.</margin>
What is the antecedent? Can the antecedent and the consequent exist without the correlatives of the principles? Is the ultimate end an antecedent or a consequent? Is there an intrinsic and extrinsic object to the act, such that the object is prior, either intrinsically or extrinsically? Go to chapter 78.

### On questions of generation, corruption, and privation. 87

<margin>On questions of generation, corruption, and privation.</margin>
What is generation? What is corruption? Does corruption exist between being and non-being? Go to chapter 79.

### On the questions of philosophy.

<margin>On the questions of philosophy.</margin>
What is philosophy? What is the matter <note>The "subject matter" or underlying substance</note> subjected to the intellect of the one philosophizing? In what way is the intellect very general? In what way is the intellect very skillfully fashioned to reach its objects? Whether philosophy is an image of theology. ### On the questions of geometry

<margin>On the questions of geometry.</margin>
What is geometry? What is the subject of geometry? With what does geometry measure the measurable? Whether a theologian can measure the principles of the first figure in the same way that geometry measures acute and right angles. From what principles do measures arise? What are the subjects of measure? Whether quantity is the habit <note>the characteristic state</note> of the "how much." Through what principle is geometry unfolded and explained in this art? Whether the nine subjects are the subjects of geometry. Whether geometry can measure the nine subjects according to their mode. With which principle and through what mode is geometry discoursed through this art? It is asked where the places applicable to geometry are. And it must be answered that it is there where quantity was discussed. ¶ In what way does the intellect find geometry and use it? In what way does geometry abstract mathematical measures from the senses and multiply them? In what way does geometry, with sensible angles, multiply angles beyond the senses? Whether geometry creates knowledge about sensed quantity or about quantity beyond the senses. Whether geometry is a subject, or a sign, or an instrument for the theologian to measure nature, and for the moralist to measure morality. In geometry, which measures are prior and which are posterior? In what way can geometry measure an extended circular line and square the circle? In what way can the circle be squared? That is, to measure a circular line with a quadrangular line, and vice versa. Go to chapter 82.

### On the questions of astronomy.

<margin>On the questions of astronomy.</margin>
What is astronomy? Whether astronomy depends on geometry. Whether there is another eighth sphere, or another world, or another starry heaven. ¶ Since the sun is not hot <note>A common medieval Aristotelian paradox: the sun causes heat but is not itself composed of the element of fire</note>, why does it heat the air? ¶ Many other questions could be made concerning astronomy, the solutions of which are involved in the third subject, which is about the heaven. As if it were asked: granted that there were another sphere, whether there would be distances and proximities between them in act or in potency. Go to chapter 83.

### On the questions of arithmetic.

<margin>On the questions of arithmetic.</margin>
What is arithmetic? Whether arithmetic depends on geometry. What are the primitive principles of arithmetic? What is the cause of number? How many species does number have? ¶ Whether an even number is prior, or an odd number. What are the correlatives of number? ¶ It is asked in what way the first unity is the principle of number, and the first and second [principles] of the third unity. Why is number perfected in three unities? Whether the third unity is as close to the first unity as to the second. What is the first multiplication of number? In what way are geometry and arithmetic similar? Go to chapter 84.

### On the questions of music.

<margin>On the questions of music.</margin>
What is music? Why is it? With what principles is the definition of music signified? Why are there six degrees of music? What are the primitive principles of the voice? Why are there five vowels, and no more, nor fewer? From what does the voice arise? From what do consonants arise? Why is this letter *e* more capable of being composed with other letters in the alphabet than *a*, and *a* more than *u*? And why do *i* and *o* not cause consonants as *a* and *u* do? In what way are vowels applied to different elements? It is asked why *o* in the voice is attributed to the heaven. Whether music descends from geometry. Go to chapter 85.

<margin>On the questions of logic.</margin>

### On questions of preaching.

<margin>On questions of preaching.</margin>

# The twelfth part: On Habituation. The thirteenth part.

How does memory relate to the common intellect and will? How does memory stand in relation to understanding and believing, and to willing and hating? ### On questions of memory through the rules.

<margin>On questions of memory through the rules.</margin>
It is asked: whether memory receives species <note>term: species (mental representations or images of objects)</note> more quickly from the intellect than from the will? Why has it been so often asked what memory is? Now it is asked what memory contains within itself essentially? What is memory in relation to knowledge? Whether memory has an act in the subject and the object? Whether memory exists of itself? Whether memory acts through its own species? To whom does memory belong? Whether memory is composed of matter and form? Toward what does memory tend? Why is memory indivisible? Whether memory can have correlatives without discrete quantity? What is the proper or appropriated passion of memory? How does memory exist in time? Why is memory stronger regarding past things than future things? Where does the memorizer preserve his species? How is memory disposed toward the object? With what is memory forgotten? Go to the rubric in which memory is discussed through the rules. ¶ We have spoken concerning the questions of the eleventh part of this book, and the doctrine has been given through which the artist <note>term: artist (a practitioner of this specific Art or system of logic)</note> may know how to form questions and transmit them to their proper places; for the practice of this Art consists chiefly in the solution of questions.

## The twelfth principal part of this work, which is on habituation.

<margin>The twelfth principal part of this work, which is on habituation.</margin>
This part concerns the habituation <note>term: habituation (the process of turning knowledge into a fixed habit or second nature through practice)</note> of this Art, and it is divided into three parts. The first of these is about the thirteen parts into which this Art is divided. And the artist of this Art ought to habituate himself to these, so that he himself may know how to apply a question to that place, or places, disposed for the question according to the condition of the mat-

<column-break/>

-ter of the question. ¶ The second part is, namely, that he should habituate the mode and process of this Art by following the manner of the text for preparing and solving foreign questions <note>original: "questiones peregrinas" (questions external to the primary examples provided)</note> in the same way through which they are explained in the text, just as one example is exemplified and declared by another.
¶ The third part is, namely, that he should possess a method for multiplying questions and solutions toward one and the same conclusion, as is signified through the third and fourth figures. ¶ And let these things suffice concerning habituation for the sake of brevity.

## The thirteenth principal part of this work, which is on doctrine.

<margin>The thirteenth principal part of this work, which is on doctrine.</margin>
This part is about doctrine <note>term: doctrine (here meaning the method of teaching or instruction)</note>, and it is divided into four parts. The first of these is: that the artist should well know the alphabet through the figures, definitions, rules, and the layout of the table by heart. ¶ The second part is that he should explain the text well and reasonably to the students, and that he should not bind himself to the authorities of others, and that the students should read the text beforehand. And if the students should doubt anything, let them ask the master about it. ¶ The third part is: that the master should form questions in the presence of the students and solve them reasonably according to the process of the Art. For without reason, the artist cannot use this Art well. ¶ Wherefore it should be known that this Art has three friends: namely, subtlety of intellect, reason, and good intention. Without these, no one can learn this Art. ¶ The fourth part is that the master should pose questions to the students so that they may respond to him concerning them. And he should tell them to multiply reasons for one and the same conclusion, to the end that they may find the "places" <note>term: places (topoi or logical locations within the system)</note> by reason of which they may know how to answer and multiply arguments. If indeed the students do not know how to answer, nor how to multiply reasons, nor how to find the places, then the master should teach the students concerning the aforesaid things.

It should be known that there are three degrees of comparison: namely, good, better, and best. And thus this science has three degrees for learning according to itself. For a man having...

# On Instruction.

A person with an excellent intellect, well-grounded in logic and natural philosophy, and possessing great diligence, will be able to master this science in two months: one month for the theory and another month for the practice. ¶ A person having a better-than-average intellect, grounded in logic and natural philosophy, and possessing diligence, will be able to master it in four months: two for the theory and two for the practice. ¶ A person having a subtle and good intellect, grounded in logic and natural philosophy, and possessing good diligence, will be able to master it in half a year: namely, three months for the theory and three for the practice. And if one cannot learn it in this time, it is a sign that they have a dull intellect, lack good diligence, or are occupied with other matters. Such a person will never be able to learn it. Nevertheless, to learn this art more quickly, I counsel that one first learn the *Short Art* <note>original: "Ars Brevis"</note> which is titled as follows: *By your grace, for the love of wisdom, here begins the Short Art, which is the image of the General Art.* For once that is known by a subtle and grounded intellect, one can then master the *General Art*.

<margin>of the shorter [art]</margin>

### ¶ The Great, General, and Ultimate Art of the enlightened man, Master Ramon Llull <note>original: "Raymundi Lull"</note>, most distinguished professor of the Sacred Pages <note>A title for a professor of Theology.</note>: which is the explanation of any other arts and sciences of the same Llull: with marginal citations and a table or index: has reached its desired end at Lyon <note>original: "Lugduni"</note> by Jacobus Marechal, the printer <term>calcographum: a copper-plate engraver or printer</term>, at the expense of Simon Vincent, faithful bookseller. In the year of the Incarnate Word 1517, on the fifth day before the Ides of May <note>May 11, 1517</note>.

### ¶ The Great, General, and Ultimate Art of the enlightened man, Master Ramon Llull <note>original: "Raymundi Lull"</note>, most distinguished professor of the Sacred Pages <note>A traditional title for a professor of Theology.</note>: which is the explanation of any other arts and sciences of the same Llull: with marginal citations and a table or index: has reached its desired end at Lyon <note>original: "Lugduni"</note> by Jacobus Marechal, the printer <term>calcographum: a printer using metal or copper plates</term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Apostles</margin>

-> **[Illustration]** <-

This woodcut depicts the foundational figures of the Christian Church, **Saint Peter** and **Saint Paul**. On the left, **Saint Peter** is shown holding a large key <note>Symbolizing the keys to the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>. On the right, **Saint Paul** holds a sword <note>The instrument of his martyrdom and a symbol of the "sword of the Spirit."</note>. 

Together, they hold up the **Veil of Veronica** <note>original: "Sudarium"</note>, a sacred relic believed to have been used by a woman named Veronica to wipe the face of **Jesus Christ** on his way to Calvary, which miraculously retained the image of his features. The face of **Christ** is shown here with a crown of thorns and a radiant halo.

Above the veil, there is a small banner or scroll containing the letters:

-> **P. V.** <-
<note>Likely stands for "Pia Vota" (Pious Wishes) or is a mark of the printer or engraver.</note>
